label: Ab
slogan: Ab is a shorthand for a type where addition is commutative and associative, zero acts as an identity, and every element has an inverse that cancels it out. Such a type supports subtraction and allows reordering of sums without changing the result. It is used to model abelian groups in mathematics.

label: AbsConvex
slogan: A set is absolutely convex if it is both convex (contains the line segment between any two points in it) and balanced (remains within itself when multiplied by any scalar of absolute value at most one). This applies to sets in a vector space over a seminormed ring, where scalar multiplication is defined and the scalars have a partial order. The conditions rely on the space having commutative addition with zero, scalar multiplication, and a normed ring structure.

label: AbsoluteValue.abs
slogan: The absolute value function takes an element from an ordered ring and returns its non-negative value, effectively removing any negative sign. It satisfies the properties that the absolute value of a sum is at most the sum of absolute values, and the absolute value of a product equals the product of absolute values. This function is defined for algebraic structures where order and arithmetic operations like addition and multiplication are compatible.

label: AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_deriv_eq_sub
slogan: If a function f is absolutely continuous on the interval from a to b, then the integral of its derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a).

label: AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_mul_deriv_eq_deriv_mul
slogan: For two absolutely continuous functions f and g on an interval [a, b], the integral of f times the derivative of g from a to b equals f(b)*g(b) minus f(a)*g(a) minus the integral of the derivative of f times g over the same interval. This relates the integrals of the products of the functions and their derivatives. It is a version of integration by parts that applies when both functions are absolutely continuous.

label: AbstractCompletion.compareEquiv
slogan: The function compareEquiv provides a uniform isomorphism between two abstract completions of the same uniform space, showing that they are essentially the same in terms of their uniform structure. It uses the compare function to define when elements in different completions are equivalent, ensuring consistency with the original space's topology and uniform properties. This means any two completions of a uniform space can be matched up in a way that preserves closeness and continuity.

label: AbstractSimplicialComplex
slogan: An AbstractSimplicialComplex is a collection of finite nonempty sets of points where every nonempty subset of a set in the collection is also included, and every single-point set is part of the collection. It builds on a PreAbstractSimplicialComplex by requiring that all singleton sets are present. The collection is based on a type ι representing the vertices.

label: AccPt
slogan: A point x is an accumulation point of a set A if every neighborhood around x contains at least one point from A other than x itself; this is formalized using filters by checking that x is a cluster point of the filter formed by intersecting A with the punctured neighborhoods of x (i.e., neighborhoods of x with x removed). The definition uses the topological structure to express proximity and set operations like complement and singleton sets to exclude x.

label: Action
slogan: An Action describes how a monoid (a set with an associative operation and an identity) can act on a type in a way that respects the monoid's structure: applying the identity element does nothing, and acting with two combined elements is the same as acting with each one in turn. It is used to model transformations or symmetries on mathematical objects. The action connects a category, a monoid, and a type, ensuring compatibility between the monoid operation and the transformations on the type.

label: Action.functorCategoryEquivalence
slogan: A monoid action on a set corresponds exactly to a functor from the single-object category of the monoid to the category of sets, where the monoid's elements act as functions on the set. This correspondence is reversible and preserves structure: applying the action of a product is the same as composing the corresponding functions, and the identity element acts as the identity function. The equivalence is supported by natural isomorphisms showing that converting between actions and functors in both directions recovers the original structure.

label: Action.ρAut
slogan: For a group action, the function that sends each group element to the corresponding automorphism of the object is a monoid homomorphism, meaning it maps the identity element to the identity automorphism and preserves multiplication.

label: AddAction.sum_card_fixedBy_eq_card_orbits_mul_card_addGroup
slogan: For a finite additive group acting on a finite set, the sum of the number of fixed points of each group element equals the number of orbits times the size of the group.

label: AddChar.doubleDualEquiv
slogan: For any finite abelian group, there is a natural one-to-one correspondence that maps each group element to a function evaluating characters on that element, and this correspondence preserves the group's addition structure. This means the group is isomorphic to its double dual through additive characters over the complex numbers.

label: AddChar.wInner_cWeight_eq_boole
slogan: For two additive characters on a finite abelian group, their weighted inner product is 1 if they are the same and 0 otherwise, using a specific weight function tied to the group's size. The inner product is defined over a real-like coefficient ring and uses the complex conjugate of one character. This result reflects the orthonormality of additive characters in a finite setting.

label: AddCircle.denseRange_zsmul_coe_iff
slogan: The set of all integer multiples of a real number a, when wrapped around a circle of circumference p, fills the circle densely if and only if the ratio a/p is an irrational number.

label: AddCircle.ergodic_nsmul
slogan: Multiplying points on a circle by a natural number n greater than 1 results in a transformation that thoroughly mixes the circle with respect to the standard measure, meaning no nontrivial part of the circle remains invariant under repeated applications of the map. This mixing property holds when the circle is parameterized by a positive real period T. The result is a special case of a more general fact about multiplication by integers with absolute value greater than 1.

label: AddCommGroup
slogan: AddCommGroup describes a type where addition is commutative and associative, zero acts as an identity element, and every element has an additive inverse; it combines the structure of a group with commutative addition.

label: AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite
slogan: Every finite abelian group can be expressed as a direct sum of cyclic groups, each consisting of integers modulo a power of a prime number. This decomposition is unique up to the order of the summands. There exists a structure-preserving bijection between the group and such a direct sum.

label: AddCommGroup.equiv_free_prod_directSum_zmod
slogan: Every finitely generated abelian group can be expressed as a combination of a free part, made up of copies of the integers, and a torsion part, made up of cyclic groups of prime power order. This means the group is structurally equivalent to a direct sum of integer sequences with finite modular arithmetic components. The decomposition reflects how such groups break down into simple, well-understood pieces.

label: AddCommGrpCat.injective_of_divisible
slogan: If an abelian group allows division by any positive integer (meaning for every element x and positive integer n, there is some y such that n*y = x), then any group homomorphism from a subgroup into this group can be extended to a homomorphism from the whole group. This means divisible abelian groups are injective objects in the category of abelian groups, allowing extensions of homomorphisms from substructures. The result links the algebraic notion of divisibility with the categorical concept of injectivity.

label: AddCommGrpCat.instAbelian
slogan: The category of abelian groups is set up so that it supports key algebraic constructions like kernels, cokernels, and exact sequences, and its morphisms can be added in a way that respects composition. This structure makes it an abelian category, which is well suited for homological algebra. Objects are commutative groups and maps between them preserve addition, with all the necessary structure built from the additive and categorical properties of these groups.

label: AddCommMonoid
slogan: An AddCommMonoid is a type where addition is associative, commutative, and has a zero element such that adding zero to any element leaves it unchanged. It combines the properties of having an additive identity (like an AddMonoid) and commutative addition (like an AddCommSemigroup). For any elements a, b, and c: a + b = b + a, (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), and a + 0 = a.

label: AddCommSemigroup
slogan: AddCommSemigroup is a type where addition is associative and commutative, so for any elements a, b, and c, (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and a + b = b + a.

label: AddMonoid.End
slogan: AddMonoid.End is the type of all functions from an additive monoid M to itself that preserve addition and map zero to zero. These functions are called endomorphisms. The structure requires M to have a zero element and an addition operation.

label: AddMonoidHom.toRealLinearMap
slogan: A continuous function between two real topological vector spaces that preserves addition also preserves scalar multiplication by real numbers, making it a linear and continuous map when the spaces have compatible topological and algebraic structures.

label: AddSubmonoid.NSMulSaturated
slogan: An additive submonoid H of a monoid G is saturated if whenever a natural number multiple n*g is in H, then either n is zero or the element g itself is in H. This means H contains all elements that can generate its members through repeated addition, except when the multiple is zero. The term NSMulSaturated distinguishes this concept from other forms of saturation in multiplicative settings.

label: AdicCompletion
slogan: The adic completion of a module M over a commutative ring R with respect to an ideal I is the set of all coherent sequences in the quotients M/I^n, where each term maps to the previous one under natural projections. It forms a new module that encodes approximate solutions to equations in M modulo higher powers of I. This object is constructed as the inverse limit of the system of quotient modules linked by transition maps.

label: AdicCompletion.flat_of_isNoetherian
slogan: The adic completion of a Noetherian ring R with respect to an ideal I is a module over R that is flat, meaning tensoring with it preserves injective linear maps. This ensures that algebraic properties involving solutions to linear equations are maintained when working with completed modules. Flatness here follows from the fact that injectivity of maps between finitely generated modules over R is preserved under adic completion.

label: Affine.Simplex
slogan: An Affine.Simplex represents a geometric shape like a point, line segment, triangle, or higher-dimensional equivalent, defined by a set of points that are affinely independent in an affine space. It is built using a ring k, a module V over k with an additive group structure, and a space P that behaves like points acted on by vectors from V. The simplex has n+1 vertices indexed by Fin (n+1), and supports affine operations such as computing centroids or checking independence.

label: Affine.Simplex.AcuteAngled
slogan: A simplex has all acute angles if every angle formed by its vertices is less than 90 degrees, meaning the inner product of any two edge vectors meeting at a vertex is positive. This property applies to geometric shapes like triangles or tetrahedrons in Euclidean space, where angles are defined using the inner product structure. The condition ensures that no angle in the simplex is right or obtuse.

label: Affine.Simplex.centroid
slogan: The centroid of a simplex is the average of its vertices, calculated by giving each vertex equal weight and combining them in an affine space. This point is the geometric center and does not depend on the choice of origin. The computation uses vector operations and division by the number of vertices, relying on the simplex having a finite, indexed set of points.

label: Affine.Simplex.circumcenter
slogan: The circumcenter of a simplex is the point in space that is equidistant from all the vertices of the simplex, and it lies at the center of the smallest sphere that passes through all those vertices. This point exists in a geometric setting where points and vectors have a well-defined distance and inner product structure. The circumcenter is part of a larger construction that includes both the sphere and its center for a given simplex.

label: Affine.Simplex.circumradius
slogan: The circumradius of a simplex is the radius of the smallest sphere that passes through all the vertices of the simplex, calculated in a space with a well-defined notion of distance and geometry. It is derived from the circumsphere of the simplex, which is the sphere centered at the circumcenter and passing through all the simplex's vertices. The value is a real number representing the radius of this sphere.

label: Affine.Simplex.circumsphere
slogan: The circumsphere of a simplex is the unique sphere that passes through all the vertices of the simplex, with its center located in the affine span of those vertices. It is defined by a center point and a radius, where the center is equidistant to all vertices of the simplex. This sphere exists and is unique for any set of affinely independent points in a Euclidean space.

label: Affine.Simplex.dist_point_centroid
slogan: In a simplex, the distance from any vertex to the centroid is n times the distance from the centroid to the center of the opposite face, where n is the dimension of the simplex.

label: Affine.Simplex.eq_centroid_of_forall_mem_median
slogan: If a point lies on every median of a simplex in an affine space, then that point must be the centroid of the simplex.

label: Affine.Simplex.face
slogan: A simplex can have lower-dimensional faces made by picking a subset of its vertices; this definition constructs such a face by selecting a specific ordered subset of vertices using an index set of the right size. The selected vertices are guaranteed to form a valid simplex because the ordering ensures they remain affinely independent.

label: Affine.Simplex.faceOpposite
slogan: Given a simplex and one of its vertices, the face opposite to that vertex is the simplex formed by all the other vertices, excluding the specified one. This new simplex has one fewer vertex and thus one lower dimension than the original. The function takes a simplex and an index of a vertex and returns the lower-dimensional simplex made from the remaining vertices.

label: Affine.Simplex.faceOppositeCentroid
slogan: For a given simplex and one of its vertices, the face opposite that vertex consists of the remaining vertices, and the centroid of this opposite face is calculated as the average position of those vertices using affine geometry and standard arithmetic.

label: Affine.Simplex.median
slogan: The median of a simplex is the line segment from a vertex to the centroid of the face opposite that vertex, where the centroid is the average of the other vertices. This is defined in an affine space over a module where division by nonzero scalars is possible, and it requires at least one vertex to define the average. The median is represented as an affine subspace connecting the chosen vertex to the centroid of the remaining vertices.

label: Affine.Simplex.mongePoint
slogan: The Monge point of a simplex is a point that generalizes the orthocenter of a triangle to higher dimensions, defined using a fixed ratio along the Euler line from the circumcenter through the centroid. It lies at the intersection of special planes called Monge planes, each passing through the centroid of a face and perpendicular to the opposite edge. In 0 or 1 dimensions, this point equals the centroid, and in higher dimensions it aligns with the geometric properties of the simplex.

label: Affine.Simplex.mongePoint_eq_smul_vsub_vadd_circumcenter
slogan: The Monge point of a simplex lies on the line joining the circumcenter and centroid, and its position is determined by scaling the vector from the circumcenter to the centroid by a factor of (n+1)/(n-1), then adding that to the circumcenter. In simpler terms, it's a specific point along the Euler line that depends on the dimension of the simplex. This point is defined so that the distances between the circumcenter, centroid, and Monge point follow a fixed ratio.

label: Affine.Triangle.dist_point_centroid
slogan: In a triangle, the distance from any vertex to the centroid is twice the distance from the centroid to the midpoint of the opposite side.

label: Affine.Triangle.orthocenter_eq_smul_vsub_vadd_circumcenter
slogan: In a triangle, the orthocenter is located at a point found by moving three times the vector from the circumcenter to the centroid, starting from the circumcenter. This places the orthocenter, centroid, and circumcenter on a straight line, with specific spacing between them. The formula expresses the orthocenter directly in terms of the circumcenter and centroid using basic vector operations.

label: Affine.Triangle.prod_dist_div_dist_eq_one_of_mem_line_of_mem_line
slogan: For a triangle and three points, each lying on a side line, if lines from the vertices through these points meet at a common point, then the product of the ratios of distances along each side equals one.

label: Affine.Triangle.prod_div_one_sub_eq_one_of_mem_line_point_lineMap
slogan: If three points lie on the sides of a triangle such that each point divides its side in a certain ratio, and these ratios are all non-zero and not equal to one, then the product of the ratios divided by one minus the ratios equals one, provided the lines from the vertices through these points meet at a common point inside the triangle.

label: AffineBasis
slogan: An AffineBasis is a set of points in an affine space such that any point in the space can be uniquely written as an affine combination of these points, where the coefficients sum to one. It is defined over a module with a ring of scalars, using an additive group of vectors that act on the space of points. This structure allows affine coordinates to be assigned relative to a chosen origin and a linear basis of direction vectors.

label: AffineBasis.toMatrix_vecMul_coords
slogan: When changing from one affine basis to another, the barycentric coordinates of a point in the new basis can be found by multiplying the coordinates in the original basis by a transformation matrix formed from the old basis's coordinates of the new basis points. This transformation matrix is built by expressing each point of the new basis in terms of the old basis. The equation shows how coordinate vectors transform under a change of affine basis.

label: AffineEquiv
slogan: An AffineEquiv is a one-to-one mapping between two affine spaces that preserves straight lines and parallelism by respecting how vectors translate points, and it comes with an inverse that does the same. It is defined using a bijective linear map between the associated vector spaces and ensures the geometry of the space is maintained under transformation. This makes it a reversible affine transformation that behaves well with vector operations and point translations.

label: AffineEquiv.equivUnitsAffineMap
slogan: An affine equivalence between two spaces induces a one-to-one correspondence between their groups of invertible affine maps, where each invertible affine map corresponds to an invertible linear map on the underlying vector space. This correspondence respects composition and inversion, meaning the group structure is preserved. The linear part of an invertible affine map determines its associated element in the general linear group.

label: AffineIndependent
slogan: A set of points in an affine space is affinely independent if no point can be written as an affine combination of the others, meaning the only way a weighted sum of vectors from one point to the others equals zero, with weights adding to zero, is if all weights are zero. This captures the idea that the points are in general position, not lying on a common line, plane, or higher-dimensional flat. The condition relies on a base ring, a module of vectors, and a torsor structure linking points and vectors.

label: AffineIndependent.existsUnique_dist_eq
slogan: For any finite, nonempty set of points that are affinely independent, there is exactly one point (the circumcenter) in the affine subspace they span that is equidistant to all of them, and that common distance is the circumradius.

label: AffineIndependent.vectorSpan_eq_top_of_card_eq_finrank_add_one
slogan: If a collection of points is affinely independent and the number of points is one more than the dimension of the space they're in, then the set of all vectors formed by taking differences between these points spans the entire vector space.

label: AffineIsometryEquiv.constVAdd
slogan: Adding a fixed vector to every point in a normed affine space defines a distance-preserving, invertible map from the space to itself that respects both the affine and metric structure. This map is an affine isometry equivalence, meaning it preserves lines and distances, and its inverse subtracts the same vector. It works over any normed field and relies on the space having a compatible normed vector structure.

label: AffineIsometryEquiv.linearIsometryEquiv
slogan: An affine isometry between two normed spaces can be split into a linear isometry that describes how it transforms vectors, obtained by shifting the affine map to act around the origin. This linear part preserves distances and vector operations, and the process of extracting it respects composition and inversion of equivalences.

label: AffineIsometryEquiv.vaddConst
slogan: An affine isometry equivalence from a normed vector space V to a normed affine space P can be shifted by adding a fixed point p in P, resulting in a new affine isometry equivalence that maps vectors in V to points in P translated by p. This shift preserves both the affine structure and distances, effectively changing the basepoint of the mapping. The operation uses the natural action of vectors on points in the affine space.

label: AffineMap
slogan: An AffineMap is a function between spaces that preserves straight lines and the relative positions of points, combining a linear transformation with a fixed shift. It works with types that support vector-like addition, subtraction, and scaling, where differences between points behave like vectors. The map acts linearly on those differences, even if it moves the origin.

label: AffineMap.comp
slogan: The composition of two affine maps results in another affine map, where the linear part is the composition of the individual linear parts and the translation is adjusted accordingly. Applying the composed map to a point gives the same result as applying the second map to the image of the first. This operation respects the structure of affine spaces by preserving both vector addition and point transformations.

label: AffineMap.ext_linear
slogan: Two affine maps are equal if they have the same linear part and agree at a single point. This means that knowing how an affine map transforms vectors and where it sends one point is enough to determine the entire map. The result follows from properties of vector spaces and affine geometry.

label: AffineMap.ofMapMidpoint
slogan: A function between real normed affine spaces that sends midpoints to midpoints and is continuous can be written as an affine map, meaning it acts by applying a linear transformation and then adding a fixed vector. Such a function automatically preserves the affine structure, including how points and vectors relate. This works because scalar multiplication by 1/2 is well-defined in real vector spaces.

label: AffineMap.toConstProdLinearMap
slogan: An affine map between two vector spaces can be uniquely broken down into a constant vector (the translation) and a linear map; this function converts such an affine map into a pair consisting of that vector and the corresponding linear map. The conversion is structured as a linear equivalence, meaning it preserves the module structure and is invertible. This decomposition reflects the fact that every affine transformation is a linear transformation followed by a shift.

label: AffineSubspace
slogan: An affine subspace is a set of points in a space where you can combine points using weighted sums, as long as the weights add up to one, and the result stays in the set. It is based on a vector space structure over a ring, where points can be moved by vectors, and the set behaves like a shifted version of a linear subspace—such as a line or plane not necessarily going through the origin. The setup requires a ring for scalars, a commutative group for vectors, a module for scalar multiplication, and a torsor structure to link points and vectors.

label: AffineSubspace.Parallel
slogan: Two affine subspaces are parallel if you can get from one to the other by adding the same vector to every point. This means one subspace is a shifted version of the other, with no rotation or scaling involved. The direction of the subspaces stays the same, like two distinct parallel lines or planes in space.

label: AffineSubspace.mk'
slogan: An affine subspace is formed by starting at a given point and adding all possible vectors from a submodule, creating a set where any point can be reached by moving from the base point along vectors in the submodule. This set is closed under affine combinations, meaning any weighted sum of points with coefficients adding to one stays in the set. The construction relies on the algebraic properties of modules and vector operations in a torsor structure.

label: AffineSubspace.mk'_eq
slogan: An affine subspace made from a base point and a direction (a set of vectors) is exactly the set of all points you get by adding vectors from the direction to that base point. This means the subspace consists of all points reachable by moving from the base point in directions allowed by the vector space. The subspace is uniquely determined by its direction and any one point it contains.

label: AlgHom
slogan: An AlgHom is a function between two algebras over the same commutative semiring of scalars that preserves addition, multiplication, the multiplicative identity, and scalar multiplication. It is a ring homomorphism that also respects the algebra structure by ensuring scalar actions are compatible via a homomorphism into the center of the target algebra. This means the function maintains both the ring and scalar multiplication properties of the algebras.

label: Algebra
slogan: An algebra combines a ring A with a commutative semiring R, allowing elements of R to multiply elements of A in a way that respects addition and multiplication in A, guided by a ring homomorphism from R into the center of A. This structure supports scalar multiplication where scalars come from R and act on elements of A, compatible with the arithmetic in both types. It generalizes linear algebra concepts to work over various number systems like natural numbers or polynomials.

label: Algebra.FiniteType
slogan: An Algebra.FiniteType is a structure where an algebra A over a commutative semiring R is finitely generated as a module, meaning there exists a finite set of elements in A such that every element of A can be written as a linear combination of these elements with coefficients from R. This implies the algebra is not too large compared to the base ring, combining ring operations, scalar multiplication, and finite generation in a compatible way. It requires A to be a semiring, R a commutative semiring, and a well-defined algebra structure between them.

label: Algebra.GrothendieckGroup
slogan: The Grothendieck group of a commutative monoid M is formed by formally adding inverses to all elements, treating the entire monoid as the set being localized. It is constructed as the localization of M at its top submonoid, which includes all elements of M. This process turns the monoid into an abelian group where differences of elements can be expressed.

label: Algebra.GrothendieckGroup.of_injective
slogan: If a commutative monoid has the property that multiplication cancels on both sides (meaning a*b = a*c implies b = c and similarly on the right), then the natural map sending each element of the monoid into its Grothendieck group is injective—distinct elements in the monoid remain distinct in the group. This means no information is lost when embedding the monoid into its Grothendieck group under these conditions.

label: Algebra.IsAlgebraic
slogan: An element of a ring A is algebraic over a commutative ring R if there is a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in R such that evaluating it at the element gives zero, and this relationship is defined when A has an algebra structure over R.

label: Algebra.IsAlgebraic.of_finite
slogan: If a ring R is both a finite module and an algebra over a commutative ring A, then every element of R satisfies a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in A. This means each element of R is algebraic over A, provided A has more than one element and the algebra structure is compatible with the ring operations. The result follows from the fact that integral elements over A are also algebraic when the module is finitely generated.

label: Algebra.IsCentral
slogan: An element is central in an algebra if it commutes with every other element, meaning multiplying it by any element in either order gives the same result. This property depends on the algebra structure over a commutative semiring, where scalars act on the algebra through a ring homomorphism. The center of an algebra consists of all such elements that satisfy this symmetry condition.

label: Algebra.IsSeparable
slogan: A separable algebra over a field F is an algebra where the structure remains well-behaved when extended to larger fields, meaning that no unnecessary algebraic dependencies are introduced. It ensures that certain bilinear forms stay non-degenerate, preserving linear independence across field extensions. This condition is key for studying field extensions in algebra and geometry.

label: Algebra.TensorProduct.instAlgebra
slogan: The tensor product of two algebras over a commutative semiring is itself an algebra over that semiring, meaning it has a multiplication, addition, and scalar action that work together as expected. Scalar multiplication is defined so that multiplying by a scalar from the base semiring acts on the whole tensor product in a way that respects both algebra structures. This makes the tensor product into a ring with scalars from the original semiring, where all operations are compatible.

label: Algebra.TensorProduct.instCommRing
slogan: If R is a commutative semiring and A and B are commutative R-algebras, then the tensor product A ⊗[R] B can be given a commutative ring structure where multiplication is defined by (a1 ⊗ b1) * (a2 ⊗ b2) = (a1 * a2) ⊗ (b1 * b2). This multiplication is commutative, associative, and compatible with the R-algebra structures. The resulting ring has a zero and a one, and all the usual ring properties hold.

label: Algebra.TensorProduct.isField_of_isAlgebraic
slogan: If two field extensions of a common base field are algebraic and linearly disjoint, then their tensor product over that base field is also a field, meaning it has no zero divisors and every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. This holds when the natural map from the base field into the tensor product is injective. The result ensures the tensor product retains the field structure under these conditions.

label: Algebra.TensorProduct.leftAlgebra
slogan: Given a commutative semiring R and two R-algebras A and B, the tensor product A ⊗[R] B can be made into an R-algebra by defining scalar multiplication as r * (a ⊗ b) = (r * a) ⊗ b, and this structure is compatible with the ring operations and the embedding of R into A ⊗[R] B via r ↦ r * 1 ⊗ 1. If there is another commutative semiring S acting on A in a way that commutes with the R-action, then S also acts on the tensor product A ⊗[R] B, making it an S-algebra. This construction uses the algebra structure of A over S and the bilinearity of the tensor product to define a well-behaved scalar mult

label: Algebra.TensorProduct.rightAlgebra
slogan: Given a commutative semiring R and two R-algebras A and B, the tensor product A ⊗_R B can be made into a B-algebra by defining multiplication as (a1 ⊗ b1) * (a2 ⊗ b2) = (a1 * a2) ⊗ (b1 * b2) and extending this operation linearly. This structure ensures that elements of B act naturally on the right side of the tensor, making the tensor product a well-defined algebra over B. The scalar action from R commutes with all operations, preserving the necessary algebraic properties.

label: Algebra.norm
slogan: The norm of an element in a finite-dimensional algebra over a commutative ring is calculated as the determinant of the linear transformation that maps each algebra element to the result of left multiplication by the given element. This determinant is taken with respect to the algebra's structure as a module over the base ring, and the result is always an element of the base ring. The norm function is multiplicative, meaning the norm of a product equals the product of the norms.

label: Algebra.trace
slogan: The trace of an element in a finite-dimensional algebra over a commutative ring is computed by viewing the element as a linear map defined by left multiplication, then taking the trace of that map. This results in a scalar value in the base ring that does not depend on the choice of basis. The operation is linear with respect to the algebra structure.

label: Algebra.trdeg
slogan: The transcendence degree of an algebra A over a commutative ring R is the largest possible size (as a cardinal number) of a set of elements in A that do not satisfy any nontrivial polynomial equation with coefficients from R. It is defined as the supremum of the cardinalities of all algebraically independent subsets of A over R. This measures how "free" or "independent" the algebra is from polynomial relations over the base ring.

label: AlgebraicClosure
slogan: The algebraic closure of a field is built by adding solutions to all non-constant polynomials through a process that uses polynomials with infinitely many variables and takes quotients by maximal ideals. This ensures the resulting structure is a field where every non-constant polynomial has a root. The construction relies on standard algebraic tools like polynomial rings, ideals, and quotient rings.

label: AlgebraicClosure.isAlgClosed
slogan: The algebraic closure of any field is a field extension where every non-constant polynomial has at least one root, ensuring no further algebraic extensions are possible. This closure is built by adjoining roots through quotienting multivariate polynomial rings by a maximal ideal. The result is a field in which all polynomials split into linear factors.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.AffineScheme
slogan: The category of affine schemes consists of schemes that are spectra of commutative rings, where morphisms come from ring homomorphisms in the opposite direction via the Spec functor. It is a subcategory of the category of schemes, built using the opposite category of commutative rings. Affine schemes and their maps form a category with standard composition and identity morphisms.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.AffineScheme.equivCommRingCat
slogan: The category of affine schemes is equivalent to the opposite category of commutative rings, meaning every affine scheme corresponds to a commutative ring and morphisms between schemes correspond to ring homomorphisms in the reverse direction. This equivalence reflects a one-to-one relationship between the structures of these two categories.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Etale
slogan: A map between schemes is called etale if, whenever you look at small enough pieces that can be described by algebra, the corresponding ring map is etale, meaning it is flat and unramified. This condition must hold for all compatible affine pieces of the schemes involved. The definition builds on the structure of schemes as spaces that locally resemble the spectrum of a commutative ring.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Flat
slogan: A morphism of schemes is flat if the induced map on sections over affine open sets is a flat ring homomorphism, meaning it preserves exact sequences when tensoring. This condition is equivalent to requiring that the induced map on stalks at every point is also a flat ring homomorphism.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.IsAffine
slogan: A scheme X is called affine if the natural map from X to the spectrum of its ring of global sections is an isomorphism. This means X can be fully described by a single commutative ring, up to isomorphism.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.IsClosedImmersion
slogan: A morphism of schemes is a closed immersion if it gives a homeomorphism onto a closed subset of the target space and the induced maps on local rings are surjective. This means the map is both a topological embedding with closed image and algebraically surjective at each point.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.IsIntegral
slogan: A scheme X is integral if it is not empty and the ring of sections over every nonempty open set U is an integral domain, meaning it has no zero divisors and 1 is not equal to 0.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.IsProper
slogan: A morphism of schemes is called proper if it is separated, universally closed, and locally of finite type. This means the map behaves like a compact map in topology, with good finiteness and closure properties when pulled back along other maps.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.LocallyRingedSpace
slogan: A locally ringed space is a topological space with a sheaf of commutative rings where each stalk is a local ring, meaning it has a unique maximal ideal and the non-units are closed under addition. A morphism between such spaces is a continuous map with a compatible sheaf map that induces local ring homomorphisms on stalks. This structure combines topology and algebra to model geometric objects in algebraic geometry.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Proj
slogan: Proj(A) is a geometric space built from a ring A that is graded by the natural numbers, where the space is constructed by focusing on homogeneous prime ideals not containing all positive-degree elements. It carries the structure of a scheme, meaning it is a topological space equipped with a sheaf of rings that locally resembles the spectrum of a commutative ring. The construction generalizes projective algebraic varieties to arbitrary graded rings.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Proj.toSpecZero
slogan: Proj A maps to the spectrum of the degree-zero part of A, where this map is a morphism of schemes derived from the graded ring structure. The degree-zero part forms a commutative ring, and its spectrum is a base scheme that Proj A naturally maps to. This structure map connects the projective spectrum to an affine one using the ring's grading.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.RingedSpace
slogan: A ringed space is a mathematical structure that combines a topological space with a sheaf of commutative rings, used to study spaces by associating algebraic data to them. It is defined as a special case of a sheafed space where the algebraic objects involved are commutative rings.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme
slogan: A Scheme is a locally ringed space where every point has an open neighborhood that looks like the spectrum of a commutative ring, in terms of both topology and algebraic structure.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.Hom
slogan: A morphism of schemes is a map that respects both the geometric structure (as a continuous map) and the algebraic structure (via sheaves of rings), where the map on each point's neighborhood behaves like a ring homomorphism that preserves local properties. It is built from a morphism of locally ringed spaces, which means it includes a continuous function and a compatible sheaf map that induces local ring homomorphisms on stalks. Schemes are defined as locally ringed spaces that locally resemble the spectrum of a commutative ring.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.RationalMap
slogan: A rational map from a scheme X to a scheme Y is defined as an equivalence class of partial maps from X to Y, where two partial maps are considered equivalent if they agree on a dense open subset of X.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.functionField
slogan: The function field of an irreducible scheme is defined as the local ring at its generic point, which exists because the scheme's underlying space is quasi-sober. This ring is a field only if the scheme is integral, meaning it is both irreducible and reduced. The construction relies on the stalk of the structure sheaf at the generic point, formed as a colimit over open neighborhoods.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.smallEtaleTopology
slogan: The small étale site of a scheme X is a collection of schemes that map to X in a way that is locally like a standard smooth map of dimension zero, where the coverings are families of such maps that are jointly surjective and preserve the étale condition. This structure forms a Grothendieck topology, meaning it satisfies certain axioms about pullbacks and composition of covering families. It is built from the category of schemes étale over X by restricting the broader étale topology on all schemes to only those over X.

label: AlgebraicGeometry.structureSheafInType
slogan: The structure sheaf on the prime spectrum of a commutative ring R is defined as the sheaf of functions that, on each open set, take values in the localizations of R at prime ideals and can locally be written as fractions of elements from R. It is constructed as a subsheaf of a larger sheaf of all possible functions into these localizations, by restricting to only those functions satisfying the "isLocallyFraction" condition. This means that around every point, there is a neighborhood where the function equals a single fraction with numerator and denominator in R, valid in the corresponding loca

label: AlgebraicIndependent
slogan: A set of elements is algebraically independent over a commutative ring R if the only multivariate polynomial with coefficients in R that evaluates to zero when applied to those elements is the zero polynomial. This means there are no nontrivial polynomial relations among the elements with coefficients from R.

label: AlgebraicTopology.AlternatingFaceMapComplex.objD
slogan: The alternating face map complex defines a differential for a simplicial object by taking the alternating sum of its face maps at each level. Specifically, for each n, the differential is built by summing the face maps composed with (-1)^i for i from 0 to n, using the abelian group structure on morphisms in a preadditive category. This differential connects the object at degree n+1 to the object at degree n, forming a chain complex.

label: AlgebraicTopology.alternatingFaceMapComplex
slogan: The alternating face map complex converts a simplicial object in a preadditive category into a chain complex by defining the differential as an alternating sum of face maps. This construction ensures that the composition of two consecutive differentials is zero, satisfying the chain complex condition. It allows homological algebra techniques to be applied to simplicial structures by organizing them into a sequence of objects and morphisms indexed by natural numbers.

label: AlternatingMap.coe_alternatization
slogan: The alternatization of a multilinear map is obtained by averaging, over all permutations of the input indices, the original map applied to the permuted inputs, with each term multiplied by the sign of the permutation. This resulting map is alternating and, when converted to a function, matches that symmetric signed sum. The output is scaled by the factorial of the number of inputs, ensuring the alternatization preserves the original map if it was already alternating.

label: AlternatingMap.map_perm
slogan: Applying a permutation to the inputs of an alternating map multiplies the output by the sign of the permutation, which is 1 for even permutations and -1 for odd ones. This means reordering the arguments changes the sign of the result based on how the permutation affects the input order.

label: AlternatingMap.map_swap
slogan: Swapping two distinct inputs to an alternating map results in the negative of the original output. This means if you exchange the values at two different positions in the input function, the map's result changes sign. The map operates on functions from an index type to a module, and the swap is defined using a permutation that exchanges two indices.

label: AnalyticAt
slogan: A function is analytic at a point if, near that point, it can be written as a convergent power series using continuous multilinear functions, with the function and its inputs coming from normed spaces over a field where the norm isn't trivial. This means the function behaves locally like its Taylor series expansion. The spaces involved must support both addition and scalar multiplication with a well-behaved notion of size given by a norm.

label: AnalyticAt.harmonicAt_log_norm
slogan: If a complex function f has no zeros and is analytic (locally representable by a convergent power series) at a point, then the real-valued function obtained by taking the logarithm of the norm of f is harmonic at that point, meaning it satisfies Laplace's equation in a neighborhood around the point.

label: AnalyticAt.harmonicAt_re
slogan: If a complex function is analytic at a point, then its real part satisfies Laplace's equation at that point, meaning the real part is harmonic.

label: AnalyticOn
slogan: A function is analytic on a set if, at every point in that set, it can be written as a convergent power series in some neighborhood around that point, with the series taking values in a normed space over a field that has a nontrivial norm. This means the function locally matches its power series expansion near each point in the set. The function must map between two normed spaces over the same nontrivially normed field for this to hold.

label: AnalyticOn.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall
slogan: If a function f is analytic on the entire ball where its Taylor series is defined, then the Taylor series converges to f within that ball, provided the underlying field behaves like the real or complex numbers. This means that on this ball, f can be exactly represented by its power series expansion around a point. The result strengthens a simpler local version by applying over the full radius of convergence.

label: AnalyticOnNhd
slogan: A function is analytic on a neighborhood if, at every point in that neighborhood, it can be written as a convergent power series in some small region around the point, provided the function maps between normed vector spaces over a field with a nontrivial norm. This means the function behaves locally like a power series everywhere in an open set. The spaces involved must support both addition and scalar multiplication with compatible norms.

label: AnalyticOnNhd.eqOn_of_preconnected_of_eventuallyEq
slogan: If two functions are analytic on a neighborhood of a connected set and agree near some point in that set, then they agree everywhere on the set.

label: AnalyticOnNhd.eqOn_of_preconnected_of_frequently_eq
slogan: If two functions are analytic on a neighborhood of a preconnected set and they agree at points that are arbitrarily close to some point in the set (excluding the point itself), then the functions are equal everywhere on that set.

label: AnalyticOnNhd.eq_of_frequently_eq
slogan: If two functions are analytic on a neighborhood in a connected normed space over a nontrivially normed field, and they are equal at points arbitrarily close to some point (but not equal to it), then the functions are equal everywhere. This means that if analytic functions match frequently near a point, they must be the same function throughout the space.

label: AnalyticOnNhd.is_constant_or_isOpen
slogan: If a complex-valued function is analytic on a connected set, then either it is constant throughout that set, or it maps open subsets to open sets in the complex plane.

label: And.symm
slogan: If a and b are both true, then b and a are also both true. The order of logical "and" does not matter.

label: Antitone.tendsto_alternating_series_of_tendsto_zero
slogan: If a sequence of real numbers decreases and approaches zero, then the alternating sum (adding the first term, subtracting the second, and so on) converges to some real number. This happens because the partial sums eventually get arbitrarily close to each other and the completeness of the real numbers guarantees a limit exists.

label: AntitoneOn.integral_le_sum_Ico
slogan: If a function f is decreasing on the interval from a to b (where a and b are natural numbers), then the integral of f from a to b is less than or equal to the sum of f evaluated at each integer point from a up to but not including b.

label: AntitoneOn.sum_le_integral
slogan: If a function f is decreasing on the interval from x0 to x0 + a, then the sum of f evaluated at integer steps from x0 + 1 to x0 + a is less than or equal to the integral of f over the continuous interval from x0 to x0 + a.

label: AntivaryOn.card_mul_sum_le_sum_mul_sum
slogan: If two functions f and g are such that one increases while the other decreases over a finite set s, then the sum of their product values across s is at most the average of their individual sums multiplied together, scaled by the size of s. Specifically, the inequality states that the total sum of f(i)*g(i) over all elements in s, when multiplied by the number of elements in s, is less than or equal to the product of the sum of f(i) and the sum of g(i). This result holds for values in a semiring with a compatible linear order and strict ordering properties.

label: Archimedean
slogan: A type has an Archimedean order when, given any two positive elements a and b, adding a to itself repeatedly will eventually produce a sum larger than b. This means no element is so large that it cannot be surpassed by adding a smaller element enough times. The type must support both a partial order and a commutative addition with zero.

label: ArithmeticFunction
slogan: An arithmetic function is a function that takes natural numbers as inputs and returns values in some type that has a zero element, where multiplying by zero gives zero. It is designed to represent number-theoretic functions like the Möbius or divisor functions. The natural numbers are assumed to follow standard rules for multiplication with zero.

label: ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative
slogan: A function from natural numbers to a type with zero is called multiplicative if, whenever two natural numbers have no common divisors other than 1, the function's value at their product equals the product of the function's values at each number. This must hold for all such coprime pairs, and the type must support multiplication and a zero element that behaves normally (anything times zero is zero).

label: ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative.mul
slogan: If two functions on natural numbers satisfy f(m*n) = f(m)*f(n) whenever m and n are coprime, then their product function (f*g)(n) = f(n)*g(n) also satisfies this property for coprime m and n.

label: ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative.prodPrimeFactors_one_sub_of_squarefree
slogan: If a natural number is squarefree, then the product of (1 - f(p)) over all its distinct prime factors p equals the sum over all divisors d of n of the Möbius function of d times f(d), provided f is a multiplicative function taking values in a commutative ring.

label: ArithmeticFunction.cardDistinctFactors_mul
slogan: If two natural numbers share no common prime factors, then the number of distinct prime factors of their product is simply the sum of the number of distinct prime factors of each number. This is because the prime factors of the two numbers are completely separate. Multiplying them combines their distinct prime factors without overlap.

label: ArithmeticFunction.cardFactors_mul
slogan: The total number of prime factors (counting repeats) of the product of two nonzero natural numbers equals the sum of the number of prime factors of each number. For example, if you factor two numbers separately, count their prime factors with repetition, and add those counts, it will match the count of prime factors in their product. This holds because prime factorization is additive over multiplication.

label: ArithmeticFunction.coe_zeta_mul_apply
slogan: Multiplying the zeta function by another arithmetic function f and evaluating at a natural number n gives the sum of f values over all positive divisors of n. Since the zeta function is the constant function 1, this sum includes f(i) for each divisor i of n. This operation follows the rule of Dirichlet convolution in number theory.

label: ArithmeticFunction.isMultiplicative_id
slogan: The identity function, which maps each natural number to itself, is multiplicative: if two natural numbers are coprime (their greatest common divisor is 1), then the value of the function at their product is equal to the product of the values at each number.

label: ArithmeticFunction.isMultiplicative_moebius
slogan: If two natural numbers have no common prime factors (their gcd is 1), then the Moebius function of their product equals the product of the Moebius function values at each number. The Moebius function returns 0 if a number has a squared prime factor, and otherwise returns 1 or -1 depending on whether the number has an even or odd number of distinct prime factors. This property holds for all coprime pairs of natural numbers.

label: ArithmeticFunction.isMultiplicative_sigma
slogan: For any fixed natural number k, the function that sums the k-th powers of the divisors of a positive integer is multiplicative: if two integers have no common factors other than 1, then the sum for their product equals the product of the sums for each integer separately.

label: ArithmeticFunction.liouville
slogan: The Liouville function assigns to each natural number n the value (-1) raised to the power of the total number of prime factors of n, counting repetitions; it returns zero when n is zero. This function maps natural numbers to integers and is defined using the count of prime factors including multiplicity.

label: ArithmeticFunction.moebius
slogan: The Moebius function takes a natural number and returns 0 if the number has a squared prime factor (i.e., is not squarefree), returns 1 if it has an even number of distinct prime factors, and -1 if it has an odd number of distinct prime factors. It is defined for all natural numbers and outputs integers.

label: ArithmeticFunction.moebius_apply_one
slogan: The Möbius function returns 1 when given the input 1, because 1 has no prime factors and is considered squarefree. Since it has zero distinct prime factors, which is an even number, the function's value is 1.

label: ArithmeticFunction.moebius_apply_prime
slogan: If p is a prime number, the Moebius function returns -1 when evaluated at p, because primes are squarefree and have exactly one distinct prime factor.

label: ArithmeticFunction.moebius_mul_coe_zeta
slogan: The product of the Moebius function and the constant function 1, when combined using Dirichlet convolution, results in the function that is 1 at 1 and 0 everywhere else. This means that summing the Moebius function over all positive divisors of a natural number n gives 1 if n is 1, and 0 for all other n. The result follows from properties of arithmetic functions and finite sums over divisors.

label: ArithmeticFunction.moebius_ne_zero_iff_squarefree
slogan: The Moebius function is nonzero at a natural number if and only if that number is squarefree, meaning it is not divisible by any perfect square greater than 1.

label: ArithmeticFunction.mul_apply
slogan: The product of two arithmetic functions at a natural number n is computed by summing the products of their values over all pairs of positive integers (a, b) such that a times b equals n. This sum runs over all divisor pairs of n, where each pair (a, b) satisfies a * b = n. The multiplication uses the underlying semiring's operations for combining function values.

label: ArithmeticFunction.prod_eq_iff_prod_pow_moebius_eq
slogan: Two arithmetic functions f and g are equal if and only if, for every positive integer n, the product of f over the divisors of n equals g(n), and equivalently, the product of g(d) raised to the power of the Möbius function at n/d over all divisor pairs (d, n/d) equals f(n). This gives a way to check function equality by transforming products involving the Möbius function. The result applies to functions from natural numbers to a commutative group.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sigma
slogan: ArithmeticFunction.sigma takes a natural number and returns the sum of all its positive divisors, calculated by adding up the elements in the finite set of numbers that divide it. For any nonzero natural number, this means summing all divisors from 1 up to the number itself that divide it evenly. Since every natural number divides zero, the sum would be infinite, so sigma is not meaningfully defined for zero.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sigma_one_apply
slogan: The function sigma_1 applied to a natural number n gives the sum of all positive divisors of n. This sum is calculated by adding up every number d that divides n, using the standard addition of natural numbers. For example, if n is 6, the divisors are 1, 2, 3, and 6, and their sum is 12.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sigma_zero_apply
slogan: The sum of 1 for each positive divisor of a natural number n equals the total number of divisors of n. This means adding 1 once for every divisor counts how many divisors there are. The result is true for all natural numbers, including zero.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sum_Ioc_sigma0_eq_sum_div
slogan: The sum of the number of divisors of all integers from 1 to N-1 is equal to the sum over d from 1 to N-1 of the number of multiples of d that are less than N. This counts the same divisor relationships in two different ways. Each divisor d of a number k contributes 1 to the count when summing over divisors, and also when summing over multiples.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sum_eq_iff_sum_mul_moebius_eq
slogan: Two arithmetic functions f and g satisfy f(1) + f(d) + ... = g(n) for every n if and only if combining g with the Möbius function through a divisor sum gives back f(n) for all n. This means summing f over the divisors of n matches g(n) exactly when f can be recovered from g using Möbius inversion. The result works for functions from positive integers to any ring-like structure.

label: ArithmeticFunction.sum_eq_iff_sum_smul_moebius_eq
slogan: Two arithmetic functions f and g are equal if and only if, for every positive integer n, the sum of f over the divisors of n equals g(n), which happens exactly when the Möbius function twisted sum of g gives back f. This means you can recover f from g using Möbius inversion, and vice versa. The equality of these sums for all n guarantees the functions are pointwise equal.

label: ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt
slogan: The vonMangoldt function returns the natural logarithm of a prime p if its input is a power of p (like p^k for k >= 1), and returns 0 otherwise. It uses the smallest prime factor of a number to determine the prime when the number is a prime power. This function is defined for natural numbers and outputs real numbers.

label: ArzelaAscoli.compactSpace_of_isClosedEmbedding
slogan: If a family of functions from a topological space X to a uniform space alpha is indexed by a space iota, and if these functions are equicontinuous on each compact set in a cover of X, map each point into a compact set, and the embedding of iota into the function space is closed, then the index space iota is compact.

label: Asymptotics.IsBigOWith
slogan: A function f is considered big-O of another function g as x approaches a certain limit if, beyond some point, the absolute value of f(x) is always less than or equal to a constant times the absolute value of g(x). This describes how fast f grows compared to g near that limit, using normal real number multiplication and comparison. The limit is defined by a filter, which captures the idea of "eventually" being close to the limit.

label: Asymptotics.IsEquivalent
slogan: Two functions are asymptotically equivalent if their difference becomes arbitrarily small compared to the norm of one of them as they approach a limit defined by a filter. This means the difference between the functions grows much slower than the norm of one function near that limit. The concept applies to functions whose outputs are in a normed abelian group.

label: Asymptotics.IsEquivalent.trans
slogan: If two functions f and g become relatively indistinguishable as their inputs approach a certain limit, and g and h also become relatively indistinguishable in the same way, then f and h will likewise become relatively indistinguishable near that limit. This means that asymptotic equivalence is transitive: if f is asymptotically equivalent to g and g to h, then f is asymptotically equivalent to h.

label: Asymptotics.IsLittleO.add
slogan: If two functions both grow much slower than a third function near a limit (meaning each is negligible compared to the third), then their sum also grows much slower than that same third function. This holds when measuring size using norms and considering limits defined by filters.

label: Asymptotics.IsLittleO.isBigO
slogan: If a function f becomes negligible compared to another function g as they approach some limit, then f is also bounded by a constant multiple of g near that limit. In other words, if f grows much slower than g, it certainly doesn't grow faster than g up to a constant factor. This follows from the definitions of little-o and big-O using norms and filters.

label: Asymptotics.IsLittleO.trans
slogan: If one function grows much slower than a second, and the second grows much slower than a third, then the first grows much slower than the third, as they approach the same limit. This is true for functions whose sizes are measured by norms and compared using real numbers. The result follows from the definition of "grows much slower" (little-o) and the ordering of real numbers.

label: Asymptotics.IsTheta
slogan: A function f is asymptotically Theta of g if, within a given limiting context (filter), f is bounded above by a constant multiple of g and g is bounded above by a constant multiple of f, using norms to measure size. This means f and g grow at the same rate asymptotically. The definition applies to functions from a type α into normed spaces E and F, with the behavior determined along a filter l on α.

label: Asymptotics.IsTheta.isBigO
slogan: If a function f grows at the same rate as a function g (meaning f is bounded both above and below by constant multiples of g) near some limit defined by a filter, then f does not grow faster than g; that is, the size of f is eventually bounded by a constant multiple of the size of g.

label: Asymptotics.isBigO_iff
slogan: A function f is big-O of another function g as x approaches a certain limit if and only if there is some positive constant c such that, for all x sufficiently close to that limit, the norm of f(x) is less than or equal to c times the norm of g(x). This means f does not grow significantly faster than g near the limit. The comparison uses the usual notion of size (norm) and multiplication by a constant.

label: Asymptotics.isBigO_iff_div_isBoundedUnder
slogan: A function f is big-O of another function g as x approaches some limit if and only if the absolute value of f(x)/g(x) stays within some fixed bound as x gets close to that limit, assuming g(x) is not zero (or both f(x) and g(x) are zero when g(x) is zero). This means f does not grow significantly faster than g near the limit. The ratio |f(x)/g(x)| must eventually remain less than or equal to some constant.

label: Asymptotics.isEquivalent_iff_tendsto_one
slogan: Two functions are asymptotically equivalent if and only if their ratio approaches 1 as they get close to a certain point, provided the denominator isn't zero near that point. This means they grow at the same rate in the limit. The condition ensures the ratio is well-defined as the input approaches the limit.

label: Asymptotics.isLittleO_pow_pow_atTop_of_lt
slogan: If p is less than q, then the function x^p grows slower than x^q as x approaches infinity, meaning x^p becomes negligible compared to x^q for large values of x.

label: BaireMeasurableSet
slogan: A set is Baire measurable if it is almost the same as an open set, except possibly on a small (meager) set. This means the set matches an open set outside of a negligible portion that is contained in a countable union of nowhere dense sets. The collection of all such sets forms a sigma-algebra.

label: BaireSpace
slogan: A Baire space is a topological space where the intersection of any countable number of dense open sets is still dense, meaning that this intersection comes arbitrarily close to every point in the space. The property depends on the topology and the fact that the sets are open. This captures the idea that in such spaces, certain "large" sets remain large even when infinitely intersected.

label: BaireSpace.instBarrelledSpace
slogan: A topological vector space over a nontrivially normed field is barrelled if it is also a Baire space, meaning every lower semicontinuous seminorm on the space is continuous. This includes important cases like Banach spaces and Fréchet spaces.

label: BaireSpace.of_completelyPseudoMetrizable
slogan: Every completely pseudometrizable space is a Baire space, meaning that in such a space, the intersection of countably many dense open sets remains dense.

label: BddAbove
slogan: A set is bounded above if there is some element that is greater than or equal to every element in the set, using the type's built-in ≤ relation. This means the set has at least one upper bound. The existence of such a bound depends on the ordering defined for the type.

label: BddBelow
slogan: A set has a lower bound if there is some element that is less than or equal to every element in the set, using the type's ≤ relation, and the set must contain at least one element.

label: Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div
slogan: For almost every point in a set s, as the radius of closed balls around that point gets smaller and smaller, the ratio of the measure of s intersected with the ball to the measure of the ball itself approaches 1, provided the space has a locally finite measure and satisfies the Besicovitch covering property. This means that at almost every point, small balls are eventually filled up by the set in terms of measure. The convergence happens as the radius approaches zero from positive values.

label: Besicovitch.exists_closedBall_covering_tsum_measure_le
slogan: In a metric space with certain regularity properties, there exists a countable collection of closed balls centered at points of a set s, with radii chosen from given families, that covers s and has total measure at most the measure of s plus a small error ε. The sum of the measures of these balls is controlled by the measure of the original set. This allows constructing efficient, non-overlapping coverings in measure-theoretic contexts.

label: Besicovitch.exists_disjoint_closedBall_covering_ae
slogan: There is a countable set of non-overlapping closed balls such that almost every point in a given set s is inside one of these balls, the radius at each center x is positive and less than a given bound R x, and each radius is chosen from a specified set of allowed radii near zero.

label: Bool.and_eq_true
slogan: The expression (a && b) equals true if and only if both a equals true and b equals true.

label: Bool.carry
slogan: The carry function takes three boolean values (x, y, and c) representing two bits and a carry-in, and returns a boolean indicating whether adding them produces a carry-out. It computes whether at least two of the three inputs are true, which corresponds to generating a carry in binary addition. This models the logic of a full adder's carry output in digital circuits.

label: Bool.instBooleanAlgebra
slogan: The Bool type, with its values true and false, is equipped with a full Boolean algebra structure, meaning it supports logical operations like and, or, and not, along with ordering (≤), and follows standard algebraic rules such as distributivity and complementation. This setup ensures that Bool behaves like a classical two-element Boolean algebra, consistent with logic and set theory. It relies on existing definitions that give Bool a bounded order and distributive lattice structure.

label: BooleanAlgebra
slogan: A BooleanAlgebra is a type of system where elements can be combined using operations like union, intersection, and complement, have a smallest value (bot) and largest value (top), and follow logical rules such as implication and set difference, all while behaving like a distributive lattice. It supports standard reasoning about sets, logic, and order in a consistent algebraic framework.

label: BooleanAlgebra.ofRegular
slogan: If every element in a Heyting algebra equals the double complement of itself, then the algebra satisfies all the properties of a Boolean algebra. This means that when an element is the same as the complement of its complement, the structure behaves like classical logic with standard true/false operations. The condition ensures that the algebra has enough symmetry between elements and their complements to support Boolean reasoning.

label: BooleanRing
slogan: A Boolean ring is a type of algebraic structure where every element multiplied by itself gives the same element, and it follows the usual rules of addition and multiplication. In other words, for any element a, a * a = a. It builds on the standard ring structure by adding this idempotent property for multiplication.

label: BorelSpace
slogan: A BorelSpace is a space that has both a topology and a sigma-algebra such that the sigma-algebra is the one generated by the open sets of the topology. This means the measurable sets include all open sets and are closed under countable unions, intersections, and complements. It links the concepts of continuity and measurability by using open sets as the foundation for measurement.

label: Bornology.IsBounded
slogan: A set is bounded in a bornology if it is part of a collection of "small" sets that includes the empty set and is closed under subsets and finite unions, meaning subsets of bounded sets are bounded and finite unions of bounded sets remain bounded.

label: BoundedContinuousFunction.arzela_ascoli
slogan: If a set of bounded continuous functions from a compact space to a Hausdorff pseudometric space is equicontinuous and all functions map into a fixed compact subset, then the closure of that set is compact.

label: BoundedContinuousFunction.exists_extension_norm_eq_of_isClosedEmbedding
slogan: If a function continuously embeds a topological space into a normal space as a closed subset, then any real-valued bounded continuous function on the original space can be extended to the larger space without changing its norm.

label: BoundedContinuousFunction.exists_norm_eq_restrict_eq
slogan: If a function is continuous and bounded on a closed subset of a normal topological space, then it can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm, meaning there exists a bounded continuous function on the entire space that matches the original function on the subset and has the same maximum absolute value.

label: BoundedContinuousFunction.instCompleteSpace
slogan: The space of bounded continuous functions from a topological space to a complete metric space is complete, meaning every uniformly Cauchy sequence of such functions converges uniformly to a bounded continuous function. This convergence happens because the completeness of the target metric space ensures that pointwise limits exist and are preserved under uniform convergence. The result depends on both the continuity of the functions and the uniform structure of the metric.

label: BoundedContinuousFunction.toLp_denseRange
slogan: The image of bounded continuous functions in the Lp space is dense when the underlying space is normal, second-countable, and equipped with a finite weakly regular Borel measure. This means that any Lp function can be approximated arbitrarily well by bounded continuous functions in the Lp norm. The result holds for real or complex scalars and requires the exponent p to be at least 1 and not infinite.

label: BoundedLatticeHom
slogan: A BoundedLatticeHom is a function between two bounded lattices that preserves the top and bottom elements, as well as the operations for taking the least upper bound (sup) and greatest lower bound (inf) of any two elements. It ensures that the structure of the lattice, including its bounds, is maintained when mapping from one lattice to another. This means the function respects sup, inf, top, and bot in both the source and target types.

label: BoundedOrder
slogan: A BoundedOrder is a type that has a minimum element (bot) and a maximum element (top), along with a less-than-or-equal-to relation (≤), such that for every element x, bot ≤ x and x ≤ top. It combines the properties of having both a smallest and largest element within an ordered structure.

label: BoundedVariationOn
slogan: A function has bounded variation on a set if the total distance it travels over that set, measured using the extended metric, is finite. This means the supremum of the sum of distances between consecutive values along any finite increasing sequence in the set is not infinite. The function's variation is defined in terms of a pseudo extended metric space, and boundedness means this variation is a real number, not infinity.

label: BoxIntegral.Box
slogan: BoxIntegral.Box defines a multidimensional box in Euclidean space by specifying an interval for each axis, using a type to index the coordinates. It is used to represent regions over which integration can be performed in multiple dimensions. The box is determined by its lower and upper bounds in each coordinate direction.

label: BoxIntegral.HasIntegral.add
slogan: If two functions are integrable over a box using a given method, then their sum is also integrable over that box, and the integral of the sum is the sum of their integrals. This result follows from the fact that limits and integral sums preserve addition.

label: BoxIntegral.hasIntegral_iff
slogan: A function has an integral equal to a specific value if and only if, for every positive error tolerance, there is a sufficiently fine partition such that all corresponding Riemann sums are within that error of the value. This means integrability is confirmed by the Riemann sums getting arbitrarily close to the integral as partitions get finer. The closeness is measured using distances in a normed space, where being within a given error means lying in a closed ball around the integral value.

label: Brauer.CSA_Setoid
slogan: For any field K, the type of finite-dimensional central simple algebras over K can be equipped with an equivalence relation called Brauer equivalence, where two algebras are equivalent if some matrix algebras over them are isomorphic as algebras over K. This equivalence relation allows the collection of such algebras to form a setoid.

label: BrauerGroup
slogan: The BrauerGroup of a field K is the collection of finite-dimensional central simple algebras over K, where two algebras are considered the same if they are Brauer equivalent. This equivalence is formalized as a setoid on the type of such algebras. The BrauerGroup is then the quotient type under this equivalence.

label: Bundle.ContMDiffRiemannianMetric
slogan: A continuous family of inner products on the fibers of a vector bundle that matches the bundle's topology and varies smoothly with the base space. It ensures each fiber has a normed vector space structure while maintaining compatibility across the bundle. This setup supports Riemannian geometry on manifolds by providing a smoothly varying notion of length and angle.

label: Bundle.Trivial
slogan: A Bundle.Trivial associates each point in a base space B with a copy of a fixed type F, effectively representing a product structure B × F without any twisting. It means the bundle looks the same everywhere, like a cylinder over B with fiber F. The type F is based on the real numbers, suggesting a geometric or analytic context.

label: Bundle.Trivial.fiberBundle
slogan: The declaration states that a trivial bundle with base space B and fiber F has the structure of a fiber bundle, meaning it is globally equivalent to the product space B × F with continuous projection onto B. This equivalence is supported by a homeomorphism between the total space of the bundle and the product space, ensuring the bundle has no twisting. The fiber bundle structure is defined using this global homeomorphism and the standard topologies on B and F.

label: Bundle.Trivial.vectorBundle
slogan: A trivial bundle over a base space B with fiber F is a vector bundle when F is a normed vector space over a nontrivially normed field 𝕜, and B is a topological space, meaning the bundle is globally a product space with linear and topological structure preserved.

label: Bundle.Trivialization
slogan: A Bundle.Trivialization describes a local equivalence between a space Z and a product space B × F, where Z maps onto a base space B, such that over an open set in B, the map from Z to B × F is a homeomorphism when restricted to the preimage of that open set, and it preserves the base coordinate. It ensures the projection from Z to B locally looks like a trivial bundle, meaning Z splits into a product of B and a fiber F over small enough regions of B. This structure relies on topological spaces for B, F, and Z, and uses an open partial homeomorphism to define the splitting.

label: Bundle.zeroSection
slogan: The zero section of a vector bundle assigns to each point in the base space B a zero vector in the corresponding fiber E x, forming a function from B to the total space of the bundle.

label: CStarAlgebra
slogan: A CStarAlgebra is a complete normed ring with a star operation (like complex conjugation) that is compatible with a scalar multiplication over the complex numbers, where the norm satisfies the C*-identity: the norm of a*a equals the square of the norm of a. It supports algebraic operations and is closed under limits of Cauchy sequences. This structure generalizes algebras of bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space.

label: CStarAlgebra.increasingApproximateUnit
slogan: In a C*-algebra with a partial order and a star operation compatible with the order, the filter generated by elements greater than or equal to a nonnegative element a and inside the closed unit ball forms an increasing approximate unit.
