This means there exists a net of positive elements, each with norm at most 1, that approximates the identity in a way that respects the order structure. The net is increasing, meaning later elements are larger in the partial order.

label: CStarRing
slogan: A CStarRing is a ring without requiring a multiplicative identity, equipped with a norm and an involution operation (like complex conjugation), where the norm of the product of an element with its involution equals the square of the norm of that element. It combines the properties of a star ring and a non-unital normed ring under the C*-identity. This structure is used to model certain algebras of operators in functional analysis.

label: CStarRing.norm_star_mul_self
slogan: In a C*-ring, the norm of the product of an element's adjoint with the element itself equals the square of the element's norm. This means that for any element x, the size of star(x) * x is exactly the square of the size of x. The result follows from the defining C*-identity and properties of the norm and star operation.

label: CStarRing.norm_star_mul_self'
slogan: In a C*-ring, the norm of the product of an element's adjoint with itself equals the product of the norms of the adjoint and the element. Since the norm of the adjoint of an element equals the norm of the element itself, this simplifies to the square of the norm of the element. This result follows from the C*-identity and the properties of the star and norm operations.

label: Cardinal
slogan: Cardinal assigns a size to every set, where two sets have the same size if there's a one-to-one correspondence between them. This "same size" relation is defined using an equivalence relation called isEquivalent, based on the existence of a bijection. The type Cardinal lives in a higher universe level than the sets it measures.

label: Cardinal.Categorical
slogan: A theory is called kappa-categorical if all models of that theory having size kappa are isomorphic to each other. This means that up to structure-preserving bijection, there is essentially only one model of the given size. The notion depends on a first-order language, a theory in that language, and a cardinal number kappa.

label: Cardinal.IsInaccessible
slogan: A cardinal number is called inaccessible if it is greater than the set of natural numbers, cannot be reached by taking the power set of any smaller cardinal, and cannot be reached by taking the cofinality of any smaller cardinal. This means it is a very large cardinal that is both regular (its cofinality equals itself) and a strong limit (the power set of any smaller cardinal is still smaller). Such cardinals are so large that they cannot be built from smaller cardinals using standard set operations like power sets or unions.

label: Cardinal.IsRegular
slogan: A cardinal is regular if it cannot be reached or covered by combining fewer smaller sets than its own size, meaning no union of a smaller number of smaller sets can exhaust it. This happens when the cardinal is not equal to its cofinality, the smallest size of a set that can map cofinally into it. Regular cardinals are important for understanding how infinite sets can or cannot be broken down into smaller pieces.

label: Cardinal.add_def
slogan: The sum of the sizes of two types is equal to the size of their disjoint union, where each element is marked as coming from the first or the second type. This means adding two cardinal numbers gives the total number of elements when the sets are combined without overlap. The definition uses the sum type (⊕) to ensure no elements are identified across the two types.

label: Cardinal.add_eq_max
slogan: If one of two infinite cardinal numbers is at least as big as the smallest infinite cardinal (aleph0), then their sum is equal to the larger of the two cardinals. In other words, adding infinite cardinals acts the same as taking their maximum value.

label: Cardinal.add_eq_self
slogan: If a cardinal number is infinite, then adding it to itself results in the same cardinal number. This means combining two disjoint sets of the same infinite size gives a set of the original size.

label: Cardinal.add_one_eq
slogan: If an infinite set is at least as big as the set of natural numbers, then adding one more element to it does not change its size. This means that for such infinite sets, the total number of elements stays the same even after adding a single element. The addition is defined using disjoint unions, and the result holds because infinite sets of this size can always absorb an extra element without changing their cardinality.

label: Cardinal.aleph
slogan: aleph n is the n-th infinite cardinal number, representing the size of the set of all ordinals less than the n-th uncountable initial ordinal, and it is defined so that each ordinal n maps strictly into a larger infinite cardinal. The function is an order embedding, meaning that if one ordinal is smaller than another, its corresponding aleph cardinal is also smaller. This sequence starts with aleph 0, the size of the natural numbers, and continues through larger infinities in increasing order.

label: Cardinal.aleph0_le_mk_iff
slogan: A set is infinite if and only if there is an injective function from the natural numbers into it, meaning its size is at least aleph0. This is equivalent to saying the cardinality of the set is greater than or equal to the cardinality of the natural numbers. The comparison uses the standard ordering of cardinals.

label: Cardinal.aleph0_lt_continuum
slogan: The size of the set of natural numbers is smaller than the size of the set of real numbers. This means there are more real numbers than natural numbers, even though both sets are infinite. It follows from the fact that the set of real numbers has the same size as the power set of the natural numbers, which is strictly larger than the set of natural numbers itself.

label: Cardinal.aleph_one_le_continuum
slogan: The size of the set of real numbers is at least as big as the smallest uncountable infinity, known as aleph1. This means there is no set whose size is strictly between that of the natural numbers and the real numbers in terms of infinity levels. It asserts that aleph1, the next infinity after countable infinity, does not exceed the size of the continuum.

label: Cardinal.aleph_zero
slogan: aleph_zero is the smallest infinite cardinal number, equal to the size of the set of natural numbers, and is defined as the cardinality of the first infinite ordinal omega0. It is the first in the sequence of aleph numbers, each representing a distinct infinite size.

label: Cardinal.beth
slogan: beth is a function that starts with the size of the natural numbers and builds larger infinite sizes by repeatedly taking power sets at each step, using ordinals to index the process; for limit steps, it takes the supremum of all previous sizes. It is defined recursively using a helper function preBeth that ensures the correct size at each ordinal stage. The result is a hierarchy of ever-larger cardinalities indexed by ordinals.

label: Cardinal.beth_one
slogan: beth one is the size of the set of all subsets of the natural numbers, which is the same as the number of real numbers, and it is strictly bigger than the number of natural numbers. It is calculated by taking the power set of the smallest infinite cardinal. This value equals the cardinality of the continuum.

label: Cardinal.cantor
slogan: For any set, the number of subsets it has is always greater than the number of elements in the set, meaning there can be no one-to-one mapping from the elements of the set onto all of its subsets. This implies that the power set is strictly larger in size than the original set.

label: Cardinal.continuum_power_aleph0
slogan: The number of all possible subsets of natural numbers (which is 2 raised to the power of aleph0) is the same as the number of real numbers, called the continuum. This means the set of all subsets of natural numbers has the same size as the set of real numbers. The result comes from rules about how infinite sizes behave when raised to powers.

label: Cardinal.eq
slogan: Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them, and this equality of size is treated as an equivalence relation. The cardinality of a set is an abstract measure of its size, and two sets get the same cardinality value exactly when such a bijection exists. This is formalized by saying that the cardinality of type α equals that of type β if and only if there is at least one equivalence (one-to-one correspondence) between α and β.

label: Cardinal.exists_uncountable_fiber
slogan: If a function sends an uncountable set into a countable one, then at least one element in the output must come from an uncountable number of inputs. This means some preimage under the function is uncountable. It's an infinite version of the pigeonhole principle.

label: Cardinal.instLE
slogan: Cardinal.instLE sets up the ≤ symbol to compare the sizes of sets by defining when one cardinal number is less than or equal to another. It uses the idea that one set's size is less than or equal to another's if there is an injective map from the first into the second. This allows standard inequality notation to work for cardinal numbers in set theory.

label: Cardinal.instNoMaxOrder
slogan: For any cardinal number, there is always a larger one, meaning no cardinal is the biggest. This is supported by the structure of cardinals having an ordering where one can always find a strictly greater element. The system ensures this unbounded growth is consistent with how cardinals are compared and operated on.

label: Cardinal.isEquivalent
slogan: Cardinal.isEquivalent defines when two types have the same size by checking if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their elements. This relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, meaning every type matches itself, the order doesn't matter, and if one type matches a second and the second matches a third, then the first matches the third. It uses the Setoid structure to formalize this notion of equivalence for types.

label: Cardinal.isRegular_aleph_add_one
slogan: The cardinal number that comes right after the n-th infinite cardinal is always regular, meaning it cannot be reached by adding up fewer than itself smaller cardinals.

label: Cardinal.isRegular_aleph_one
slogan: The cardinal number that comes right after the size of the natural numbers (aleph0) is called aleph1, and it has the property that you can't reach it by combining fewer than aleph1 sets each of size less than aleph1. This means aleph1 is regular, so any collection of smaller sets that tries to cover it must be at least as big as aleph1 itself.

label: Cardinal.isRegular_cof
slogan: The cofinality of any ordinal that is not minimal and has no immediate predecessor is a regular cardinal, meaning its cofinality equals itself. This means repeatedly taking cofinalities leads to cardinals that cannot be broken down into smaller pieces in this way. In simple terms, the process of finding how "reachable" the top of such an ordinal is will always result in a cardinal that is its own cofinality.

label: Cardinal.isSuccLimit_omega
slogan: The smallest infinite cardinal, aleph0, corresponds to an ordinal that is not a successor of any other ordinal and has no immediate predecessor. This ordinal, known as omega, comes after all finite ordinals and represents the first infinite stage in the sequence of ordinals. It is a limit ordinal, meaning it is reached by taking a limit rather than by adding one to a previous ordinal.

label: Cardinal.isSuccLimit_ord
slogan: The smallest infinite cardinal, aleph0, corresponds to an ordinal that is not a successor of any other ordinal and is not the smallest ordinal, meaning it has no immediate predecessor. This ordinal is a limit point in the order of ordinals, coming after all finite ordinals without being one more than any specific finite or infinite ordinal. Any cardinal at least as large as aleph0 also has this limit property in its ordinal form.

label: Cardinal.le_def
slogan: A cardinal number A is less than or equal to a cardinal number B if there is an injective function from a set of size A into a set of size B. This means A ≤ B whenever the elements of a set with cardinality A can be mapped one-to-one into a set with cardinality B. The definition uses the existence of such a one-to-one mapping to formalize the idea that one set is no larger than another.

label: Cardinal.linearOrder
slogan: Cardinal numbers can always be compared: for any two cardinals, one is less than, equal to, or greater than the other. This ordering is based on whether there exists an injection between the corresponding sets, and it extends the partial order of cardinals to a total (linear) order using classical logic. The structure ensures that the usual properties of comparison, like transitivity and antisymmetry, hold.

label: Cardinal.lt_aleph0
slogan: A set has fewer elements than the natural numbers if and only if it is finite. This means every infinite set has at least as many elements as the natural numbers. The statement links the idea of finiteness directly to cardinal number comparisons.

label: Cardinal.mk
slogan: Cardinal.mk takes a set and returns its cardinal number, which represents the size of the set based on whether it can be put into one-to-one correspondence with other sets. Two sets have the same cardinal if there is a bijection between them, meaning they are equinumerous. This allows sets to be classified by size without considering what their elements are.

label: Cardinal.mkRat
slogan: The set of rational numbers is countably infinite, meaning it has the same size as the set of natural numbers. This is because there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the rationals and the naturals, which can be shown by effectively encoding each rational number as a unique natural number. As a result, the cardinality of the rational numbers is aleph0, the smallest infinite cardinal.

label: Cardinal.mk_complex
slogan: The size of the set of complex numbers is the same as the size of the set of real numbers. This is because each complex number can be written as a pair of real numbers, and the number of such pairs is the same as the number of real numbers. So, the complex numbers have the same cardinality as the real numbers.

label: Cardinal.mk_congr
slogan: If two sets can be put in one-to-one correspondence (there is a bijection between them), then they have the same cardinality. The function mk_congr ensures that whenever there is a bijection between two types, their assigned cardinal numbers are equal. This reflects the idea that cardinality depends only on the size of a set, not on its specific elements.

label: Cardinal.mk_eq_aleph0
slogan: A set is countably infinite if and only if its size is equal to aleph0, the cardinality of the natural numbers. This means that any infinite set that can be put in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers has the same size as the natural numbers. The result follows from the fact that aleph0 is the smallest infinite cardinal and serves as both a lower bound for infinite sets and an upper bound for countable sets.

label: Cardinal.mk_int
slogan: The cardinality of the integers is the same as the cardinality of the natural numbers, both being equal to aleph0, which means the integers are countably infinite. This means there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the integers and the natural numbers.

label: Cardinal.mk_le_of_surjective
slogan: If there is a surjective function from set α to set β, then the size of β is less than or equal to the size of α. This means that every element in β is mapped to by at least one element in α, so α must have at least as many elements as β. The statement compares the cardinalities of the two sets using this surjection.

label: Cardinal.mk_powerset
slogan: The size of the set of all subsets of a set is equal to 2 raised to the power of the size of the original set. This holds for both finite and infinite sets when using cardinal arithmetic. For any set, the number of its subsets is exactly 2^n, where n is the number of elements in the set.

label: Cardinal.mk_real
slogan: The number of real numbers is the same as the number of subsets of natural numbers, which is 2 to the power of countable infinity (aleph0). This shows that the set of real numbers is uncountably infinite and strictly larger than the set of natural numbers.

label: Cardinal.mk_set
slogan: The size of the set of all subsets of a type α is equal to 2 raised to the power of the number of elements in α. This means the number of possible subsets of a set is determined by exponentiating 2 by the size of the set. It equates the cardinality of the power set with an exponential expression involving the cardinality of the original set.

label: Cardinal.mk_set_nat
slogan: The cardinality of the set of all subsets of natural numbers is equal to 2 raised to the power of aleph0, where aleph0 is the size of the set of natural numbers. This value, known as the continuum, represents the cardinality of the real numbers. The theorem states that the cardinality of the power set of the natural numbers is exactly the continuum.

label: Cardinal.mk_subset_mk_lt_cof
slogan: If a cardinal number is large enough that its cofinality is greater than aleph0, then the number of subsets with size smaller than the cofinality is exactly the same as the size of the whole set. This means most small subsets do not add up to the full cardinal when the cofinality is large. It shows how the size of a cardinal is controlled by its cofinality.

label: Cardinal.mul_eq_max
slogan: If two infinite sets are each at least as large as the set of natural numbers, then the size of their Cartesian product is equal to the size of the larger set. In other words, multiplying two infinite cardinal numbers gives the bigger one. This applies to all infinite sizes starting from countable infinity.

label: Cardinal.mul_eq_self
slogan: If k is an infinite cardinal number, then k times k equals k. This means multiplying an infinite cardinal by itself doesn't change its size.

label: Cardinal.not_countable_real
slogan: There is no way to list all real numbers in a sequence, even an infinite one. This is because the set of real numbers is too large to be countable. Any attempt to pair each real number with a natural number will always miss some real numbers.

label: Cardinal.one_power
slogan: One raised to any cardinality equals one, meaning that for any set, there is exactly one function from that set into a set with only one element.

label: Cardinal.ord_aleph
slogan: The function aleph assigns to each ordinal a corresponding infinite cardinal number such that the resulting cardinals are ordered the same way as the ordinals. The order type of the cardinal aleph(o) is equal to the ordinal omega raised to the power of o. This means the aleph function enumerates all infinite cardinals in order, with each one being strictly larger than all previous ones.

label: Cardinal.power_def
slogan: The number of functions from a set B to a set A has a cardinality equal to the cardinality of A raised to the power of the cardinality of B. This means |A|^|B| counts the functions from B to A. The definition works for both finite and infinite sets.

label: Cardinal.power_eq_two_power
slogan: For any infinite cardinal number c that is at least as big as the smallest infinity, and for any cardinal number b between 2 and c, raising b to the power of c gives the same result as raising 2 to the power of c. This means the number of functions from a set of size c to itself is the same as the number of its subsets. The equality follows from order properties of cardinals and the fact that exponentiation preserves inequalities.

label: Cardinal.power_mul
slogan: For any three infinite cardinal numbers a, b, and c, raising a to the power of b times c is the same as first raising a to the power of b, then raising that result to the power of c. This means exponentiation of cardinals follows the rule a^(b*c) = (a^b)^c, which is consistent with how powers and multiplication work in cardinal arithmetic.

label: Cardinal.range_aleph
slogan: The range of the aleph function is the set of all infinite cardinals, meaning every infinite cardinal number can be expressed as aleph of some ordinal. This set starts from aleph0 and includes all cardinals greater than or equal to it.

label: CartanMatrix.E₆
slogan: CartanMatrix.E₆ is a 6x6 matrix of integers that encodes the structure of the E₆ root system in Lie algebra, with rows and columns indexed by the numbers 0 through 5. It is defined using integer entries that reflect the geometric relationships between simple roots. This matrix is used in the classification of semisimple Lie algebras.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian
slogan: A category is abelian if it has a zero object, binary products, kernels, and cokernels, all morphisms can be added in a way that respects composition, and every monomorphism is the kernel of some morphism while every epimorphism is the cokernel of some morphism. This structure ensures that exact sequences and standard constructions from homological algebra make sense. It combines algebraic operations on morphisms with strong conditions on the existence and behavior of limits and colimits.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.Ext
slogan: The Ext-group in an abelian category C is defined as a type that represents certain morphisms between objects X and Y after shifting in the derived category, provided the category has well-behaved hom-sets under shifting. It depends on the category being abelian and satisfying a size condition (HasExt) that ensures these morphism sets are small enough to work with formally. The group is indexed by natural numbers n, which correspond to the degree of extension.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.extFunctor
slogan: For a fixed natural number n, this functor takes a pair of objects X and Y from an abelian category C and assigns to them the abelian group Ext^n(X, Y), in a way that is contravariant in X and covariant in Y. It organizes the Ext groups into a functor from the opposite category of C and C into the category of abelian groups. The category C must support enough structure for Ext groups to be defined and well-behaved.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.freyd_mitchell
slogan: For any abelian category C, there exists a ring R and a functor F from C to the category of R-modules such that F is fully faithful and preserves both finite limits and finite colimits. This means C can be embedded into the category of modules over R in a way that respects exact sequences and the abelian structure. The embedding allows arguments in C to be carried out using module-like elements.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.functorCategoryAbelian
slogan: If D is an abelian category and C is any category, then the category of functors from C to D is also abelian. This means that functors between C and D form a category with kernels, cokernels, and exact sequences, all defined pointwise. As a result, standard tools of homological algebra apply to such functor categories.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.isIso_of_epi_of_isIso_of_isIso_of_mono
slogan: In an abelian category, if you have a commutative diagram of two exact sequences of four maps each, and a natural transformation between them, then the middle map of the transformation is an isomorphism if the first map is epic, the second and fourth maps are isomorphisms, and the fifth map is monic.

label: CategoryTheory.Abelian.mono_of_epi_of_mono_of_mono
slogan: In an abelian category, if you have a commutative diagram of three composable morphisms and the first and third vertical maps are monomorphisms, and the composite of the first two maps is an epimorphism, then the second vertical map is also a monomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.ActionCategory
slogan: When a monoid M acts on a set X, you can form a category where the objects are in one-to-one correspondence with elements of X, and each morphism from x to y is an element of M that sends x to y under the action. The category structure comes from viewing the action as a functor from the one-object category of M into sets. Although the objects are not literally the elements of X, they behave as if they are, via a bijection.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction
slogan: Two functors F and G are adjoint when there is a natural one-to-one correspondence between morphisms from F(X) to Y and morphisms from X to G(Y); this means applying F on one side matches applying G on the other, forming a symmetric relationship central to many constructions in category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.CoreHomEquivUnitCounit
slogan: An adjunction between two functors F and G consists of natural transformations called unit and counit that satisfy specific coherence conditions, making them inverses in a structured way. This setup creates a one-to-one correspondence between morphisms in the categories involved, linking the action of F and G through these transformations. The adjunction is defined by this equivalence, which ensures the functors are related via the unit and counit.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.adjunctionOfEquivLeft
slogan: If there is a natural one-to-one correspondence between maps from F(X) to Y and maps from X to G(Y), and this correspondence respects composition in the appropriate way, then F is the left adjoint of G; this function constructs that adjunction from the given equivalence.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.comp
slogan: Composing two pairs of adjoint functors results in a new adjoint pair, where the left adjoint of the composition is the composition of the left adjoints, and the right adjoint is the composition of the right adjoints, with the adjunction relationship preserved through natural transformations.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.homEquiv
slogan: The homEquiv function provides a one-to-one match between arrows from F(X) to Y and arrows from X to G(Y), where F and G are functors in an adjunction. This match is given by a pair of inverse functions that convert each arrow into the other in a way that respects category structure. It expresses the idea that mapping out of F(X) is naturally equivalent to mapping into G(Y).

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.isRightAdjoint
slogan: A functor G is a right adjoint if there is another functor F such that for every pair of objects X and Y, morphisms from F(X) to Y correspond naturally to morphisms from X to G(Y). This correspondence defines an adjunction where F is the left adjoint and G is the right adjoint. The theorem states that given such an adjunction, G satisfies the condition of being a right adjoint.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.left_triangle
slogan: If F is left adjoint to G, then composing the unit of the adjunction with F on the right and the counit on the left gives back the identity transformation on F. This means the unit and counit transformations are compatible in a way that ensures coherence in the adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.mkOfHomEquiv
slogan: If there is a natural one-to-one correspondence between morphisms from F(X) to Y and morphisms from X to G(Y) for two functors F and G, then F is left adjoint to G, and this adjunction can be built using that correspondence.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.ofNatIsoRight
slogan: If two functors G and H are naturally isomorphic and one of them (G) is right adjoint to a functor F, then the other functor (H) is also right adjoint to F. The adjunction between F and H is constructed by using the natural isomorphism to transfer the unit and counit from the original adjunction. This allows replacing a right adjoint with a naturally isomorphic functor while preserving the adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.rightAdjointUniq
slogan: If two functors G and G' are both right adjoints to the same functor F, then G and G' are naturally isomorphic, meaning there is a natural, invertible transformation between them.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.rightAdjoint_preservesLimits
slogan: If two categories are connected by a pair of adjoint functors, then the right adjoint will always map limits in the source category to corresponding limits in the target category, preserving their limiting structure.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.right_adjoint_additive
slogan: If two categories are preadditive and a pair of functors between them form an adjunction where the left functor is additive, then the right adjoint functor automatically preserves the addition of morphisms and is also additive. This means that additivity is inherited by the right adjoint when the left adjoint has it.

label: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.toMonad
slogan: Given a pair of functors F and G where F is left adjoint to G, the composition G after F forms a monad on the domain category of F. The monad's unit comes from the adjunction's unit, and its multiplication is built using the adjunction's counit composed with G. This construction automatically satisfies the monad laws because of the naturality and triangle identities of the adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.Arrow
slogan: A morphism in a category, defined by its source and target objects, with an identity arrow provided when the source and target are identical.

label: CategoryTheory.Aut
slogan: Aut is a function that takes an object X in a category C and returns the type of all automorphisms of X, which are invertible morphisms from X to itself, with composition defined in the usual way where applying g then f gives f ∘ g.

label: CategoryTheory.Aut.instGroup
slogan: The declaration sets up a group structure for invertible morphisms from an object to itself in a category, where the group operation is composition of morphisms, the identity morphism acts as the identity element, and inverses are given by reversing the morphisms. This allows automorphisms to be composed, inverted, and raised to integer powers in a way consistent with group theory.

label: CategoryTheory.Balanced
slogan: A category is balanced if every morphism that is both left-cancellable (mono) and right-cancellable (epi) has a two-sided inverse (is an isomorphism).

label: CategoryTheory.BasedCategory
slogan: A based category over a category S consists of another category X and a functor from X to S. It is a way of relating two categories by mapping objects and morphisms from one to the other in a structure-preserving way. The declaration defines this relationship as a type that bundles the category X and the functor p together.

label: CategoryTheory.BasedFunctor
slogan: A based functor is a functor between two based categories that respects their projections to the base category, meaning the functor fits into a commutative diagram with the projections. It is a structure preserving map over a fixed base category.

label: CategoryTheory.Bicategory.Strict
slogan: A strict bicategory is a type of bicategory where composition of morphisms is strictly associative and has strict identity laws, meaning no isomorphisms are needed to make them hold. It includes objects, morphisms between objects, and 2-cells that act as morphisms between those morphisms. This structure is built on top of standard category theory and requires the underlying bicategory laws to hold exactly, not just up to isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.BimonObj
slogan: A bimonoid object in a braided monoidal category is an object that has both a monoid and a comonoid structure, where the multiplication and unit maps are compatible with the comultiplication and counit maps in a way that respects the braiding. It combines the structures of a monoid object and a comonoid object so that they interact consistently. Such an object generalizes the idea of a bialgebra in algebra.

label: CategoryTheory.CartesianClosed
slogan: A Cartesian closed category is a category with finite products that is also monoidal closed, meaning it supports an internal hom-functor (exponential objects) representing morphisms between objects. It allows currying of morphisms, so a function taking a pair of inputs can be transformed into a function returning a function. This structure generalizes the behavior of function spaces in set theory.

label: CategoryTheory.CartesianMonoidalCategory
slogan: A Cartesian monoidal category is a category that has all finite products, where the tensor product of any two objects is their categorical product and the unit object is terminal. It builds on a semicartesian monoidal category by ensuring the monoidal structure comes directly from the product structure, using limits of diagrams from discrete categories to define products properly. This means for any pair of objects, their product exists and behaves universally, with unique maps factoring through it.

label: CategoryTheory.Cat
slogan: A category is a collection of objects and arrows (morphisms) between them, where each object has an identity arrow and arrows can be composed in an associative way.

label: CategoryTheory.Cat.bicategory
slogan: The category of categories, functors, and natural transformations supports a bicategory structure where functor composition is associative up to coherent natural isomorphism and identity functors serve as units up to natural isomorphism, with left and right whiskering defining how natural transformations interact with functors. This structure includes natural isomorphisms for associativity (the associator) and unitality (the left and right unitors) that satisfy coherence conditions. Functors compose in a way that is not strictly associative but associative up to invertible natural transformati

label: CategoryTheory.Cat.category
slogan: The collection of small categories forms a large category where the objects are categories, the morphisms are functors between categories, composition is the usual composition of functors, and each category has an identity functor. This structure satisfies the standard axioms of a category: composition is associative and identity functors act as units. The term "large" indicates that the collection of all small categories is too big to be a set.

label: CategoryTheory.Cat.objects
slogan: The declaration specifies that the objects of the category Cat are small categories, meaning Cat is a category whose elements are themselves categories. It uses a functor to map Cat to a universe of types, formalizing how categories serve as objects in Cat. This helps build the foundation for working with categories and functors in the system.

label: CategoryTheory.Category
slogan: A category is a collection of objects and arrows between them, where every object has an identity arrow and arrows can be combined in an associative way. It extends a basic structure that includes objects, morphisms, composition, and identities. The category class enforces the rules that composition must be associative and that identity arrows must behave correctly.

label: CategoryTheory.Category.opposite
slogan: The opposite category keeps the same objects but reverses the direction of all morphisms, so a morphism from A to B becomes a morphism from B to A. Composition is also reversed: to compose two morphisms in the opposite category, you compose them in the original category in the reverse order. This allows switching between left and right actions in a consistent way.

label: CategoryTheory.Classifier
slogan: A subobject classifier consists of a monomorphism "truth" from an object Ω₀ to an object Ω such that every monomorphism into any object X can be uniquely represented as a pullback of "truth" via a characteristic map to Ω. This means that subobjects of any object X correspond uniquely to maps from X to Ω. Sometimes Ω₀ is taken to be the terminal object.

label: CategoryTheory.CohomologicalSpectralSequence
slogan: A cohomological spectral sequence is a structure in homological algebra that organizes a sequence of approximations to the cohomology of a complex, where on the r-th page, the differential maps increase the first grading by r and the second grading by 1 - r. It is defined in an abelian category, ensuring the existence of kernels, cokernels, and exact sequences. The differentials follow a specific bidegree pattern determined by the integer r.

label: CategoryTheory.CommSq
slogan: A commutative square consists of four objects W, X, Y, Z and four morphisms f: W->X, g: W->Y, h: X->Z, i: Y->Z in a category, such that the composition h ∘ f equals i ∘ g, meaning the path from W to Z via X is the same as the path via Y.

label: CategoryTheory.ComposableArrows.Exact
slogan: A sequence of connected morphisms in a category is exact if, at each step, the image of the previous morphism equals the kernel of the next, meaning the output of the first is precisely what the second needs to map to zero; this requires the category to have zero morphisms and the sequence to form a complex, with each morphism starting where the last ended.

label: CategoryTheory.ConcreteCategory.injective_of_mono_of_preservesPullback
slogan: If a functor from a concrete category preserves pullbacks and the underlying function of a morphism is injective, then that morphism being left-cancellable (a monomorphism) implies its underlying function is injective in the category of sets. This connects the abstract categorical notion of monomorphisms with the concrete set-theoretic idea of one-to-one functions when pullbacks are preserved.

label: CategoryTheory.ConcreteCategory.mono_iff_injective_of_preservesPullback
slogan: In a concrete category where the forgetful functor preserves pullbacks, a morphism is a monomorphism if and only if the underlying function between the sets is injective. This means that a map is left-cancellable in the category precisely when it sends distinct elements to distinct elements. The condition relies on the forgetful functor preserving certain limits to ensure the equivalence.

label: CategoryTheory.ConcreteCategory.mono_of_injective
slogan: In a concrete category, if a morphism's underlying function maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs (is injective), then the morphism is a monomorphism, meaning it can be left-canceled in compositions. This is because the forgetful functor to the category of types preserves differences between morphisms and reflects monomorphisms. Thus, injectivity of the function implies the morphism has the left-cancellation property.

label: CategoryTheory.Dial
slogan: The Dialectica category has objects that are triples consisting of two objects U and X and a subset α of U × X, while morphisms between such triples are pairs of functions satisfying a logical implication encoded via a subset condition involving composition and products. The structure relies on the base category having finite products to define these objects and morphisms properly.

label: CategoryTheory.Discrete
slogan: A discrete category is formed from a type where the only morphisms are identities, meaning no nontrivial relationships exist between distinct objects. It treats each element of the type as a separate object with no connections to others. This structure imposes no additional data beyond the underlying type itself.

label: CategoryTheory.End
slogan: End gives the type of all morphisms from an object X to itself in a category C, where morphisms can be composed associatively and include an identity; it relies on the category structure to define composition and ensure proper behavior.

label: CategoryTheory.End.monoid
slogan: The endomorphisms of an object in a category form a monoid, meaning they can be combined using composition (treated as multiplication) and include an identity morphism that acts as a neutral element. Composition is associative, and the identity morphism leaves others unchanged when composed with them. This structure supports repeated composition, allowing expressions like f ^ n to denote f composed with itself n times.

label: CategoryTheory.Endofunctor.Algebra
slogan: An algebra for an endofunctor F consists of an object A in a category C along with a morphism from F(A) to A, called the structure morphism. This structure captures the idea of "evaluating" the functor F on A to get back an element of A. It is used to model recursive structures in category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.EnrichedCategory
slogan: A V-category is a category where the hom-sets are replaced by objects in a monoidal category V, and composition is defined using the monoidal structure of V. There may not be an ordinary underlying category, since V does not need to be a concrete category. This structure generalizes ordinary categories by allowing richer types of morphism collections.

label: CategoryTheory.Epi
slogan: A morphism f from X to Y is an epimorphism if, for any two morphisms that go from Y to some other object, composing each with f gives the same result only if the two morphisms were identical to begin with. This means f can be canceled on the right in composition. It generalizes the idea of a surjective function, where every element in the target is hit by the function.

label: CategoryTheory.Equivalence
slogan: A category equivalence consists of two functors between categories that are inverses up to natural isomorphism, meaning composing them gives functors naturally isomorphic to the identity functors. It shows that two categories have the same structure even if their objects and morphisms aren't identical. The equivalence is specified by the functors and the natural isomorphisms confirming their inverse relationship.

label: CategoryTheory.Equivalence.isLeftAdjoint_functor
slogan: If two categories are equivalent, then the functor going from one to the other has a right adjoint, meaning there is a natural correspondence between certain morphisms in the two categories. This functor automatically satisfies the conditions to be a left adjoint as part of the equivalence. The equivalence provides the necessary unit and counit to form an adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.Equivalence.toAdjunction
slogan: Given an equivalence of categories, the forward and inverse functors involved are adjoint to each other, with the unit and counit of the equivalence providing the necessary natural transformations to define the adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.Fiber
slogan: Fiber p S represents the collection of objects in the category 𝒳 that are mapped by the functor p to a specific object S in the category 𝒮. It consists of all elements in 𝒳 such that applying p sends them to S. This forms a subcategory over S within the structure defined by p.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsFibered
slogan: A functor p from a category X to a category S is fibered if it is prefibered and the composition of Cartesian morphisms is Cartesian. This means that for every morphism in S and object in X above its target, there is a universal lift to X that is closed under composition. The condition ensures that Cartesian lifts exist and behave well with respect to composition in X.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsLeftAdjoint
slogan: A functor F is called a left adjoint if there exists another functor G such that for every object X in the source category of F and every object Y in the target category of G, there is a natural one-to-one match between arrows from F(X) to Y and arrows from X to G(Y). This means F and G form a dual pair in a way that links their actions across categories. The existence of such a G defines F as a left adjoint.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsPreFibered.pullbackMap
slogan: Given a prefibered functor p from category X to category S, for any morphism f from R to S and any object a in X that maps to S under p, pullbackMap provides a chosen morphism in X that is Cartesian over f and has a as its target. This morphism comes from a specific object, called the pullbackObj, which serves as its source. The existence of such a morphism is guaranteed by the prefibered structure.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsPreFibered.pullbackObj
slogan: Given a prefibered functor p from a category X to a category S, a morphism f from R to S in S, and an object a in X lying over S, the pullbackObj is an object in X that serves as the domain of a Cartesian morphism over f with codomain a.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsRepresentable
slogan: A functor F from the opposite of a category C to the category of types is representable if there exists an object X in C such that F(Y) is naturally equivalent to the set of morphisms from Y to X for every object Y. This means the behavior of F is completely determined by morphisms into a single object X. Representability captures the idea that F can be represented as Hom(-, X) for some X.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsStronglyCartesian
slogan: A morphism φ from a to b that lies over a morphism f from R to S is called strongly Cartesian if, whenever there is another morphism φ' from a' to b lying over a composite morphism g followed by f, there exists a unique morphism χ from a' to a lying over g such that composing χ with φ gives φ'. This means any map into b that fits a certain base diagram can be factored uniquely through φ via a lift of the base map. The property ensures φ is optimal for lifting maps relative to the functor p.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsStronglyCocartesian
slogan: A morphism φ in a category 𝒳 that maps to a morphism f in another category 𝒮 is called strongly co-Cartesian if, whenever there is a morphism φ' starting from the same object as φ and covering the composition f followed by some other morphism g, then φ' can be factored through a morphism χ that covers g and comes after φ. This means every such lift φ' must equal the composition of φ with some lift χ of g. The property ensures that certain diagrams involving lifts of morphisms can always be completed in a unique way.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.additive_of_preservesBinaryBiproducts
slogan: A functor between preadditive categories that preserves zero morphisms and binary biproducts also preserves the addition of morphisms, meaning it maps sums of morphisms to sums of their images. This happens because the image of a biproduct under the functor is naturally isomorphic to the biproduct of the images, and this isomorphism respects the structure needed for addition. As a result, the functor is additive.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.category
slogan: Functors between two categories can be treated as objects in their own category, where the morphisms are natural transformations, identity transformations act as identities, and vertical composition of natural transformations serves as the composition operation. This structure satisfies the axioms of a category when the target category does. The identity and composition are defined componentwise, and equality of natural transformations is determined by their components at each object.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.comp
slogan: The composition of two functors F and G, written as F.comp G, creates a new functor that first applies F to objects and morphisms in a category and then applies G to the results, maintaining the categorical structure. This composition is associative, and combining any functor with an identity functor leaves it unchanged.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.const
slogan: The constant functor takes a fixed category C and a category J, then creates a functor that maps every object in C to a constant functor from J to C, which sends all objects and morphisms in J to a single object and its identity morphism in C. It effectively treats the source category as irrelevant, producing a trivial functor that does not change with input. This models unchanging or static mappings across categories.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.diag
slogan: The diag function takes a category C and returns a functor that maps each object a to the pair (a, a) in the product category C × C, and each morphism f to the pair (f, f). This functor duplicates objects and morphisms along the diagonal using the standard product structure.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.hom
slogan: A functor's hom maps pairs of objects (A, B) from a category and its opposite to the type of morphisms from A to B, such that each morphism f from B to A in the original category corresponds to a function from F(A) to F(B), preserving identity and composition. This mapping works by reversing the direction of morphisms using the opposite category structure. It is part of how a functor handles morphisms between objects in a way consistent with category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.id
slogan: The identity functor on a category C maps every object and every morphism to itself, maintaining the same structure within the category. It acts as a neutral operation in the context of functors from C to C.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.map_isIso
slogan: A functor preserves isomorphisms: if a morphism has an inverse (is invertible) in one category, then applying the functor to that morphism yields another invertible morphism in the target category. This means the image of an isomorphism under a functor is always an isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.op
slogan: The Functor.op function takes a functor that maps from one category to another and returns a new functor that works in the opposite direction by reversing all the morphisms, turning a functor from C to D into a functor from the opposite of C to the opposite of D. It uses the opposite category construction to flip the direction of mappings while preserving the structure of the original functor. This allows functors to be used in dual contexts by simply reversing the flow of morphisms.

label: CategoryTheory.Functor.rightDerived
slogan: Given an additive functor between abelian categories where the source category has enough injectives, the right derived functor at degree n is a new functor that maps each object to the n-th cohomology of the image of its injective resolution under the original functor. This construction relies on resolving objects by injective complexes and then applying the functor and taking cohomology in the target category. The result is a sequence of functors, one for each degree n, that extend the original functor to include higher derived information.

label: CategoryTheory.Grothendieck
slogan: A Grothendieck category is a category equipped with a functor to the category of small categories, satisfying specific structural conditions that allow it to model advanced algebraic and topological concepts like sheaves and abelian categories. It extends ordinary category theory by adding properties that support richer constructions in homological algebra. The functor F maps objects and morphisms from a base category C to categories and functors, playing a central role in defining the structure.

label: CategoryTheory.GrothendieckTopology
slogan: A Grothendieck topology on a category C assigns to each object X a collection of sieves on X, called covering sieves, such that: the sieve containing all morphisms into X is always covering, any pullback of a covering sieve is covering, and if a sieve R pulls back to a covering sieve along every morphism in another covering sieve S, then R is itself covering.

label: CategoryTheory.Groupoid
slogan: A groupoid is a category in which every morphism (or arrow) between objects has an inverse, so that each transformation can be undone. This means for any arrow from A to B, there is a reverse arrow from B to A such that going back and forth gives the identity. All structure-preserving maps in the category are reversible.

label: CategoryTheory.GrpObj
slogan: A group object in a category with finite products, meaning an object equipped with multiplication, identity, and inversion maps that satisfy the usual group axioms, formulated using the category's product structure. It generalizes the notion of a group to categories where the product plays the role of the monoidal operation. This builds on the idea of a monoid object by adding an inverse operation.

label: CategoryTheory.HasExactColimitsOfShape
slogan: A category C has exact colimits of shape J if colimits of that shape exist in C and these colimits preserve finite limits. This means that forming colimits indexed by J commutes with taking finite limits. The property combines existence of colimits with a compatibility condition between colimits and finite limits.

label: CategoryTheory.HasExactLimitsOfShape
slogan: A category C has exact limits of shape J if all diagrams of shape J in C have limits, and the operation of taking such limits preserves finite colimits. This means that computing limits of shape J commutes with forming finite colimits in C. The property combines the existence of certain limits with a compatibility condition between limits and colimits.

label: CategoryTheory.HopfObj
slogan: A Hopf object in a braided monoidal category is a bimonoid (an object with compatible monoid and comonoid structures) that also has an antipode map, which generalizes the notion of inverses in algebraic structures like Hopf algebras. The antipode provides a way to "invert" elements in a manner consistent with the monoidal and braided structure of the category. This structure is defined for objects in categories that support both monoidal products and braiding.

label: CategoryTheory.Idempotents.Karoubi
slogan: The Karoubi structure creates a new category from an existing one by adding objects for each idempotent morphism, effectively splitting those idempotents into projections onto their images. Each new object corresponds to a pair consisting of an original object and an idempotent endomorphism on it. This allows every idempotent to have a well-defined image as a retract of its source object.

label: CategoryTheory.IsIso
slogan: A morphism f from object X to object Y is an isomorphism if there exists a morphism in the reverse direction such that composing f with it in both orders results in the identity morphisms on X and Y. This means f has both a left inverse and a right inverse, which are the same. Being an isomorphism is a property that ensures the morphism can be reversed in a way that preserves structure.

label: CategoryTheory.IsIso.inv_eq_of_hom_inv_id
slogan: If a morphism has an inverse, and composing it with some morphism on the right gives the identity, then that morphism must be the inverse; in particular, the inverse of an isomorphism is uniquely determined by this condition.

label: CategoryTheory.IsIsomorphic
slogan: Two objects in a category are isomorphic if there is a morphism between them with an inverse, such that composing the morphisms in either direction gives the identity on the respective object. This declaration defines a property that is true when such an invertible morphism exists. It expresses when two objects have the same structure in the context of a category.

label: CategoryTheory.IsSplitEpi
slogan: A split epimorphism is a map between two objects such that there is another map going back which, when composed with the original, gives the identity map on the target object.

label: CategoryTheory.IsSplitEpi.epi
slogan: A split epimorphism is a morphism that has a right inverse, and this declaration ensures that any such morphism is automatically an epimorphism. This means if a morphism can be "undone" from the right by another morphism, then it satisfies the right-cancellation property. It provides a way to infer the epi property whenever a split epi structure is present.

label: CategoryTheory.IsSplitMono
slogan: A split monomorphism is a morphism f from X to Y for which there exists another morphism g from Y to X such that composing g with f gives the identity morphism on X. The property IsSplitMono holds for f if such a left inverse g exists. This guarantees that f behaves like an injective map in the context of category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.IsSplitMono.mono
slogan: If a morphism has a left inverse, then it is left-cancellable: whenever two morphisms composed with it on the left are equal, the two must be the same. This means every split monomorphism is a monomorphism. The existence of a left inverse guarantees the cancellative property.

label: CategoryTheory.Iso
slogan: An Iso is a pair of objects in a category connected by two morphisms going in opposite directions, such that each morphism undoes the other, making them inverses. This means composing one after the other gives the identity morphism on either object. It expresses the idea that two objects are structurally the same within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.Iso.trans
slogan: If A is isomorphic to B and B is isomorphic to C, then A is isomorphic to C. The composition of these isomorphisms gives a direct isomorphism from A to C. This allows isomorphisms to be chained together in a category.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.Cone
slogan: A cone over a functor F is made up of an object and a set of morphisms from that object to every value F takes, arranged so that all the necessary diagrams commute, meaning the mappings are consistent with the structure of the category. It represents a way to map uniformly into the diagram described by F.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.HasFiniteBiproducts
slogan: A category has finite biproducts if it has a zero object, zero morphisms between any two objects, and for every finite list of objects (indexed by natural numbers less than some n), there is an object that serves as both their product and coproduct in a compatible way. This means you can combine any finite number of objects into one that supports both projections and inclusions satisfying the necessary universal properties. The structure is defined for all finite indexing sets, using the type Fin n to represent indices from 0 to n-1.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.HasLimits
slogan: A category C has limits if, for any small diagram in C, there is a limiting object that maps to each part of the diagram in a way that satisfies the universal property. This ensures that all standard limit constructions, such as products and pullbacks, exist within the category. The declaration states this condition as a proposition depending on the universe levels of the category.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.HasProducts
slogan: A category has products if, for any collection of objects indexed by a discrete category (where there are no nontrivial maps between objects), there exists a limiting object that serves as their product. This means the category supports a generalized form of pairing or combining objects in a way that respects their projections. The existence of such a limit ensures that all products of that shape can be constructed within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.HasZeroMorphisms
slogan: A category has zero morphisms if there is a zero arrow between any two objects, and composing any morphism with a zero morphism gives another zero morphism. This means every set of morphisms has a special zero element that behaves like a multiplicative zero under composition. The structure relies on having a notion of zero for the hom-sets, provided by the Zero type class.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.IsImage.isoExt
slogan: If a morphism has two image factorizations that both satisfy the universal property of images, then there is a unique isomorphism between their image objects that makes all the relevant diagrams commute. This isomorphism respects the factorization maps and the monomorphism structure. It shows that the image of a morphism is unique up to a canonical isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.IsInitial
slogan: An object X in a category C is initial if for every object Y in C, there is exactly one arrow from X to Y. This is equivalent to saying that the cocone with X as its tip over the empty diagram is a colimit. The definition uses the unique empty functor from the empty category to C and relies on the discrete structure to ensure the uniqueness of the cocone.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.IsLimit
slogan: A structure that checks whether a given cone over a functor F is a limit, meaning it provides a unique way to map any other cone into F’s diagram through its apex object, ensuring universality and uniqueness of these maps. It formalizes the idea that the cone is the most efficient or smallest one compatible with the diagram defined by F.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.IsZero
slogan: An object X in a category C is a zero object if for every object Y, there is exactly one morphism from X to Y and exactly one morphism from Y to X. This means X is both initial and terminal, and all hom-sets involving X are singletons. The condition is expressed using the Unique type, which ensures there is only one possible morphism in each case.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.PreservesLimits
slogan: A functor F preserves limits if, whenever a diagram has a limit in the source category, applying F to that limit gives a limit of the corresponding diagram in the target category. In other words, F turns limit cones into limit cones. This does not mean F creates limits, only that it respects existing ones.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.Types.isInitialPEmpty
slogan: In the category of types, the empty type (which has no elements) is initial, meaning there is exactly one function from it to any other type. This is because there are no values in the empty type to map, so any such function exists vacuously and uniquely. The declaration confirms that the empty type satisfies this universal property of being initial.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.colimConstAdj
slogan: The colimit functor is left adjoint to the constant functor, meaning that a map from the colimit of a diagram to an object corresponds naturally to a cocone over the diagram with that object as apex. This adjunction exists when the target category has colimits of the given shape.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.constLimAdj
slogan: The constLimAdj function establishes a natural correspondence between maps from a fixed object to the limit of a diagram and cones over that diagram with the fixed object as the apex; this means the constant functor, which sends everything to a fixed object, is left adjoint to the limit functor, which takes diagrams to their limits.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.coprod
slogan: The coprod function returns an object in a category that is the binary coproduct of two given objects, meaning it comes with maps from each of them and satisfies the universal property that any pair of maps to a third object factors uniquely through it. It is defined as the colimit of a diagram consisting of the two objects with no nontrivial maps between them. This coproduct exists when the category has binary coproducts for the given objects.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.kernel
slogan: In a category where every pair of objects has a zero morphism, the kernel of a morphism f from X to Y is an object that maps to X such that composing with f gives the zero morphism, and it is universal with this property. It is the same as the equalizer of f and the zero morphism from X to Y. A kernel exists if such a universal object exists for the given morphism.

label: CategoryTheory.Limits.lim
slogan: lim is a function that takes a diagram (a functor from a small category to another category) and returns its limit object, if limits of that shape exist, along with projection maps to each object in the diagram. It ensures that any compatible family of maps into the diagram factors uniquely through the limit. When diagrams are related by a natural transformation, lim induces a corresponding map between their limit objects in a way that respects the projections.

label: CategoryTheory.LocallySmall
slogan: A category is called locally small if, for any two objects, the set of morphisms between them is actually a set in the usual sense—meaning it's not too large to handle. This avoids problems with size in foundations by requiring that hom-sets fit within a standard universe of sets. The condition is defined using a class called Small that ensures types are not larger than allowed.

label: CategoryTheory.Mat_
slogan: Mat_ C is a type where each object is a finite list of objects from a category C, relying on the idea that the indices for the list come from a finite type.

label: CategoryTheory.Monad.adj
slogan: For any monad T on a category C, the free functor that builds T-algebras is left adjoint to the forgetful functor that strips away the algebra structure and returns the underlying object. This adjunction means there is a natural one-to-one correspondence between morphisms from an object X to the underlying object of a T-algebra and algebra homomorphisms from the free T-algebra on X to that T-algebra. The unit and counit of this adjunction are given by the monad's unit and multiplication operations.

label: CategoryTheory.Mono
slogan: A mono is a type of morphism in a category such that if two morphisms composed with it on the left yield the same result, then those two morphisms must be identical. It represents the idea of a left-cancellable map in abstract category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.MonoidalCategory
slogan: A monoidal category is a category with a tensor product that lets you combine objects and morphisms, plus a unit object, where the ways of reassociating and adding the unit are handled by natural isomorphisms. These isomorphisms ensure that combining objects in different orders still behaves consistently. The structure satisfies coherence conditions so all relevant diagrams commute.

label: CategoryTheory.MonoidalCategory.tensor
slogan: The tensor operation in a monoidal category takes two objects or two morphisms and combines them into a single object or morphism, similar to how pairs are formed in the Cartesian product of types. When applied to identity morphisms, it produces the identity on the combined objects. This operation is part of a structured way to handle combining objects and processes in a category, with consistent rules for associativity and unit behavior.

label: CategoryTheory.MonoidalClosed
slogan: A closed monoidal category is a category with a tensor product operation and a unit object, such that for every object Y, the process of forming the tensor product with Y has a corresponding "function object" construction called the internal hom. This means that a morphism from X tensor Y to Z corresponds naturally to a morphism from X to the internal hom from Y to Z. The structure supports both the algebraic properties of tensor products and the ability to represent mappings as objects within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.MonoidalClosed.internalHom
slogan: In a monoidal closed category, for every pair of objects A and B, there is an object called the internal hom (ihom) that represents the morphisms from A to B as an object inside the category. There is a natural correspondence between morphisms from the tensor product A ⊗ B to C and morphisms from A to the internal hom of B to C. This allows the category to "internalize" its own hom-sets, turning external mappings into objects and morphisms within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.NatTrans
slogan: A natural transformation is a collection of morphisms between the outputs of two functors that commute with the action of the functors on morphisms in the categories. It ensures that transforming one functor to another respects the structure of the categories involved. In this case, it applies to functors between categories C and D, not to the real number F or the complex function G mentioned elsewhere.

label: CategoryTheory.ObjectProperty.FullSubcategory
slogan: A full subcategory is made up of objects from a given category that satisfy a specific property, including all the morphisms between those objects that exist in the original category. It is formed by selecting objects based on a condition while keeping all the original maps between them. The property used to select objects depends on the categorical structure, such as how morphisms compose.

label: CategoryTheory.ObjectProperty.IsSerreClass
slogan: A Serre class in an abelian category is a property of objects that includes the zero object and is preserved under taking subobjects, quotient objects, and extensions. Specifically, if an object has the property, then so do its subobjects and quotients, and if two objects in a short exact sequence have the property, then so does the middle object. This ensures the property is stable under common algebraic constructions within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.Over
slogan: CategoryTheory.Over creates a category where every object is a morphism pointing to a fixed object X, and morphisms are commutative triangles over X. It uses the costructured arrow construction with the identity functor, meaning it organizes maps into X and how they relate through commuting diagrams. This helps analyze how objects map into X in a structured way.

label: CategoryTheory.Paths
slogan: CategoryTheory.Paths is a type that represents all possible paths in a directed graph (quiver) where vertices are elements of a type V. Each path is a sequence of connected edges following the direction of the graph. This type forms a category where objects are vertices and morphisms are paths between them.

label: CategoryTheory.Preadditive
slogan: A preadditive category is a category where, for any two objects, the collection of morphisms between them forms an abelian group, meaning morphisms can be added in a way that is commutative and associative, with a zero morphism and additive inverses, and where composition of morphisms respects addition on both sides.

label: CategoryTheory.Presheaf.IsSeparated
slogan: A presheaf is separated for a Grothendieck topology if, whenever two sections over an object agree when restricted to all objects in a covering sieve, then the two sections are equal. This means that values of the presheaf are uniquely determined by their restrictions along covering families. It is a weaker condition than being a sheaf, requiring only uniqueness, not existence, of glued sections.

label: CategoryTheory.Presheaf.isSheaf_iff_isLimit
slogan: A presheaf P is a sheaf for a Grothendieck topology J if and only if, for every object X and every covering sieve S of X in J, the natural cone formed by applying P to the diagram of S has the universal property of a limit cone. This means that P turns covering sieves into limit cones in the target category. The condition ensures that sections of P over X are uniquely determined by their restrictions to the covering sieve S.

label: CategoryTheory.Projective.Type.enoughProjectives
slogan: In the category of types and functions, every type has a surjective map coming from a projective type, meaning projective types are abundant enough to cover all types. This confirms that the category of types has enough projectives. The declaration asserts this property as a formal instance for the category of types.

label: CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution
slogan: A projective resolution of an object Z in a category is a chain complex that starts with Z and replaces it with a sequence of projective objects, connected by maps such that the homology of the complex matches that of Z. The category must have a zero object and zero morphisms, and the resolution is linked to Z by a quasi-isomorphism, meaning it preserves homology. This setup allows working with Z in a simpler, projective approximation, useful for computing derived functors in homological algebra.

label: CategoryTheory.Pseudofunctor
slogan: A Pseudofunctor is a mapping between two bicategories that sends objects, morphisms, and 2-morphisms from one to the other, preserving identity and composition not strictly, but up to invertible 2-morphisms that satisfy coherence conditions. It is a refinement of a PrelaxFunctor where the structural transformations for composition and identity are required to be isomorphisms. This ensures the mapping respects the weak, isomorphism-based structure inherent in bicategories.

label: CategoryTheory.Quiv
slogan: CategoryTheory.Quiv refers to the category of quivers, where a quiver is a directed graph that allows multiple edges and loops. It is defined in a way that supports category theory constructions involving such graphs. The type lives in a universe level determined by the maximum of u+1 and v+1.

label: CategoryTheory.Quiv.forget
slogan: The forgetful functor from categories to quivers maps each category to its underlying directed graph, where objects become vertices and morphisms become directed edges, forgetting the composition and identity structure. It sends functors between categories to prefunctors between quivers by preserving only the mapping of objects and morphisms. This construction respects the structure of categories and quivers as organized in a categorical framework.

label: CategoryTheory.Quotient
slogan: A quotient category groups morphisms into equivalence classes based on a given relation on hom-sets, effectively treating some morphisms as the same. It constructs a new category from an existing one by enforcing specified identifications between morphisms. The relation determining these identifications must be provided as part of the structure.

label: CategoryTheory.Reflective
slogan: A reflective functor is a fully faithful functor (one that preserves and reflects all morphisms) from a category D to a category C, such that there is a left adjoint functor from C to D. This left adjoint provides, for each object in C, a "best approximation" by an object in the image of D. The adjunction ensures a natural one-to-one correspondence between morphisms in the two categories.

label: CategoryTheory.RelCat
slogan: RelCat is a type that represents types with a category structure where the morphisms between objects are binary relations instead of functions. It is essentially a renamed version of Type u, equipped with this specific categorical interpretation. The category's objects are types, and its arrows are relations between them.

label: CategoryTheory.RelCat.graphFunctor
slogan: The graphFunctor maps types and functions into types and relations by sending each function to its graph, which is a relation consisting of pairs (x, f(x)); it embeds the category of types and functions into the category of types and relations in a way that preserves structure and covers all objects up to equivalence.

label: CategoryTheory.Retract
slogan: A retract in category theory describes a relationship between two objects, X and Y, where a morphism from X to Y and another from Y back to X compose to give the identity map on X. This means X can be recovered exactly after mapping to Y and back. It captures the idea of projecting part of a structure and then restoring it perfectly.

label: CategoryTheory.RightRigidCategory
slogan: A right rigid category is a category with a tensor product where every object has a right dual, meaning for each object A there is another object A* and specific morphisms that let A and A* interact like duals in a way that respects the tensor product and unit object. These morphisms satisfy conditions similar to evaluation and coevaluation, ensuring consistent behavior across the category. The structure builds on a monoidal category and requires that all objects have such duals.

label: CategoryTheory.Sheaf
slogan: The type CategoryTheory.Sheaf represents the collection of sheaves valued in a category A over a category C equipped with a Grothendieck topology J, where a sheaf is a presheaf satisfying a gluing condition for compatible families over covering sieves. It combines the structure of a functor from the opposite category of C to A with the property that it satisfies the sheaf condition with respect to J. This construction generalizes the classical notion of sheaves from topology to arbitrary categories with a suitable notion of covering.

label: CategoryTheory.Sheaf.H
slogan: The cohomology of an abelian sheaf F on a site defined by a Grothendieck topology, in degree n, is defined using Ext groups in the category of sheaves, assuming sheafification and Ext groups exist. It assigns to each natural number n a type representing the nth cohomology group of F. This construction relies on the sheaf being valued in abelian groups and the site having sufficient structure to support sheafification and derived functors.

label: CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.ShortExact.homology_exact₂
slogan: If a short complex is exact in an abelian category, then the induced sequence of homology objects at each degree is also exact, meaning the image of one map equals the kernel of the next. This result uses the fact that homology preserves exactness when applied to exact short complexes. It relies on the structure of chain maps and the functorial behavior of homology.

label: CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.ShortExact.δ
slogan: The δ function takes a short exact sequence of chain complexes in an abelian category and produces a connecting homomorphism between the homology of one object at degree i and the homology of another at degree j, whenever the indexing shape relates i and j. This map links the homology of the third complex at i to the homology of the first complex at j, forming part of the long exact sequence in homology. It is constructed using the universal properties of kernels and cokernels, ensuring the sequence remains exact.

label: CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.SnakeInput.snake_lemma
slogan: In an abelian category, given two short complexes linked by a morphism where the top row is exact in the middle, the left vertical map is surjective, and the right vertical map is injective, there exists a long exact sequence connecting the kernels and cokernels of the vertical maps, with a connecting morphism built using pullbacks and pushouts.

label: CategoryTheory.SimplicialObject
slogan: A simplicial object assigns an object in a category C for each natural number n, along with morphisms in C corresponding to order-preserving maps between finite sets {0,...,m-1} and {0,...,n-1}, in a way that respects composition and identities. It is defined as a contravariant functor from the simplex category to C, where the simplex category has finite ordered sets as objects and order-preserving functions as morphisms. The opposite category is used to reverse morphism directions, making the functor contravariant.

label: CategoryTheory.SingleObj
slogan: A category with only one object is determined entirely by a type of morphisms from that object to itself, together with an identity morphism and a composition operation that satisfy associativity and identity laws. The structure is built on a single vertex represented by the Unit type, and all morphisms are loops on this vertex. This construction lifts a type of self-maps into a category with one object.

label: CategoryTheory.SingleObj.category
slogan: A category with just one object is completely determined by a type of morphisms that forms a monoid, meaning the morphisms can be composed like elements of a monoid with an associative operation and an identity element. Composition of morphisms corresponds to the monoid's multiplication, and the identity morphism acts as the monoid's unit. This establishes a direct correspondence between single-object categories and monoids.

label: CategoryTheory.SingleObj.mapHom
slogan: The mapHom function links monoid homomorphisms between two monoids M and N to functors between the corresponding single-object categories built from M and N, by turning each monoid map into a functor that acts on morphisms. It establishes a one-to-one correspondence where structure-preserving maps between monoids match structure-preserving maps between their associated one-object categories. This means converting a monoid homomorphism to a functor preserves composition and identity in a way that respects the category structure.

label: CategoryTheory.SmallCategory
