slogan: A small category is a category in which both the objects and the morphisms between any two objects form sets, ensuring the category is not too large to run into set-theoretic problems. The type CategoryTheory.SmallCategory C represents this property for a type C, living in a universe one level higher than C.

label: CategoryTheory.SpectralSequence
slogan: A spectral sequence is a sequence of chain complexes in an abelian category, indexed by integers, where the homology of each complex is isomorphic to the next complex in the sequence, starting from a specified page and following a given shape pattern.

label: CategoryTheory.SpectralSequence.Hom
slogan: A morphism of spectral sequences is a collection of maps between corresponding pages of two spectral sequences that respect the homology isomorphisms linking each page to the next. These maps must commute with the differentials and the structural isomorphisms of the spectral sequences. It is defined within an abelian category, where the sequences follow a given shape indexed by integers.

label: CategoryTheory.SplitEpi
slogan: A split epimorphism is a map f from object X to object Y such that there exists another map from Y back to X, where composing f with this map gives the identity map on Y. This means f has a right inverse in the category. The structure records both the map f and the existence of this right inverse.

label: CategoryTheory.SplitEpi.epi
slogan: If a morphism has a right inverse (meaning composing it with another morphism gives the identity), then it is an epimorphism, which means it can be canceled on the right in compositions.

label: CategoryTheory.SplitMono
slogan: A split monomorphism is a morphism f from X to Y such that there exists another morphism g from Y to X where g composed with f gives the identity morphism on X. This means f has a left inverse, ensuring it behaves like an injective map in category theory. The structure records the existence of this left inverse.

label: CategoryTheory.SplitMono.mono
slogan: A split monomorphism has a left inverse, and this result confirms that any such morphism is also a monomorphism, meaning it can be left-cancelled in compositions. In other words, if a morphism has a left inverse, then it satisfies the property that whenever two morphisms composed with it on the left are equal, the original two morphisms must have been equal. This establishes a stronger property (being a mono) from the existence of a left inverse.

label: CategoryTheory.SplitMono.splitEpi
slogan: If a morphism has a left inverse (so composing it with another morphism on the left gives the identity), then that same morphism, when viewed in the opposite direction, has a right inverse, meaning it is a split epimorphism. The function converts a proof that a morphism is a split monomorphism into a proof that it is a split epimorphism in the dual category. This reflects the duality between monomorphisms and epimorphisms in category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.Subfunctor.sheafify
slogan: The sheafify function turns a subpresheaf into another subpresheaf that is closer to being a sheaf, by including sections that locally lie in the original subpresheaf. It uses a Grothendieck topology to determine what "locally" means. The result is a sheaf only if the original presheaf was already a sheaf.

label: CategoryTheory.Tor
slogan: Tor C n is a functor that takes two objects from a monoidal abelian category C and produces another object in C, computed by fixing the first object and deriving the tensor product in the second variable using projective resolutions. It generalizes the idea of taking homology of the tensor product after resolving one factor. This construction is defined for each natural number n, giving the n-th left derived functor of the tensor product.

label: CategoryTheory.Tor'
slogan: Tor' is a functor that computes the derived functors of the tensor product in a monoidal abelian category by resolving the first input with projective objects and then applying the tensor product. It is defined for each natural number n and takes two objects to the nth homology of the resulting complex. This construction assumes the category has enough projectives and that the tensor product is additive in both arguments.

label: CategoryTheory.Under
slogan: The Under category consists of all morphisms from a fixed object X to objects obtained by applying a given functor, where the functor involved is the identity. It forms a category whose objects are arrows starting from X and ending at any object in the category, with commutative triangles as morphisms. This setup organizes all maps from X into the image of the identity functor.

label: CategoryTheory.actionAsFunctor
slogan: A monoid M acting on a set X can be seen as a functor that sends the single object of M to X, and each element of M to the function on X that multiplies by that element.

label: CategoryTheory.adjunctionOfStructuredArrowInitials
slogan: If for every object in category C there is an initial object in the category of arrows from that object to images under functor G, then G has a left adjoint. This left adjoint assigns to each object the source of the initial arrow over it, using the unique morphisms from initial objects to build the adjunction. The condition ensures a natural correspondence between morphisms in the two categories, forming the adjoint relationship.

label: CategoryTheory.constantSheaf
slogan: The constant sheaf functor takes an object from a category D and assigns to it the sheafification of the constant presheaf at that object, resulting in a sheaf over a site defined by a Grothendieck topology on a category C. It requires that sheafification exists for the given categories and topology. This construction maps objects in D to sheaves valued in D over the site.

label: CategoryTheory.coyoneda
slogan: The coyoneda construction maps each object in a category to a functor that collects all incoming morphisms to that object, turning them into a set-valued functor in a way that reverses the original morphism directions using the opposite category. It is a dual version of the Yoneda embedding, focusing on how other objects map into a given object rather than how it maps out to others. This mapping forms a well-behaved, structure-preserving functor from the opposite category into the category of functors to types.

label: CategoryTheory.epi_iff_surjective
slogan: In the category of types and functions, a function is right-cancellable (an epimorphism) if and only if it is surjective, meaning every element in the output type is mapped to by at least one element from the input type.

label: CategoryTheory.exp.adjunction
slogan: For any object A in a closed monoidal category, the functor that tensors with A has a right adjoint given by the internal hom functor associated with A. This means there is a natural one-to-one correspondence between morphisms from A ⊗ X to Y and morphisms from X to ihom(A, Y). The adjunction captures the idea that forming tensor products with A is dual to forming internal homs out of A.

label: CategoryTheory.forget
slogan: The forget function takes an object from a concrete category and returns its underlying set, while mapping morphisms to the corresponding functions between these sets. It allows categorical structures to be viewed in terms of plain types and functions by stripping away extra structure. This functor preserves the behavior of identity and composition as seen in ordinary function application.

label: CategoryTheory.id_of_comp_left_id
slogan: If a morphism f composed with any morphism g on the left results in g itself, then f must be the identity morphism on its domain. This means that the only morphism that acts as a left identity for all compositions from a given object is the identity morphism of that object. It expresses a fundamental uniqueness property of identity morphisms in category theory.

label: CategoryTheory.ihom
slogan: In a closed monoidal category, for every object A, there is a functor ihom A that maps each object B to the internal hom object representing morphisms from A to B, such that this functor is right adjoint to tensoring with A. This means that combining objects via tensor product relates naturally to having an object that behaves like a function space. The ihom function provides this right adjoint, turning external morphisms into an internal object within the category.

label: CategoryTheory.ihom.adjunction
slogan: In a closed monoidal category, for any object A, the operation of tensoring with A on the left has a right adjoint given by the internal hom functor; this means that maps from A ⊗ B to C correspond naturally to maps from B to the object of morphisms from A to C.

label: CategoryTheory.isIso_iff_bijective
slogan: In the category of types, a function is invertible if and only if it is bijective, meaning it pairs each element of one type with exactly one element of another type and vice versa. This means a function has an inverse if and only if it is both one-to-one (no two inputs map to the same output) and onto (every output is covered). Being an isomorphism in this category is the same as being a bijective function.

label: CategoryTheory.isIso_of_epi_of_isSplitMono
slogan: If a morphism has a left inverse and is right-cancellable (meaning it can be canceled from the right in equations), then it has a two-sided inverse and is an isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.isIso_of_mono_of_isSplitEpi
slogan: If a morphism in a category can be canceled on the left (mono) and has a right inverse (split epi), then it has a two-sided inverse and is an isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.isIsomorphicSetoid
slogan: In a category, two objects are isomorphic if there is a reversible map between them, and this isomorphism relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, forming an equivalence relation on the objects of the category. This declaration defines that the relation "is isomorphic to" gives a setoid structure on the type of objects, meaning it behaves like equality for the purpose of grouping objects into equivalence classes.

label: CategoryTheory.isRightAdjoint_of_preservesLimits_of_solutionSetCondition
slogan: If a functor G from category D to category C preserves all limits and D has all limits, and if G satisfies the solution set condition, then G has a left adjoint. The solution set condition means that for every object in C, there is a small set of objects in D through which all morphisms into G's image can be factored. This result gives a sufficient condition for a functor to be a right adjoint.

label: CategoryTheory.isomorphismClasses
slogan: The declaration defines a functor that sends each category to its set of isomorphism classes, grouping together objects that are isomorphic to each other. It uses the fact that isomorphism is an equivalence relation to form a quotient set where isomorphic objects are treated as equal. This allows structural comparisons between categories by reducing them to their essential, non-redundant objects up to isomorphism.

label: CategoryTheory.leftAdjointOfStructuredArrowInitials
slogan: If for every object in category C there is an initial object in the category of arrows from that object to images under functor G, then G has a left adjoint. This left adjoint maps each object in C to the source of the initial arrow over it. The construction uses the universal property of initial objects to define the adjunction.

label: CategoryTheory.mono_iff_injective
slogan: In the category of types, a function is a monomorphism if and only if it is injective, meaning that f(x) = f(y) implies x = y. This equivalence links the categorical property of being left-cancellable with the set-theoretic notion of one-to-one mapping.

label: CategoryTheory.prod
slogan: Prod combines two categories C and D into a new category where objects are pairs (X, Y) with X from C and Y from D, and morphisms are pairs of morphisms from C and D, composed componentwise. The result is a category that represents the Cartesian product of the two original categories. This construction uses the standard product type α × β to form pairs of objects and morphisms.

label: CategoryTheory.projectiveDimension
slogan: The projective dimension of an object in an abelian category is defined as a value in the set of natural numbers extended with infinity and a bottom element, where the bottom element represents objects with no finite projective resolution. It measures the shortest length of a projective resolution for the object, or infinity if no such finite resolution exists.

label: CategoryTheory.projective_iff_hasProjectiveDimensionLT_one
slogan: An object X in an abelian category is projective if and only if its projective dimension is less than 1, meaning that all Ext groups Ext^i(X, Y) vanish for i >= 1. This is equivalent to saying that there are no nontrivial extensions of X by any object Y. The condition simplifies to checking that Ext^1(X, Y) has at most one element for every Y.

label: CategoryTheory.sheafHom
slogan: Given two sheaves F and G on a category C with a Grothendieck topology, the sheafHom F G is a new sheaf that assigns to each object X in C the set of morphisms between the restrictions of F and G to the slice category over X. This construction yields a sheaf of types from the original sheaves valued in any category A. It is built so that the homomorphisms between sheaves behave like a sheaf themselves.

label: CategoryTheory.sheafIsAbelian
slogan: If D is an abelian category and sheafification exists for presheaves on a category C with a Grothendieck topology J taking values in D, then the category of sheaves on C with values in D is also abelian. This means the sheaf category has well-behaved kernels, cokernels, and exact sequences just like D. The result follows from the existence of a suitable adjunction between presheaves and sheaves.

label: CategoryTheory.sheafificationAdjunction
slogan: The sheafification functor turns presheaves into sheaves in a universal way, and it is left adjoint to the inclusion functor that views sheaves as presheaves. This means there is a natural correspondence between maps from a presheaf to a sheaf and maps from the associated sheafification to the same sheaf. The adjunction exists when the category supports sheafification.

label: CategoryTheory.sheafify
slogan: Given a presheaf P on a category C with values in a category D, and a Grothendieck topology J on C, the sheafify function produces a new presheaf that is the closest sheaf to P, meaning it satisfies the sheaf condition for J and is obtained from P by a universal process. This operation is only possible when sheafification exists for the given topology and target category, as witnessed by the HasWeakSheafify condition. The result is a functor from the opposite category of C to D that behaves like P but respects gluing conditions defined by J.

label: CategoryTheory.skeleton_isSkeleton
slogan: A skeleton of a category is made by picking one representative from each group of isomorphic objects and keeping only those objects and their morphisms. The resulting subcategory has no two distinct objects that are isomorphic, and the mapping from this skeleton back into the original category is an equivalence, meaning it preserves all essential categorical structure. This ensures the skeleton is a simplified version of the original category where isomorphic objects are treated as the same.

label: CategoryTheory.yoneda
slogan: The Yoneda embedding takes a category and maps each object to a functor that assigns to every other object the set of morphisms into it, using the opposite category to ensure the mapping is covariant. It turns objects and morphisms into representable functors and natural transformations between them. This mapping preserves the structure of the original category, being fully faithful.

label: CategoryTheory.yonedaEquiv
slogan: The yonedaEquiv function establishes a one-to-one correspondence between natural transformations from the Yoneda embedding of an object X to a functor F and elements of the type obtained by applying F to X. This means that for any object X in a category and any functor F valued in types, there is an exact match between how X maps into F via natural transformations and the actual values F produces at X. The result is a foundational bridge between abstract functor mappings and concrete data in the target category.

label: CategoryTheory.yonedaLemma
slogan: The yoneda lemma says that for any object X in a category and any functor F from that category to sets, there is a natural one-to-one match between natural transformations from the hom-functor Hom(X, -) to F and the elements of the set F(X). This match respects how objects and functors change under mappings, meaning it works consistently across the category. It shows that the behavior of X relative to other objects fully determines the values of F on X, up to equivalence.

label: CauSeq.equiv
slogan: CauSeq.equiv defines when two Cauchy sequences are equivalent by saying they must have a difference that converges to zero. This equivalence respects addition, negation, and the zero sequence, meaning operations on equivalent sequences yield equivalent results. It allows building a new type where equivalent sequences are treated as equal, supporting the completion of ordered fields.

label: Cauchy
slogan: A Cauchy filter in a uniform space is a filter where, for every measure of closeness (entourage), there is a set in the filter containing points that are all uniformly close to each other. This means the filter's sets eventually become arbitrarily small in diameter. Such filters are key to defining completeness, as they converge in complete spaces.

label: CauchySeq
slogan: A sequence is Cauchy if, for any given degree of closeness, all its terms eventually stay close to each other, judged by the uniform structure of the space. This means the image of the "at infinity" filter (from a preordered index set) under the sequence map must satisfy the Cauchy filter condition: for every measure of closeness, some set in the filter has all its points mutually close. The definition applies to sequences indexed by any preordered set and relies on the space having a uniform structure to define closeness.

label: CauchySeq.isBounded_range
slogan: Every Cauchy sequence in a pseudometric space has a range where all points are within some fixed finite distance of each other, meaning the sequence doesn't spread out indefinitely. This is because, beyond a certain index, all terms of the sequence stay uniformly close, and in such spaces, this uniform closeness ensures the entire sequence remains bounded. The result uses the fact that on the natural numbers, the cofinite filter (capturing "all but finitely many") is the same as the atTop filter (capturing "all sufficiently large" indices).

label: CauchySeq.tendsto_limUnder
slogan: If a sequence is Cauchy in a complete uniform space, then it converges to the limit given by limUnder, meaning that as the sequence progresses, its values eventually stay arbitrarily close to that limit. Convergence is defined in terms of the neighborhood filter at the limit point and the "at infinity" behavior of the sequence. This result relies on the space being complete and the sequence satisfying the Cauchy condition.

label: ChainCompletePartialOrder
slogan: A chain complete partial order is a nonempty set with a partial ordering where every nonempty chain of elements has a least upper bound, called cSup. The ordering must be reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, and any sequence of comparable elements (a chain) that is not empty must have a supremum in the set.

label: ChainCompletePartialOrder.nonempty_fixedPoints_of_inflationary
slogan: If a function f on a nonempty chain complete partial order always maps elements to greater or equal ones, then f has at least one fixed point — an element x such that f(x) = x.

label: ChainComplex
slogan: A chain complex is a sequence of objects and maps in a category where each map goes from one object to the next in the sequence, and composing any two consecutive maps gives zero; the sequence is indexed by a type that supports addition and shifting indices down by one, and the category must have zero maps and allow cancellation under addition.

label: CharP.cast_eq_zero
slogan: In a ring R with characteristic p, the natural number p becomes zero when converted to an element of R; this happens if and only if p divides the number.

label: CharTwo.add_self_eq_zero
slogan: In a ring where the characteristic is two, adding any element to itself results in zero, because the number 2 is equivalent to 0 in such a ring.

label: ChartedSpace
slogan: A ChartedSpace is a topological space equipped with a set of local coordinate maps that align open regions of the space with open regions of a model space, where each map and its inverse are continuous and transitions between overlapping maps are smooth. These local maps, called charts, allow the space to be studied using coordinates from the model space. The structure relies on the space having a topology and uses partial homeomorphisms defined on open sets to ensure consistency and continuity.

label: Chebyshev.eventually_primeCounting_le
slogan: For any small positive number ε, the number of primes less than or equal to x is eventually at most (log(4) + ε) * x / log(x) for all sufficiently large x.

label: Chebyshev.pi_le_log4_mul_div
slogan: For any real number x greater than 1, the number of primes less than or equal to x is at most (log 4 times x) divided by the log of the square root of x, plus the square root of x. This gives an upper bound on the prime counting function using basic logarithmic and square root terms.

label: Chebyshev.psi
slogan: Chebyshev.psi(x) is the sum of the vonMangoldt function values for all natural numbers n less than or equal to the floor of x, where the vonMangoldt function returns the natural logarithm of a prime p if n is a power of p, and zero otherwise. This sum is computed over the finite set of integers from 1 to floor(x) using standard addition of real numbers.

label: Chebyshev.theta
slogan: Chebyshev.theta(x) is the sum of the natural logarithms of all prime numbers less than or equal to x. It is defined for real numbers x by summing log(p) over primes p ≤ floor(x). The function uses standard arithmetic and set operations to compute the sum over primes in a finite interval.

label: Choose.choose_modEq_prod_range_choose_nat
slogan: For a prime number p, the binomial coefficient "n choose k" modulo p is equal to the product of binomial coefficients formed by taking the digits of n and k in base p, computed for each digit position up to a certain number of digits a, and then multiplying those together modulo p. This holds when both n and k are less than p raised to the power a.

label: Choose.lucas_theorem_nat
slogan: For a prime number p and natural numbers n and k less than p^a, the binomial coefficient "n choose k" modulo p equals the product of binomial coefficients formed by the base-p digits of n and k, taken digit by digit up to a digits, all computed modulo p.

label: Circle.exp
slogan: Circle.exp is a continuous function that maps a real number t to the complex number exp(t * i), which lies on the unit circle in the complex plane. It describes how multiplying the imaginary unit i by a real number and applying the exponential function wraps the real line around the unit circle. This mapping is continuous and traces out the circle as t varies.

label: CircularOrder
slogan: A circular order is a way of arranging elements in a circle where each pair of distinct elements has a defined clockwise direction, and no two different elements can be clockwise from each other; this ensures a consistent, antisymmetric circular arrangement.

label: Class.univ_notMem_univ
slogan: There is no set that contains everything, because the class of all sets does not belong to itself. This means no universal set can exist. It follows from the fact that no object can be a member of itself.

label: Classical.axiomOfChoice
slogan: If for every x of some type there exists a y such that a relation r(x, y) holds, then there is a function f that assigns to each x a corresponding y such that r(x, f(x)) is true. This function f is guaranteed to exist even if it cannot be explicitly constructed. The statement asserts the existence of a choice function based on the existence of related elements.

label: Classical.byContradiction
slogan: If assuming that a statement p is false leads to a contradiction, then p must be true. This is known as proof by contradiction. From a false assumption, any conclusion can follow, so the contradiction implies the assumption was wrong.

label: Classical.em
slogan: For any proposition p, either p is true or p is false. This principle, known as the law of excluded middle, is derived using classical reasoning, function extensionality, and propositional extensionality. The result is expressed as p or not p.

label: CliffordAlgebra
slogan: The Clifford algebra is a mathematical structure built from a module over a commutative ring, equipped with a quadratic form, that generalizes complex numbers and quaternions. It is constructed by taking a tensor algebra and imposing relations that link the square of a vector to its value under the quadratic form. This allows geometric operations like reflections and rotations to be represented algebraically.

label: CliffordAlgebra.Rel
slogan: Rel is a relation that identifies each element ι m * ι m in the tensor algebra with the value Q m, where Q is a quadratic form on a module M over a commutative ring R; the Clifford algebra is formed by taking the tensor algebra and quotienting out by this relation.

label: CliffordAlgebra.equivEven
slogan: Every Clifford algebra is algebraically equivalent to the even part of another Clifford algebra that has one extra dimension, where the new dimension contributes negatively to the quadratic form. This equivalence arises by extending the original vector space with a new direction that squares to -1. The isomorphism preserves the algebra structure over the base ring.

label: CliffordAlgebra.even
slogan: The even part of a Clifford algebra, defined by a quadratic form over a module, forms a subalgebra because it contains the identity, is closed under addition and multiplication, and respects scalar operations. This means the even elements alone can act as a smaller algebra within the full Clifford algebra. It is constructed by restricting to elements of even degree in the natural grading of the algebra.

label: CliffordAlgebra.gradedAlgebra
slogan: The Clifford algebra is split into two parts—even and odd—based on the powers of elements, and this split respects multiplication so that multiplying elements from the even and odd parts follows a predictable pattern. This structure is defined using integers modulo 2 to label the two parts, with 0 for even and 1 for odd. The algebra as a whole is built from these two submodules, and their interaction follows the rules of a graded algebra over a ring.

label: CliffordAlgebra.hom_ext
slogan: If two algebra homomorphisms from a Clifford algebra to another algebra agree on the images of the original module elements, then they are equal. This means a homomorphism out of a Clifford algebra is completely determined by where it sends the embedded module elements. The condition checks equality after composing with the inclusion map from the module into the Clifford algebra.

label: CliffordAlgebra.involute
slogan: The involute operation on a Clifford algebra negates each basis vector and extends this sign flip to the entire algebra in a way that respects multiplication and scalar operations. It is an algebra automorphism that inverts the sign of all grade-1 elements while leaving scalars unchanged. Applying the involute twice returns any element to its original value.

label: CliffordAlgebra.lift
slogan: For any linear map from a module M to an R-algebra A that satisfies f(m)*f(m) = Q(m) for all m in M, there exists a unique algebra homomorphism from the Clifford algebra of Q to A that extends the map. This extension provides a one-to-one correspondence between such linear maps and algebra homomorphisms. It allows constructing algebra maps out of a Clifford algebra by checking a simple condition on generators.

label: CliffordAlgebra.map
slogan: A linear map between two modules that preserves their quadratic forms can be extended to a ring homomorphism between their corresponding Clifford algebras. This means if a map respects the quadratic structure on the underlying modules, it induces a well-defined algebra homomorphism on the Clifford algebras built from those modules. The resulting homomorphism is compatible with the algebra structure over the base ring.

label: CliffordAlgebra.reverse
slogan: CliffordAlgebra.reverse is a linear map that reverses the order of multiplication for basis vectors in a Clifford algebra, effectively applying a kind of transpose operation while preserving the algebraic structure over a commutative ring.

label: CliffordAlgebra.ι
slogan: The function ι maps elements from a module M over a commutative ring R into the Clifford algebra built from M and a quadratic form Q, preserving the module's linear structure. This map is linear and serves as the core building block for constructing the Clifford algebra. Every element of M is embedded into the algebra in a way that respects scalar multiplication and addition.

label: CliffordAlgebra.ι_mul_ι_add_swap
slogan: For any two vectors a and b, the sum of the products a*b and b*a in the Clifford algebra equals the scalar value obtained from the polar form of the quadratic form evaluated at a and b, where scalars are embedded into the algebra via the natural ring map.

label: CliffordAlgebra.ι_mul_ι_comm_of_isOrtho
slogan: If two vectors a and b are orthogonal with respect to a quadratic form Q, then the product of their images in the Clifford algebra anticommutes, meaning ι(a) * ι(b) = -ι(b) * ι(a).

label: CliffordAlgebraComplex.equiv
slogan: The Clifford algebra constructed using the quadratic form Q(x) = -x^2 on the real numbers is algebraically equivalent to the complex numbers, meaning its elements and operations behave exactly like those of the complex plane. This equivalence preserves addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication by real numbers. The generator of the algebra corresponds to the imaginary unit i, whose square is -1.

label: CliffordAlgebraQuaternion.equiv
slogan: The Clifford algebra built from a specific quadratic form on pairs of elements from a commutative ring R is algebraically equivalent to a quaternion algebra over the same ring, with parameters c₁ and c₂ determining the multiplication rules. This equivalence means that operations in the Clifford algebra correspond directly to operations in the quaternion algebra. The two structures can be converted to each other in a way that preserves addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication.

label: ClosureOperator
slogan: A closure operator is a function on a preordered type that is increasing (every element is less than or equal to its image), preserves order (if a ≤ b then f(a) ≤ f(b)), and repeating it doesn't change the result (f(f(x)) = f(x)). It sends each element to the smallest "closed" element that is greater than or equal to it, representing a process of completing or closing an element in a way that respects the order.

label: ClusterPt
slogan: A cluster point of a filter is a point where every neighborhood around it meets every set in the filter, meaning the filter comes arbitrarily close to the point infinitely often. Such a point lies in the closure of every set in the filter. This idea captures limiting behavior in topological spaces using the structure of filters.

label: CochainComplex
slogan: A cochain complex is a sequence of objects connected by maps where each map goes from one object to the next, and applying two maps in a row always results in zero; the sequence follows an ordered indexing pattern like the integers, and the category must support zero maps and addition that can be canceled on the right.

label: CochainComplex.HomComplex.Cocycle
slogan: The Cocycle type represents the collection of cochains of degree n between two cochain complexes F and G that are cocycles, meaning they satisfy the condition of having zero coboundary; it is defined as a subgroup of the additive group of cochains in degree n. This subgroup consists of those cochains whose differential maps to zero, capturing the idea of "closed" elements in the homological sense. The structure relies on the ambient category being preadditive to support addition of morphisms and the formation of kernels.

label: CofiniteTopology
slogan: The cofinite topology on a type X is defined so that a subset is open if its complement is finite or the subset is empty. The closed sets in this topology are exactly the finite subsets and the entire space X. This construction provides a topology on any type, independent of its underlying structure.

label: Collinear
slogan: Three points are collinear if one of them can be written as a combination of the other two using vector addition and scalar multiplication over a division ring, within a space where points and vectors are related by a group action. This means all three points lie on a single straight line. The condition depends on the underlying algebraic structures of the space, including a division ring, a module, and an affine setup.

label: Combinatorics.Line.exists_mono_in_high_dimension
slogan: For any finite sets of symbols and colors, there is a high enough dimension such that any coloring of the hypercube (functions from positions to symbols) must contain a monochromatic combinatorial line — a line where all points have the same color.

label: Combinatorics.Subspace.exists_mono_in_high_dimension
slogan: For any finite sets of symbols, colors, and dimensions, there is a sufficiently large finite set such that any coloring of all functions from this set to the symbols using the given colors must contain a monochromatic combinatorial subspace of the specified dimension. A monochromatic subspace means all its points are assigned the same color. This is the multidimensional version of the Hales-Jewett theorem.

label: Combinatorics.exists_mono_homothetic_copy
slogan: If the elements of a commutative monoid are colored using finitely many colors, then for any finite set S, there exists a scaled and shifted copy of S (a homothetic copy) where all elements have the same color.

label: CommGroup
slogan: A CommGroup is a set where you can multiply elements in any order, always get a result in the set, have an identity element for multiplication, and every element has an inverse. It is both a group and commutative, meaning multiplication is associative, invertible, and order does not matter. This structure supports operations like cancellation and rearrangement without changing outcomes.

label: CommGroup.fg_of_descent'
slogan: If a commutative group G has a function h from G to the real numbers such that h is non-negative, grows in a controlled way when combining group elements, and only finitely many elements have h-values below any fixed bound, and if the quotient group G/G^2 is finite, then G must be finitely generated.

label: CommGroup.isNilpotent
slogan: In a commutative group, every element commutes with every other element, so the center of the group is the whole group. Since the upper central series starts at the center and grows to include the entire group in one step, the group is nilpotent. Therefore, every commutative group is nilpotent.

label: CommGroup.isSolvable
slogan: Every commutative group is solvable because repeatedly taking commutator subgroups eventually results in the trivial subgroup containing only the identity. This happens since all commutators are trivial in a commutative group, making the derived series shrink to the bottom subgroup. The structure of subgroups and their ordering supports this progression through well-defined steps.

label: CommGroup.is_simple_iff_prime_card
slogan: A finite commutative group has no nontrivial normal subgroups if and only if the number of its elements is a prime number. This means such a group is simple exactly when its size is prime.

label: CommMonoid
slogan: A CommMonoid is a set with a multiplication operation that is associative, commutative, and has an identity element (called one), meaning multiplying any element by one leaves it unchanged. It satisfies the rules of both a monoid and a commutative semigroup. The operation is closed, so multiplying any two elements gives another element in the set.

label: CommRing
slogan: A CommRing is a type of algebraic structure where you can add, subtract, and multiply elements such that addition and multiplication are both commutative, multiplication respects addition, and there are identity elements for both operations. It includes zero, one, and every element has an opposite for addition. This structure satisfies the rules of both a commutative monoid under multiplication and a ring where multiplication is commutative.

label: CommRing.Pic
slogan: The Picard group of a commutative ring is the group of isomorphism classes of invertible modules over that ring, using tensor product as the group operation and the ring itself as the identity element. It is constructed by forming a skeleton of the category of semimodules to ensure the group is well-defined and small. Invertible modules are those for which there exists another module such that their tensor product is isomorphic to the ring.

label: CommRingCat.epi_iff_epi
slogan: A ring homomorphism between commutative rings is an epimorphism in the category of commutative rings if and only if the corresponding algebra map makes the target ring an epimorphic algebra over the source, meaning the multiplication map from the tensor product of the algebra with itself to the algebra is injective.

label: CommSemigroup
slogan: A CommSemigroup is a set with a multiplication operation that is associative and commutative, so (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) and a * b = b * a for all elements a, b, c. It requires no identity element or inverses. This structure combines the associativity of a semigroup with the commutativity of a commutative magma.

label: Commute
slogan: Two elements a and b in a type with multiplication are said to commute if a * b equals b * a. This means the order of multiplication does not affect the result. The definition applies to any type equipped with a multiplication operation via the Mul typeclass.

label: Commute.add_pow
slogan: If two elements x and y in a semiring commute (meaning x * y = y * x), then the nth power of their sum (x + y)^n is equal to the sum of terms x^k * y^(n-k) multiplied by the binomial coefficient (n choose k), for k ranging from 0 to n.

label: CompRel
slogan: CompRel r a b means that either r a b is true or r b a is true, indicating that a and b are comparable under the relation r.

label: CompactSpace
slogan: A compact space is a type of topological space where every collection of open sets that covers the space has a finite subset that still covers it. This property relies on the space already having a topology defined by open sets. Being compact is a condition that may or may not hold for a given topological space.

label: CompactSpace.iInter_nonempty
slogan: In a compact topological space, if a collection of closed sets has the property that any finite number of them have a nonempty intersection, then the intersection of all the sets in the collection is also nonempty.

label: CompactSpace.uniformContinuous_of_continuous
slogan: If a function is continuous and its domain is a compact space, then the function is uniformly continuous: this means that for any desired closeness in the output, there is a single level of input closeness that works across the entire domain.

label: ComplementedLattice
slogan: A complemented lattice is a type with a partial order that has a bottom and top element, where every element has a complement such that the smallest element greater than both the element and its complement is the top, and the largest element less than both is the bottom.

label: CompleteLattice
slogan: A CompleteLattice is a type with a partial order where every subset has both a greatest lower bound (infimum) and a least upper bound (supremum), ensuring that all meets and joins exist. It combines the structures of a lattice, a bounded order with top and bottom elements, and the ability to take arbitrary infima and suprema. This allows consistent reasoning about bounds in ordered sets.

label: CompleteOrthogonalIdempotents
slogan: A CompleteOrthogonalIdempotents is a finite collection of elements in a semiring where each element squared equals itself, any two different elements multiply to zero, and their sum equals one. This describes a way to break the semiring into independent pieces that add up to the whole. The index set for the collection must be finite, and the operations used are those of the semiring.

label: CompleteOrthogonalIdempotents.ringEquivOfComm
slogan: If a ring has finitely many central, orthogonal idempotents that add up to one, then the ring is isomorphic to the product of rings formed by taking elements fixed under multiplication by each idempotent on both sides. Each component in the product corresponds to one idempotent, and the isomorphism preserves both addition and multiplication. The result holds when the idempotents commute with all elements of the ring.

label: CompleteSpace
slogan: A complete space is a uniform space where every Cauchy filter has a limit point in the space. This means that if the elements of a filter get arbitrarily close to each other, they must converge to some point within the space. Such a space contains all the points needed for Cauchy filters to converge.

label: CompleteSpace.prod
slogan: If two spaces are complete, meaning every Cauchy sequence in each space converges, then their product space with the product uniform structure is also complete. Any Cauchy sequence in the product space will converge to a point in that space. The uniform structure on the product is defined using the uniform structures of the individual spaces, and completeness is preserved under this construction.

label: CompletelyNormalSpace
slogan: A completely normal space is a topological space where every subset, when given the subspace topology, is a normal space; this means that any two disjoint closed sets in any subspace can be separated by disjoint open sets. It is a stronger separation property than normality, ensuring that separation holds not just in the whole space but in all its parts. The condition relies on the underlying structure of open and closed sets defined by the topology.

label: CompletelyRegularSpace
slogan: A completely regular space is a topological space where, for any point and any closed set not containing that point, there exists a continuous function from the space to the unit interval [0,1] that maps the point to 0 and the closed set to 1. This property allows points and closed sets to be separated by real-valued continuous functions. It requires the space to have a topology and involves the concepts of continuous functions, closed sets, and logical conjunction in its definition.

label: CompletelyRegularSpace.instRegularSpace
slogan: A completely regular space is automatically a regular space, meaning that for any point and a disjoint closed set, there are separate open neighborhoods around each. This follows because complete regularity allows separation by continuous functions, which implies the weaker topological separation property. No extra assumptions are needed beyond the definitions of the spaces involved.

label: Complex.Gamma
slogan: Complex.Gamma is a function that extends the factorial to complex numbers, defined for all complex numbers except non-positive integers where it has poles. It uses properties of real numbers like order, arithmetic, and the floor function, along with auxiliary definitions, to construct the gamma function in the complex plane. The function takes a complex input and returns a complex number.

label: Complex.GammaIntegral
slogan: The Gamma function for a complex number s is defined as the integral from 0 to infinity of t^(s-1) * e^(-t) dt, where t is a positive real variable, using the standard measure on the real line. This integral combines the exponential decay of e^(-t) with the power function t^(s-1) over the positive reals. The result is a complex number obtained by integrating this product with respect to the usual length measure on the real numbers.

label: Complex.GammaIntegral_add_one
slogan: For complex numbers z with positive real part, the integral defining the Gamma function at z + 1 equals z multiplied by the integral defining the Gamma function at z, reflecting the identity Gamma(z + 1) = z * Gamma(z) in terms of convergent integrals involving exponential and power functions.

label: Complex.GammaIntegral_eq_mellin
slogan: The integral of t^(s-1) times e^(-t) over the positive real numbers equals the Mellin transform of the exponential function at s, for complex numbers s with positive real part, and this integral defines the complex Gamma function.

label: Complex.GammaSeq
slogan: For a complex number s and natural number n, GammaSeq gives the value of n raised to the power s, multiplied by n factorial, then divided by the product of s, s+1, up to s+n. This sequence approaches the gamma function of s as n gets larger and goes to infinity.

label: Complex.GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma
slogan: For any complex number s, the sequence defined by (n^s * n!) / (s * (s+1) * ... * (s+n)) gets arbitrarily close to the value of the complex gamma function Gamma(s) as n increases without bound.

label: Complex.Gamma_add_one
slogan: The gamma function of a complex number z plus 1 is equal to z multiplied by the gamma function of z, as long as z is not zero or a negative integer. This identity shows how the gamma function grows by multiplying at each step in the complex plane. It generalizes the factorial property n! = n * (n-1)! to complex numbers.

label: Complex.Gamma_conj
slogan: The gamma function of the complex conjugate of a number z is the same as the complex conjugate of the gamma function of z. This means you can swap the order of taking the gamma function and taking the complex conjugate. In symbols: Gamma(conj(z)) = conj(Gamma(z)).

label: Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_add_half
slogan: For any complex number s, the product of the gamma function at s and at s plus one half equals the gamma function at 2s multiplied by 2 raised to the power of (1 minus 2s), all multiplied by the square root of pi.

label: Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub
slogan: For any complex number z, the product of the gamma function at z and at 1 minus z equals pi divided by the sine of pi times z, as long as z is not an integer. This identity relates the gamma function and trigonometric functions in the complex plane. It is valid everywhere except where the gamma function has poles or the sine function is zero.

label: Complex.Gamma_nat_eq_factorial
slogan: The gamma function of a natural number n plus one equals the factorial of n, when both are converted to complex numbers. This means Gamma(n+1) = n! holds for natural numbers in the complex domain. It connects the gamma function to the standard factorial operation.

label: Complex.I
slogan: The imaginary unit i is defined as a complex number with real part 0 and imaginary part 1. It is represented as a value of type complex number (ℂ). This definition relies on the real numbers having zero and one as defined values.

label: Complex.I_sq
slogan: The imaginary unit i, defined as the complex number with real part 0 and imaginary part 1, when squared, equals -1. This follows from the standard rule for multiplying complex numbers.

label: Complex.Rectangle
slogan: Complex.Rectangle defines a rectangle in the complex plane by using intervals of real numbers for both the real and imaginary parts, where the bounds are determined by min and max operations on the coordinates of two complex numbers. The region includes all complex numbers whose real and imaginary parts lie between the corresponding parts of the two given numbers. This construction relies on lattice properties of the real numbers and set operations to define measurable rectangular regions.

label: Complex.analyticOnNhd_univ_iff_differentiable
slogan: A complex function is analytic everywhere if and only if it is differentiable at every point in the complex plane. This means that being smooth (having a derivative everywhere) is the same as being expressible as a convergent power series around each point. The result applies to functions from the complex numbers to a complete normed vector space over the complex numbers.

label: Complex.arctan
slogan: The complex arctangent function takes a complex number z and returns a complex number, calculated using the complex logarithm. It is defined for all complex inputs and extends the real arctangent function into the complex plane. The function relies on standard arithmetic operations and the imaginary unit i, along with the complex logarithm.

label: Complex.arg
slogan: The function Complex.arg takes a complex number and returns a real number representing the angle in radians between the positive real axis and the line connecting the origin to the point in the complex plane. This angle is always between -pi and pi, with positive values for points above the real axis and negative values for those below. The result is computed using standard real arithmetic, including pi and the arcsin function.

label: Complex.arg_mem_Ioc
slogan: The argument (angle) of a nonzero complex number is always a real number greater than -pi and less than or equal to pi. This angle represents the direction of the complex number in the plane relative to the positive real axis. Every nonzero complex number has exactly one such angle in this range.

label: Complex.arg_mul
slogan: The angle of the product of two nonzero complex numbers equals the sum of their angles, provided that the sum is between -pi and pi; otherwise, adding or subtracting 2*pi brings it into that range.

label: Complex.arg_mul_coe_angle
slogan: The angle of the product of two nonzero complex numbers equals the sum of their angles, modulo 2*pi. This means multiplying complex numbers adds their directions in the plane. The result is given as a real angle, which automatically handles the modulo 2*pi equivalence.

label: Complex.arg_mul_eq_add_arg_iff
slogan: The argument of the product of two nonzero complex numbers equals the sum of their arguments if and only if that sum lies in the interval (-pi, pi]. This means angle addition works directly without adjustment exactly when the total angle doesn't cross the boundary at -pi or pi. Otherwise, the result wraps around due to modular arithmetic.

label: Complex.arg_neg_one
slogan: The argument of the complex number -1 is equal to pi, meaning the angle it makes with the positive real axis in the complex plane is 180 degrees or pi radians.

label: Complex.betaIntegral
slogan: The beta function B(u, v) is defined as the integral from 0 to 1 of x raised to the power (u - 1) times (1 - x) raised to the power (v - 1), where u and v are complex numbers and the integration is performed over real numbers in the interval [0, 1].

label: Complex.betaIntegral_eq_Gamma_mul_div
slogan: For complex numbers u and v with positive real parts, the beta integral of u and v equals the product of the gamma function at u and the gamma function at v, divided by the gamma function at u plus v. This expresses a fundamental relationship between the beta and gamma functions in complex analysis. The result holds when the real parts of both u and v are greater than zero.

label: Complex.circleIntegral_div_sub_of_differentiable_on_off_countable
slogan: If a complex function is continuous on a closed disk and differentiable inside the disk except at a countable number of points, then the integral around the boundary of the disk of f(z)/(z-w) dz equals 2 * pi * i times f(w), for any point w inside the disk.

label: Complex.circleIntegral_sub_inv_smul_of_differentiable_on_off_countable
slogan: If a function is continuous on a closed disk in the complex plane and differentiable everywhere inside that disk except at countably many points, then the integral of the function divided by (z - w) around the boundary circle equals 2 * pi * i times the value of the function at any point w inside the disk. This means the integral over the circle captures the function's value inside, even if differentiability fails at some isolated points.

label: Complex.conjAe
slogan: The conjAe function maps each complex number to its complex conjugate and is an algebra isomorphism over the real numbers, meaning it preserves addition, multiplication, and multiplication by real numbers. It shows that complex conjugation respects the full algebraic structure of the complex numbers as an algebra over the reals. This map is built using the star operation and is its own inverse, since conjugating twice returns the original number.

label: Complex.conj_eq_iff_im
slogan: A complex number is equal to its conjugate if and only if its imaginary part is zero. This means the number must be a real number. The conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part, so it only matches the original when that part is zero.

label: Complex.cos
slogan: The cosine of a complex number z is defined as (exp(i*z) + exp(-i*z)) / 2, where i is the imaginary unit with real part 0 and imaginary part 1. This uses the complex exponential function, addition, multiplication, and division to extend the familiar cosine function from real to complex numbers. The definition ensures that key properties of cosine continue to hold in the complex plane.

label: Complex.cos_add_sin_I
slogan: For any complex number z, the cosine of z plus i times the sine of z equals the exponential of i times z. This equation links the trigonometric functions cosine and sine with the exponential function in the complex plane. It is a form of Euler's formula that holds for all complex numbers.

label: Complex.cos_add_sin_mul_I_pow
slogan: For any natural number n and complex number z, raising (cos(z) + i*sin(z)) to the nth power gives cos(n*z) + i*sin(n*z), where i is the imaginary unit. This shows that exponentiation of a complex trigonometric expression scales the angle by n. The result follows from Euler's formula and properties of the complex exponential function.

label: Complex.cos_eq_tsum
slogan: The cosine of any complex number z is equal to the infinite sum of terms where each term is (-1) raised to the power n, multiplied by z raised to the power 2n, and divided by the factorial of 2n. This series converges to the value of the complex cosine function for all complex numbers z.

label: Complex.cos_two_mul
slogan: The cosine of twice a complex number z is equal to two times the square of the cosine of z, minus one. This formula works for all complex numbers and matches the familiar double-angle rule from trigonometry, extended to complex inputs.

label: Complex.cosh_add_sinh
slogan: For any complex number z, the sum of the hyperbolic cosine of z and the hyperbolic sine of z equals the exponential of z. This is because both cosh and sinh are defined using exponentials, and their sum simplifies directly to exp(z).

label: Complex.cosh_eq_tsum
slogan: The hyperbolic cosine of a complex number z is equal to the infinite sum of z raised to the power of 2n, divided by the factorial of 2n, for all natural numbers n starting from 0.

label: Complex.cosh_sq_sub_sinh_sq
slogan: For any complex number x, the square of the hyperbolic cosine of x minus the square of the hyperbolic sine of x equals 1. This identity is derived from the exponential definitions of cosh and sinh and holds due to algebraic simplification.

label: Complex.cpow
slogan: The cpow function raises a nonzero complex number a to the power of another complex number b by computing exp(b * log(a)), using the complex exponential and logarithm functions. It extends exponentiation to complex numbers while depending on standard operations like multiplication and addition in the complex plane. This definition applies to all nonzero complex bases and any complex exponent.

label: Complex.cpow_def
slogan: The complex power z ^ w is defined as exp(w * log(z)) when z is not zero, and is 1 when both z and w are zero, or 0 when z is zero and w is not zero. This uses the principal branch of the complex logarithm and handles the case of zero base separately to avoid undefined log(0). The definition ensures complex exponentiation is well-defined for all inputs.

label: Complex.cpow_def_of_ne_zero
slogan: For any nonzero complex number x and any complex number y, the power x^y is equal to the complex exponential of y times the complex logarithm of x. This definition uses the standard exp and log functions for complex numbers and requires x to be non-zero.

label: Complex.differentiableAt_Gamma
slogan: The Gamma function is differentiable at every complex number except at the non-positive integers, where it is not defined to have a derivative. This means the function behaves smoothly and has a well-defined slope everywhere in the complex plane except at 0, -1, -2, and so on. The result relies on showing the Gamma function relates to another function that is known to be differentiable.

label: Complex.differentiableOn_sqrt
slogan: The complex square root function has a derivative at every point in the complex plane except on the negative real axis and zero. This means the function is smooth and can be approximated by a linear map in that region. The set where it is differentiable is called the slit plane, defined as all complex numbers with either a nonzero imaginary part or a positive real part.

label: Complex.digamma
slogan: The digamma function is defined as the derivative of the logarithm of the Gamma function, or equivalently, the derivative of the Gamma function divided by the Gamma function itself, for complex numbers. It is a complex-valued function defined everywhere except at the non-positive integers, where the Gamma function has poles. This function is constructed using the general notion of a logarithmic derivative in the context of complex analysis.

label: Complex.digamma_one
slogan: The digamma function evaluated at 1 equals the negative of the Euler-Mascheroni constant. This constant is the limiting difference between the harmonic series and the natural logarithm. The result holds for the complex digamma function, which is the logarithmic derivative of the gamma function.

label: Complex.dist_eq
slogan: The distance between two complex numbers is the same as the magnitude of their difference, where magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary parts. This magnitude is computed using the standard norm operation for complex numbers, and distance is defined via subtraction in the complex plane.

label: Complex.dist_eq_re_im
slogan: The distance between two complex numbers equals the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences between their real parts and their imaginary parts. This is calculated by subtracting the real and imaginary components separately, squaring those differences, adding them, and taking the square root of the result.

label: Complex.dist_le_dist_of_mapsTo_ball
slogan: If a complex analytic function maps a ball of radius R around a point c into a closed ball of the same radius R centered at f(c), then the distance from f(z) to f(c) is less than or equal to the distance from z to c for any point z in the ball.

label: Complex.eqOn_of_isPreconnected_of_isMaxOn_norm
slogan: If a complex differentiable function on a connected open set has a point where the norm of the function reaches its maximum, then the function is constant throughout that set.

label: Complex.equivRealProd
slogan: The complex numbers can be represented as pairs of real numbers, where each complex number corresponds uniquely to an ordered pair (a, b) of reals. This correspondence is reversible, with functions to convert between complex numbers and these pairs. The equivalence means the two representations carry the same structure and information.

label: Complex.exists_root
slogan: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root, meaning there is always a complex number that makes the polynomial equal zero when substituted in. The result applies to any polynomial whose degree is greater than zero. This is guaranteed by the properties of complex numbers and polynomial evaluation.

label: Complex.exp_add
slogan: The exponential of the sum of two complex numbers equals the product of their individual exponentials. In other words, exp(x + y) = exp(x) * exp(y) for any complex numbers x and y. This property mirrors how exponents work with real numbers but applies to complex values.

label: Complex.exp_eq_exp_re_mul_sin_add_cos
slogan: The exponential of a complex number x + i*y is equal to e^x times (cos(y) + i*sin(y)). This means the complex exponential can be broken down into a real exponential and trigonometric functions. It is a version of Euler's formula for complex numbers.

label: Complex.exp_log
slogan: For any nonzero complex number z, taking the complex logarithm of z and then applying the complex exponential function gives back z. This means that exp undoes what log does, as long as z is not zero. The result depends on how exp and log are defined for complex numbers and their algebraic behavior.

label: Complex.exp_mul_I
slogan: The exponential of i times a complex number z is equal to the cosine of z plus i times the sine of z. This equation shows how the exponential function with imaginary exponent connects to the trigonometric functions cosine and sine for all complex numbers. It is a fundamental identity in complex analysis.

label: Complex.exp_pi_mul_I
slogan: The exponential of pi times the imaginary unit i equals -1. This means that when you raise the number e to the power of pi*i, the result is -1. It connects exponential functions with complex numbers and trigonometry.

label: Complex.exp_two_pi_mul_I
slogan: The exponential of 2 times pi times the imaginary unit i equals 1. This means that when you raise the number e to the power of 2 * pi * i, the result is the complex number 1. It shows that the complex exponential function repeats every 2 * pi * i.

label: Complex.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_of_differentiable_off_countable
slogan: If a complex function is continuous on a closed disk and differentiable at all but countably many points inside the open disk, then it equals a convergent power series centered at the disk's center, and this series represents the function everywhere in the disk.

label: Complex.hasSum_arctan
slogan: For any complex number z with absolute value less than 1, the sum of the series (-1)^n * z^(2n+1) / (2n+1) from n=0 to infinity equals the complex arctangent of z.

label: Complex.hasSum_cos
slogan: The cosine of a complex number z is equal to the sum of the infinite series where each term is (-1)^n times z raised to the power 2n, divided by the factorial of 2n. This series converges to the value of the complex cosine function for any complex number z.

label: Complex.hasSum_cosh
slogan: The hyperbolic cosine of a complex number z is equal to the sum of the series where each term is z raised to the power of 2n, divided by the factorial of 2n, for all natural numbers n.

label: Complex.hasSum_sin
slogan: The sine of any complex number z can be expressed as the sum of an infinite series where each term is (-1)^n times z raised to the power (2n+1), divided by the factorial of (2n+1), and this series converges to the value of sin(z).

label: Complex.hasSum_sinh
slogan: The sum of the series where each term is z raised to the power (2n+1), divided by the factorial of (2n+1), equals the hyperbolic sine of the complex number z, for any complex number z.

label: Complex.instAdd
slogan: This declaration sets up the addition operation for complex numbers by adding their real parts and imaginary parts separately, using the standard addition of real numbers. It allows complex numbers to be added together in a way that matches the usual mathematical definition. This makes expressions like z + w work when z and w are complex numbers.

label: Complex.instCompleteSpace
slogan: The complex numbers are a complete space, meaning every Cauchy sequence of complex numbers converges to a complex number. This is because the complex plane is uniformly equivalent to the product of two real lines, and since the real numbers are complete, so is their product.

label: Complex.instZero
slogan: The complex numbers have a zero element, which is formed by embedding the real number zero into the complex numbers using the function that maps a real number to a complex number with zero imaginary part. This relies on the real numbers already having a defined zero. The zero complex number has both real and imaginary parts equal to zero.

label: Complex.integral_boundary_rect_of_hasFDerivAt_real_off_countable
slogan: If a complex function is continuous on the boundary of a rectangle and has a real derivative at all but countably many points inside the rectangle, then the integral of the function around the boundary of the rectangle is zero. This result connects the behavior of the function's derivative over the plane to the value of its contour integral. The integral is computed as a combination of line integrals along the edges of the rectangle.

label: Complex.integral_cpow_mul_exp_neg_mul_Ioi
slogan: For a complex number s with positive real part and a positive real number r, the integral from 0 to infinity of t^(s-1) times e^(-r*t) dt equals (1/r)^s times the gamma function of s, where t is a real variable and the integral is taken in the Lebesgue sense over the positive real line.

label: Complex.isAbsoluteValueNorm
slogan: The absolute value of a complex number, calculated as the square root of the sum of the squares of its real and imaginary parts, is always non-negative, is zero only when the number itself is zero, and satisfies the property that the absolute value of a product equals the product of the absolute values. It also obeys the triangle inequality: the absolute value of the sum of two complex numbers is less than or equal to the sum of their absolute values. This confirms that the complex absolute value behaves as a proper norm.

label: Complex.isAlgClosed
slogan: The complex numbers are algebraically closed, meaning every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. This implies that any such polynomial can be fully factored into linear terms using complex numbers. The result follows from the fact that every non-constant polynomial over the complex numbers has a root, and the complex numbers form a field.

label: Complex.isPrimitiveRoot_exp
slogan: The complex number e^(2 * pi * i / n) is a primitive n-th root of unity, meaning its powers generate all solutions to x^n = 1 and no smaller positive power equals 1, provided n is a positive integer. This result follows from the properties of the complex exponential function and the fact that 1 and n are coprime. The expression uses real pi, integer casting, and the imaginary unit i to define the root in terms of standard mathematical constants.

label: Complex.log
slogan: The complex logarithm function takes any nonzero complex number and returns a complex number whose real part is the natural log of the magnitude of the input and whose imaginary part is the angle (in radians) of the input in the complex plane. It generalizes the real logarithm to complex numbers using the imaginary unit i, where the angle is measured from the positive real axis. The function is defined for all complex numbers except zero.

label: Complex.log_I
slogan: The logarithm of the imaginary unit i is equal to (pi / 2) * i, because i has a magnitude of 1 and an angle of pi/2 radians in the complex plane. Since the natural log of 1 is 0, the real part of the log is 0 and the imaginary part is pi/2, making the result purely imaginary.

label: Complex.log_exp
slogan: For any complex number z whose imaginary part is between -pi and pi, the logarithm of e^z is equal to z; this holds because the complex logarithm is only defined up to multiples of 2*pi*i, and the principal value is chosen to lie in this standard range.

label: Complex.log_exp_exists
slogan: For any complex number z, there is some integer n such that the complex logarithm of e^z equals z plus 2 * pi * i * n. This reflects the fact that the complex exponential function repeats every 2 * pi * i, so the logarithm can only recover the original input up to adding multiples of this period.

label: Complex.log_im
slogan: The imaginary part of the complex logarithm of a nonzero complex number equals the angle that the number makes with the positive real axis, measured in radians. This angle, called the argument, is always between -pi and pi.

label: Complex.measurable_re
slogan: The real part of a complex-valued function is measurable whenever the function itself is measurable, because taking the real part is a continuous operation and continuous functions preserve measurability with respect to Borel sigma-algebras. This relies on the standard Borel structures on both the real and complex numbers.

label: Complex.mul_conj
slogan: For any complex number z, multiplying z by its complex conjugate gives a real number equal to the square of the real part of z plus the square of the imaginary part of z, and this result is always greater than or equal to zero.

label: Complex.mul_re
slogan: The real part of the product of two complex numbers is equal to the product of their real parts minus the product of their imaginary parts. This uses standard multiplication and subtraction of real numbers to compute the result.

label: Complex.norm_def
slogan: The norm of a complex number is the square root of the sum of the squares of its real and imaginary parts, which equals the square root of its norm squared. This value is always a non-negative real number and represents the distance from the origin in the complex plane.

label: Complex.norm_deriv_le_one_of_mapsTo_ball
slogan: If a complex analytic function maps an open disk of positive radius R centered at a point c into a closed ball of the same radius R centered at f(c), then the norm of its derivative at c is at most 1.

label: Complex.norm_eventually_eq_of_isLocalMax
slogan: If a complex differentiable function f has a point c where the norm of f(z) reaches a local maximum, then the norm of f(z) is constant in some neighborhood around c.

label: Complex.norm_exp
slogan: The absolute value of e^z for any complex number z is equal to e raised to the real part of z. This means the magnitude of the complex exponential depends only on the real part of the input.

label: Complex.norm_iteratedDeriv_le_of_forall_mem_sphere_norm_le
slogan: If a complex function is smooth inside and on a circle of radius R around a point c, and the function's values on the circle are bounded by C, then the norm of its n-th derivative at c is at most n! times C divided by R to the power n. This gives a way to bound how large the derivatives of a well-behaved complex function can be at a point, based on its behavior on a surrounding circle. The result follows from integral estimates using complex analysis.

label: Complex.norm_le_of_forall_mem_frontier_norm_le
slogan: If a complex differentiable function on a bounded set has values whose magnitudes are at most C on the boundary of the set, then the magnitudes of its values are at most C everywhere in the closure of the set.

label: Complex.norm_mul
slogan: The absolute value of the product of two complex numbers is equal to the product of their absolute values. This means multiplying two complex numbers and then taking the absolute value gives the same result as taking the absolute values first and then multiplying them.

label: Complex.one_add_cpow_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero
slogan: The function (1 + x)^a, where a is a complex number, can be expressed as a power series centered at 0 with radius of convergence 1, and the coefficients of this series are given by the binomial series for a.

label: Complex.one_div_one_sub_cpow_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero
slogan: For any complex number a, the function 1 / (1 - x)^a can be expressed as a convergent power series around 0 with radius of convergence 1, where the coefficient of x^n is the generalized binomial coefficient (a + n - 1) choose n.

label: Complex.one_div_one_sub_pow_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero
slogan: The function 1 / (1 - x)^(a+1) can be represented as a power series around 0 with radius of convergence 1, where the coefficient of x^n is the binomial coefficient (a + n choose a) interpreted as a complex number.

label: Complex.orientation
slogan: The complex numbers are treated as a 2-dimensional vector space over the real numbers, with the standard basis 1 and i. This declaration defines the standard orientation of that space, based on the order of the basis elements where 1 comes first, then i.

label: Complex.range_exp_mul_I
slogan: The set of all values of exp(i * x), where x is a real number, is exactly the set of complex numbers that lie on the unit circle centered at the origin, meaning all complex numbers with absolute value 1.

label: Complex.rotation
slogan: Multiplying a complex number z by the complex number corresponding to an angle θ (on the unit circle) rotates z by θ radians around the origin in the complex plane. This rotation is equivalent to applying a geometric rotation operator defined by the standard orientation of the complex plane. The result is a new complex number obtained by scaling and adding the real and imaginary parts according to the cosine and sine of θ.

label: Complex.sin
slogan: The Complex.sin function computes the sine of a complex number z using the formula (exp(i*z) - exp(-i*z)) / (2*i), where i is the imaginary unit and exp is the complex exponential function. It extends the familiar sine function from real numbers to complex numbers using standard complex arithmetic. This definition works for all complex inputs and aligns with Euler's formula.

label: Complex.sin_eq
slogan: The sine of a complex number z is equal to the sine of its real part times the hyperbolic cosine of its imaginary part, plus the cosine of its real part times the hyperbolic sine of its imaginary part multiplied by the imaginary unit i. This formula expresses the complex sine function in terms of real trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. It holds for all complex numbers and matches the standard definition using complex exponentials.

label: Complex.sinh_add
slogan: The hyperbolic sine of the sum of two complex numbers equals the sum of the products of their hyperbolic sines and cosines: sinh(a + b) = sinh(a)*cosh(b) + cosh(a)*sinh(b).

label: Complex.sqrt
slogan: Complex.sqrt is a function that takes a complex number and returns its square root, also as a complex number. It is defined as part of the complex number operations, where the square root is computed in a way consistent with complex arithmetic.

label: Complex.sqrt_I
slogan: The square root of the imaginary unit i is equal to (1/sqrt(2)) times (1 + i), where i is the complex number with real part 0 and imaginary part 1. This expresses the principal square root of i in terms of real and imaginary components. The result is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both 1/sqrt(2).

label: Complex.sqrt_eq_real_add_ite
slogan: The square root of a complex number a is equal to the sum of two terms: the first is the real square root of half the sum of the magnitude of a and its real part, and the second depends on the sign of the imaginary part of a—positive or negative—times the real square root of half the difference between the magnitude and the real part, multiplied by the imaginary unit i.

label: Complex.sqrt_neg_of_nonneg
slogan: If a complex number a is non-negative real, then the square root of -a equals i times the square root of a.

label: Complex.taylorSeries_eq_on_ball
slogan: If a function is complex differentiable everywhere inside an open ball of radius r around a point c, then the function's value at any point z inside that ball equals the sum of its Taylor series centered at c, where each term involves the n-th derivative of the function at c, multiplied by (z - c)^n and divided by n!.

label: Complex.tendsto_euler_sin_prod
slogan: For any complex number z, the infinite product formed by multiplying pi, z, and terms (1 - z^2/j^2) for positive integers j converges to sin(pi * z) as the number of terms goes to infinity.

label: Complex.tendsto_one_add_div_pow_exp
slogan: As n gets larger, the value of (1 + t/n) raised to the power n gets arbitrarily close to exp(t), where t is any complex number. This means the sequence (1 + t/n)^n converges to exp(t) in the complex plane as n approaches infinity.

label: Complex.tendsto_self_mul_Gamma_nhds_zero
slogan: As z gets close to 0 (but not equal to 0), the value of z multiplied by the Gamma function of z gets arbitrarily close to 1. This describes how the Gamma function behaves near zero when scaled by its input.

label: Complex.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_lt
slogan: If the partial sums of a complex sequence f converge to a limit l, then the power series formed by f, when evaluated at complex numbers approaching 1 from below along the real line, also converges to l.

label: Complex.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_stolzCone
slogan: If a complex power series converges at the point 1, then the sum of the series approaches the same limit as the input approaches 1 from within any Stolz cone—a region near 1 that stays away from the boundary of the unit disk. The convergence happens uniformly within such cones, ensuring continuity at 1 when approaching from inside the cone. This result is a version of Abel's limit theorem for complex power series.

label: Complex.two_cos
slogan: Twice the cosine of a complex number z is equal to the sum of the exponential of i times z and the exponential of negative i times z, where i is the imaginary unit with real part 0 and imaginary part 1. This identity expresses the complex cosine function in terms of complex exponentials.

label: Complex.two_pi_I_inv_smul_circleIntegral_sub_inv_smul_of_differentiable_on_off_countable
slogan: If a function is continuous on a closed disk and complex differentiable everywhere inside that disk except at countably many points, then the value of the function at any point inside the disk equals the integral of the function divided by (z - w) around the boundary circle, multiplied by 1/(2πi).

label: Computable
slogan: A function between two types that can be encoded and decoded as natural numbers in a simple, computable way is called computable if it can be described as a partially recursive function. This means the function is computable if it can be defined using basic computational rules that allow for undefined outputs. The definition links ordinary functions to partial recursive ones by treating them as partial functions that always return a value.

label: Computable.comp
slogan: If f and g are computable functions on types that support primitive recursive encoding, then their composition—applying g first and then f—is also computable.
