This holds for functions taking values in the extended non-negative real numbers. When c is infinity, the result may not hold due to indeterminate behavior.

label: ENNReal.lintegral_Lp_add_le
slogan: For two measurable functions f and g that take nonnegative real values (possibly infinite), and for any exponent p greater than or equal to 1, the Lp norm of their sum is less than or equal to the sum of their individual Lp norms, where integration is with respect to a given measure. This result holds even when dealing with infinite values, using standard conventions for powers and arithmetic involving infinity.

label: ENNReal.lintegral_mul_le_Lp_mul_Lq
slogan: For two measurable functions with values in the extended nonnegative real numbers, the integral of their product is less than or equal to the product of their L^p and L^q norms, provided that p and q are Holder conjugate exponents. This inequality holds even if some integrals are infinite. The result is a version of Holder's inequality in the context of extended nonnegative reals.

label: ENNReal.lintegral_prod_norm_pow_le
slogan: For a finite collection of measurable functions that take nonnegative extended real values, the integral of the product of each function raised to a given power is less than or equal to the product of the integrals of the individual functions each raised to the same power, provided the powers are nonnegative and sum to one. This result holds in a product measure space and generalizes Hölder's inequality to extended nonnegative real-valued functions.

label: ENNReal.tsum_comm
slogan: The sum of a function that takes two indices and returns a non-negative real number (possibly infinity) is the same no matter which order you sum over the indices, as long as both index sets are countable. This means you can swap the order of summation without changing the result. The reason this works is that addition is commutative and the topology on these extended non-negative reals ensures the sums behave continuously.

label: EReal
slogan: EReal is a type that includes all real numbers along with negative infinity and positive infinity. It is built by first adding negative infinity using WithBot and then adding positive infinity using WithTop. This lets EReals represent values that are unbounded below or above.

label: Eq.subst
slogan: If two values a and b are equal, and a property holds for a, then the same property must also hold for b. This allows replacing a with b in logical statements when they are proven equal. The property in question is often specified using a function called the "motive".

label: Eq.symm
slogan: If a equals b, then b also equals a; equality works both ways. This means that from any proof that a = b, you can get a proof that b = a just by reversing the equality.

label: Eq.trans
slogan: If a equals b and b equals c, then a equals c. This rule applies to any type of value, meaning equality can be chained: from a = b and b = c, we conclude a = c.

label: Equicontinuous.tendsto_uniformFun_iff_pi
slogan: If a family of functions from a compact space X to a uniform space α is equicontinuous, then it converges uniformly to a function f if and only if it converges pointwise to f, with respect to a given filter on the index set.

label: Equidecomp
slogan: An equidecomposition is a partial bijection between two subsets of a space X, where each piece of the source subset can be mapped to the corresponding piece of the target subset by applying a group element from a finite set of transformations. The group acts on the space, and the bijection is built by breaking the source into finitely many parts and moving each part using a single group action. This captures the idea of cutting a set into pieces and reassembling them using symmetries to form another set.

label: Equiv
slogan: Equiv represents a one-to-one correspondence between two types by pairing two functions that reverse each other's actions. It ensures every element of one type maps to exactly one element of the other type, and vice versa. This creates a reversible transformation between the types.

label: Equiv.Perm
slogan: Equiv.Perm defines a permutation of a type as a function from the type to itself that is both injective and surjective, meaning every element maps to exactly one other element and every element is reached. It represents symmetries or rearrangements of the elements of the type.

label: Equiv.Perm.Disjoint
slogan: Two permutations are disjoint if they do not move any common elements, meaning each element is either fixed or moved by only one of the permutations. This happens exactly when the sets of elements they change (their supports) have no overlap. The condition can be effectively checked for any pair of permutations.

label: Equiv.Perm.Disjoint.commute
slogan: If two permutations move completely different sets of elements, then applying them in either order has the same effect, so their composition is commutative.

label: Equiv.Perm.IsCycle
slogan: A permutation is called a cycle if it moves only finitely many elements and there exists at least one element such that repeatedly applying the permutation to it will eventually produce every element that is moved by the permutation.

label: Equiv.Perm.IsCycle.conj
slogan: If a permutation is a cycle, then conjugating it by another permutation results in a cycle of the same length, where each element in the new cycle is the image of an element from the original cycle under the conjugating permutation. This shows that conjugation preserves the cyclic structure of permutations.

label: Equiv.Perm.IsCycle.orderOf
slogan: The order of a cyclic permutation — the number of times it must be applied to return all elements to their original positions — equals the number of elements it actually moves. This number is the size of the permutation's support, and the result holds for permutations on finite types where equality between elements can be decided.

label: Equiv.Perm.applyMulAction
slogan: Permutations of a type act on elements by applying the permutation as a function, where composing permutations corresponds to applying them in sequence. This action respects the group structure: the identity permutation does nothing, and applying an inverse permutation undoes the action. The operation follows the rules of function application and matches the group behavior of permutations under composition.

label: Equiv.Perm.card_of_cycleType
slogan: The number of permutations of a finite set with a given cycle type is calculated by dividing the factorial of the set's size by the product of the factorials of the cycle lengths and their multiplicities, adjusted for unused elements; if the total cycle length exceeds the set size or any cycle is shorter than 2, the count is zero.

label: Equiv.Perm.card_support_eq_two
slogan: A permutation swaps exactly two distinct elements if and only if the number of elements it moves (its support) is exactly two.

label: Equiv.Perm.closure_isSwap
slogan: Every permutation of a finite type with decidable equality can be built by combining simple swaps of two elements. The set of all such permutations is exactly the group closure of the swap operations. This means that repeatedly applying and inverting swaps generates every possible permutation.

label: Equiv.Perm.cycleFactorsFinset
slogan: Every permutation can be uniquely expressed as a finite set of disjoint cycles, and the permutation is equal to the product of these cycles, with the order of multiplication not mattering due to disjointness.

label: Equiv.Perm.cycleFactorsFinset_noncommProd
slogan: Every permutation can be written as a product of disjoint cycles, and since these cycles do not affect each other's elements, they commute, meaning the order in which they are multiplied does not change the result.

label: Equiv.Perm.cycleOf
slogan: Given a permutation and an element, cycleOf returns the cyclic part of the permutation that includes the element, representing all the elements it reaches by repeatedly applying the permutation. It forms a new permutation that acts only on the orbit of the given element. The function assumes it is decidable whether any two elements are in the same cycle.

label: Equiv.Perm.cycleType
slogan: The cycleType function takes a permutation of a finite set and returns a multiset containing the lengths of its disjoint cycles. It does this by breaking the permutation into cycles, computing the size of each cycle's support (the elements it moves), and collecting these sizes. The result is an unordered list of cycle lengths that describes the permutation's structure.

label: Equiv.Perm.fin_5_not_solvable
slogan: The group of all permutations of five elements cannot be solved using a sequence of abelian normal subgroups, meaning it is not solvable. This is because repeatedly taking commutators does not lead to the trivial subgroup after any finite number of steps. As a result, there is no general solution in radicals for polynomial equations of degree five or higher.

label: Equiv.Perm.isConj_iff_cycleType_eq
slogan: Two permutations are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type, meaning the lengths of their disjoint cycles match when counted with multiplicity, regardless of the order of the cycles or the elements they permute.

label: Equiv.Perm.isMultiplyPretransitive
slogan: The group of all permutations of a type α acts in a way that is n-transitive for every natural number n, meaning it can map any n distinct elements to any other n distinct elements. This action is defined through the standard permutation action on the type α. The result holds for any type α and any n >= 0.

label: Equiv.Perm.lcm_cycleType
slogan: The order of a permutation is the smallest positive number of times you must apply it to get back to the identity, and this number equals the least common multiple (LCM) of the lengths of its disjoint cycles. The cycle type of a permutation, which lists the lengths of these cycles, determines the order through this LCM calculation. For example, if a permutation breaks into cycles of lengths 3 and 4, the order is LCM(3, 4) = 12.

label: Equiv.Perm.mclosure_swap_castSucc_succ
slogan: The set of permutations of a finite set of size n+1, generated by swapping adjacent elements (where one is the successor of the other), includes all possible permutations of that set. These swaps involve elements i.castSucc and i.succ in Fin (n+1), and repeatedly composing them produces every permutation in the symmetric group. This means the smallest submonoid containing these adjacent swaps is the entire permutation group on Fin (n+1).

label: Equiv.Perm.mul_apply
slogan: Multiplying two permutations is the same as composing them as functions, so applying the product permutation to an element means first applying the second permutation and then the first. This composition always results in another permutation. The operation is defined so that (f * g)(x) = f(g(x)) for any element x.

label: Equiv.Perm.not_solvable
slogan: The group of all permutations of a set with five or more elements is not solvable, meaning it cannot be constructed from abelian groups using group extensions. This holds no matter how large the universe level of the set.

label: Equiv.Perm.one_def
slogan: The identity permutation, denoted as 1, is the function that maps every element of a type to itself, matching each element with itself in a one-to-one way. It is defined as the reflexive equivalence on the type, meaning it represents the simplest form of a permutation where nothing changes. Composing any permutation with this identity leaves the permutation unchanged.

label: Equiv.Perm.partition
slogan: Every permutation of a finite set can be split into cycles that don't share elements, and the lengths of these cycles add up to the total number of elements in the set. The collection of cycle lengths forms a partition of the set's size, meaning it is a list of positive integers that sum to the total. This partition describes the structure of the permutation in terms of how it rearranges elements.

label: Equiv.Perm.partition_eq_of_isConj
slogan: If two permutations are conjugate, then they have the same cycle type, meaning the lengths of their disjoint cycles form the same multiset. This means conjugate permutations break down into cycles of matching lengths, just possibly arranged differently. The partition of the permutation's support into cycle lengths is preserved under conjugation.

label: Equiv.Perm.permGroup
slogan: Permutations of a type form a group, meaning they can be composed associatively, every permutation has an inverse, and there is an identity permutation. Composition of permutations serves as the group's multiplication operation. This structure ensures permutations can be combined and reversed consistently.

label: Equiv.Perm.permMatrix
slogan: The permMatrix function creates a square matrix that represents a permutation of a finite type, where each row and column has exactly one entry equal to 1 and all others are 0, based on how the permutation rearranges elements. The matrix is defined over a type with decidable equality and requires the underlying type to support zero and one values. This matrix is constructed by converting the permutation into a partial equivalence and then using its mapping to place ones in the correct positions.

label: Equiv.Perm.sign
slogan: The sign of a permutation is a function that returns 1 if the permutation can be built using an even number of swaps, and -1 if it requires an odd number of swaps. It maps permutations to the multiplicative group {1, -1} in a way that respects composition, meaning the sign of a combination of permutations equals the product of their individual signs. This function is defined for any finite type where equality between elements can be decided.

label: Equiv.Perm.sign_mul
slogan: The sign of the composition of two permutations equals the product of their signs, meaning that combining two permutations results in a sign that multiplies the individual signs, where each sign is either 1 or -1 based on whether the permutation is even or odd.

label: Equiv.Perm.sign_prod_list_swap
slogan: The sign of a permutation made by composing a list of swaps is -1 raised to the power of the number of swaps in the list, since each swap contributes a factor of -1 to the overall sign.

label: Equiv.Perm.subgroupOfMulAction
slogan: Every group G can be represented as a subgroup of the group of permutations of some set H, provided G acts faithfully on H; this generalizes Cayley's theorem, which says every group is a subgroup of the symmetric group on itself.

label: Equiv.Perm.truncCycleFactors
slogan: Every permutation can be broken down into a list of disjoint cycles whose product equals the original permutation, and this decomposition exists even though the order of the cycles is not specified; the function returns a proof of such a decomposition's existence without choosing a particular ordering.

label: Equiv.Perm.truncSwapFactors
slogan: Any permutation can be broken down into a sequence of swaps, and while the exact sequence isn't unique, the evenness or oddness of the number of swaps is always well-defined; this result is expressed by saying there exists such a list of swaps whose composition gives the permutation, with all elements of the list being actual transpositions, and the existence is treated in a way that ignores irrelevant differences between possible lists.

label: Equiv.Set.powerset
slogan: There is a one-to-one correspondence between the subsets of a set S and the functions from S to the set of truth values (true or false), where each subset corresponds to a function that returns true exactly on the elements of that subset. This means every subset can be uniquely described by a membership function. The power set of S is equivalent to the set of all such boolean-valued functions on S.

label: Equiv.curry
slogan: There is a one-to-one correspondence between functions that take a pair of inputs (a, b) and return a result, and functions that take the first input a and return a function that takes the second input b and returns the same result. This equivalence is established by converting between the two forms using curry and uncurry, which are inverse operations. Both forms can be converted back and forth without losing any information.

label: Equiv.intEquivNat
slogan: There is a one-to-one correspondence between integers and natural numbers, meaning every integer can be uniquely paired with a natural number and vice versa. This is done by first mapping integers to pairs of naturals with a sign tag, then mapping those pairs to single naturals. The result shows the integers and naturals have the same size in terms of countability.

label: Equiv.mulLeft
slogan: For any element a in a group G, the function that maps each element x to a * x is a bijection on G, meaning left multiplication by a permutes the elements of the group. This permutation is invertible, with the inverse given by left multiplication by a inverse. The function is also multiplicative, preserving the group operation.

label: Equiv.ofInjective
slogan: If a function f maps elements from one type to another in a way that no two different inputs give the same output, then there is a one-to-one match between the inputs and the outputs actually produced by f. This match is expressed as a two-way invertible function (equivalence) between the input type and the set of outputs of f. The invertibility relies on f being injective, ensuring each output comes from exactly one input.

label: Equiv.refl
slogan: Equiv.refl takes a type and returns an equivalence from that type to itself, using the identity function in both directions. This means every type is equivalent to itself.

label: EquivLike.bijective
slogan: A function-like equivalence between two types maps each element of the source to a unique element of the target, and every target element is covered by exactly one source element. This means the function is both one-to-one and onto. Such a mapping ensures a perfect pairing between the elements of the two types.

label: Equivalence
slogan: An equivalence relation is a binary relation that is reflexive (every element is related to itself), symmetric (if a is related to b, then b is related to a), and transitive (if a is related to b and b is related to c, then a is related to c). Such relations behave similarly to equality in many ways. The declaration defines a structure that captures these three properties for a given relation r on a type α.

label: Ergodic
slogan: A function f from a measurable space to itself is ergodic with respect to a measure μ if it preserves the measure and every measurable set that is invariant under f has either zero measure or full measure (its complement has zero measure). This means the system cannot be split into smaller invariant parts of positive measure. The measure μ assigns sizes to sets in a way consistent with the space's structure.

label: EuclideanDomain
slogan: A Euclidean domain is a type of algebraic structure where elements can be divided to give a quotient and a remainder, with the remainder being either zero or smaller than the divisor according to a special size function; it supports standard arithmetic and requires the ring to be commutative, have at least two elements, and allow unique factorization.

label: EuclideanDomain.div_add_mod
slogan: When you divide element a by nonzero element b in a Euclidean domain, you get a quotient and a remainder such that a equals b times the quotient plus the remainder, and the remainder is either zero or smaller than b according to a size function.

label: EuclideanDomain.gcd
slogan: The gcd function computes the greatest common divisor of two elements in a Euclidean domain by repeatedly replacing the larger element with the remainder of dividing it by the smaller one, stopping when one element becomes zero. It uses the domain's size function to ensure the process eventually terminates. The result is the last nonzero remainder, which divides both original elements.

label: EuclideanDomain.gcd_dvd_left
slogan: In a Euclidean domain, the greatest common divisor of two elements divides the first element. This means that for any two elements a and b, gcd(a, b) is a divisor of a. The result follows from the properties of the Euclidean algorithm and the structure of divisibility in such domains.

label: EuclideanDomain.gcd_eq_gcd_ab
slogan: In a Euclidean domain, the greatest common divisor of two elements a and b can always be written as a combination of a and b, meaning there are elements x and y such that gcd(a, b) = x*a + y*b. The functions gcdA and gcdB provide those specific coefficients x and y. This result is guaranteed by the extended Euclidean algorithm used in the domain.

label: EuclideanDomain.gcd_self
slogan: In a Euclidean domain, the greatest common divisor of any element a with itself is a, meaning gcd(a, a) = a. This holds because every element divides itself, and when one element divides another, their gcd is the divisor. The result follows from basic divisibility properties and the definition of gcd in such domains.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Cospherical.two_zsmul_oangle_eq
slogan: If four points lie on a circle, then twice the oriented angle from one point to two others relative to a common vertex is equal to twice the oriented angle subtended by the same arc at another point on the circle, using angles treated modulo pi. This captures the classical geometry facts that angles in the same segment are equal and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to pi, but expressed uniformly through doubled oriented angles. The result holds as long as the relevant points are distinct.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere
slogan: A Sphere in a metric space P consists of a center point and a radius value, where the radius does not have to be positive. It is defined for any type P that has a distance function (metric space structure). The sphere represents the set of points at a fixed distance (radius) from the center.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.IsExtTangent
slogan: Two spheres in Euclidean space are externally tangent if they touch at exactly one point and their centers are separated by a distance equal to the sum of their radii. This means the spheres just barely touch without overlapping. The definition applies to spheres defined in any metric space with the necessary geometric structure.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.angle_eq_pi_div_two_iff_mem_sphere_of_isDiameter
slogan: If a point lies on a circle where the line between two other points is a diameter, then the angle at that point between the two endpoints of the diameter is a right angle, and conversely, if that angle is a right angle, then the point must lie on the circle.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.dist_sq_eq_mul_dist_of_tangent_and_secant
slogan: If a line from a point outside a circle touches the circle at one point (tangent) and another line from the same point cuts through the circle at two points (secant), then the square of the distance from the external point to the point of tangency equals the product of the distances from the external point to each of the two points where the secant intersects the circle.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.inner_vsub_center_midpoint_vsub
slogan: The line from the center of a sphere to the midpoint of any chord is perpendicular to that chord. This means the vector between the center and midpoint forms a right angle with the chord. Points on the sphere that are endpoints of a chord are equidistant from the center, making this property consistent for all such chords.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.isExtTangent_iff_dist_center
slogan: Two spheres in Euclidean space touch externally if and only if the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii and both radii are non-negative.

label: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.thales_theorem
slogan: If a point lies on a circle and forms a triangle with the endpoints of a diameter of that circle, then the angle at that point is a right angle, and conversely, if the angle at a point is a right angle, then that point lies on the circle having the segment between the other two points as diameter.

label: EuclideanGeometry.angle
slogan: The angle at point p2 between the line segments to points p1 and p3 is defined as the undirected angle in Euclidean space, calculated using the arccosine of the normalized inner product of the vectors from p2 to p1 and from p2 to p3; if either p1 or p3 coincides with p2, the angle is taken to be pi/2. This value is always a real number between 0 and pi, representing the smallest angle formed at p2. The notation ∠ p1 p2 p3 can be used when the EuclideanGeometry scope is open.

label: EuclideanGeometry.angle_eq_angle_of_dist_eq
slogan: If a point p1 is equidistant from two other points p2 and p3, then the angle formed at p1 between p2 and p3 is equal to the angle at p1 between p3 and p2. This means the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal. The result holds in any Euclidean space with the usual notions of distance and angle.

label: EuclideanGeometry.dist_orthogonalProjection_eq_infDist
slogan: The distance from a point to its closest point in a nonempty affine subspace (where orthogonal projection is defined) is equal to the shortest distance from that point to any point in the subspace. This shortest distance is given by the infimum of all distances to points in the subspace. The result confirms that orthogonal projection achieves the minimum possible distance.

label: EuclideanGeometry.dist_sq_add_dist_sq_eq_two_mul_dist_midpoint_sq_add_half_dist_sq
slogan: In a Euclidean space, the sum of the squares of the distances from a point to two other points equals twice the sum of the square of the distance to their midpoint and the square of half the distance between them.

label: EuclideanGeometry.dist_sq_eq_dist_sq_add_dist_sq_iff_angle_eq_pi_div_two
slogan: In a Euclidean space, the square of the distance from p1 to p3 equals the sum of the squares of the distances from p1 to p2 and from p3 to p2 if and only if the angle at p2 between p1 and p3 is exactly 90 degrees.

label: EuclideanGeometry.dist_sq_mul_dist_add_dist_sq_mul_dist
slogan: If point p lies on the line segment bc such that the angle at p is 180 degrees, then the sum of the squares of the distances from a to b and from a to c, each multiplied by the distance from c to p and b to p respectively, equals the distance from b to c multiplied by the sum of the square of the distance from a to p and the product of the distances from b to p and c to p.

label: EuclideanGeometry.inversion
slogan: Inversion in a sphere maps a point x to another point y such that y lies on the line from the center c to x, and the distance from c to y is R squared divided by the distance from c to x, where R is the radius of the sphere.

label: EuclideanGeometry.mul_dist_add_mul_dist_eq_mul_dist_of_cospherical
slogan: If four points lie on a circle and two opposite angles at a fifth point are each 180 degrees, then the sum of the products of the lengths of opposite sides of the quadrilateral equals the product of the lengths of the diagonals.

label: EuclideanGeometry.mul_dist_eq_mul_dist_of_cospherical_of_angle_eq_zero
slogan: If four points lie on a circle and two lines through them intersect at a point p such that the angles at p are zero (meaning the points are aligned in straight lines through p), then the product of the distances from p to the first pair of points equals the product of the distances from p to the second pair.

label: EuclideanGeometry.mul_dist_le_mul_dist_add_mul_dist
slogan: In any quadrilateral ABCD, the product of the lengths of the diagonals (AC and BD) is less than or equal to the sum of the products of the lengths of opposite sides (AB with CD and BC with AD). This relationship holds in Euclidean geometry for any four points.

label: EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjection
slogan: The orthogonal projection maps a point in a Euclidean space to the closest point in a given nonempty affine subspace, such that the line connecting the original point and its projection is perpendicular to the subspace. This operation is well-defined when the subspace has a direction that supports orthogonal projections. The result is a continuous affine map from the ambient space to the subspace.

label: EuclideanGeometry.side_angle_side
slogan: If two triangles have two sides of equal length and the angle between those sides is also equal, then the triangles are congruent, meaning all corresponding sides and angles match, even if the triangles are flat or degenerate.

label: EuclideanGeometry.side_side_side
slogan: If the three sides of one triangle have the same lengths as the three sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent, meaning all corresponding distances between points match, even if the triangles are flat or degenerate.

label: EuclideanGeometry.similar_of_angle_angle
slogan: If two triangles each have two angles that are equal, and the three points of each triangle don't lie on a straight line, then the triangles are similar, meaning their corresponding angles are equal and their sides are in proportion.

label: EuclideanGeometry.similar_of_side_angle_side
slogan: If two triangles have two pairs of sides whose lengths are in proportion and the angle between those sides is the same in both triangles, then the triangles are similar. This means one triangle can be scaled to match the other exactly in shape, though not necessarily in size.

label: EuclideanGeometry.triangle_congruent_iff_dist_eq
slogan: Two triangles are congruent if and only if the distances between each pair of corresponding vertices are equal. This means that their side lengths are the same, regardless of the space they are in. The result applies to any metric spaces and uses standard distance measurements.

label: EuclideanSpace.dist_eq
slogan: The distance between two points in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is calculated by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences between their corresponding coordinates. This formula applies to spaces formed as products of real-like components, where the total number of dimensions is finite. Each coordinate difference is measured, squared, added together, and then the square root of that sum gives the final distance.

label: EuclideanSpace.norm_eq
slogan: The length of a vector in a Euclidean space is found by squaring each of its components, adding those squares together, and taking the square root of the sum. This gives the usual straight-line distance from the origin to the point represented by the vector. The result is always a non-negative real number.

label: EuclideanSpace.volume_ball
slogan: The volume of a ball in n-dimensional Euclidean space is equal to the volume of the unit ball in that space multiplied by the radius raised to the power of n. The volume of the unit ball depends on the dimension n and is calculated using powers of pi and the gamma function. This formula applies to any non-negative radius and any finite dimension n.

label: EuclideanSpace.volume_ball_fin_three
slogan: The volume of a ball in 3D space is (4/3) * pi * r^3, where r is the radius. This value is represented as an extended nonnegative real number, meaning it can be infinite if r is infinite. The formula uses standard real arithmetic with pi as the usual constant.

label: EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd
slogan: If a function f from natural numbers to a complete normed commutative ring satisfies f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, is multiplicative for coprime inputs, and the sum of its norms is convergent, then the infinite product over all primes p of the sum over exponents e of f(p^e) equals the sum over all natural numbers n of f(n). This means the total sum can be reconstructed by multiplying together local sums at each prime. The equality holds in the sense that the infinite product converges to the infinite sum.

label: ExpGrowth.expGrowthSup
slogan: The expression ExpGrowth.expGrowthSup(u) computes the upper limit of the logarithm of a sequence u of nonnegative extended real numbers, divided by n, as n goes to infinity. It measures the fastest rate at which the sequence grows exponentially, returning a value in the extended real numbers. For example, if u(n) grows like a constant raised to the power n, the result is the natural logarithm of that constant.

label: Ext
slogan: Ext is a function that, for a given ring R and an abelian category with enough projectives, assigns to each pair of objects a sequence of abelian groups parameterized by natural numbers, built by taking projective resolutions of one object and applying the Hom functor in a derived way. It measures the failure of Hom to preserve exact sequences, with higher Ext groups capturing deeper obstructions to exactness. The construction treats the first object contravariantly and the second covariantly, forming a bifunctor from the product of the opposite category and the original category to R-modules.

label: ExteriorAlgebra
slogan: The exterior algebra of an R-module M is a mathematical structure built from a commutative ring R and an additive commutative group M that supports scalar multiplication by elements of R, forming a new algebra where elements of M anti-commute. It is used to study volumes, determinants, and higher-dimensional analogs of cross products in linear algebra. This construction generalizes the idea of forming alternating multilinear expressions from vectors in M.

label: ExteriorAlgebra.gradedAlgebra
slogan: The exterior algebra over a module M is structured as a graded algebra, where each grade consists of the i-th exterior power of M, and the product of elements from grades i and j lands in grade i+j. This grading is built from the image of the canonical map from M into the exterior algebra. The entire algebra decomposes into the direct sum of these graded components.

label: FDRep.char_conj
slogan: The character of a finite-dimensional representation of a group over a field has the same value on any two elements that are conjugate to each other. In other words, if you take an element g and conjugate it by h (forming h * g * h^-1), the character evaluated at this conjugated element equals the character at g. This follows from the fact that the trace of a linear map is invariant under conjugation.

label: FDRep.char_iso
slogan: If two finite-dimensional representations of a monoid over a field are isomorphic, then their characters are equal. The character of a representation is defined as the trace of the linear map associated with each group element.

label: FDRep.char_one
slogan: The character of a finite-dimensional representation V of a group G over a field k, evaluated at the identity element of G, equals the dimension of the representation space V as a vector space over k, where this dimension is expressed as an element of the field.

label: FDRep.char_orthonormal
slogan: The characters of irreducible representations of a finite group over an algebraically closed field, where the field's characteristic does not divide the group's order, are orthonormal with respect to the inner product defined by averaging the product of one character with the conjugate of another over all group elements; this average equals 1 if the representations are isomorphic and 0 otherwise.

label: FDRep.char_tensor
slogan: The character of the tensor product of two finite-dimensional representations of a monoid over a field is equal to the product of their individual characters. In other words, evaluating the character of the combined representation at any group element gives the product of the traces of the actions on each representation. This shows that the character map respects the tensor product structure multiplicatively.

label: FDRep.character
slogan: The character of a finite-dimensional representation V of a monoid G over a field k is a function that takes an element g of G and returns the trace of the linear transformation V.ρ g, which represents how g acts on the vector space of the representation. This trace is an element of the field k.

label: FDRep.finrank_hom_simple_simple
slogan: If V and W are finite-dimensional representations of a group over an algebraically closed field, and both are simple (meaning they have no nontrivial subrepresentations), then the space of intertwining operators from V to W has dimension 1 if V and W are isomorphic, and dimension 0 otherwise.

label: False.elim
slogan: From a false statement, any conclusion can be drawn, no matter what it is. This rule allows deriving any proposition or type when starting from a contradiction. It has no practical execution because reaching it means something impossible has occurred.

label: FermatLastTheorem
slogan: Fermat's Last Theorem states that no three positive integers a, b, and c can satisfy the equation a^n + b^n = c^n if n is an integer greater than 2.

label: FermatLastTheorem.of_odd_primes
slogan: If a natural number n is greater than 2 and divisible by an odd prime, then there are no positive integers a, b, and c such that a^n + b^n = c^n. This means Fermat's Last Theorem holds for any such exponent n. The result relies on knowing the theorem is true for all odd prime exponents.

label: FermatLastTheoremWith
slogan: For any integer n greater than 2 and any semiring R (a structure with addition and multiplication like the natural numbers), there are no positive elements a, b, c in R such that a^n + b^n = c^n.

label: FiberBundle
slogan: A fiber bundle is a topological space that maps onto a base space B such that each point in B has a neighborhood where the space looks like a product of that neighborhood with a fixed fiber space F, and all fibers are homeomorphic to F. The total space of the bundle consists of pairs (b, e) where b is a point in B and e is an element of the fiber over b. This structure is defined using local trivializations, which are homeomorphisms from parts of the total space to product spaces that preserve the base point.

label: FiberBundle.isOpenMap_proj
slogan: The projection map from the total space of a fiber bundle to its base space sends open sets to open sets. This means that if you take any open set in the total space and project it down to the base, the resulting set is open in the base space.

label: FiberBundle.mem_baseSet_trivializationAt
slogan: For any point in the base space of a fiber bundle, that point lies in the neighborhood where the local trivialization around it is defined. This means the trivialization at a point is always valid in some open set containing that point. The total space includes all pairs of base points and their corresponding fiber elements, and the bundle structure ensures this local product behavior everywhere.

label: FiberBundleCore.fiberBundle
slogan: A fiber bundle can be built from core data that specifies how local trivializations cover the base space and map continuously to the fiber, and this construction satisfies the conditions to be a genuine fiber bundle. The core data includes an indexing type, open sets covering the base, and continuous transition functions between overlapping regions. This instance confirms that the resulting structure meets the definition of a topological fiber bundle with the given fiber.

label: Field
slogan: A Field is a mathematical structure where you can add, subtract, multiply, and divide numbers following familiar arithmetic rules, and every nonzero number has a multiplicative inverse, meaning division by nonzero values is always possible; it is based on a commutative ring and supports operations like inversion and division through typeclasses like Inv and Div.

label: Field.absoluteGaloisGroup
slogan: The absolute Galois group of a field K is the group of all automorphisms of its algebraic closure that fix every element of K. It consists of symmetries of the algebraic closure that leave the original field unchanged. This group helps describe the structure and symmetries of all algebraic extensions of the field.

label: Field.exists_primitive_element
slogan: In a finite separable field extension, there is always one element that, when added to the base field, generates the entire extension through field operations.

label: Field.instIsLocalRing
slogan: In a field, every nonzero element has an inverse, so for any element x, either x or 1 - x is invertible; this property ensures that every field is a local ring, meaning it has a unique maximal ideal.

label: Field.isDomain
slogan: Every field has no zero divisors and allows cancellation of nonzero elements in multiplication, meaning if a nonzero element multiplies two values to give equal results, the original values must be equal. This is because fields support division by nonzero elements, ensuring their algebraic structure meets the conditions of an integral domain. The declaration affirms that any type with a field structure automatically satisfies the properties of a domain.

label: Filter.HasBasis.lebesgue_number_lemma
slogan: In a compact uniform space, for any open cover of a set, there is a single entourage such that the neighborhood of every point in the set, defined by that entourage, lies entirely within some set of the cover. This means there exists a uniform "scale" where all small enough neighborhoods fit completely into the covering sets. The result ensures a form of uniform local fineness for the cover across the compact set.

label: Filter.NeBot
slogan: A filter is not the smallest possible filter (the empty one) if it contains at least one set, meaning it actually represents a nontrivial collection of subsets that can describe meaningful limiting behavior. In the lattice of all filters, this means the filter is not the least element. Such a filter must satisfy the usual properties, like being closed under finite intersections and supersets.

label: Filter.Tendsto.add
slogan: If two functions get arbitrarily close to their limit values as their inputs approach a certain point (in terms of a given filter), and if addition is continuous in the space's topology, then the sum of the functions gets arbitrarily close to the sum of their limits at that same point. This means the limit of the sum is the sum of the limits when both functions converge and addition behaves continuously.

label: Filter.Tendsto.cesaro
slogan: If a sequence of real numbers converges to a limit, then the average of its first n terms also converges to the same limit as n goes to infinity.

label: Filter.Tendsto.inv
slogan: If a function approaches a limit in a space where taking inverses is continuous, then the inverses of the function values approach the inverse of the limit. This holds in any topological space equipped with a continuous inversion operation.

label: Filter.cofinite
slogan: The cofinite filter on a type includes all sets whose complements contain only finitely many elements. A set is part of this filter if it excludes only a finite number of points from the type. This construction captures the notion that a property holds "almost everywhere" except on a finite set.

label: Filter.liminf_eq_iSup_iInf_of_nat
slogan: The limit inferior of a sequence of natural numbers is the largest value that appears in every tail of the sequence, computed by taking the supremum over all n of the infimum of the sequence values from n onward. This means it captures the eventual lower bound of the sequence using lattice operations. It relies on the natural numbers having a complete lattice structure under reversed ordering.

label: Filter.liminf_le_limsup
slogan: For any non-degenerate filter and a function into a conditionally complete lattice, the limit inferior of the function is less than or equal to its limit superior, provided the function is both bounded above and below along the filter. This means the smallest eventual value the function approaches does not exceed the largest eventual value it approaches. The result follows from the order structure and definitions of liminf and limsup in terms of filter behavior.

label: Filter.limsup_eq_iInf_iSup_of_nat
slogan: The limsup of a sequence of sets is the infimum over all n of the supremum of the sets from index n onward, meaning it takes the largest values that appear infinitely often as the sequence progresses. It describes the eventual upper bound by looking at the tails of the sequence and finding the common accumulation points. This value is computed by taking the inf of the sups of all suffixes of the sequence.

label: FinTopCat
slogan: FinTopCat represents a topological space that has a finite underlying set, combining the structures of finite types and topological spaces into a single bundled object. It is built by extending the TopCat structure with the condition that the space is finite via the Fintype class. This allows finite topological spaces to be treated as objects in a category with continuous maps as morphisms.

label: Finite
slogan: Finite is a property that says a type has only a limited number of values, even if we don't know exactly how many or what they are. It means there could be a list containing all the elements, but we don't necessarily have that list. This is weaker than Fintype, which requires an actual list of all elements.

label: Finite.compactSpace
slogan: If a topological space has only finitely many points, then it is compact, meaning every open cover has a finite subcover. This is because the entire space is a finite set, and finite sets in a topological space are always compact.

label: Finite.exists_infinite_fiber
slogan: If a function maps an infinite set to a finite set, then at least one value in the finite set must be hit by infinitely many elements from the infinite set. This means that some output value has an infinite number of inputs mapping to it.

label: Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite
slogan: If a function maps an infinite set to a finite set, then at least two distinct inputs must map to the same output. This means no such function can be injective. In fact, at least one output value must be shared by infinitely many inputs.

label: Finite.injective_iff_bijective
slogan: For a function that maps a finite set to itself, being injective (no two different inputs give the same output) is the same as being bijective (every output is hit exactly once). This means that if the function doesn't repeat values, it must also cover all possible values. The set must be finite for this to hold.

label: Finite.injective_iff_surjective
slogan: For a function that maps a finite set to itself, being one-to-one (no two inputs give the same output) is the same as being onto (every possible output is produced by some input).

label: Finite.isField_of_domain
slogan: A finite commutative ring with no zero divisors and decidable equality is a field, meaning every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. This ensures that division by any nonzero element is always possible. The finiteness of the ring, together with its algebraic properties, guarantees that inverses exist for all nonzero elements.

label: FiniteDimensional.complete
slogan: Every finite-dimensional vector space over a complete, nontrivially normed field is complete, meaning all Cauchy sequences in the space converge to a point within the space. This is because such a vector space is uniformly equivalent to a finite-dimensional Euclidean-type space, which is complete. The result relies on the existence of continuous linear isomorphisms between finite-dimensional spaces of the same dimension.

label: FiniteDimensional.of_isCompactOperator_id
slogan: If the identity map on a complete normed vector space over a nontrivially normed field is a compact operator, then the space must be finite-dimensional. This is because compactness of the identity implies the space is locally compact, and locally compact normed spaces over such fields are finite-dimensional. The result connects compactness of an operator to the algebraic dimension of the space.

label: FiniteDimensional.of_isCompact_closedBall
slogan: If a closed ball of positive radius is compact in a normed vector space over a complete normed field like the real numbers, then the space must have finite dimension. This is because compactness of a ball at any point implies compactness at the origin, and only finite-dimensional spaces support compact closed balls. The result uses translation invariance of the norm and the fact that continuous operations preserve compactness.

label: FiniteField.Extension
slogan: For any finite field k with prime characteristic p, and for any positive integer n, there exists a field extension of k of degree n, though the construction depends on choices and is not unique. This extension is another field containing k where the dimension of the extension as a vector space over k is exactly n. Such extensions are guaranteed to exist for all positive degrees when the base field is finite.

label: FiniteField.card
slogan: The size of any finite field is a power of a prime number, meaning it can be expressed as p^n where p is a prime and n is a positive integer.

label: FiniteField.card'
slogan: Every finite field has a size that is a power of a prime number, where the prime is the field's characteristic and the exponent is a positive integer.

label: FiniteField.frobenius_pow
slogan: In a finite field with p^n elements, where p is a prime, raising each element to the p-th power repeatedly n times results in the original element; this operation, known as the Frobenius map, when composed with itself n times, acts as the identity function on the field.

label: FiniteField.instIsCyclicAlgEquivOfFinite
slogan: The multiplicative group of a finite field extension L over a field K is cyclic, meaning some nonzero element can generate all other nonzero elements through its powers. This structure supports an algebraic equivalence tied to the field's operations. The Galois group of such an extension is therefore cyclic, reflecting the symmetry of the field extension.

label: FiniteField.pow_card
slogan: In a finite field, every element raised to the power of the total number of elements in the field equals itself. This is because nonzero elements follow a cyclic pattern where raising them to one less than the field size gives 1, and zero raised to any positive power remains zero. The field's size is always a positive whole number, so the operation is always defined.

label: FiniteField.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one
slogan: In a finite field, if you take any nonzero element and raise it to the power of (the total number of elements in the field minus one), the result is always 1. This happens because the nonzero elements form a multiplicative group, and the size of this group is one less than the size of the field.

label: FiniteField.ringEquivOfCardEq
slogan: If two finite fields have the same number of elements, and that number is a power of a prime, then there is a one-to-one mapping between them that preserves both addition and multiplication, making them structurally identical as rings.

label: FiniteField.roots_X_pow_card_sub_X
slogan: In a finite field with n elements, every element satisfies the equation x^n - x = 0. The set of all roots of the polynomial x^n - x is exactly the set of all elements in the field. There are no repeated roots, and no elements outside the field satisfy this equation.

label: FiniteGrp
slogan: FiniteGrp is a type that represents the category of finite groups, where each object is a group with a finite number of elements and the morphisms are group homomorphisms. It is built by restricting the general category of groups (GrpCat) to only include finite groups. This enables categorical reasoning about finite groups and the functions between them that preserve the group operation.

label: Finpartition.instLE
slogan: We can compare two finite partitions P and Q of an element in a lattice by saying P is less than or equal to Q if every part of P fits entirely within some part of Q, meaning P breaks the element into smaller or equal pieces compared to Q. This defines a way to order finite partitions based on how finely they divide the element. The ordering is built using the structure of the lattice and the existence of a smallest element.

label: Finset.Shatters
slogan: A set family A shatters a set s if, for every subset of s, there is some set in A whose intersection with s equals that subset. This means all possible subsets of s can be "traced" by intersecting s with members of A. The condition requires the elements of s and A to come from a type where equality can be algorithmically decided.

label: Finset.affineCombination
slogan: Given a finite set of points in an affine space and weights that sum to one, the affine combination is computed by taking a weighted sum of the vectors from a base point to each point, then adding that sum back to the base point. The result is a single point in the affine space and does not depend on which base point is chosen, as long as the weights add up to one. This operation is defined for any affine space modeled on a module over a ring with an additive commutative group structure.

label: Finset.all_card_le_biUnion_card_iff_exists_injective
slogan: For a family of finite sets indexed by a type, there exists an injective function that picks a distinct element from each set if and only if every collection of k sets has a union containing at least k elements. This means a system of distinct representatives exists precisely when the union of any k sets is large enough to support k unique choices. The condition ensures no group of sets is too small to allow distinct selection.

label: Finset.card_lt_card
slogan: If one finite set is a proper subset of another, then its size is strictly smaller, meaning the number of elements it contains is less than that of the larger set, according to the usual ordering of natural numbers.

label: Finset.card_powerset
slogan: The number of subsets of a finite set is 2 raised to the power of the number of elements in the set. For any finite set with n elements, there are exactly 2^n possible subsets, including the empty set and the set itself. This count includes all combinations of elements, regardless of order.

label: Finset.card_powersetCard
slogan: The number of subsets with exactly k elements that can be made from a finite set of n elements is equal to the binomial coefficient "n choose k". This value counts the combinations of k elements selected from a total of n, without considering the order of selection. The result is always a natural number that gives the exact count of such subsets.

label: Finset.centerMass_le_sup
slogan: The weighted average of a finite set of points, using positive weights, is always less than or equal to the largest value among those points, provided the values are in an ordered type that supports compatible scalar multiplication. This result relies on the fact that each point is bounded by the supremum and that scaling and summing preserve order. The weights must be non-negative and their sum must be positive.

label: Finset.centroid_eq_centerMass
slogan: The centroid of a nonempty finite set of points is the same as the center of mass when each point is given equal weight, where the weight for each point is one divided by the total number of points. These equal weights add up to one, and the calculation takes place in a vector space over a field with an ordered ring structure. The result is an affine combination that does not depend on the choice of origin.

label: Finset.centroid_mem_convexHull
slogan: The centroid of a nonempty finite set of points in a real vector space is always inside the convex hull of those points. This means the average of the points, when equally weighted, lies within the smallest convex region containing all of them. The result depends on standard properties of real numbers, vector spaces, and convex combinations.

label: Finset.convexHull_eq
slogan: The convex hull of a finite set of points is the collection of all points that can be expressed as weighted averages of the points in the set, where each weight is nonnegative and the sum of all weights equals one. This means every point in the convex hull can be formed by taking a combination of the original points using such weights. The result applies in any vector space over an ordered field where linear combinations make sense.

label: Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le
slogan: If a finite set s is contained in another finite set t, and the number of elements in t is no greater than in s, then s and t must be the same set. This means a subset that is not smaller in size must include all elements of the set it is contained in. The result uses natural number comparisons and the subset relation to establish equality.

label: Finset.erdos_ko_rado
slogan: If you have a collection of r-element subsets of an n-element set where every two subsets share at least one element, and r is at most n/2, then the maximum number of such subsets is (n-1) choose (r-1). This bound is the best possible.

label: Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to
slogan: If a function maps a finite set s into a smaller finite set t, then at least two different elements of s must map to the same element in t.

label: Finset.ext_iff
slogan: Two finite sets are equal if and only if they contain exactly the same elements. This means that for any element, it is in one set if and only if it is in the other. The order or way the sets are built does not affect their equality.

label: Finset.inclusion_exclusion_card_biUnion
slogan: The size of the union of a finite number of finite sets is calculated by adding the sizes of the individual sets, subtracting the sizes of all pairwise intersections, adding back the sizes of all triple intersections, and so on, alternating signs for intersections of more sets. This process corrects for overcounting elements that appear in multiple sets. The formula works for any finite collection of finite sets where equality between elements can be decided.

label: Finset.prod_empty
slogan: The product of a function over an empty finite set is equal to 1, the multiplicative identity in a commutative monoid. This means that if there are no elements to multiply, the result is the identity element by default. The property relies on the monoid being commutative, associative, and having an identity.

label: Finset.sum_Ico_by_parts
slogan: The sum of f(i) times g(i) for i from m to n-1 equals f(n-1) times the sum of g from 0 to n-1 minus f(m) times the sum of g from 0 to m-1, minus the sum of (f(i+1) - f(i)) times the sum of g from 0 to i, for i from m to n-2. This formula lets you reorganize sums of products into expressions that may be easier to evaluate. It's the discrete version of integration by parts, but for finite sums over integers.

label: Finset.sum_empty
slogan: The sum of the values produced by any function over an empty finite set is zero. This applies to any type where addition is commutative and has a zero element. The empty set is written as {}.

label: Finset.sum_pow
slogan: The sum of the n-th powers of values assigned to elements of a finite set equals the sum over all multisets of size n formed from that set, where each term is the product of the values weighted by the multinomial coefficient counting how many ways that multiset can be arranged.

label: Finset.sum_range_id
slogan: The sum of all whole numbers from 0 up to but not including n is equal to n times (n minus 1), divided by 2.

label: Finset.vcDim
slogan: The Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension of a family of finite sets is the largest size of a set that can be completely shattered by the family, meaning every subset of that set can be obtained by intersecting it with some set in the family. It is computed as the maximum cardinality of any set in the collection of shattered sets. The result is a natural number representing this maximal size.

label: Fintype.card_eq
slogan: Two finite types have the same number of elements if and only if there is a one-to-one correspondence between them. The size of a finite type is well-defined and matches the size of any other finite type with an equivalent structure. This means counting elements in finite types is consistent and depends only on the number of elements, not their names or arrangement.

label: Fintype.card_finset
slogan: The total number of subsets of a finite set is equal to 2 raised to the power of the number of elements in that set. This means if a set has n elements, there are exactly 2^n possible subsets, including the empty set and the set itself. The result holds for any type with a finite number of elements where the size can be computed.

label: Fintype.card_fun
slogan: The total number of functions from a finite type A to a finite type B is equal to the number of elements in B raised to the power of the number of elements in A, using ordinary natural number exponentiation. This assumes both types have a finite, computable set of values and that equality between elements can be decided. The size of the function space is calculated purely from the sizes of the input and output types.

label: Fintype.card_le_of_injective
slogan: If a function maps distinct elements of one finite set to distinct elements of another finite set, then the first set has at most as many elements as the second. This means that an injective function from a finite type to another cannot increase the number of elements. The size of the domain is less than or equal to the size of the codomain.

label: Fintype.card_le_of_surjective
slogan: If a function maps every element of a finite set A onto a finite set B, such that every element in B is hit at least once, then the number of elements in A is at least as large as the number of elements in B.

label: Fintype.exists_card_fiber_lt_of_card_lt_mul
slogan: If a function maps a finite set with fewer than n * m elements to a set with m elements, then at least one element in the target set has fewer than n elements mapping to it.

label: Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt
slogan: If a function maps a finite set of elements to another finite set that has fewer elements, then at least two different inputs must map to the same output.

label: Fintype.nonempty_field_iff
slogan: A finite type can support a field structure if and only if its size is a prime power. This means there exists a field with that many elements exactly when the number of elements is p^n for some prime p and natural number n.

label: FirstCountableTopology
slogan: A first countable topology is a space where each point has a countable collection of neighborhoods such that any neighborhood of the point contains at least one from the collection. This means the local structure around each point can be described using a sequence of open sets. It simplifies the study of limits and convergence by reducing general topological behavior to countable approximations.

label: FirstCountableTopology.frechetUrysohnSpace
slogan: In a topological space where each point has a countable neighborhood basis, a point belongs to the closure of a set if and only if there is a sequence from that set converging to the point. This means closure can be completely described using limits of sequences. Such spaces satisfy the Frechet-Urysohn property, linking sequential convergence to topological structure.

label: FirstOrder.Field.ACF_isComplete
slogan: The theory of algebraically closed fields of a given characteristic p (where p is either 0 or a prime number) is complete, meaning that for every sentence in the language of rings, either the sentence or its negation is true in all such fields. This holds because all models of a certain infinite size are isomorphic, ensuring the theory decides every statement. The result follows from general model-theoretic criteria for completeness.

label: FirstOrder.Field.ACF_zero_realize_iff_infinite_ACF_prime_realize
slogan: A first-order sentence is true in all algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero if and only if it is true in algebraically closed fields of characteristic p for infinitely many prime numbers p.

label: FirstOrder.Language
slogan: A first-order language is defined by specifying a collection of function symbols and relation symbols, each with a given number of arguments. These symbols are organized by their arity, meaning how many inputs they take. The language is built from types that classify all possible functions and relations for every possible number of arguments.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula
slogan: BoundedFormula L α n represents logical formulas in a first-order language L, where free variables come from a type α and there are exactly n bound variables available, indexed from 0 to n-1. These bound variables are used to interpret quantified expressions within the formula. The type system ensures that formulas track both the source of free variables and the number of bound variables in scope.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsAtomic
slogan: An atomic formula is either an equality between terms or a relation symbol applied to terms, but does not include logical constants like true or false. This property applies to formulas in a first-order language with bounded quantifiers and specified free and bound variables. The declaration defines a criterion to identify such atomic formulas within that framework.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsPrenex
slogan: A bounded formula is in prenex normal form if all its quantifiers are at the front, followed by a part of the formula that has no quantifiers. This property applies to formulas in a first-order language with specified free and bound variables. The declaration defines a way to check or state that a given bounded formula has this structure.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsQF
slogan: A quantifier-free formula is one that does not use quantifiers like "for all" or "there exists" and can be expressed just using basic logical operations on atomic formulas. Such formulas are built only from combinations of simple relations and functions connected by AND, OR, and NOT. The property IsQF identifies which bounded formulas meet this condition.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.freeVarFinset
slogan: Given a formula in a first-order language with variables from a type α, this function returns the finite set of free variables that appear in the formula. It works only when equality between variables can be decided, and it processes the structure of the formula to collect all variables not bound by quantifiers. For example, in an implication or universal quantification, it combines or excludes variables accordingly.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.subst
slogan: Replaces free variables in a logical formula with specified terms, while keeping bound variables unchanged.

label: FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.toPrenex_isPrenex
slogan: Every bounded formula in a first-order language can be converted into an equivalent formula in prenex normal form, where all quantifiers are moved to the front. This conversion preserves the logical meaning of the original formula. The resulting formula has no quantifiers appearing after any connectives.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ClosedUnder
slogan: A set s in a structure M is closed under a function symbol f if applying f to any n-tuple of elements from s results in an element that is still in s. This means the function f, interpreted in M, maps tuples from s back into s. It describes a subset that remains unchanged when the function f is applied to its elements.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Constants
slogan: The Constants of a first-order language L is the type of all constant symbols in L, where each constant is a symbol with no arguments. It is derived from the language's structure, which organizes function and relation symbols by their arity. This type lives in the same universe as the language's function symbols.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ElementarilyEquivalent
slogan: Two structures are elementarily equivalent if they satisfy exactly the same sentences in a given first-order language. This means that any sentence that is true in one structure is also true in the other, and vice versa. The equivalence depends only on the language's symbols and how the structures interpret them.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ElementaryEmbedding
slogan: An elementary embedding between two structures in a first-order language is a map that preserves the truth of all formulas, meaning any statement expressible in the language holds in one structure if and only if it holds in the other after applying the map. It is a function between the underlying sets that respects the interpretations of functions, relations, and logical structure. Such an embedding ensures that the two models are elementarily equivalent from the perspective of the language.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ElementarySubstructure
slogan: An elementary substructure is a subset of a mathematical structure that is closed under the functions of the language and satisfies the same first-order formulas as the larger structure when evaluated on elements from the subset. This means any logical statement about elements in the substructure holds true in the substructure if and only if it holds true in the whole structure. It builds on the idea of a substructure by adding the requirement that formulas preserve their truth values.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ElementarySubstructure.theory_model_iff
slogan: A substructure S of a structure M satisfies all sentences in a theory T if and only if the entire structure M satisfies T, provided S is an elementary substructure. This means that truth of first-order sentences in S matches their truth in M. Thus, S is a model of T exactly when M is.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Embedding
slogan: An embedding between two structures in a first-order language is a function that preserves the structure of functions and relations, meaning it maps elements in a way that respects how functions and relations are interpreted in both structures. It is injective and ensures that the interpretation of any function or relation in one structure corresponds correctly to the other. Such an embedding is defined between two types equipped with interpretations of the same language.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Embedding.toHom
slogan: Every first-order embedding between two structures is also a first-order homomorphism, meaning it preserves the structure's functions and relations when mapping elements from one structure to another.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Formula
slogan: Formula α represents the set of logical formulas in a first-order language where the free variables come from a type α, and there are no bound variables present. The language itself is defined by its function and relation symbols, each with a specified number of arguments. This structure allows building formulas using only the given symbols and variables from α.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Formula.Realize
slogan: A formula in a first-order language can be assigned a truth value (true or false) by assigning elements from a structure M to its free variables. The function Realize takes a formula φ with free variables indexed by a type α, a variable assignment v mapping each variable in α to an element of M, and returns the proposition that φ is true under that assignment. This evaluation depends on the interpretation of function and relation symbols in the structure M.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Hom
slogan: A homomorphism between two structures in a first-order language is a function between their underlying types that preserves the interpretation of functions and relations: it maps elements so that functions commute and relations that hold in the source structure also hold in the target structure under the mapping.

label: FirstOrder.Language.IsAlgebraic
slogan: A first-order language is called algebraic if it only has function symbols and no relation symbols. This means the language can express operations on elements but cannot express relations between them.

label: FirstOrder.Language.IsFraisseLimit
slogan: A structure M is a Fraisse limit for a class K if M is countable, every finitely generated substructure of M is in K, and M is ultrahomogeneous, meaning any isomorphism between finitely generated substructures extends to an automorphism of M.

label: FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous
slogan: A structure M is ultrahomogeneous if, whenever a finite part of M can be mapped into M in a way that preserves the language's functions and relations, that mapping can be extended to a bijective transformation of the entire structure M that also preserves all functions and relations. In simpler terms, any local symmetry on a finitely generated part of M can be extended to a global symmetry of M.

label: FirstOrder.Language.LHom.reduct
slogan: Given a mapping between two first-order languages, any structure interpreting the second language can be turned into a structure for the first language by interpreting each symbol through the mapping. This process uses the original interpretations in the second language's structure but applies them to the symbols of the first language. It allows one to view a model of one language as a model of another via a translation of symbols.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Sentence
slogan: A sentence is a logical formula in a first-order language that has no free variables, meaning all variables are bound by quantifiers. It is built from a language consisting of function and relation symbols with specified arities. The type of sentences depends on the language and the universe levels of its components.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Sentence.Realize
slogan: A sentence in a first-order language can be determined to be true or false in a given structure, based on how the symbols in the language are interpreted in that structure. This truth value depends only on the structure and the sentence, since sentences have no free variables. The function Realize computes this truth value as a proposition.

label: FirstOrder.Language.StrongHomClass
slogan: StrongHomClass L F M N means that F is a type of functions from M to N which preserve all relations in the first-order language L in both directions: if a relation holds in M, it holds in N and vice versa. This makes F a strong homomorphism between structures M and N for language L.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Structure
slogan: A first-order structure assigns meanings to all function and relation symbols in a first-order language by interpreting each function of arity n as a real function from n-tuples of elements (represented as functions from Fin n to a type M) to elements of M, and each relation of arity n as a function from n-tuples of elements to propositions.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Substructure
slogan: A substructure of a first-order structure M is a subset of M that is closed under all function symbols of the language L, meaning applying any function from L to elements in the subset results in an element still in the subset.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Substructure.closure
slogan: The closure of a set in a first-order structure is the smallest substructure that contains the set, formed by closing the set under all functions of the language. It is the minimal subset closed under the operations defined by the language and includes all elements that must be present to satisfy the structure's function symbols. This closure operation maps any subset of a structure to the substructure it generates.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Substructure.instCompleteLattice
slogan: The set of all substructures of a first-order structure forms a complete lattice, meaning that every collection of substructures has both a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. This allows for the intersection and union-like combinations of any family of substructures, with the entire structure serving as the largest substructure.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Substructure.isElementary_of_exists
slogan: If for every formula and parameters in a substructure S, whenever there's a solution in the larger structure M, there's also a corresponding solution within S, then S is an elementary substructure of M. This means S and M satisfy the same first-order formulas with parameters from S.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Substructure.subtype
slogan: The subtype function embeds a substructure S of a first-order structure M into M itself, preserving the structure's functions and relations. It treats elements of the substructure as elements of the larger structure via a natural inclusion map. This embedding is injective and respects the first-order language operations.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Term
slogan: A term in a first-order language is either a variable from a given set or a function symbol applied to other, simpler terms. The language defines functions and relations of various arities over a domain. Terms are built inductively using variables and function applications.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Term.realize
slogan: A term in a first-order language can be evaluated in a structure by assigning elements of the structure to the variables and interpreting function symbols as actual functions on the structure. The evaluation depends on a variable assignment and follows the inductive construction of terms. Function symbols are applied to the evaluated subterms to produce a value in the structure.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory
slogan: A theory is a collection of sentences in a first-order language, where each sentence has no free variables. It is defined as a set of statements that can be expressed using the functions and relations of the language. The theory itself is represented as a type based on the language's structure.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ACF
slogan: ACF(p) is the first-order theory in the language of rings that describes algebraically closed fields of characteristic p, combining the axioms for fields of characteristic p with additional axioms stating that every monic polynomial of degree n has a root for all natural numbers n.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.CompleteType
slogan: A complete type over a theory is a maximal consistent set of formulas in a given variable type, meaning it contains as many formulas as possible without causing a logical contradiction with the theory. It is defined within a first-order language that includes functions and relations of various arities. The theory itself is a collection of sentences with no free variables.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.Iff
slogan: Two bounded formulas are semantically equivalent over a theory T if, in every model of T, they are true under exactly the same variable assignments. This means the formulas have identical meanings in all structures where the theory holds. The relation is defined as a proposition that depends on the theory and the two formulas involved.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsComplete
slogan: A theory is complete if it has at least one model and for every sentence, either the sentence or its negation is true in all models of the theory.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsMaximal
slogan: A theory is called maximal if it is satisfiable and for every sentence, either the sentence or its negation is included in the theory. Such a theory is necessarily complete, meaning it decides the truth or falsity of every sentence in the language.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsSatisfiable
