slogan: A theory is satisfiable if there exists a structure that makes all its sentences true. This means the theory has at least one model in which every sentence in the theory holds. Satisfiability depends on the language's function and relation symbols and the sentences built from them.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.Model
slogan: A model of a theory is a structure where all the sentences in the theory are true, given that the structure interprets the language's functions and relations appropriately and the theory is a set of statements with no free variables.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelType
slogan: ModelType is the type of nonempty structures that satisfy all sentences in a given first-order theory, where the structures interpret the function and relation symbols of the language in a way that makes every statement in the theory true.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelsBoundedFormula
slogan: A theory satisfies a bounded formula if, in every nonempty structure that models the theory, the formula is true for all possible assignments of values to its free and bound variables. This means the formula holds universally across all interpretations that satisfy the theory. The condition applies to formulas with a specified set of free variables and a fixed number of bound variables.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.exists_large_model_of_infinite_model
slogan: If a first-order theory has an infinite model, then for any given size, there exists a model of the theory that is at least as large. This means the theory has models of arbitrarily large infinite sizes. The size comparison accounts for universe levels using cardinal lifting.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.exists_model_card_eq
slogan: If a first-order theory has an infinite model and the cardinality of the language is no greater than some infinite cardinal κ, which is at least the size of the natural numbers, then there exists a model of the theory with exactly κ elements.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.isSatisfiable_iff_isFinitelySatisfiable
slogan: A first-order theory has a model if and only if every finite subset of it has a model. This means a set of sentences is consistent as a whole exactly when all its finite parts are consistent.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.models_iff_not_satisfiable
slogan: A theory T models a sentence φ if and only if the theory together with the negation of φ has no model. This means T logically implies φ exactly when adding "not φ" to T results in an unsatisfiable set of sentences. In other words, T ⊨ φ is equivalent to there being no structure that satisfies both T and ¬φ.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.models_sentence_iff
slogan: A theory T satisfies a sentence φ if and only if φ is true in every model of T.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.models_sentence_of_mem
slogan: If a sentence is part of a theory, then the theory logically entails that sentence, meaning the sentence is true in every model of the theory.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.typeOf
slogan: Given a first-order language and a theory T, for any nonempty structure M that models T and any tuple of elements from M, the set of all formulas true at that tuple forms a complete type over T.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Ultraproduct.sentence_realize
slogan: A sentence is true in an ultraproduct of structures if and only if the set of indices where the sentence is true in the individual structures belongs to the ultrafilter. This means truth in the ultraproduct depends on whether the collection of structures satisfying the sentence is "large" according to the ultrafilter. The result holds under the assumption that all structures in the product are nonempty.

label: FirstOrder.Language.Ultraproduct.structure
slogan: Given a first-order language L and a family of L-structures indexed by a set α, if u is an ultrafilter on α, then the ultraproduct of the structures with respect to u naturally forms a new L-structure. This means functions and relations from L are interpreted in the ultraproduct by applying them pointwise on representatives and using the ultrafilter to determine equivalence. The construction relies on defining an appropriate equivalence relation (via a setoid) on sequences, then lifting the logical structure to equivalence classes.

label: FirstOrder.Language.completeTheory
slogan: The complete theory of a structure M in a first-order language L is the set of all sentences in L that are true when interpreted in M. It consists of every sentence that M satisfies, meaning the ones for which the Realize function returns true. This set of true sentences forms a theory, which is just a collection of statements in the language.

label: FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq
slogan: If a first-order language L and an infinite structure M are both smaller in size than a cardinal κ, then there exists a structure N of size κ that is elementarily equivalent to M, meaning there is an elementary embedding from M into N or from N into M.

label: FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq_of_ge
slogan: If a first-order language L and an infinite structure M have sizes smaller than a given cardinal κ, then there exists a larger structure N of size κ that contains M in a way that preserves all first-order properties of M.

label: FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementarySubstructure_card_eq
slogan: If a first-order structure M contains a set s and the language has cardinality such that the maximum of |s| and the size of the language is less than or equal to an infinite cardinal κ, and κ is also less than or equal to the size of M, then there exists an elementary substructure of M that contains s and has exactly κ elements.

label: FirstOrder.Language.order
slogan: The declaration defines a first-order language with a single binary relation symbol representing "less than or equal to" (≤). This language contains no function symbols or other relations, just the order relation. It is used to formally describe ordered structures in model theory.

label: FirstOrder.Language.presburger
slogan: The language of Presburger arithmetic includes the constant symbols 0 and 1, and the addition operation +, with no other functions or relations. It is a first-order language used to express statements about natural numbers with addition. This language does not include multiplication or any other operations.

label: FirstOrder.Language.ring
slogan: The language of rings includes the basic operations of addition, multiplication, negation, zero, and one. These operations are part of a formal system used to describe rings in first-order logic. The language is defined by specifying these symbols along with their argument counts.

label: FixedPoints.subalgebra
slogan: The set of elements in an algebra that remain unchanged under a multiplicative group action forms a subalgebra, meaning it is closed under addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and contains the image of the base ring.

label: Flow
slogan: A flow is a continuous action of an additive topological monoid τ on a topological space α, meaning that adding elements of τ corresponds to continuously transforming points in α. The action respects both the algebraic structure of addition in τ and the continuity required by the topologies on τ and α. This setup models systems that evolve continuously over time, where τ often represents time and α the space of states.

label: Flow.orbit
slogan: The orbit of a point under a flow is the set of all points it can reach by following the flow for any amount of time. It is defined for a continuous action of a topological monoid on a topological space. This is the same as the orbit from the underlying additive monoid action.

label: FormalMultilinearSeries.ofScalars_radius_eq_inv_of_tendsto
slogan: The radius of convergence of a power series with scalar coefficients is the reciprocal of the limit of the ratio of consecutive coefficient norms, provided this limit exists and is nonzero.

label: FormalMultilinearSeries.radius
slogan: The radius of convergence of a formal multilinear series is the largest nonnegative real number or infinity such that the series converges when evaluated at inputs with norm smaller than this value, and it is calculated using the norms of the series' coefficients and the structure of the underlying spaces. This value is expressed as an extended nonnegative real number, meaning it can be finite or infinite. Convergence depends on the properties of a nontrivially normed field, ensuring meaningful behavior under scaling and limits.

label: FormalMultilinearSeries.radius_eq_liminf
slogan: The radius of convergence of a formal multilinear series is given by the limit inferior of the sequence 1 divided by the n-th root of the norm of the n-th term of the series, as n approaches infinity. This value is expressed using non-negative real numbers and appropriate coercions. The result characterizes how large the inputs can be for the series to still converge.

label: FormalMultilinearSeries.radius_inv_eq_limsup
slogan: The reciprocal of the radius of convergence of a formal multilinear series is equal to the limit superior of the n-th root of the norm of its n-th term as n approaches infinity.

label: Fourier.fourierIntegral
slogan: The Fourier transform integral computes a function that maps each element w to the integral of f(x) multiplied by a complex character e evaluated at w and x, using a given measure μ on a commutative ring 𝕜. The function f takes values in a normed space E over the complex numbers, and the character e maps elements of 𝕜 to the unit circle in the complex plane. This integral generalizes the classical Fourier transform to settings involving abstract rings, measures, and vector-valued functions.

label: Fourier.fourierIntegral_comp_add_right
slogan: The Fourier transform of a function that has been shifted to the right by a fixed amount is equal to the original Fourier transform multiplied by a complex phase factor that depends on the shift and the frequency variable. This phase factor comes from the additive character applied to the product of the shift and the frequency. The measure used in the transform is invariant under right addition, ensuring the property holds.

label: FractionRing
slogan: FractionRing takes a commutative ring R and constructs a new ring where elements are fractions made from elements of R, with denominators that don't turn nonzero elements into zero when multiplying. This new ring is built by allowing division by all non-zero divisors, making those elements invertible. It uses the general method of localization applied to the set of non-zero divisors in R.

label: FractionalIdeal
slogan: A fractional ideal is a subset of the fraction field of a commutative ring that becomes an actual ideal when multiplied by some nonzero element of the ring. It extends the notion of ideals to include certain collections of fractions, provided they can be scaled back into the ring. This concept relies on structures like commutative rings, submonoids, and algebras to define how elements interact under multiplication and scaling.

label: FreeAbelianGroup.lift
slogan: Every function from a set S to an abelian group A can be extended in exactly one way to a group homomorphism from the free abelian group on S to A, where the homomorphism respects addition and matches the original function on the elements of S.

label: FreeGroup
slogan: FreeGroup takes a type and constructs a group whose elements are sequences of symbols from that type, with only the minimal simplifications needed for group structure, like canceling a symbol with its inverse. Each symbol is embedded as a one-letter sequence via FreeGroup.of, and FreeGroup.lift lets you define a group homomorphism out of the free group by just specifying where each symbol goes.

label: FreeGroup.Red.church_rosser
slogan: If a word in a free group can be reduced in two different ways, then both reduced forms can eventually be reduced further to reach a common word. This means the reduction process is confluent, so the order of reductions does not matter. The result follows from the fact that each individual reduction step has the diamond property and from the general Church-Rosser theorem for relations.

label: FreeGroup.lift
slogan: Every function from a set S to a group G can be uniquely extended to a group homomorphism from the free group on S to G, where the homomorphism maps each generator to its assigned value in G and respects multiplication and inverses.

label: FreeLieAlgebra
slogan: FreeLieAlgebra R α is a Lie algebra over a commutative ring R, built from a type α, such that every element is an R-linear combination of nested brackets of elements from α, and any function from α to a Lie algebra L extends uniquely to a Lie algebra homomorphism from FreeLieAlgebra R α to L.

label: FreeLieAlgebra.universalEnvelopingEquivFreeAlgebra
slogan: The universal enveloping algebra of the free Lie algebra over a set X with coefficients in a commutative ring R is algebraically the same as the free associative algebra over X with coefficients in R. This means that turning the free Lie algebra into an associative algebra via the universal enveloping construction gives back the simplest possible associative algebra generated by X.

label: FreeMagma
slogan: FreeMagma α is a type representing all possible ways to combine elements of α using a binary operation that is not associative, meaning the order of grouping matters. Each element is like a binary tree with leaves labeled by elements of α, and operations follow no simplifying rules like associativity or commutativity. There is a function FreeMagma.of that embeds each element of α into FreeMagma α, and any function from α to a magma M extends uniquely to a magma homomorphism from FreeMagma α to M.

label: FreeMagma.lift
slogan: There is a one-to-one correspondence between functions from a type α to a magma β and magma homomorphisms from the free magma on α to β, meaning every function from α to β extends uniquely to a homomorphism that respects the binary operation.

label: FreeMonoid
slogan: FreeMonoid creates a monoid where elements are lists of values from a given type, with list concatenation as the operation and the empty list as the identity. It allows embedding single values into the monoid via FreeMonoid.of and extending functions from the base type to any monoid using FreeMonoid.lift, which maps lists to products in the target monoid. This structure satisfies the universal property of free monoids.

label: FreeMonoid.lift
slogan: FreeMonoid.lift turns a function from a set to a monoid into a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on that set, by mapping each list to the product of the function's values on its elements. It ensures that the empty list goes to the identity and that the image of a concatenated list is the product of the images. This extension is unique and fully determined by where the individual elements are sent.

label: FreeSemigroup
slogan: FreeSemigroup α is the set of all nonempty sequences of elements from α, where the operation is concatenation. It comes with a natural way to turn any function from α to a semigroup M into a unique semigroup homomorphism from FreeSemigroup α to M. This means every element of α can be embedded into FreeSemigroup α, and any mapping from α to a semigroup extends uniquely to a multiplicative map on the entire free semigroup.

label: FrobeniusNumber
slogan: The Frobenius number of a set of natural numbers is the largest natural number that cannot be written as a sum of elements from that set, using addition repeatedly. It exists only when the set has no common divisor greater than 1. This number is an upper bound on all other numbers that cannot be expressed in such a way.

label: Function.Antiperiodic
slogan: A function f is antiperiodic with period T if shifting the input by T and applying the function gives the negative of the original output, that is, f(x + T) = -f(x) for all x. The function's domain must support addition, and its codomain must support negation. This condition must hold for every point in the domain.

label: Function.Bijective
slogan: A function is bijective if it is both one-to-one and onto, meaning each input maps to a unique output and every output is covered by some input. This means no two different inputs give the same output, and every element in the output set has exactly one corresponding element in the input set. Such a function creates a perfect pairing between inputs and outputs.

label: Function.Bijective.comp
slogan: If two functions are both one-to-one and onto, then applying one after the other (in sequence) also results in a function that is one-to-one and onto. This means the combined function matches each input to a unique output, covering all outputs exactly once.

label: Function.Bijective.of_comp_iff
slogan: A function f is bijective if and only if composing it with any bijective function g results in a bijective function exactly when f itself is bijective. This means that f preserves bijectivity under composition with bijective functions. The property holds for all functions with matching domains and codomains.

label: Function.Embedding.antisymm
slogan: If there is an injective function from set A to set B and another injective function from B to A, then there exists a bijective function between A and B, meaning the sets have the same size.

label: Function.Embedding.injective
slogan: A function embedding ensures that different inputs always map to different outputs, so if two outputs are the same, the inputs must also be the same. This property is called injectivity, and it is guaranteed for all embeddings by their definition.

label: Function.Embedding.schroeder_bernstein
slogan: If one set can be mapped into another set in a one-to-one way, and the second set can also be mapped one-to-one back into the first, then there is a one-to-one correspondence between the two sets, meaning they have the same size.

label: Function.End
slogan: Function.End is the type of functions from a given type to itself, where functions can be composed in sequence and include an identity function, forming a structure where composition is associative and has an identity.

label: Function.Even
slogan: A function is called even if applying it to the negative of an input gives the same result as applying it to the input itself, meaning f(-x) equals f(x) for all x. This requires the input type to support negation through the Neg typeclass. The definition applies to functions from any type with negation to any other type.

label: Function.Exact
slogan: A function f followed by a function g is called exact if every output of f is exactly the input that makes g return zero, meaning the image of f matches the kernel of g with respect to the zero element in g's target space. This means that g(f(x)) = 0 for all x, and any element y such that g(y) = 0 must come from some x via y = f(x). It captures a precise fit between the range of one function and the solutions to g(y) = 0.

label: Function.HasTemperateGrowth.toTemperedDistribution
slogan: A smooth function that grows no faster than a polynomial, and whose derivatives do the same, can be turned into a tempered distribution by integrating it against Schwartz functions. The resulting distribution maps each Schwartz function g to the integral of g(x) times f(x) with respect to a measure that also has temperate growth. This integral is well-defined and produces a continuous linear functional on the space of Schwartz functions.

label: Function.Injective
slogan: A function is injective if different inputs always produce different outputs, meaning that whenever the outputs of two inputs are equal, the inputs themselves must be equal.

label: Function.Injective.comp
slogan: If two functions f and g are injective, then their composition g ∘ f is also injective. This means that applying f and then g preserves distinctness: different inputs remain different after both functions are applied.

label: Function.Involutive
slogan: A function f is involutive if applying it twice returns the original input, so f(f(x)) = x for all x.

label: Function.IsFixedPt
slogan: A fixed point of a function f is a value x such that f(x) equals x. This means applying the function to x returns x itself. The property checks whether x remains unchanged under the function f.

label: Function.IsPeriodicPt
slogan: A point x is periodic under a function f if, after applying f repeatedly for some number n times, the result is x again. This means the nth iterate of f at x equals x, so x is a fixed point of the nth iterate of f. It captures the idea that the function eventually cycles back to the starting point after a finite number of steps.

label: Function.LeftInverse
slogan: LeftInverse g f means that applying f and then g gets you back to where you started, so g undoes the action of f. In other words, g(f(x)) = x for all x. This is the same as saying the composition of g and f equals the identity function.

label: Function.Odd
slogan: A function f is odd if f(-x) = -f(x) for all x in its domain, meaning the function's value at -x is the negative of its value at x. This requires both the input and output types to support negation.

label: Function.Odd.zero
slogan: If a function is odd, then f(0) = 0, as long as -0 = 0 in the codomain. This is because the definition of an odd function requires f(-x) = -f(x), and substituting x = 0 gives f(0) = -f(0), which implies f(0) = 0. The result holds when the output type supports both negation and a zero element.

label: Function.Periodic
slogan: A function f from type α to type β is periodic with period c if, for every x in α, adding c to x and then applying f gives the same result as applying f to x alone; this means the function repeats its values every time c is added to the input. The type α must support addition. The period c is an element of α, and the function f maps elements of α to elements of β.

label: Function.Periodic.intervalIntegral_add_eq
slogan: If a function repeats every T units, then the integral of the function over any interval of length T is the same, no matter where the interval starts. Shifting the interval by any amount does not change the value of the integral.

label: Function.RightInverse
slogan: RightInverse g f means that applying f after g returns the original input, so f undoes what g does; in other words, f(g(x)) = x for all x.

label: Function.Semiconj
slogan: A function f semiconjugates two functions ga and gb if applying ga, then h, is the same as applying h and then f; that is, h(ga(x)) = f(h(x)) for all x. This means the function h links the behavior of ga and gb through f in a consistent way.

label: Function.Surjective
slogan: A function f from type α to type β is surjective if for every element b in β, there is at least one element a in α such that f(a) equals b.

label: Function.Surjective.comp
slogan: If function f maps elements from set α onto all of set β, and function g maps elements from set β onto all of set γ, then the composition of g after f maps elements from α onto all of set γ. This means that when two functions are both surjective, their composition is also surjective. In simpler terms, if every element in the second set comes from the first, and every element in the third comes from the second, then every element in the third set can be reached from the first.

label: Function.Surjective.hasRightInverse
slogan: If a function f maps from one type to another and covers every element in the target type (surjective), then there exists a function g that, when applied after f, returns the original input for every element in the target type. This means f has a right inverse function g such that f(g(b)) = b for all b.

label: Function.argmin
slogan: Given a function f from a nonempty type to a type with a well-founded less-than relation, argmin f returns an input value that minimizes f, meaning no other input gives a strictly smaller output, and among all such minimizing inputs, it returns the smallest one.

label: Function.bijective_id
slogan: The identity function, which maps every element to itself, is bijective because it is both injective (no two different inputs map to the same output) and surjective (every element in the output set is mapped to by some input).

label: Function.bijective_iff_has_inverse
slogan: A function has an inverse if and only if it is both one-to-one (different inputs give different outputs) and onto (every element in the output set is hit by some input); this means there exists another function that reverses its action completely, both when applied before and after it.

label: Function.cantor_injective
slogan: There is no way to map each subset of a set to a unique element of the set without at least two subsets sharing the same element, because the collection of all subsets is inherently larger than the set itself.

label: Function.cantor_surjective
slogan: There is no function that can map every element of a set to every possible subset of that set, because the collection of subsets is always larger than the set itself. This means no such function can cover all subsets, so it cannot be surjective. As a result, such a function cannot have a fixed point where an element maps to itself.

label: Function.comp
slogan: Function.comp creates a new function by combining two functions, where the output of the second function (g) is passed as input to the first function (f), resulting in a function that maps from the input type of g to the output type of f.

label: Function.comp_assoc
slogan: Function composition is associative: given three functions f, g, and h, the order in which they are grouped when composed does not affect the result, so (f composed with g) composed with h is the same as f composed with (g composed with h).

label: Function.comp_id
slogan: The composition of any function f with the identity function id on its input type is equal to f itself. This means applying id before f has no effect on the result. In other words, f(id(x)) is the same as f(x) for all x.

label: Function.exists_fixed_point_of_surjective
slogan: If a function f from a type to itself covers every element in the target (meaning for every output there is some input that maps to it), then there is at least one element x such that applying a related function g to x returns x itself.

label: Function.extend
slogan: Function.extend takes a function f from type α to β, a function g from α to γ, and a function j from β to γ, and returns a new function from β to γ that agrees with g on the image of f and extends it arbitrarily elsewhere using j. The result is defined for all elements of β, even those not in the range of f. This allows building functions on larger domains while preserving behavior on a core subset.

label: Function.graph
slogan: The graph of a function f from type α to type β is the set of all pairs (x, y) where y is equal to f(x). It is defined using setOf to collect pairs that satisfy the relation y = f(x). This graph is a relation between elements of α and β.

label: Function.id_comp
slogan: Composing any function f with the identity function on the left results in f itself. This means applying the identity function after f has no effect, so id ∘ f is the same as f. It reflects that the identity function returns its input unchanged.

label: Function.injective_comp_right_iff_surjective
slogan: A function f is surjective if and only if, for any function g, the composition g ∘ f being injective implies that g is also injective, provided the codomain of g has at least two distinct elements.

label: Function.injective_iff_hasLeftInverse
slogan: A function maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs if and only if there is another function that can undo its effect by mapping outputs back to their original inputs, but only when the function's domain has at least one element.

label: Function.leftLim
slogan: The left-side limit of a function at a point is the value the function gets close to as inputs approach that point from values less than it, within an ordered topological space. It uses neighborhoods restricted to the left of the point (values strictly less than it) and defines the limit through filter convergence. This limit is computed by seeing how the function behaves as inputs get near the point from the left, using the limUnder operation.

label: Function.mt
slogan: If a implies b, and b is not true, then a cannot be true either.

label: Function.not_surjective_Type
slogan: No function can map elements of a type to all of its possible subsets, because there will always be some subset that is not in the image of the function.

label: Function.periodicPts
slogan: The periodicPts function takes a function f from a type to itself and returns the set of all points that eventually map back to themselves after repeated applications of f. A point is included in this set if some iterate of the function sends it back to its original value. This set is constructed using the IsPeriodicPt condition, which checks whether a point returns to itself after a finite number of steps.

label: Function.surjective_id
slogan: The identity function, which maps every element to itself, is surjective because every element in the target set is the image of some element in the source set.

label: Function.surjective_iff_hasRightInverse
slogan: A function maps every output to at least one input if and only if there is another function that picks an input for each output such that applying the original function to that input gives back the output.

label: FunctionField
slogan: A function field F over a finite field Fq is a field that extends the field of rational functions in one variable over Fq, meaning F contains all such rational functions and is finite-dimensional when viewed as a vector space over them. The field F can be a function field over different finite fields Fq that are not necessarily isomorphic. This setup relies on Fq being a field, F being a field, and there being a well-defined algebra structure from the rational functions over Fq into F.

label: FundamentalGroup
slogan: The fundamental group of a topological space X at a point x is the set of loops at x, where two loops are considered the same if one can be continuously deformed into the other, and the group operation is concatenation of loops. It is formed by taking the automorphisms of x in the fundamental groupoid of X, which captures paths in X up to homotopy. This gives a group structure with the constant loop as the identity and path reversal as inversion.

label: FundamentalGroup.fundamentalGroupMulEquivOfPathConnected
slogan: In a path-connected space, the fundamental group at any point is isomorphic to the fundamental group at any other point, meaning the group structure does not depend on the choice of basepoint. This isomorphism arises because any two points can be connected by a continuous path, which induces a group isomorphism via conjugation of loops. As a result, all fundamental groups of the space are algebraically equivalent.

label: FundamentalGroup.map
slogan: Given a continuous function f from space X to space Y, and a base point x in X, there is an induced group homomorphism from the fundamental group of X at x to the fundamental group of Y at f(x). This homomorphism maps loops in X based at x to loops in Y based at f(x) by composing them with f. It preserves the group structure of loop concatenation and the identity loop.

label: FundamentalGroup.mapOfEq
slogan: Given a continuous function f from space X to space Y that maps point x to point y, this defines a group homomorphism from the fundamental group of X at x to the fundamental group of Y at y. It captures how loops based at x are transformed into loops based at y under f.

label: FundamentalGroupoid
slogan: The fundamental groupoid of a space X is a mathematical structure that wraps the points of X and treats paths between points as invertible morphisms, forming a category where every path has an inverse. It captures the idea of connectedness and loops in the space without focusing on a single base point. This structure is built by defining X as a groupoid, meaning all its morphisms (paths) are reversible.

label: FundamentalGroupoid.fundamentalGroupoidFunctor
slogan: This defines a functor that takes a topological space to its fundamental groupoid, and a continuous map between spaces to the corresponding functor between their fundamental groupoids. It formalizes how topological spaces and continuous maps are transformed into groupoids and functors in a way that preserves identities and composition. The construction relies on the category structures of topological spaces and groupoids.

label: FundamentalGroupoidFunctor.equivOfHomotopyEquiv
slogan: If two topological spaces are homotopy equivalent, then their fundamental groupoids are equivalent as categories. This means there is a pair of functors between the groupoids that are inverses up to natural isomorphism. The equivalence arises from the continuous maps that define the homotopy equivalence, lifted to the level of paths and homotopy classes.

label: FundamentalGroupoidFunctor.preservesProduct
slogan: The fundamental groupoid functor takes a product of topological spaces and maps it to the corresponding product of their fundamental groupoids, preserving the structure of the product. This means that the way spaces are combined continuously is reflected in how their groupoids of paths and homotopies are combined. The functor respects the universal property of products in both categories.

label: FundamentalGroupoidFunctor.prodIso
slogan: The fundamental groupoid of the product of two topological spaces is naturally isomorphic to the product of their fundamental groupoids, meaning paths in the product space correspond exactly to pairs of paths in the individual spaces. This isomorphism is given by mapping a path in the product to its projections and vice versa. The forward and inverse maps are continuous and preserve the homotopy classes of paths.

label: GCDMonoid
slogan: A GCDMonoid is a type with a commutative multiplication and zero, where every pair of elements has a greatest common divisor (unique up to units), and where you can cancel nonzero elements in multiplication. It requires that multiplication is commutative, has an identity and zero, and that if a nonzero element multiplies two equal products, the other factors must be equal. This structure supports both GCDs and safe cancellation of nonzero factors.

label: GE.ge
slogan: a >= b means the same as b <= a, using the standard less-than-or-equal relation defined for a type. The notation 'ge' is used in code to represent the greater-than-or-equal relationship. This definition relies on the LE typeclass, which provides the <= operation for a given type.

label: GaloisConnection
slogan: A Galois connection consists of two functions between preordered sets where one function maps an element to be less than or equal to a value in one set if and only if the other function maps the corresponding element to be greater than or equal to the original value in the other set. These functions maintain a reverse order relationship without needing to be inverses. The connection relies on the preorder structures of both sets.

label: GaloisConnection.closureOperator
slogan: A closure operator is a function that maps each element in a partially ordered set to a larger or equal element in a way that is monotone and idempotent, meaning repeating the operation has no extra effect, and it arises from the composition of the lower and upper functions in a Galois connection.

label: GaloisField
slogan: A Galois field is a finite number system with p^n elements, where p is a prime number and n is a positive integer, built using arithmetic modulo p and polynomials. It supports all basic arithmetic operations, including division by nonzero elements, and follows strict algebraic rules. These fields are used in cryptography and coding theory because of their predictable structure and limited size.

label: GaloisField.algEquivGaloisField
slogan: For any prime p and positive integer n, any finite field with p^n elements can be matched perfectly with the Galois field of the same size in a way that preserves all field operations and the underlying modular arithmetic over the integers mod p. This matching is a bijective algebra isomorphism that respects the base field structure. The result follows from the fact that both fields are splitting fields of the polynomial X^(p^n) - X over ZMod p.

label: GaloisField.algEquivGaloisFieldOfFintype
slogan: For any prime p and positive integer n, every finite field with p^n elements can be matched perfectly with the splitting field of the polynomial X^(p^n) - X over the integers modulo p, in a way that preserves all algebraic operations and the underlying modular arithmetic. This means all finite fields of the same size are structurally the same when viewed as algebras over the integers modulo p.

label: GaloisField.card
slogan: A finite field with characteristic p, where p is a prime number, and dimension n over its prime subfield has exactly p^n elements. The size of the field is always a power of the prime p, specifically p raised to the dimension n. This gives the total number of elements in the field as p^n.

label: GaloisField.instIsGaloisOfFinite
slogan: Every finite field is a Galois extension of its prime subfield, meaning it has a symmetric algebraic structure where all roots of certain polynomials are treated uniformly. This symmetry arises because finite fields have prime characteristic and their nonzero elements form a cyclic multiplicative group. The extension is both separable and normal, which guarantees the Galois property.

label: GaussianInt
slogan: The Gaussian integers are numbers of the form a + b√(-1), where a and b are integers. They are represented here as a type called GaussianInt. This definition builds on standard integer operations like negation and natural number conversion.

label: GaussianInt.instEuclideanDomain
slogan: The Gaussian integers support division with remainder, where the remainder is always smaller in size than the divisor, using the absolute value of the norm as the measure of size. This makes the Gaussian integers a Euclidean domain, ensuring that arithmetic behaves well and allows for unique factorization. The norm of a Gaussian integer a + bi is a*a + b*b, and the division algorithm guarantees that remainders decrease in this norm.

label: GenContFract
slogan: A generalized continued fraction consists of a head term h and a sequence of pairs of values, where each pair contains a partial numerator and a partial denominator. These components define a fraction that can extend infinitely in a nested structure. The entire expression is built from a starting value and successive layers of numerators and denominators.

label: GenContFract.abs_sub_convs_le
slogan: For a value v in an ordered field with a floor function, if the generalized continued fraction of v has not terminated by step n, then the absolute difference between v and its nth convergent (A_n / B_n) is at most 1 divided by the product of the nth and (n+1)th denominators.

label: GenContFract.succ_nth_fib_le_of_nth_den
slogan: The nth denominator of a continued fraction is at least as large as the (n+1)th Fibonacci number, provided the continued fraction has not terminated earlier or n is zero.

label: GenContFract.terminates_iff_rat
slogan: The continued fraction expansion of a value v stops after a finite number of steps if and only if v is a rational number. This means that rational values produce finite continued fractions, while irrational values produce infinite ones. The result holds for any field with an order and a floor function, such as the real numbers.

label: GeneralSchauderBasis
slogan: A GeneralSchauderBasis is a family of vectors and corresponding functionals indexed by a type β, such that every vector in the space can be expressed as a sum of basis vectors weighted by the functionals, where convergence is defined along a specified filter on finite subsets. The basis vectors and functionals satisfy a biorthogonality condition: each functional maps its corresponding basis vector to 1 and all others to 0. This generalizes classical Schauder bases by allowing non-sequential convergence over arbitrary index sets.

label: GeneralizedBooleanAlgebra
slogan: A GeneralizedBooleanAlgebra is a type that has a bottom element, supports meet and join operations that distribute over each other, and includes a set difference operation (like removing one element from another). It generalizes Boolean algebras by allowing this difference operation on types with finite, logically structured values. This setup is useful for reasoning about finite data types where logical and set-like operations behave consistently.

label: Geometry.SimplicialComplex
slogan: A simplicial complex is a collection of geometric shapes called simplices, such as points, lines, and triangles, that fit together in a structured way within a module over a ring with a partial order; these shapes are combined so that their intersections are also simplices in the collection. The structure ensures that overlapping parts of any two simplices form another simplex already present in the set. It is built using finite sets of points and relies on convex hulls to define how the pieces connect.

label: GradedLieAlgebra
slogan: A graded Lie algebra is a Lie algebra that is split into parts indexed by an additive commutative monoid, such that the Lie bracket of elements from two parts lands in the part indexed by the sum of their indices, and each part is a submodule over a commutative ring. This structure ensures the bracket operation respects the grading. The indexing set must have decidable equality to allow algorithmic checking of index conditions.

label: Graph
slogan: A graph consists of a set of vertices of type α and a set of edges of type β, where each edge connects two vertices as defined by a relation IsLink; the edge set can be derived from this connection relation, but is included explicitly for convenience and better definitional control.

label: Graph.IsLoopAt
slogan: G.IsLoopAt e x means that edge e in graph G is a loop, connecting vertex x to itself.

label: GromovHausdorff.GHSpace
slogan: GromovHausdorff.GHSpace is a type representing the space of all nonempty compact metric spaces, where two spaces are considered the same if they are isometric, and the distance between them is defined by the Gromov-Hausdorff metric. This space is constructed using a quotient of compact subsets of the infinite-dimensional space ℓ^∞(ℝ) under isometry equivalence. The setup allows comparing shapes and metric spaces in a unified geometric framework.

label: GromovHausdorff.ghDist
slogan: The Gromov-Hausdorff distance between two nonempty compact metric spaces is the distance between their equivalence classes in the Gromov-Hausdorff space, where spaces are considered equivalent if they are isometric. This distance is defined by embedding the spaces into a common metric space and measuring the smallest possible Hausdorff distance between them. It provides a way to compare the shapes of compact metric spaces up to isometry.

label: GromovHausdorff.instMetricSpaceGHSpace
slogan: The Gromov-Hausdorff space is equipped with a distance function that measures how far apart two compact metric spaces are, and this distance satisfies all the properties of a metric space. This means the distance is non-negative, symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and is zero exactly when the spaces are isometric. The distance is defined as the smallest Hausdorff distance possible between isometric copies of the spaces in a common metric space.

label: Group
slogan: A group is a set with an operation that combines any two elements to give another element of the set, where there is a special identity element that leaves others unchanged when combined, every element has an inverse that cancels it out to give the identity, and the operation is associative. The group structure can be proven using either left-sided or right-sided rules for the identity and inverse properties. It extends simpler structures like monoids and includes operations for multiplication, inversion, and division.

label: Group.FG
slogan: A group is finitely generated if some finite set of elements can be combined using the group operation and inverses to produce every element in the group. This means the entire group can be built from a finite starting set through repeated application of the group's multiplication and inverse operations.

label: Group.IsFinitelyPresented
slogan: A group is finitely presented if it can be generated by a finite set of elements and all the relations among those generators can be captured by a finite list of equations. This means the group is a quotient of a free group on finitely many generators by the smallest normal subgroup containing a finite number of relators.

label: Group.IsNilpotent
slogan: A group is nilpotent if it has a sequence of subgroups starting from the trivial subgroup and ending with the whole group, where each subgroup is contained in the center of the next. This means the group is built up step by step through central extensions, making it structurally close to being abelian. The property depends only on the group's internal structure and subgroup relationships.

label: Group.nat_card_center_add_sum_card_noncenter_eq_card
slogan: The size of a finite group equals the number of elements in its center plus the sum of the sizes of all conjugacy classes that contain elements not in the center. Each of these non-center conjugacy classes consists of elements that do not commute with every element of the group. This equation accounts for every element of the group exactly once.

label: Group.nilpotencyClass
slogan: The nilpotency class of a group is the smallest number n such that the nth step of the upper central series, which builds larger central subgroups step by step, reaches the whole group; if the group is nilpotent, this number exists and is found using Nat.find; otherwise, the class is not defined.

label: GroupLieAlgebra
slogan: The Lie algebra of a Lie group is defined as the tangent space at the identity element of the group, using the term GroupLieAlgebra to avoid confusion with the general Lie algebra class. It combines structures of a group, a topological space, and a smooth manifold modeled on a normed space over a nontrivially normed field. This definition sets up the foundation for studying continuous symmetries through their linear approximations at the identity.

label: GroupLike.instGroup
slogan: The set of group-like elements in a Hopf algebra forms a group, meaning these elements have inverses, an identity, and associative multiplication under the given algebraic structure. This builds on the fact that they already form a monoid and adds the existence of inverses through the Hopf algebra structure.

label: GroupLike.toUnits
slogan: A group-like element in a Hopf algebra can be turned into an invertible element (unit), where its inverse is given by applying the antipode operation. This conversion respects multiplication and sends the group-like element to a unit whose product with its antipode is 1 on both sides. The map from group-like elements to units is a multiplicative homomorphism.

label: GroupTopology
slogan: A GroupTopology is a group that also has a topology, where multiplying elements and taking inverses are continuous operations. This means the group's algebraic structure works smoothly with the concept of open sets and limits. It is equivalent to saying the group is a topological group.

label: GrpCat
slogan: GrpCat is the category of groups, where objects are types with a group structure (identity, inverses, and associative multiplication) and morphisms are group homomorphisms. It allows reasoning about groups and structure-preserving functions between them using category theory. The type GrpCat lives in a universe one level above the types it is built from.

label: GrpCat.abelianizeAdj
slogan: The abelianization functor from the category of groups to the category of abelian groups is left adjoint to the forgetful functor that treats an abelian group as a general group. This means group homomorphisms from a group G to an abelian group A correspond naturally to homomorphisms from the abelianization of G to A. The adjunction captures the universal property of abelianization.

label: GrpCat.adj
slogan: The free group functor from types to groups is left adjoint to the forgetful functor from groups to types, meaning group homomorphisms from the free group on a type X to a group G correspond naturally to functions from X to the underlying set of G.

label: HNNExtension
slogan: The HNN Extension of a group G adds a new generator t to G such that conjugating elements of a subgroup A by t gives their images under an isomorphism φ mapping A to another subgroup B. This creates a larger group where A and B are made conjugate through the new element t. The construction is defined by taking the free product of G with the integers and imposing relations that enforce t * a * t^-1 = φ(a) for all a in A.

label: HahnSeries
slogan: HahnSeries defines a type of formal series where terms are indexed by a linearly ordered set Γ and have coefficients in a type R that has a zero element; the support of each series (the set of indices with non-zero coefficients) must be well-founded. This means no infinite descending chains of indices with non-zero coefficients are allowed. The series are written as R⟦Γ⟧ and require Γ to have a partial order and R to have a zero.

label: HallMarriageTheorem.hall_hard_inductive
slogan: If for every subset of indices, the number of elements in the union of their associated sets is at least as large as the size of the subset, then there exists an injective function that picks a distinct element from each set. This result holds for finite index types with decidable equality. It guarantees a system of distinct representatives when Hall's condition is satisfied.

label: HarmonicAt.analyticAt
slogan: If a function from the complex numbers to the real numbers is harmonic at a point (meaning it is twice continuously differentiable and its Laplacian vanishes near that point), then it is analytic at that point, so it can be represented by a convergent power series in a neighborhood around it.

label: HarmonicOnNhd.circleAverage_eq
slogan: If a real-valued function is harmonic near and inside a closed disc in the complex plane, then the average value of the function on the circle surrounding the disc equals the value of the function at the center of the disc.

label: HasCompactSupport
slogan: A function has compact support if it is zero outside of some compact set, meaning the region where the function is nonzero, along with its limit points, forms a compact set. This requires the domain to be a topological space and the function to map into a type with a zero element. The concept combines topology, compactness, and the idea of vanishing outside a bounded region.

label: HasCompactSupport.contDiff_convolution_right
slogan: If a function g has compact support and is n-times continuously differentiable, and f is locally integrable, then their convolution with respect to a continuous bilinear map is also n-times continuously differentiable.

label: HasCompactSupport.convolution
slogan: If two functions have compact support and are defined on a topological additive group with a measure, then their convolution — formed by integrating their values combined through a continuous bilinear map — also has compact support. This means the convolution is zero outside some compact set. The result holds under standard assumptions about the spaces involved, including measurability, topology, and normed structure.

label: HasCompactSupport.convolutionExists_left
slogan: If a function f has compact support and is continuous, and g is locally integrable on a topological abelian group G with a suitable invariant measure, then the convolution of f and g exists for all points in G, meaning the integral defining the convolution is well-defined everywhere.

label: HasCompactSupport.hasDerivAt_convolution_right
slogan: If one function has compact support and is continuously differentiable, and another is locally integrable, then the convolution of the two is differentiable at a point, and its derivative equals the convolution of the first function with the derivative of the second. The result holds for functions between normed spaces with respect to an invariant and s-finite measure. The bilinear structure of the convolution ensures compatibility with the derivative operation.

label: HasCompactSupport.hasFDerivAt_convolution_right
slogan: If g has compact support and is continuously differentiable, and f is locally integrable, then the derivative of the convolution f ⋆ g at a point is equal to the convolution of f with the derivative of g, using an appropriate linear map to combine the values.

label: HasDerivAt
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if, near that point, the difference between the function's values and its linear approximation (based on the derivative) becomes arbitrarily small compared to the distance from the point, using the topology and scalar multiplication of the space. This means the function behaves more and more like a straight line as you zoom in on the point, with the derivative giving the slope of that line. The definition uses neighborhood filters to formalize "near" and requires the space to support addition, scalar multiplication, and a topology that works well with tho

label: HasDerivAt.add
slogan: If two functions are differentiable at a point, then their sum is also differentiable at that point, and the derivative of the sum is the sum of their derivatives. This applies to functions from a normed field to a normed vector space, using the standard notion of derivative based on neighborhood limits.

label: HasDerivAt.comp
slogan: If a function h has a derivative at a point x, and another function h2 has a derivative at h(x), then the composition h2 ∘ h has a derivative at x, and that derivative is the product of the derivatives of h2 and h. This holds when both functions map between spaces over nontrivially normed fields with compatible algebraic structure.

label: HasDerivAt.inner
slogan: If two functions from the real numbers to an inner product space are differentiable at a point, then the function formed by taking their inner product is also differentiable at that point, and its derivative is the sum of the inner product of the first function's value with the second function's derivative and the inner product of the first function's derivative with the second function's value.

label: HasDerivAt.lhopital_zero_nhds
slogan: If two functions f and g both approach 0 as x approaches a, and their derivatives f' and g' exist near a with g' not zero near a, then the limit of f(x)/g(x) as x approaches a equals the limit of f'(x)/g'(x), provided the latter limit exists.

label: HasDerivAt.lhopital_zero_nhdsNE
slogan: If two functions f and g both approach zero as x approaches a point a (but x is not equal to a), and if their derivatives f' and g' exist near a (except possibly at a) with g' not zero, then the limit of f(x)/g(x) as x approaches a is equal to the limit of f'(x)/g'(x), provided the latter limit exists.

label: HasDerivAt.lhopital_zero_right_on_Ioo
slogan: If two functions f and g both approach 0 as x approaches a from the right, and their derivatives f' and g' exist and g' is never zero near a on the interval (a, b), then the limit of f(x)/g(x) as x approaches a from the right equals the limit of f'(x)/g'(x), provided that latter limit exists.

label: HasDerivAt.log
slogan: The derivative of the natural logarithm of a function f at a point x is equal to the derivative of f at x divided by the value of f at x, provided f(x) is not zero. This means the rate of change of log(f(y)) near y = x depends on both how fast f is changing and the current value of f. The rule applies wherever the function f is positive and differentiable.

label: HasDerivAt.of_local_left_inverse
slogan: If a function g is continuous at a point a, and another function f has a derivative f' at g(a) with f' not zero, and f(g(y)) = y for all y near a, then g is differentiable at a and its derivative is the inverse of f'. This result holds for functions between spaces over a nontrivially normed field.

label: HasDerivAt.smul
slogan: If a function f has a derivative at a point x, and another function c maps into scalars with its own derivative at x, then the derivative of the product function (c scaled times f) at x is equal to c(x) times the derivative of f plus the derivative of c times f(x), following the product rule in the context of normed spaces with compatible scalar multiplication.

label: HasDerivWithinAt
slogan: A function has a derivative within a set at a point if, when only considering points in that set, the function's difference quotient gets arbitrarily close to a specific linear map as the input change approaches zero. This means the function looks approximately linear near the point, but only along directions that stay within the given subset. The definition uses the limit of the difference quotient with respect to the neighborhood filter restricted to the set.

label: HasFDerivAt
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if, near that point, it can be written as its value plus a continuous linear map applied to small changes in the input, plus an error term that becomes very small compared to the size of the input change. The smallness of the error is defined using neighborhood filters and scalar multiplication on filters, ensuring the approximation improves as you get closer to the point. This definition works in spaces with both algebraic structure (like vector spaces) and topological structure (like continuity).

label: HasFDerivAt.comp
slogan: If a function f has a Fréchet derivative at a point x, and another function g has a Fréchet derivative at f(x), then the composition g ∘ f has a Fréchet derivative at x, and this derivative is the composition of the derivatives of g and f.

label: HasFDerivAt.hasLineDerivAt
slogan: If a function is Fréchet differentiable at a point with derivative L, then it has a directional derivative in every direction v, and that directional derivative is given by applying the derivative map L to the vector v.

label: HasFDerivAt.inner
slogan: If two functions f and g from a real normed space to an inner product space are differentiable at a point x, then the function that maps t to the inner product of f(t) and g(t) is also differentiable at x, and its derivative is given by applying the chain rule through the derivative of the inner product combined with the derivatives of f and g.

label: HasFPowerSeriesAt
slogan: A function f from one normed space to another has a formal power series at a point x if there exists a series of continuous multilinear maps such that the Taylor expansion of f around x, built using these maps, converges to f in a neighborhood of x, with convergence defined using norms over a field whose norm is not trivial. The series must match the function values near x when evaluated as a sum of scaled and iterated linear operations. This captures the idea of analyticity in a general setting beyond real or complex spaces.

label: HasFPowerSeriesAt.comp
slogan: If a function f has a formal power series at a point x, and another function g has a formal power series at f(x), then the composite function g(f(x)) also has a formal power series at x, formed by composing the series of g with that of f. This composition reflects how analytic functions behave when nested within one another near a point. The result holds in normed vector spaces over a nontrivially normed field.

label: HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.add
slogan: If two functions can be expressed as power series that converge near a point, then their sum can also be expressed as a power series that converges at least as far as the smaller of the two convergence radii, and the series for the sum is simply the sum of the individual series terms.

label: HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.fderiv
slogan: If a function can be represented by a convergent power series in a ball around a point, then its derivative also has a convergent power series in the same ball, obtained by differentiating each term of the original series. The radius of convergence for the derivative's series is at least as large as that of the original series. This applies to functions between normed spaces over fields with a nontrivial norm.

label: HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.hasSum_iteratedFDeriv
slogan: If a function has a power series representation on a ball around a point, then the function's value at a nearby point can be computed by summing up its iterated derivatives at the center, each divided by the corresponding factorial and applied to the displacement. This sum converges unconditionally in a complete normed space over a field of characteristic zero. The result confirms that the function is analytic and locally equal to its power series expansion.

label: HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.tendstoUniformlyOn
slogan: If a function has a power series that converges on a ball around a point, then on any smaller closed ball, the partial sums of the series get uniformly close to the function as more terms are added. This means that for any desired accuracy, there is a single point in the sequence of partial sums beyond which all values stay within that accuracy of the function across the entire smaller ball. The convergence is uniform on that smaller ball.

label: HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn.comp
slogan: If a function f has a Taylor approximation up to order n at a point, and another function g has a Taylor approximation up to the same order at the value of f at that point, then the composite function g after f also has a Taylor approximation up to order n at the original point, and this approximation is built from the approximations of g and f using a specific composition operation.

label: HasGradientAt.fderiv_apply
slogan: If a function has a gradient at a point, then the derivative of the function at that point, when applied to a vector, equals the inner product of the gradient and that vector.

label: HasLineDerivAt
slogan: A function f has a directional derivative f' at point x in the direction v if, as t approaches 0, the change in f along the line x + t*v is approximately t times f', with the error smaller than any linear term in t. This means f(x + t*v) ≈ f(x) + t*f' for small t, where the approximation error becomes negligible compared to t. This notion focuses on behavior along a specific direction rather than overall differentiability.

label: HasMFDerivAt.comp
slogan: If a function f is differentiable at a point x on a manifold and another function g is differentiable at f(x), then the composition g(f(x)) is differentiable at x, and its derivative is the composition of the derivatives of g and f, viewed as continuous linear maps between tangent spaces.

label: HasStrictFDerivAt.localInverse
slogan: If a function has a strictly differentiable derivative at a point, and that derivative is an invertible continuous linear map, then the function has a local inverse near that point. This inverse is continuous, defined on an open set, and both the function and its inverse map open sets to open sets. The result applies in complete normed vector spaces over a field with a nontrivial norm.

label: HasStrictFDerivAt.toOpenPartialHomeomorph
slogan: If a function has a derivative at a point that is invertible and behaves like a continuous linear isomorphism in a strict sense, then the function is locally invertible near that point, and both the function and its inverse are continuous on some open neighborhood around the point.

label: HasStrictFDerivAt.to_localInverse
slogan: If a function has an invertible strict Frechet derivative at a point in a complete normed space over a nontrivially normed field, then near that point it has a continuously differentiable local inverse defined on an open set, and this inverse function has a derivative equal to the inverse of the original derivative. The local inverse is continuous, maps open sets to open sets, and the function and its inverse are locally homeomorphic. This result applies to functions between normed vector spaces and ensures smooth local invertibility when the derivative is invertible.

label: HasSumUniformlyOn.of_norm_le_summable
slogan: If the norms of the functions f n x are bounded by a summable sequence u n for all x in a set s, and the target space is a complete normed abelian group, then the series sum of f n x converges uniformly on s.

label: HenselianLocalRing
slogan: A Henselian local ring is a commutative ring with a unique maximal ideal where roots of polynomials can be lifted from the residue field back to the ring, provided the ring satisfies Hensel's lemma. It combines the algebraic structure of a commutative ring with the special lifting property of a Henselian ring and the uniqueness of a maximal ideal in a local ring. This concept is useful in algebraic geometry and number theory for studying solutions to polynomial equations.

label: HenselianRing
slogan: A HenselianRing is a commutative ring with a special ideal such that any polynomial equation that has a solution modulo the ideal can be "lifted" to an actual solution in the ring, under mild conditions. This lifting property allows solving polynomial equations approximately and then refining the solutions to higher precision. It is useful in number theory and geometry when working with completions or local properties of rings.

label: Heyting.IsRegular
slogan: An element a in a Heyting algebra is regular if, after taking the complement of a and then the complement of that result, you get back to a. This means that the double complement of a equals a. The property relies on the existence of a complement operation on the type.

label: Heyting.Regular.instBooleanAlgebra
slogan: The set of elements in a Heyting algebra that are equal to their double complement forms a Boolean algebra, meaning they support operations like meet, join, complement, and implication in a way that satisfies the laws of classical logic. These regular elements inherit their structure from the original algebra and are closed under the Boolean operations. This construction ensures that double negation elimination holds for these elements.

label: Heyting.Regular.toRegular
slogan: For any element a in a Heyting algebra, toRegular(a) gives the smallest regular element (one that equals its double complement) that is greater than or equal to a. This operation maps elements into the subtype of regular elements, which form a Boolean algebra under the inherited order and operations.

label: Heyting.isRegular_compl
slogan: In a Heyting algebra, the complement of any element is regular, meaning that taking the complement twice brings you back to the original element. This relies on the algebraic structure providing a complement operation. The result follows from the general property that three complements equal one.

label: HeytingAlgebra
slogan: A HeytingAlgebra is a type of ordered structure that includes a meet operation, a join operation, a top element, a bottom element (bot), a complement operation ('), and an implication operation (=>), where the complement and implication follow rules consistent with constructive logic. It builds on a lattice with a smallest element and a logical "not" operation, ensuring that the complement interacts properly with the order and logical operations. This structure supports reasoning about propositions where truth values are not necessarily boolean.

label: HeytingAlgebra.ofHImp
slogan: A Heyting algebra is built from a distributive lattice with a bottom element, where an implication operation is defined such that x implies y is the largest element z for which the meet of x and z is less than or equal to y. This means x ≤ (y implies z) exactly when (x and y) ≤ z, capturing a form of logical implication that aligns with intuitionistic logic. The structure supports reasoning about propositions in constructive mathematics and generalizes the behavior of open sets in topology.

label: HeytingHom
slogan: A HeytingHom is a function between two Heyting algebras that preserves the operations for combining elements (meet and join) and also preserves the implication operation. It ensures that logical structure, including how elements relate under implication, is maintained when mapping from one algebra to another. This function respects the core operations of constructive logic represented in the algebra.

label: HilbertBasis
slogan: A Hilbert basis for an inner product space E over a real-like field 𝕜 is a way to represent E as the space of square-summable sequences indexed by ι, meaning E is structurally equivalent to the l2 space of functions from ι to 𝕜. This provides a coordinate system for E where vectors correspond to sequences with finite squared norm. The basis ensures a one-to-one, structure-preserving match between elements of E and those sequences.

label: HilbertBasis.hasSum_repr
slogan: For any vector in a Hilbert space with a given Hilbert basis, the sum of the basis vectors scaled by their corresponding coefficients in the basis representation converges to the original vector. This means decomposing a vector into basis components and then summing those components reconstructs the vector exactly. The convergence is unconditional, meaning the sum is stable under rearrangement of terms.

label: HilbertBasis.mkOfOrthogonalEqBot
slogan: If a family of vectors is orthonormal and the only vector orthogonal to all of them is zero, then they form a Hilbert basis for the space. This means the vectors provide a complete coordinate system where every element of the space can be uniquely represented as a square-summable sequence. The space must be complete, and the field must behave like the real or complex numbers.

label: HilbertBasis.tsum_inner_mul_inner
slogan: For any Hilbert basis in an inner product space, the sum over all basis elements of the product of the inner product of x with a basis element and the inner product of that basis element with y equals the inner product of x and y. This sum converges unconditionally, meaning the result does not depend on the order of summation. It reflects the completeness and orthonormality of the basis in representing inner products through coordinate-wise operations.

label: HilbertSpace
slogan: A Hilbert space is a vector space with an inner product that allows measuring angles and distances, where every Cauchy sequence converges to a point inside the space. It combines the algebraic properties of vectors and inner products with the analytic property of completeness. This makes it a natural setting for extending finite-dimensional geometry to infinite dimensions, such as in functional analysis.

label: HolderWith
slogan: A function f between two spaces with a generalized distance measure is called Holder continuous with constant C and exponent r if the distance between f(x) and f(y) is at most C times the distance between x and y raised to the power r, for all points x and y. The values C and r are non-negative real numbers, and the condition must hold using extended non-negative distances. This property describes how much the function can stretch distances between points, controlled by the exponent r.

label: Homeomorph
slogan: A Homeomorph is a one-to-one and onto function between two topological spaces such that both the function and its inverse are continuous, meaning open sets in one space correspond exactly to open sets in the other. It ensures the spaces have the same topological structure. This combines a set-level equivalence (Equiv) with continuity in both directions.

label: Homeomorph.addRight
slogan: The function Homeomorph.addRight takes a fixed element a in a topological additive group G and maps each element x to x + a, producing a homeomorphism from G to itself; this means the map is bijective, continuous, and has a continuous inverse because addition is continuous and every element has an additive inverse.

label: Homeomorph.inv
slogan: Homeomorph.inv gives a function that maps each element of a topological space with a continuous, involutive inverse to its inverse, and this function is a homeomorphism — meaning it is continuous, bijective, and its inverse is also continuous. It ensures the inverse operation respects both the topology and the algebraic structure. This works when inversion is well-behaved, meaning applying it twice returns the original element and it interacts nicely with open sets.

label: Homeomorph.isOpenMap
slogan: A homeomorphism is a function between two topological spaces that maps open sets to open sets. This means if a set is open in the first space, its image under the homeomorphism is open in the second space. Such a function preserves the topological structure, ensuring continuity in both directions.

label: Homeomorph.mulLeft
slogan: Multiplying all elements of a topological group on the left by a fixed element gives a function that is continuous, bijective, and has a continuous inverse. This function preserves both the group's algebraic structure and the space's topological structure. It is a homeomorphism from the group to itself.

label: Homeomorph.symm
slogan: A homeomorphism is a reversible, continuous mapping between two topological spaces, and the symm function gives its inverse, which is also continuous and bijective. This inverse is itself a homeomorphism, allowing safe conversion in both directions while preserving open sets. The operation ensures that if two spaces are homeomorphic, going back and forth between them maintains their full topological structure.

label: Homeomorph.toHomotopyEquiv
slogan: A homeomorphism between two topological spaces is automatically a homotopy equivalence, meaning that if two spaces are homeomorphic, then they are also homotopy equivalent. This is because a homeomorphism provides continuous maps in both directions whose compositions are homotopic to the identity maps.

label: Homeomorph.unitBall
slogan: A real normed vector space is topologically equivalent to its open unit ball, meaning there is a continuous, invertible mapping between the entire space and the ball of radius 1 centered at zero. This mapping sends each point x to (1 + ||x||^2)^(-1/2) times x, effectively scaling it to fit inside the unit ball. The inverse mapping is also continuous, preserving the space's topological structure.

label: HomologicalComplex
slogan: A HomologicalComplex represents a sequence of objects and maps in a category that has zero morphisms, where each map goes from one object to the next according to an index shape like a chain or cochain complex, and composing two consecutive maps always results in the zero map. It generalizes chain and cochain complexes to different indexing patterns and categories. The structure depends on the category, the indexing shape, and the presence of zero morphisms.

label: HomologicalComplex.Acyclic
slogan: A homological complex is called acyclic if, at every position, the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map, meaning no homology exists anywhere in the sequence. This requires the complex to be in a category with zero morphisms and to follow a specific indexing shape. Acyclicity generalizes exact sequences to various kinds of complexes in different categorical contexts.

label: HomologicalComplex.ExactAt
slogan: A HomologicalComplex.ExactAt checks that at a specific position in a sequence of objects and maps, the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map, meaning no unwanted elements are carried forward. This ensures the sequence is exact at that point, generalizing the idea of exactness in chain or cochain complexes. The sequence must follow a given index shape and have consecutive maps that compose to zero.

label: HomologicalComplex.Hom
slogan: HomologicalComplex.Hom describes a type of structure-preserving map between two homological complexes, which are sequences of objects and arrows where each consecutive pair composes to zero. These maps must respect the underlying shape and categorical structure, such as the presence of zero morphisms. It provides a formal way to handle morphisms between complexes in algebraic settings like homology theory.

label: HomologicalComplex.d_comp_d
slogan: In a homological complex, applying one differential map after another in sequence always gives the zero map, meaning the image of one map is contained in the kernel of the next. This property holds for any three consecutive positions in the complex, within a category that supports zero morphisms and a defined complex structure.

label: HomologicalComplex.eulerChar
slogan: The Euler characteristic of a homological complex is calculated by summing the ranks of its components at each index, with each term multiplied by a sign determined by the complex's shape, using a finite sum; if the complex has infinitely many non-zero components, the characteristic is zero. This value is always an integer and depends on the underlying algebraic structure of modules over a ring. The computation relies on the complex having a well-defined shape that supports assigning alternating signs to the terms.

label: HomologicalComplex.homology
slogan: The homology of a homological complex at a given position is the quotient of cycles (elements mapped to zero) by boundaries (elements that come from the previous map), computed using kernels and images in a category with zero morphisms. It measures how far the complex is from being exact at that position, meaning how much the image of one map fails to cover the kernel of the next. This is defined for complexes indexed by shapes like chain or cochain complexes, where consecutive maps compose to zero.

label: HomologicalComplex.homologyEulerChar
slogan: The homology Euler characteristic is defined as the alternating sum of the ranks of the homology groups of a complex, taken over all indices, with signs determined by the complex shape; it returns zero if infinitely many homology groups have non-zero rank.

label: HomologicalComplex.homologyFunctor
slogan: The homologyFunctor takes a chain map between homological complexes and produces a map between their homology objects, in a way that sends identity maps to identity maps and preserves the composition of maps. It operates in any category with zero morphisms where homology can be defined, turning complexes and chain maps into objects and morphisms in the base category. This makes homology a well-behaved functor from the category of complexes to the underlying category.

label: HomologicalComplex₂
slogan: A bicomplex in a category C with two given shapes c1 and c2 is a complex of complexes: it is a complex indexed by c1, where each object in the complex is itself a complex in C indexed by c2. The object at position (i1, i2) in the bicomplex is obtained by taking the i2-th object of the i1-th complex. This structure requires the category C to have zero morphisms and allows building double complexes in homological algebra.

label: HomologicalComplex₂.total
