slogan: The set of elements in a Lie algebra that act trivially under the adjoint map is exactly the set of elements that commute with all others under the Lie bracket. In other words, the kernel of the adjoint representation equals the center of the Lie algebra. This means an element is in the center if and only if it induces zero derivation via the adjoint action.

label: LieDerivation.inner
slogan: For a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring R and an L-module M, the inner derivation map sends each element of M to a derivation from L to M, where the derivation is defined by the Lie action of L on M. This map is linear over R. It provides a canonical way to view elements of M as Lie derivations.

label: LieEquiv
slogan: A LieEquiv is a bijective linear map between two Lie algebras that preserves addition, scalar multiplication, and the Lie bracket, meaning it fully respects both the vector space and Lie algebra structures; because it is invertible and structure-preserving, it shows the two Lie algebras are algebraically identical in every aspect.

label: LieGroup
slogan: A LieGroup is a group that is also a smooth manifold, where multiplying elements and taking inverses are smooth operations. It combines the algebraic structure of a group with the geometric and topological structure of a manifold in a way that ensures compatibility between the two. The smoothness is defined relative to a model space over a normed field, using charts to coordinate the local geometry.

label: LieHom
slogan: A LieHom is a function between two Lie algebras over the same commutative ring that preserves addition, scalar multiplication, and the Lie bracket operation. It is a linear map that also respects the algebraic structure defined by the bracket. This means the map commutes with both the vector space operations and the bracket of elements.

label: LieHom.quotKerEquivRange
slogan: For a Lie algebra homomorphism f from L to L', the quotient of L by the kernel of f is isomorphic to the image of f, with the isomorphism preserving both the module and Lie bracket structure.

label: LieIdeal
slogan: A Lie ideal is a subset of a Lie ring that is closed under addition, additive inverses, and taking Lie brackets with any element of the ring, so bracketing an ideal element with any ring element stays in the ideal. When the Lie ring is part of a Lie algebra over a commutative ring, the ideal also respects the module structure.

label: LieModule
slogan: A Lie module is a setup where a Lie algebra, built over a commutative ring, acts on a module in a way that respects both the module's addition and scalar multiplication, as well as the Lie bracket operation. This action generalizes how vectors transform under symmetries encoded by the Lie algebra. The structure combines linear algebra with the algebraic properties of Lie brackets.

label: LieModule.IsFaithful
slogan: A Lie module is faithful if the only element of the Lie algebra that acts as zero on all elements of the module is the zero element itself. This means the action of the Lie algebra on the module is injective, so the module fully captures the algebra's structure. If an algebra element does nothing to any module element, it must be zero.

label: LieModule.IsNilpotent
slogan: A Lie module is nilpotent if repeatedly applying the Lie bracket action eventually sends everything to zero after finitely many steps. This means the module's structure becomes trivial under repeated bracket operations. It combines the idea of a group with a special kind of multiplication that measures non-commutativity.

label: LieModule.weightSpace
slogan: Given a Lie algebra representation M and a function χ mapping elements of the Lie algebra to scalars, the weight space for χ is the set of all vectors in M that are eigenvectors for the action of every element x in the Lie algebra with eigenvalue χ(x), and this set forms a Lie submodule of M.

label: LieRing
slogan: A Lie ring is a set with addition and negation that work like in regular arithmetic, plus a bracket operation [a, b] that is bilinear, alternating, and satisfies the Jacobi identity. It combines the structure of an abelian group under addition with a non-commutative multiplication-like operation. This setup is used to study infinitesimal symmetries in algebra and geometry.

label: LieRing.ofAssociativeRing
slogan: Any ring with standard addition and multiplication can be viewed as a Lie ring by defining the Lie bracket of two elements a and b as the commutator a * b - b * a, using the ring's own operations.

label: LieRing.of_associative_ring_bracket
slogan: Any ring with multiplication and subtraction can form a Lie ring by defining the bracket of two elements a and b as a * b - b * a; this operation satisfies antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity, making the ring a Lie ring.

label: LieSubalgebra
slogan: A Lie subalgebra is a subset of a Lie algebra that includes zero, is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, and remains closed when the Lie bracket of any two of its elements is taken. It is both a submodule and a Lie ring under the same operations. This means it preserves the combined module and Lie algebra structure over a commutative ring.

label: LieSubalgebra.IsCartanSubalgebra
slogan: A Cartan subalgebra is a nilpotent subalgebra that is equal to its own normalizer within the Lie algebra. It is a special kind of subalgebra that plays a key role in the structure theory of Lie algebras, particularly when it can diagonalize the action on the full algebra via the adjoint representation. A splitting Cartan subalgebra further requires that this action is triangularizable over the base ring.

label: LieSubalgebra.lieSpan
slogan: The lieSpan of a set in a Lie algebra is the smallest Lie subalgebra containing that set, formed by taking the intersection of all Lie subalgebras that include the set. It includes all elements needed to be closed under addition, scalar multiplication, and the Lie bracket operation. This gives a way to generate a subalgebra from any subset of the Lie algebra.

label: LieSubalgebra.normalizer
slogan: For any Lie subalgebra H of a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring, the set of elements in L that normalize H forms a Lie subalgebra of L. This means the normalizer is closed under the Lie bracket, addition, and scalar multiplication, and contains zero. It extends the structure of H while preserving the algebraic properties needed for a Lie subalgebra.

label: LieSubmodule.Quotient.lieQuotientLieAlgebra
slogan: When you take a Lie algebra and divide it by a Lie ideal, the resulting quotient space naturally forms a new Lie algebra over the same ring, with the Lie bracket defined on cosets in a way that respects the original bracket structure.

label: LinOrd
slogan: LinOrd describes a type with a total order where any two elements can be compared, and the ordering is reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and total. It is used to define ordered structures up to isomorphism, meaning two ordered types are equivalent if they have the same order pattern. The collection of all such order-equivalent types is captured by the OrderType universe.

label: LindelofSpace
slogan: A Lindelof space is a topological space where every open cover has a countable subcover, meaning that any collection of open sets covering the space can be reduced to a countable number of sets that still cover the whole space. It is a weaker form of compactness that only requires countable subcovers.

label: LinearEquiv.finrank_eq
slogan: If two modules over the same semiring are connected by a bijective linear map (a structure-preserving bijection), then their finite dimensions (the sizes of their bases) are equal as natural numbers. This means that isomorphic modules have the same rank when the rank is finite. The result relies on the fact that linear isomorphisms preserve linear independence and spanning sets.

label: LinearEquiv.isReflexive_of_equiv_dual_of_isReflexive
slogan: If a module N is linearly isomorphic to the dual of a reflexive module M over a commutative ring, then N is also reflexive, meaning it is naturally isomorphic to its double dual via evaluation.

label: LinearExtension
slogan: A linear extension of a partial order on a type α is a total order on α such that whenever one element is less than or equal to another in the original partial order, it remains so in the total order.

label: LinearIndependent
slogan: A set of vectors is linearly independent if the only way to combine them using scalars and addition to get zero is by using all zero scalars. This means no vector in the set can be expressed as a sum of scalar multiples of the others. The definition works in a general setting where vectors form an additive commutative monoid and scalars form a semiring, using functions with finite support to handle the combinations.

label: LinearIsometry
slogan: A LinearIsometry is a linear map between two normed spaces that preserves vector lengths, meaning the norm of f(x) equals the norm of x for all vectors x. It respects both the algebraic structure of modules and the geometric notion of distance. The map is defined over semirings and modules, using a ring homomorphism to relate the scalar actions.

label: LinearIsometry.inner_map_map
slogan: A linear isometry between inner product spaces preserves the inner product, meaning the inner product of two vectors is the same as the inner product of their images under the map. This holds because the map respects vector addition, scalar multiplication, and norm, and therefore also preserves subtraction and the overall structure of the space. The result follows from the fact that such structure-preserving maps maintain all geometric relationships defined by the inner product.

label: LinearIsometry.isConformalMap
slogan: A linear isometry between two normed spaces over the same normed field preserves angles and acts as a conformal map, meaning it scales all vectors uniformly by a nonzero factor without distorting angles. Even though it preserves lengths exactly, it still satisfies the condition of being a nonzero scalar multiple of an isometry—specifically, the scalar is 1. Thus, every linear isometry is automatically a conformal map.

label: LinearIsometryEquiv
slogan: A LinearIsometryEquiv is a bijective linear map between two normed modules that preserves distances and the algebraic structure, with an inverse that does the same, ensuring the spaces are identical in both shape and vector properties. It combines a linear equivalence and a distance-preserving map, using compatible ring homomorphisms to relate the scalar actions. The spaces involved are seminormed abelian groups with scalar multiplication over semirings.

label: LinearIsometryEquiv.measurePreserving
slogan: A linear isometry between finite-dimensional real inner product spaces preserves volume, meaning the measure of any set stays the same after applying the transformation. This happens because such a map does not stretch or shrink space, as its determinant has absolute value 1. The volume measure on both spaces remains unchanged under the mapping.

label: LinearIsometryEquiv.reflections_generate_dim
slogan: In a finite-dimensional real inner product space, every linear isometry (a distance-preserving linear map from the space to itself) can be written as a composition of reflections across hyperplanes orthogonal to nonzero vectors, and the number of such reflections needed is at most the dimension of the space.

label: LinearIsometryEquiv.toMatrix_mem_unitaryGroup
slogan: If a linear isometry between two finite-dimensional inner product spaces over the complex numbers is expressed as a matrix using orthonormal bases, then that matrix has the property that its conjugate transpose is its inverse, meaning it belongs to the unitary group.

label: LinearMap
slogan: A LinearMap is a function between two modules that preserves addition and scalar multiplication, so f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b) and f(r * a) = r * f(a) for all scalars r and elements a, b. It combines the properties of a function that respects both additive structure and scaling. This ensures the map is compatible with the algebraic operations defined by the semiring.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm
slogan: A bilinear form is a function that takes two vectors from a module over a commutative semiring and returns a scalar, being linear in each vector when the other is fixed. It is defined for types equipped with addition and scalar multiplication that follow standard algebraic rules. The types R and M represent coefficient and module structures used in this context, though they are not part of the form itself.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.IsAlt.neg_eq
slogan: If a bilinear form is alternating, meaning it gives zero when both inputs are the same, then applying it to the negatives of two vectors gives the same result as applying it to the original vectors: B(-x, -y) = B(x, y). This follows from the form's linearity and the fact that alternating forms vanish on equal arguments.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.IsOrtho
slogan: Two elements are orthogonal with respect to a bilinear form if the form evaluated at those elements equals zero. This means the bilinear map returns zero when applied to the pair of elements. Orthogonality here is defined relative to a given bilinear form over a module with a commutative semiring of scalars.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate
slogan: A bilinear form is nondegenerate if the only vector that pairs to zero with every other vector is the zero vector itself, meaning no nonzero vector is orthogonal to the whole space. This condition ensures the form distinguishes between vectors on both inputs. It is equivalent to saying the associated maps in either argument are injective.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.apply_dualBasis_left
slogan: If you have a nondegenerate bilinear form B on a finite-dimensional vector space with a basis b, then applying B to a dual basis vector (from the dual basis induced by B and b) and a basis vector b_j gives 1 if they correspond to the same index and 0 otherwise. This means the dual basis vectors act as coordinate extractors under the bilinear form. The result follows from how the dual basis is defined and how B interacts with the basis and its dual.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.dualBasis
slogan: Given a finite basis for a vector space over a field and a nondegenerate bilinear form, the dual basis consists of linear functionals that return 1 on their corresponding basis vector and 0 on all others, and this dual basis spans the entire dual space.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.dualBasis_dualBasis_flip
slogan: If a bilinear form is nondegenerate and the vector space is finite-dimensional with a given basis, then taking the dual basis of the flipped dual basis recovers the original basis; this means the bilinear form, when applied with the flipped dual elements, acts as the identity on the basis vectors.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.exists_orthogonal_basis
slogan: For any symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field where 2 has an inverse, there is a basis in which all basis vectors are pairwise orthogonal with respect to the form.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.iIsOrtho
slogan: A set of vectors v is considered orthogonal with respect to a bilinear form B if, whenever two vectors in the set are different (i ≠ j), the form B applied to those two vectors equals zero. This means orthogonality is defined pairwise across the index set n. The property depends on the algebraic structures of the ring R, the module M, and the bilinear map B.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.nondegenerate_iff_ker_eq_bot
slogan: A bilinear form is nondegenerate exactly when the only vector that pairs to zero with every other vector is the zero vector, which means the kernel of the associated linear map contains only the zero element.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.toDual
slogan: A nondegenerate bilinear form on a finite-dimensional vector space lets you turn each vector into a linear function on the space, by fixing one argument of the form. This mapping from vectors to linear functions is injective, and because the space is finite-dimensional, it is also surjective, making it a one-to-one correspondence that preserves linear structure. The key requirement is that the only vector which pairs to zero with every other vector is the zero vector itself.

label: LinearMap.BilinForm.toMatrix
slogan: Given a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional module over a commutative semiring and a chosen basis, this function maps the bilinear form to a matrix whose entries are the values of the form evaluated on all pairs of basis vectors. The matrix has rows and columns indexed by the basis elements, and the function is an isomorphism between bilinear forms and square matrices when the basis index set is finite and has decidable equality.

label: LinearMap.GeneralLinearGroup.generalLinearEquiv
slogan: The generalLinearEquiv function sets up a one-to-one match between invertible linear maps from a module M to itself and the elements of the general linear group of M, showing that each invertible linear map corresponds exactly to a linear equivalence. This correspondence preserves the way these maps compose, meaning the group structure is maintained on both sides. It essentially says that working with invertible linear maps is the same as working with the group of linear equivalences.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric
slogan: A linear map T is symmetric if, for any two vectors v and w, the inner product of T(v) with w equals the inner product of v with T(w). This must hold for all vector pairs in a space equipped with an inner product over a real-like or complex-like field. The map T must also preserve vector addition and scalar multiplication.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.conj_eigenvalue_eq_self
slogan: The eigenvalues of a self-adjoint linear operator are real numbers. This means that if a linear map satisfies the symmetry condition in an inner product space, then any eigenvalue associated with it must equal its own complex conjugate. In other words, complex conjugation does not change the eigenvalue, so it must be a real number.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.direct_sum_isInternal
slogan: A self-adjoint linear operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space has eigenspaces that together form a direct sum decomposition of the entire space. This means every vector in the space can be uniquely written as a sum of vectors from each eigenspace. The result relies on the operator being symmetric and the space having finite dimension.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.eigenvectorBasis
slogan: For a self-adjoint linear operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space, this provides a basis of eigenvectors that are orthonormal and ordered so that their corresponding eigenvalues decrease. The basis is indexed by the numbers 0 to n-1, where n is the dimension of the space. Each vector in the basis is an eigenvector of the operator, and no two are in the same direction.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.eigenvectorBasis_apply_self_apply
slogan: A self-adjoint linear operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space can be represented as a diagonal matrix when using an orthonormal basis made up of its eigenvectors, and the diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues. Applying the operator to a vector is the same as scaling each component of the vector (in the eigenvector basis) by the corresponding eigenvalue. This means the operator acts component-wise in that basis, with each component multiplied by a real eigenvalue.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.hasEigenvalue_iSup_of_finiteDimensional
slogan: The largest value of the Rayleigh quotient for a symmetric linear operator on a finite-dimensional real or complex vector space is an eigenvalue of that operator. This holds when the space has more than just the zero vector. The Rayleigh quotient measures the ratio of the inner product of the operator applied to a vector with itself, divided by the squared norm of the vector.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.orthogonalFamily_eigenspaces
slogan: For a self-adjoint linear operator on an inner product space, the eigenspaces corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal to each other.

label: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.toSelfAdjoint
slogan: If a linear map on a complete inner product space over the real or complex numbers is symmetric (meaning the inner product of T(x) with y equals the inner product of x with T(y) for all vectors x and y), then it is continuous and can be viewed as a self-adjoint operator in the space of continuous linear maps. This result relies on the completeness of the space and the fact that symmetric operators defined everywhere are automatically continuous. The theorem provides a way to treat such symmetric maps as self-adjoint elements within the algebra of bounded operators.

label: LinearMap.aeval_self_charpoly
slogan: When a linear transformation acts on a finite-dimensional module over a commutative ring, substituting the transformation into its own characteristic polynomial gives the zero transformation. This means every linear map satisfies its characteristic equation.

label: LinearMap.card_support_singularValues
slogan: The number of nonzero singular values of a linear map T between finite-dimensional inner product spaces equals the dimension of the range of T. This count includes each singular value only once, regardless of multiplicity, and matches the rank of the map. The result holds for vector spaces over real-like fields with complete normed structure.

label: LinearMap.charpoly
slogan: The charpoly of a linear map is found by turning the map into a matrix with respect to chosen bases and then computing the characteristic polynomial of that matrix, which is the determinant of (x times the identity matrix minus the matrix). This polynomial has coefficients in the same commutative ring as the matrix entries and is used to study eigenvalues and other properties of the map.

label: LinearMap.comp
slogan: LinearMap.comp takes two linear maps, one from M1 to M2 and another from M2 to M3, and returns their composition as a new linear map from M1 to M3. This composition applies the first map and then the second, preserving both addition and scalar multiplication. The result is guaranteed to be a linear map when the underlying ring homomorphisms are compatible.

label: LinearMap.continuous_iff_isClosed_ker
slogan: A linear map from a finite-dimensional topological vector space to the underlying normed field is continuous if and only if the set of vectors it sends to zero (its kernel) is a closed set. This means the map respects limits precisely when the kernel contains all its limit points. The result connects continuity of linear maps to the topological behavior of their kernels.

label: LinearMap.continuous_of_finiteDimensional
slogan: Any linear map from a finite-dimensional vector space over a complete nontrivially normed field to a normed space is automatically continuous, because all norms on such a space induce the same topology and force linear maps to preserve limits.

label: LinearMap.continuous_of_isClosed_graph
slogan: If a linear map between two Banach spaces has a graph that is a closed set, then the map is continuous. This means that whenever the set of all input-output pairs forms a closed subset of the product space, the function preserves limits. As a result, small changes in the input lead to small changes in the output.

label: LinearMap.continuous_of_seq_closed_graph
slogan: If a linear map between two complete normed spaces sends convergent sequences of inputs to sequences whose outputs converge to the right limit, then the map is continuous. Specifically, whenever a sequence of input-output pairs converges to (x, y) and the inputs converge to x, then y must equal the map's value at x. This ensures continuity based on the behavior of sequences in normed spaces.

label: LinearMap.convMul
slogan: Given a commutative semiring R, an R-algebra A, and an R-coalgebra C, the convolution product of two R-linear maps from C to A is defined by composing their tensor product with the multiplication in A and the comultiplication in C, resulting in another R-linear map from C to A. This operation equips the space of linear maps with a multiplicative structure. It generalizes the idea of multiplying functions via convolution in algebraic settings.

label: LinearMap.convSemiring
slogan: If R is a commutative semiring, A is a semiring that is also an R-algebra, and C is a coalgebra over R, then the set of R-linear maps from C to A can be given a semiring structure where multiplication is defined by convolution. This means you can add such linear maps pointwise and multiply them using the coalgebra structure of C and the algebra structure of A. The resulting structure satisfies the usual rules of a semiring, including distributivity and the existence of additive and multiplicative identities.

label: LinearMap.det
slogan: The det function takes a linear map from a module to itself and returns a scalar value from the underlying commutative ring, representing the factor by which the map scales volumes. This value is multiplicative: the determinant of a composition of maps equals the product of their determinants. The function is defined only for endomorphisms on modules over commutative rings, and it respects the algebraic structure of linear maps.

label: LinearMap.dualMap
slogan: Given a linear map f from module M1 to module M2 over a commutative semiring R, the dualMap creates a linear map from the dual of M2 to the dual of M1 by composing each linear functional on M2 with f; this turns a functional that acts on M2 into one that acts on M1, preserving linearity and scalar multiplication.

label: LinearMap.finrank_eigenspace_le
slogan: The dimension of the eigenspace for a given eigenvalue is less than or equal to the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial. This means the number of linearly independent eigenvectors for an eigenvalue cannot exceed how many times it appears as a root in the characteristic equation.

label: LinearMap.finrank_maxGenEigenspace_eq
slogan: The dimension of the largest generalized eigenspace of a linear operator φ corresponding to an eigenvalue μ is equal to the multiplicity of μ as a root of the characteristic polynomial of φ. This holds for linear operators on finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field. The result connects the algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue to the size of its generalized eigenspace.

label: LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker
slogan: For a linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces, the dimension of the output space (range) plus the dimension of the input space that maps to zero (kernel) equals the dimension of the full input space.

label: LinearMap.hasEigenvalue_adjoint_comp_self_sq_singularValues
slogan: For a linear map T between finite-dimensional inner product spaces, the square of each singular value of T is an eigenvalue of the composition of the adjoint of T with T itself.

label: LinearMap.injective_iff_surjective_of_finrank_eq_finrank
slogan: For a linear map between two finite-dimensional vector spaces of the same dimension, being injective (sending distinct inputs to distinct outputs) is equivalent to being surjective (hitting every point in the output space). This means that if the map doesn't collapse any nonzero vectors to zero, then it must cover the entire target space, and vice versa. The result depends on the equality of the dimensions of the domain and codomain.

label: LinearMap.isUnit_iff_isUnit_det
slogan: A linear map from a finite-dimensional free module to itself is invertible if and only if its determinant is an invertible element in the base ring. This means the map can be reversed precisely when its determinant has a multiplicative inverse. The result links the invertibility of the map to the algebraic property of its determinant.

label: LinearMap.ker
slogan: LinearMap.ker takes a linear map between two modules and returns the set of all elements in the domain that are mapped to zero, forming a submodule. This set includes zero, is closed under addition, and remains closed when elements are multiplied by scalars from the underlying semiring. It is constructed by taking the preimage of the zero submodule under the linear map.

label: LinearMap.ker_eq_bot
slogan: A linear map sends only the zero element to zero if and only if it is injective, meaning different inputs always produce different outputs.

label: LinearMap.lsmul
slogan: LinearMap.lsmul is a function that takes a scalar and a vector and returns the scalar multiple of that vector, and it does so in a way that is linear with respect to both the scalar and the vector. This means scaling a vector and then applying the map behaves the same as applying the map first and then scaling, and adding vectors or scalars before applying the map works the same as doing so after. The operation follows the standard rules of distributivity and associativity for scalar multiplication.

label: LinearMap.map_add
slogan: A linear map f satisfies f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) for all elements x and y, meaning it respects addition. This holds between modules over semirings, where the map also preserves scalar multiplication. The function thus maintains the additive structure of the module.

label: LinearMap.map_zero
slogan: A linear map takes the zero element of a module to the zero element of another module, meaning applying the map to zero always results in zero. This holds because linear maps preserve the structure of addition and scalar multiplication.

label: LinearMap.proj
slogan: LinearMap.proj i is a function that picks out the i-th component from a tuple of elements in a product of modules, and it does so in a way that respects addition and scalar multiplication. It maps from the full product space to just the i-th module, preserving the module operations. This projection is defined for any index i in the indexing type and works within the structure of modules over a semiring.

label: LinearMap.quotKerEquivRange
slogan: Every linear map gives a natural one-to-one linear correspondence between the quotient space of its domain modulo its kernel and its image, where each coset in the quotient maps to the image of any representative under the original map. This induced map is both linear and bijective, effectively making the quotient space isomorphic to the range. The result shows that factoring out the kernel recovers the full structure of the map's output space.

label: LinearMap.quotientInfEquivSupQuotient
slogan: For two submodules p and p' of a module M over a ring R, the quotient of p by the intersection of p and p' is isomorphic to a submodule of the product of the quotients of p and p' by their sum; this isomorphism maps each coset in the intersection quotient to a pair of corresponding cosets in the individual quotients and preserves module operations. The map is one-to-one and onto its image, ensuring a perfect structural match. This allows the quotient by an intersection to be understood in terms of simpler, separate quotients.

label: LinearMap.rank
slogan: The rank of a linear map is the size of a basis for the set of all outputs the map can produce, measured as a cardinal number. It is defined as the dimension of the range, which is the subspace in the target space formed by applying the map to every element of the domain. This definition relies on the general notion of module rank, which counts the maximum number of linearly independent vectors in a module.

label: LinearMap.rank_range_add_rank_ker
slogan: The dimension of the output space of a linear map plus the dimension of the space that maps to zero equals the dimension of the input space, assuming the input space has a well-defined finite dimension. This result holds for linear maps between modules over a ring where the necessary rank conditions are satisfied.

label: LinearMap.sq_singularValues_fin
slogan: For a linear map T between finite-dimensional inner product spaces over the real or complex numbers, the square of the i-th singular value of T equals the i-th eigenvalue of the self-adjoint operator T*∘T, where the eigenvalues are listed in decreasing order and indexed from 0 to n-1 with n being the dimension of the domain space.

label: LinearMap.toAffineMap
slogan: A linear map between two modules can be turned into an affine map by adding a fixed vector to the result, making it act like a linear transformation followed by a shift; this works because every additive group naturally acts on itself by addition, allowing the linear part to fit into the structure of an affine space.

label: LinearMap.toContinuousLinearMap
slogan: In a finite-dimensional vector space over a complete field with a nontrivial norm, every linear map to another normed space is automatically continuous, so it can be treated as a continuous linear map without additional assumptions.

label: LinearMap.toMatrix_comp
slogan: The matrix of the composition of two linear maps is the same as the product of their matrices, when using consistent bases for all spaces. This means you can either compose the maps first and then convert to a matrix, or convert each to a matrix first and then multiply. The result holds for finite-dimensional modules over a commutative semiring with decidable basis equality.

label: LinearMap.toMatrix_id
slogan: The matrix of the identity linear map, when computed with respect to any finite basis, is the identity matrix. This means multiplying a vector's coordinate representation by this matrix leaves the coordinates unchanged. The result applies to modules over a commutative semiring where the basis is finite and has decidable equality.

label: LinearMap.toMatrix_transpose
slogan: The matrix of the transpose of a linear map, with respect to the dual bases, is the transpose of the matrix of the original linear map. This means that dualizing the map and converting it to a matrix is the same as transposing the matrix after converting the original map. The result holds when using paired dual bases on the domain and codomain.

label: LinearMap.toMatrix₂
slogan: Given a linear map from one finite-dimensional module to another over a commutative semiring, with fixed bases on both modules, this function turns the map into a matrix by recording the images of the source basis vectors in terms of the target basis. The entries of the matrix are elements of the target module, indexed by the basis coordinates, and the conversion assumes decidable equality on the index types. This establishes a one-to-one correspondence between such linear maps and matrices of appropriate dimensions.

label: LinearMap.trace
slogan: The trace function takes a linear map from a finite-dimensional module to itself over a commutative semiring and returns a scalar value equal to the sum of the diagonal elements of any matrix representation of the map, with this sum being independent of the choice of basis. It is defined as a linear map from the space of endomorphisms to the underlying semiring. The result captures a fundamental, basis-independent property of the linear transformation.

label: LinearOrder
slogan: A LinearOrder is a way to arrange elements of a type so that any two elements can be compared, with clear rules for minimum and maximum, and where the ordering is consistent (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric) and total (any two elements are ordered). It combines the ability to take mins and maxes with the logical structure of a partial order and requires that all elements are comparable. This setup ensures a full, consistent ranking of all elements in the type.

label: LinearPMap.IsClosable
slogan: A partial linear map between topological modules is closable if the closure of its graph, as a set of pairs, still forms the graph of some linear map. This means that extending the map by including limit points of its graph does not break its linearity or single-valued nature. The condition ensures the map can be meaningfully extended in a continuous way.

label: LinearPMap.IsClosed
slogan: A partial linear map between two topological modules is considered closed if its graph, meaning the set of all pairs (x, f(x)) where x is in the domain, forms a closed subset of the product space. This means that whenever a sequence of points in the graph converges, the limit point is also in the graph. The map must respect both the algebraic structure (linearity) and the topology (closedness in the product space).

label: LinearPMap.IsFormalAdjoint
slogan: Two linear maps T and S are formal adjoints if the inner product of T(x) with y equals the inner product of x with S(y) for all x and y in their respective domains. This means the action of one map on the first argument of the inner product can be transferred to the other map acting on the second argument. The definition applies to partial linear maps between inner product spaces over real-like scalars.

label: LinearPMap.adjoint
slogan: The adjoint of a linear map T between two inner product spaces is a new linear map that goes from the target space back to the source space, defined only on a certain subset where a specific inner product condition holds. It satisfies the property that the inner product of T(x) with y equals the inner product of x with the adjoint applied to y, whenever the adjoint is defined. This adjoint operator exists when the source space is complete.

label: LinearPMap.closure
slogan: If a partial linear map has a graph whose closure still defines a linear map, then its closure is that extended linear map; otherwise, the closure is just the original map itself.

label: LinearPMap.graph
slogan: The graph of a partial linear map consists of all pairs (x, y) where x is in the domain and y is the image of x under the map, forming a submodule of the product space E × F. This set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, preserving the linear structure even when the map is not defined on the whole space. It generalizes the graph of a linear map to cases where the domain may be restricted.

label: LinearRecurrence
slogan: A linear recurrence relation over a commutative semiring is defined by its order n and a list of n coefficients from the semiring, which determine how each term in a sequence is computed as a linear combination of the previous n terms.

label: LinearRecurrence.charPoly
slogan: The characteristic polynomial of a linear recurrence E over a commutative ring R is a polynomial formed by taking X raised to the order of E, minus the sum of each coefficient of E multiplied by X raised to the corresponding power. It is expressed using standard polynomial operations in R. This polynomial helps analyze the behavior of the recurrence relation.

label: Liouville
slogan: A Liouville number is a real number x such that for every natural number n, there are integers a and b, with b greater than 1, where the distance between x and the fraction a/b is positive and smaller than 1 divided by b to the power n. This means x can be approximated extremely closely by rational numbers. The definition uses x not equal to a/b to ensure the approximation is non-trivial.

label: Liouville.exists_pos_real_of_irrational_root
slogan: If a real number is irrational and is a root of a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients, then there exists a positive constant A such that for all integers a and natural numbers b, the distance between the irrational number and the fraction a/(b+1) is at least A divided by (b+1) raised to the degree of the polynomial.

label: Liouville.irrational
slogan: If a real number can be approximated extremely well by rational numbers, meaning for any natural number n there is a fraction a/b (with b > 1) such that the distance between the number and the fraction is positive and less than 1/b^n, then that number cannot be rational.

label: Liouville.transcendental
slogan: If a real number x can be approximated by rational numbers a/b so closely that for every natural number n there is a fraction a/b (with b > 1) such that the distance between x and a/b is less than 1/b^n, then x is transcendental, meaning it is not a root of any non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients.

label: LiouvilleWith
slogan: A real number x is called a Liouville number with exponent p if there is some constant C such that, for infinitely many positive integers n, there exists an integer m where x is not equal to m/n but the distance between x and m/n is less than C divided by n raised to the power p.

label: LipschitzOnWith
slogan: A function f is Lipschitz on a subset s of a space with an extended pseudometric if there is a non-negative real number K such that for any two points in s, the distance between their images under f is at most K times their original distance, where distances are measured in the extended non-negative reals (including infinity) and K is embedded into this system via ENNReal.ofNNReal.

label: LipschitzWith
slogan: A function f is K-Lipschitz if, for any two points, the distance between their images under f is at most K times the distance between the points, where distances can be infinite and K is a non-negative real number. This uses extended non-negative real numbers (including infinity) to handle cases where distances may be unbounded. The condition ensures the function does not stretch distances by more than a fixed factor K.

label: LipschitzWith.ae_differentiableAt
slogan: A Lipschitz continuous function between finite-dimensional real vector spaces is differentiable at almost every point with respect to Lebesgue measure.

label: LipschitzWith.locallyBoundedVariationOn
slogan: If a function from the real numbers to a pseudometric space is Lipschitz continuous with some constant C, then it has locally bounded variation on any subset of the real line. This means that on any bounded interval intersected with the set, the total variation of the function is finite.

label: LipschitzWith.uniformContinuous
slogan: A function whose outputs don't change faster than a fixed multiple of the input distance is uniformly continuous, meaning that for any desired output closeness, there's a single input closeness threshold that works everywhere in the space. This holds even when distances can be infinite, as in extended metric spaces. The Lipschitz condition directly provides the global control needed for uniform continuity.

label: List.Vector
slogan: List.Vector α n represents a list of exactly n elements, each of type α, where the length n is part of the type to ensure size correctness at compile time.

label: List.length
slogan: List.length counts the number of elements in a linked list and returns that count as a natural number. It works on lists of any type and is optimized to use constant stack space during execution. For example, an empty list has length 0, and a list with two items has length 2.

label: List.permutations
slogan: List.permutations takes a list and returns all possible ways to reorder its elements, with each permutation as a separate list in the result. It uses a helper function to build these orderings step by step, inserting each element into every position of existing partial arrangements. The output contains every unique arrangement of the original elements, with no duplicates.

label: List.prod
slogan: List.prod calculates the product of all elements in a list by multiplying them together from right to left, starting with 1 as the default if the list is empty. It works for any type that supports multiplication and has a multiplicative identity (1). The operation is implemented using a right fold (List.foldr) with multiplication as the combining function.

label: LocPathConnectedSpace
slogan: A space is locally path connected if, around every point, there are arbitrarily small neighborhoods that are path connected, meaning any two points in the neighborhood can be joined by a continuous path within it. This is defined by requiring that the neighborhood filter at each point has a basis made up entirely of path-connected sets. In simpler terms, for every point and every open set around it, there is a smaller open, path-connected set containing the point.

label: Localization.AtPrime
slogan: Localization at a prime ideal takes a commutative semiring and a prime ideal, then forms a new ring by allowing division by all elements not in the ideal. The set of elements outside the prime ideal is closed under multiplication and does not include 1, making it suitable for inversion. This localized ring reflects the structure of the original semiring near the prime ideal.

label: Localization.AtPrime.isLocalRing
slogan: When you form a new ring by allowing all elements outside a prime ideal to have multiplicative inverses, the resulting ring has exactly one maximal ideal, which consists of all elements that are not invertible. This new ring satisfies the definition of a local ring because the set of non-units is closed under addition. The construction uses standard algebraic operations and relies on the original ring being commutative and the ideal being prime.

label: LocalizedModule
slogan: LocalizedModule creates a new module from an existing module M over a commutative semiring R, where elements are fractions formed by pairing elements of M with denominators from a multiplicative submonoid S of R, and scalar multiplication is extended to allow fractions in the localized ring. The construction uses the Ore condition to define when two such fractions are equal and ensures that addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined. This allows working with modules over localized rings in a way that generalizes the original module structure.

label: LocallyConnectedSpace
slogan: A locally connected space is a topological space where every point has arbitrarily small connected open neighborhoods, meaning each neighborhood of a point contains a connected open set that includes the point. This is equivalent to saying the connected open sets form a basis for the topology. The property ensures the space is connected in a small enough region around each point.

label: LocallyConvexSpace
slogan: A locally convex space is a topological vector space where the topology around zero is generated by a collection of sets that are convex, balanced, and absorbing, and which respect the algebraic operations of addition and scalar multiplication. It is defined over a semiring with a partial order, and the space has a filter basis of neighborhoods of zero that ensure continuity of the vector space operations. The structure combines a topological space with a module structure, requiring the existence of a neighborhood basis with specific algebraic and topological properties.

label: LocallyConvexSpace.ofBases
slogan: A locally convex space is defined by having a neighborhood basis at each point where every neighborhood is convex, balanced, and absorbing, and the topology is compatible with the module structure over a semiring. The topology is determined by these convex neighborhoods, meaning a set is open if it contains a translate of one of these convex sets around each of its points. This setup ensures the space has a local base of convex sets at zero, making the vector space operations continuous and preserving the geometric structure needed for functional analysis.

label: LoopSpace
slogan: LoopSpace defines the set of all continuous paths in a topological space X that start and end at a given point x. This set of loops is itself treated as a space under the compact-open topology. It is denoted by Ω and is used to study the structure of the space X around the point x.

label: LowerSemicontinuous
slogan: A function is lower semicontinuous if, for every real number c, the set of points where the function value is greater than c is an open set in the given topology. This means the function does not suddenly drop below values in any neighborhood around a point. The function maps from a topological space into a set with a preorder relation.

label: LowerSemicontinuousOn.exists_isMinOn
slogan: If a function is lower semicontinuous on a nonempty compact set, then there is at least one point in that set where the function achieves its smallest value. This means the function actually reaches its minimum on the set. The result depends on the topology of the space and the ordering of the function's output values.

label: MDifferentiable
slogan: A function between manifolds is differentiable if, when you look at it in local coordinates, the corresponding function between normed vector spaces has a Fréchet derivative at each point, meaning it is well-approximated by a linear map near that point. This definition relies on the manifolds being modeled on normed spaces over a nontrivially normed field, with smoothly compatible charts. It generalizes the usual idea of differentiability to curved spaces by using coordinate patches.

label: MDifferentiable.comp
slogan: If two functions between manifolds are differentiable and their domains and codomains match up correctly, then their composition is also differentiable. This means that applying one differentiable function after another preserves smoothness on manifolds. The result relies on the spaces involved having compatible topological and normed structures with well-defined charts.

label: MDifferentiable.exists_eq_const_of_compactSpace
slogan: A holomorphic function defined on a compact and connected complex manifold must be constant, meaning it takes the same value everywhere on the manifold. That value is some fixed element in the target space.

label: MDifferentiableAt
slogan: A function between two manifolds is differentiable at a point if, when you map it into local coordinates using charts, the resulting function between normed vector spaces has a Fréchet derivative at that point, meaning it can be well-approximated by a linear map near the point. This definition depends on the manifolds having smooth structures modeled on normed spaces over a field with a nontrivial norm, and uses the idea that differentiability can be checked in coordinate patches. The property is defined by lifting the notion of differentiability from normed spaces to manifolds via compatible

label: MagmaCat
slogan: MagmaCat is the category whose objects are magmas—sets equipped with a binary operation written as multiplication—and whose morphisms are functions that preserve this operation. It is built using types where each type has a multiplication operation defined by the Mul class. The category is indexed by universe levels and lives in a higher universe.

label: Manifold.IsImmersion
slogan: A function f from manifold M to manifold N is a C^n immersion if, near each point in M, it can be represented in suitable local coordinates as the map u ↦ (u, 0), meaning it smoothly embeds a neighborhood into a higher-dimensional space by padding with zeros. This definition assumes a fixed choice of complement space that splits the target tangent space into the image of the source and an additional part. The condition requires this local behavior to hold consistently around every point in the domain.

label: Manifold.pathELength
slogan: The length of a path in a manifold, defined over the entire real line but restricted to a closed interval [a, b], is computed using the norm of the manifold derivative (mfderiv) integrated over that interval. This length is expressed as an extended nonnegative real number (including infinity) and accounts for the geometry of the manifold through its tangent space structure. The definition avoids complications from subtypes by working on the full real line while remaining equivalent to formulations using only the interval [a, b].

label: Manifold.pathELength_comp_of_monotoneOn
slogan: The length of a path in a manifold does not change when the path is reparametrized by a monotone and differentiable function over a closed interval. Specifically, composing the path with such a function preserves the path's length. This means that how fast or slow you traverse the path, as long as the direction isn't reversed, doesn't affect the total length.

label: Manifold.riemannianEDist
slogan: The Riemannian extended distance between two points in a manifold is the smallest total length of any continuously differentiable path connecting them, where path length is computed using an extended norm on tangent spaces. This distance is defined as the infimum over all such path lengths and takes values in the extended non-negative real numbers. It applies to manifolds whose tangent spaces are equipped with a structure that allows for infinite or finite norm values.

label: Manifold.riemannianEDist_le_pathELength
slogan: The Riemannian distance between two points on a manifold is always less than or equal to the length of any continuously differentiable path connecting them, as measured by integrating the norm of the path's derivative over a closed interval.

label: ManyOneReducible
slogan: A property p is many-one reducible to a property q if there is a computable function that turns any question about p into a question about q. This means deciding whether p holds can be effectively translated into deciding whether q holds, using a function that is guaranteed to be computable. The types involved must support simple, primitive recursive encoding into natural numbers.

label: ManyOneReducible.trans
slogan: If a property p can be transformed into a property q using a computable function, and q can similarly be transformed into a property r, then p can also be transformed into r using a computable function. This means many-one reducibility is transitive.

label: MapClusterPt
slogan: A point x is a cluster point of a filter F under a function u if, for every neighborhood around x, the set of inputs that map into that neighborhood is included in the filter F. This means the function u sends elements of the filter arbitrarily close to x. It combines the idea of filters capturing "eventual" behavior with the function's tendency to accumulate near x.

label: Matrix.BlockTriangular
slogan: A block triangular matrix is one that is split into rectangular blocks, where all blocks below (or above) the diagonal are zero, forming a triangular pattern at the block level. The structure depends on an ordering of index sets and requires a zero element in the underlying ring or field to define the zero blocks. This definition specifies when a square matrix, indexed by a type m and valued in a ring R, has such a block triangular form based on a function b mapping indices to an ordered type α.

label: Matrix.BlockTriangular.charmatrix
slogan: If a matrix is block triangular over a commutative ring, then its characteristic matrix, formed by subtracting the matrix from X times the identity matrix, is also block triangular with the same block structure. This means the polynomial matrix respects the original block form, and the computation can be done block by block. The result applies to finite-dimensional matrices where equality of indices can be decided.

label: Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup
slogan: The GeneralLinearGroup is the type of invertible square matrices with entries from a semiring R, where the matrix size is determined by a finite index type n that supports decidable equality. These matrices form a group under multiplication because each has a two-sided inverse. The structure ensures that matrix operations are well-defined and computationally effective.

label: Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.det
slogan: The determinant of an invertible square matrix is a unit in the ring, and the determinant function maps invertible matrices to units in a way that respects multiplication: the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, and the identity matrix maps to the multiplicative identity.

label: Matrix.IsHermitian
slogan: A matrix is Hermitian if it is equal to its conjugate transpose, meaning each element equals the complex conjugate of the element in the transposed position. For real matrices, this is the same as being symmetric. The definition requires a star operation on the underlying type, which generalizes complex conjugation.

label: Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues
slogan: The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are returned as a function from the matrix's index type n to real numbers, using the same indexing as the matrix entries. This relies on the matrix being equal to its conjugate transpose and the index type having a finite, decidable structure. The result is a list of real eigenvalues corresponding to the matrix's size and structure.

label: Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues_mem_spectrum_real
slogan: The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix with entries in a real-closed field-like type are real numbers and belong to the spectrum of the matrix over the real numbers. This means every eigenvalue of such a matrix is a real number that lies in the set of values where the matrix fails to be invertible over the reals. The result holds for finite-dimensional matrices with decidable index types.

label: Matrix.IsHermitian.posDef_iff_eigenvalues_pos
slogan: A Hermitian matrix is positive definite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are positive real numbers. The eigenvalues are obtained as a function from the matrix's index type to the reals, relying on the matrix being equal to its conjugate transpose and the index type being finite and decidable. This result connects the algebraic property of positive definiteness with the spectral property of having strictly positive eigenvalues.

label: Matrix.IsHermitian.spectral_theorem
slogan: A Hermitian matrix can be transformed into a diagonal matrix using a unitary transformation, where the diagonal entries are real numbers corresponding to its eigenvalues. This means there exists a basis of eigenvectors that are orthogonal and span the space. The transformation preserves the structure of the matrix while simplifying it to its eigenvalue form.

label: Matrix.IsHyperbolic
slogan: A 2x2 matrix over a commutative ring is called hyperbolic if its determinant is 1 and the square of its trace minus 4 is a perfect square in the ring. The matrix entries are indexed by the finite types Fin 2, meaning it is a 2x2 matrix with rows and columns labeled by 0 and 1. This condition ensures the matrix is conjugate to a diagonal matrix with reciprocal eigenvalues.

label: Matrix.IsParabolic
slogan: A 2x2 matrix over a commutative ring is called parabolic if it is invertible and the square of its trace equals 4 times its determinant, which means it has a repeated eigenvalue of 1 or -1 but only one independent eigenvector. The matrix entries are indexed by the numbers 0 and 1, and the definition uses standard matrix operations available for matrices over a semiring. This condition ensures the matrix is not diagonalizable but still has determinant and trace related in a specific way.

label: Matrix.IsPrimitive
slogan: A matrix is primitive if all its entries are nonnegative and some power of the matrix has all positive entries. The matrix must be square and finite-dimensional, with entries from a ring that has a linear order. The type of the matrix indices must have decidable equality and be finite.

label: Matrix.IsSimplyLaced
slogan: A Cartan matrix is called simply laced when all its off-diagonal entries are either 0 or -1. This means that for any two different rows and columns, the value in the matrix at that position must be one of those two integers. The property is used to classify certain types of algebraic structures based on their associated matrices.

label: Matrix.IsSymm
slogan: A matrix is symmetric if swapping its rows and columns leaves it unchanged, meaning the value at row i and column j is the same as the value at row j and column i for all i and j. This is equivalent to saying the matrix is equal to its transpose.

label: Matrix.IsSymm.apply
slogan: If a matrix is symmetric, then the element at row i and column j is equal to the element at row j and column i for any indices i and j.

label: Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular
slogan: A matrix is totally unimodular if the determinant of every square submatrix (not necessarily made of contiguous rows and columns) is either 0, 1, or -1. This means all such determinants must be values that can be obtained by casting the signs positive, negative, or zero into the underlying ring. The condition applies to any square submatrix formed by selecting any subset of rows and columns from the original matrix.

label: Matrix.Pivot.exists_list_transvec_mul_mul_list_transvec_eq_diagonal
slogan: For any square matrix over a field, there are lists of elementary row and column operations (called transvections) that, when applied to the matrix, transform it into a diagonal matrix. The operations are invertible and preserve the structure of the matrix algebra. This means every square matrix can be simplified to diagonal form using these basic transformations.

label: Matrix.PosDef
slogan: A matrix M is positive definite if it is equal to its conjugate transpose and the product xᴴ*M*x is positive for every nonzero vector x. This means M must be Hermitian and produce positive values when multiplied with any nonzero vector in a specific quadratic form. The structure assumes M is over a ring with a partial order and a conjugation operation.

label: Matrix.PosSemidef
slogan: A matrix M is positive semidefinite if it is equal to its conjugate transpose and the expression xᴴ * M * x is greater than or equal to zero for all vectors x with finite support, where the matrix and vectors are defined over a ring with a partial order and a conjugate operation.

label: Matrix.PosSemidef.eigenvalues_nonneg
slogan: The eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are all greater than or equal to zero. This applies to matrices that are equal to their conjugate transpose and produce non-negative values when used in quadratic forms. The result holds for matrices over real-like types with finite, decidable index sets.

label: Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup
slogan: The projective general linear group PGL(n, R) is formed by taking the group of invertible n by n matrices over a commutative ring R and dividing it by its center, which consists of scalar matrices. This results in a new group where matrices that differ only by a scalar factor are considered equivalent. The type PGL(n, R) is defined when n is a finite type with decidable equality and R is a commutative ring.

label: Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup
slogan: The special linear group consists of all square matrices of a fixed finite size over a commutative ring where the determinant is exactly 1. These matrices are invertible and form a group under matrix multiplication. The definition requires the matrix indices to have decidable equality and the size to be finite so that the determinant can be computed.

label: Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.det_coe
slogan: Every matrix in the special linear group has determinant equal to 1, as long as it is a square matrix over a commutative ring with finitely many entries and decidable equality. The group includes only those invertible matrices whose determinant is exactly 1, preserving volume and orientation. This result follows from the definition of the special linear group and the properties of determinants.

label: Matrix.TransvectionStruct.inv_mul
slogan: The inverse of a transvection matrix, when multiplied by the original matrix, gives the identity matrix, meaning the inverse operation cancels out the row addition. This holds for matrices over a commutative ring with decidable equality and finite dimensions.

label: Matrix.UnitaryGroup.det_isUnit
slogan: Every unitary matrix has a determinant that is invertible in the ring, meaning there exists another element in the ring such that their product is 1. This holds for square matrices over a commutative star ring with finite dimensions and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.add_apply
slogan: Matrix addition combines two matrices by adding their corresponding entries one by one, resulting in a new matrix of the same size. Each entry in the result is the sum of the entries from the same position in the original matrices, provided the entries can be added together. This operation requires both matrices to have entries from a type that supports addition.

label: Matrix.add_mul_mul_inv_eq_sub
slogan: If A, C, and C⁻¹ + V * A⁻¹ * U are invertible matrices, then the inverse of A + U * C * V equals A⁻¹ minus A⁻¹ * U * (C⁻¹ + V * A⁻¹ * U)⁻¹ * V * A⁻¹, provided all operations are defined over a commutative ring with finite dimensions and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.adjugate
slogan: Matrix.adjugate takes a square matrix over a commutative ring and returns a new matrix where each entry is the determinant of a modified version of the original matrix, with one column replaced by a standard basis vector. Multiplying the original matrix by its adjugate results in a diagonal matrix where each diagonal entry is the determinant of the original matrix. This adjugate matrix can be used to compute the inverse of the original matrix when the determinant is invertible.

label: Matrix.adjugate_fin_two_of
slogan: For a 2x2 matrix with entries a, b, c, d in a commutative ring, the adjugate matrix is formed by swapping the diagonal elements a and d, and negating the off-diagonal elements b and c, resulting in the matrix [d, -b; -c, a]. This formula holds when the matrix indices are modeled by the finite type Fin 2. The computation uses cofactor expansion and properties of determinants for 2x2 matrices.

label: Matrix.aeval_eq_aeval_mod_charpoly
slogan: When you evaluate a polynomial at a square matrix, the result is the same as evaluating the remainder of that polynomial divided by the matrix's characteristic polynomial. This works because the characteristic polynomial is monic and the matrix is a root of it. So, only the part of the polynomial left over after division matters for the evaluation.

label: Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly
slogan: Substituting a square matrix into its own characteristic polynomial results in the zero matrix, meaning every matrix satisfies its characteristic equation. The coefficients of the polynomial are interpreted as scalar multiples of the identity matrix through the natural embedding of the base ring into the matrix ring.

label: Matrix.card_GL_field
slogan: The number of invertible n by n matrices over a finite field with q elements is equal to the product over i from 0 to n-1 of (q^n - q^i). This counts the number of ways to choose n linearly independent vectors in an n-dimensional vector space over the field. Each factor in the product represents the number of valid choices for the next vector that does not lie in the span of the previous ones.

label: Matrix.charpoly
slogan: The charpoly function takes a square matrix with entries from a commutative ring and returns its characteristic polynomial, computed as the determinant of (x * I - M), where x is a variable, I is the identity matrix, and M is the given matrix. This polynomial has coefficients in the same ring as the matrix entries and is used to analyze properties like eigenvalues. It is defined for matrices with a finite index type that supports decidable equality.

label: Matrix.charpoly_diagonal
slogan: The characteristic polynomial of a diagonal matrix is found by multiplying together terms of the form (X - a), where X is the polynomial variable and each a is one of the diagonal entries. This means the polynomial is completely determined by the diagonal elements of the matrix. The product is taken over all diagonal entries, using the standard multiplication of polynomials.

label: Matrix.charpoly_fin_two
slogan: For a 2x2 matrix with entries in a commutative ring, the characteristic polynomial is x^2 minus the trace of the matrix times x, plus the determinant of the matrix. The formula uses the standard polynomial variable x and relies on the matrix having exactly two rows and two columns. This result holds for any ring where not all elements are equal, ensuring the algebraic structure is rich enough.

label: Matrix.charpoly_monic
slogan: The characteristic polynomial of any square matrix has a leading coefficient of 1, meaning it is monic, no matter what commutative ring the matrix entries come from. This is because the polynomial is defined as the determinant of (x times the identity matrix minus the matrix), and the highest-degree term in this determinant comes only from the product of the diagonal entries. The structure of the determinant ensures that this top coefficient is always 1.

label: Matrix.charpoly_mul_comm
slogan: If two square matrices A and B commute, meaning A times B equals B times A, then the characteristic polynomial of A times B is the same as the characteristic polynomial of B times A, and this works when the matrices have entries in a commutative ring.

label: Matrix.charpoly_transpose
slogan: The characteristic polynomial of a matrix is the same as that of its transpose, meaning flipping the rows and columns of a matrix does not change the polynomial derived from it. This holds for square matrices over any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.circulant
slogan: Given a type n with subtraction and a function v from n to a type a, circulant v is a square matrix where each entry at row i and column j is the value of v at i minus j.

label: Matrix.commute_diagonal
slogan: If the entries of two diagonal matrices come from a commutative semiring and the matrix size is finite with decidable equality, then multiplying them in either order gives the same result. This means that for such matrices, A times B equals B times A. The reason is that the multiplication of their diagonal entries is commutative.

label: Matrix.conjTranspose
slogan: The conjTranspose of a matrix is created by flipping the matrix over its diagonal (transposing it) and then applying the star operation, such as complex conjugation, to each element. It results in a new matrix where the entry at position (i, j) is the conjugate of the original entry at (j, i). This operation requires that the elements of the matrix support the star operation.

label: Matrix.conjTranspose_mul
slogan: The conjugate transpose of the product of two matrices is the same as multiplying their conjugate transposes in reverse order. This means you can either multiply the matrices first and then take the conjugate transpose, or take the conjugate transpose of each matrix first and then multiply them in the opposite order — the result is the same. The property holds for matrices over a star ring when the index types are finite.

label: Matrix.conjTranspose_vecMulVec
slogan: The conjugate transpose of the matrix formed by multiplying a vector w with a vector v is equal to the matrix formed by multiplying the conjugate of v with the conjugate of w. This means flipping the order of the vectors and applying conjugation to each entry achieves the same result as conjugate transposing the original matrix. The equality holds for any types supporting multiplication and a conjugate-like star operation.

label: Matrix.cramer_apply
slogan: The cramer function applied to a matrix A and a vector b returns a new vector where each entry at index i equals the determinant of the matrix formed by replacing column i of A with b. This holds for square matrices over a commutative ring with finitely many rows and columns, using standard determinant properties. The result gives a component-wise solution to linear systems via Cramer's rule.

label: Matrix.derivative_det_one_add_X_smul
slogan: The derivative of the determinant of the matrix (I + t*A) with respect to t, evaluated at t=0, equals the trace of A, where A is a square matrix over a commutative ring. This identity links the rate of change of the determinant near the identity matrix to the trace, a fundamental linear algebra quantity. The result is expressed using polynomials and their derivatives, evaluated at zero.

label: Matrix.det
slogan: The determinant is a function that takes a square matrix with entries from a commutative ring and returns a single value from that ring, computed using a sum over permutations of the columns with appropriate signs. It is linear in each row, changes sign when two rows are swapped, and gives 1 for the identity matrix. The matrix must have a finite index type with decidable equality for the determinant to be defined.

label: Matrix.detRowAlternating
slogan: The determinant of a matrix is a function that is linear in each row, changes sign when two rows are swapped, and becomes zero if any two rows are the same. It is built by summing over all permutations of the rows, with each term multiplied by the sign of the permutation. This alternating and multilinear behavior uniquely defines the determinant up to a scalar factor.

label: Matrix.det_apply
slogan: The determinant of a square matrix is calculated by adding up, for every possible way to pick one element from each row and column without repetition, the product of those elements multiplied by +1 or -1 depending on the parity of the permutation used. Each term in the sum corresponds to a permutation of the column indices, with the sign determined by whether the permutation is even or odd. The result is a single value that captures important algebraic properties of the matrix.

label: Matrix.det_apply'
slogan: The determinant of a square matrix over a commutative ring is calculated by summing, over all permutations of the matrix indices, the product of selected matrix entries (one from each row and column) multiplied by the sign of the permutation, where the sign is converted into the ring via the canonical integer map.

label: Matrix.det_conj
slogan: The determinant of a matrix stays the same when you conjugate it by an invertible matrix, meaning that for any square matrix N and invertible matrix M, the determinant of M * N * M^(-1) equals the determinant of N. This holds for matrices over a commutative ring with finitely many indices and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.det_eq_prod_roots_charpoly
slogan: The determinant of a square matrix over an algebraically closed field equals the product of the roots of its characteristic polynomial, counting multiplicities. This holds because in such a field, every polynomial splits completely into linear factors. The roots are taken with their multiplicities as given by the polynomial's factorization.

label: Matrix.det_eq_zero_of_not_linearIndependent_cols
slogan: If the columns of a square matrix cannot be combined in a way that only the zero combination gives zero, then the determinant of the matrix is zero. This applies to matrices over commutative rings with no zero divisors, where the index set is finite and equality is decidable.

label: Matrix.det_fin_three
slogan: The determinant of a 3x3 matrix is calculated by multiplying entries from different rows and columns in specific combinations, adding some products and subtracting others based on the pattern of their positions. The formula expands the determinant into six terms: three positive and three negative, each being the product of three elements from the matrix. This gives a single value that reflects properties like invertibility and scaling behavior of the matrix.

label: Matrix.det_fin_zero
slogan: If a matrix has zero rows and zero columns, its determinant is 1, no matter what commutative ring the entries are from. This is because the only permutation of an empty set contributes a product of 1. Such a matrix is defined over an empty index set, and the result holds by convention in algebra.

label: Matrix.det_fromBlocks_zero₂₁
slogan: The determinant of a block matrix that has a zero block in the bottom-left corner equals the product of the determinants of the top-left and bottom-right blocks, as long as those blocks are square and the matrix entries come from a commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_isEmpty
slogan: If a matrix has no rows and no columns, its determinant is 1. This is because the determinant in this case comes from the product over the only permutation of an empty set, and that product is defined to be 1. The result holds for matrices over any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_mul
slogan: The determinant of the product of two square matrices is the same as the product of their individual determinants. This means that when you multiply two matrices and then compute the determinant, it gives the same result as computing each determinant first and then multiplying those numbers together.

label: Matrix.det_nonsing_inv
slogan: If a square matrix has a nonzero determinant, then it has an inverse, and the determinant of the inverse is 1 divided by the determinant of the original matrix.

label: Matrix.det_of_mem_unitary
slogan: If a square matrix with complex entries is unitary—meaning its conjugate transpose is its inverse—then the absolute value of its determinant is 1, so the determinant lies on the unit circle in the complex plane. This follows from properties of determinants, conjugate transposes, and the fact that the determinant of the identity matrix is 1.

label: Matrix.det_of_upperTriangular
slogan: The determinant of an upper triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on its main diagonal. This means that if all the elements below the diagonal are zero, you can find the determinant just by multiplying the diagonal elements together. The result applies to square matrices over any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_one
slogan: The determinant of the identity matrix is 1, because the identity matrix is diagonal with all diagonal entries equal to 1, and the determinant of any diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries. Since the product of 1 over a finite set is 1, the result follows.

label: Matrix.det_one_add_mul_comm
slogan: The determinant of the identity matrix plus the product of two matrices A and B is the same as the determinant of the identity matrix plus the product of B and A, even if the matrices are not square or invertible, as long as they are defined over a commutative ring and their sizes are finite. This means det(I + AB) equals det(I + BA). The result does not depend on the order of multiplication in the product term.

label: Matrix.det_permutation
slogan: The determinant of a matrix that represents a permutation is equal to the sign of that permutation, where the sign is converted into the ring where the matrix entries live.

label: Matrix.det_permute
slogan: The determinant of a matrix changes by a factor equal to the sign of a permutation when its rows are reordered according to that permutation. The sign is +1 if the permutation is even and -1 if it is odd, so the determinant stays the same for even permutations and flips sign for odd ones. This means permuting the rows of a matrix multiplies its determinant by the sign of the row permutation.

label: Matrix.det_smul
slogan: The determinant of a matrix multiplied by a scalar is equal to the scalar raised to the power of the matrix's size, times the determinant of the original matrix.

label: Matrix.det_succ_row
slogan: The determinant of a square matrix with n+1 rows and columns can be calculated by adding up the products of each element in a chosen row with the determinant of the smaller matrix that remains after removing that row and the element's column, multiplying each term by -1 raised to the sum of the row and column indices. This process is known as cofactor expansion along a row. The formula applies to matrices over any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_succ_row_zero
slogan: If the first row of a square matrix is all zeros, then the determinant of the matrix is zero.
