This is because each term in the determinant sum involves an element from the first row, and multiplying by zero makes every term zero. The formula expands the determinant using cofactors along the first row, but since all entries in that row are zero, the total sum is zero.

label: Matrix.det_transpose
slogan: The determinant of a matrix stays the same when you flip the matrix over its diagonal, meaning the determinant of a matrix equals the determinant of its transpose. This holds for square matrices with entries in any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_updateCol_add_smul_self
slogan: Adding a multiple of one column of a square matrix to a different column does not change the matrix's determinant, as long as the matrix entries are from a commutative ring. The operation modifies only the target column by adding a scaled version of another column to it, leaving all other columns unchanged. This property is similar to the row version, where adding a scaled row to another row also preserves the determinant.

label: Matrix.det_updateCol_smul
slogan: If you multiply one column of a matrix by a scalar and replace that column with the result, the determinant of the new matrix is the scalar times the determinant of the original matrix with the same column replaced by the unscaled values. This holds for square matrices over a commutative ring with finitely many columns.

label: Matrix.det_updateRow_smul
slogan: The determinant of a matrix scales by a factor s when you replace one of its rows with s times a given vector, meaning the new determinant equals s multiplied by the determinant of the matrix with that row replaced by the original vector. This holds for square matrices over a commutative ring with finitely many rows and decidable row indices. The result follows from the determinant's linearity in each row.

label: Matrix.det_vandermonde
slogan: The determinant of a Vandermonde matrix formed from a list of values is equal to the product of all differences (v_j - v_i) where i < j, taken over all pairs of indices. This formula holds for matrices with entries in any commutative ring.

label: Matrix.det_zero_of_row_eq
slogan: If a square matrix has two different rows that are exactly the same, then its determinant is zero, regardless of the underlying commutative ring. This is because the determinant changes sign when rows are swapped, but if the rows are equal, swapping them doesn't change the matrix, forcing the determinant to be zero.

label: Matrix.diag
slogan: Matrix.diag creates a square matrix where only the diagonal entries may be nonzero, setting each diagonal element using a given function and making all other entries zero.

label: Matrix.exists_mulVec_eq_zero_iff
slogan: A square matrix has a nonzero vector that it sends to zero when multiplied if and only if its determinant is zero, meaning the matrix is not invertible. This happens exactly when the matrix has a nontrivial kernel. The condition is equivalent to the matrix failing to have an inverse.

label: Matrix.frobenius_norm_def
slogan: The Frobenius norm of a matrix is the square root of the sum of the squares of all its entries. It is computed by adding up the squared magnitudes of each element across every row and column, then taking the square root of the total. This results in a non-negative real number that measures the overall size of the matrix.

label: Matrix.fromBlocks
slogan: Matrix.fromBlocks combines four smaller matrices into a larger matrix by arranging them in a 2x2 grid, where the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right blocks are filled by the given matrices A, B, C, and D respectively, and the row and column indices of the resulting matrix come from the disjoint union of the original index types. The entry at any position in the resulting matrix is determined by checking whether the row and column indices come from the first or second type using case analysis on sum types. This construction uses functions to map indices appropriately based on the

label: Matrix.fromCols_mul_fromRows
slogan: Multiplying a matrix made by joining two column blocks with a matrix made by joining two row blocks gives the same result as adding the products of the corresponding blocks.

label: Matrix.hadamard
slogan: Matrix.hadamard defines the element-wise multiplication of two matrices of the same size, where each entry in the resulting matrix is the product of the corresponding entries from the input matrices, using the multiplication operation from the Mul typeclass.

label: Matrix.instAlgebra
slogan: If R is a commutative semiring and n is a finite type with decidable equality, then n-by-n matrices over a semiring α form an R-algebra, meaning they support scalar multiplication by elements of R and have a ring structure where matrix addition and multiplication follow standard algebraic rules. The embedding of R into the matrices sends each scalar to the corresponding diagonal matrix via algebraMap. This structure ensures that scaling matrices by elements of R interacts correctly with matrix operations and R's arithmetic.

label: Matrix.inv
slogan: Matrix.inv defines a multiplicative inverse for square matrices over a commutative ring, provided the matrix's determinant is invertible; the inverse is computed as (1/det(A)) times the adjugate matrix. This allows writing A⁻¹ for a matrix A when the ring supports division by the determinant. It requires the matrix indices to be finite and decidable, and the entries to come from a commutative ring.

label: Matrix.invOf_fromBlocks₁₁_eq
slogan: If a block matrix made of four parts is invertible, and both the top-left block and its Schur complement are invertible, then the top-left block of the inverse matrix is equal to the inverse of the top-left block plus a correction term involving the other blocks.

label: Matrix.invOf_fromBlocks₂₂_eq
slogan: If a block matrix made from submatrices A, B, C, and D is invertible and the bottom-right block D is invertible, then the inverse of the whole matrix has a specific block form where the bottom-right block of the inverse is equal to the inverse of D plus a correction term involving the other blocks. This result holds for matrices over a commutative ring with finite dimensions and relies on the invertibility of D and the Schur complement of D. The formula explicitly expresses the inverse of the full block matrix in terms of the inverses of D and the Schur complement.

label: Matrix.inv_def
slogan: The inverse of a square matrix A is defined as (1 divided by the determinant of A) multiplied by the adjugate of A, and this inverse exists only when the determinant has a multiplicative inverse in the ring. The matrix must have entries from a commutative ring with decidable equality, and its size must be finite. When these conditions are met, the notation A⁻¹ refers to this inverse matrix.

label: Matrix.inv_eq_left_inv
slogan: If a square matrix A has a left inverse B (so B * A equals the identity matrix), and the matrix entries are from a commutative ring with decidable equality and finite dimensions, then the inverse of A is exactly B. This means the matrix inverse, when it exists, is the same as any left inverse. The result relies on the properties of nonsingular matrices and the invertibility of the determinant.

label: Matrix.inv_mulVec_eq_vec
slogan: If a matrix has an inverse, then multiplying that inverse by a vector u gives the vector v such that the original matrix times v equals u. This means solving the equation A*v = u by applying the inverse of A to u. The matrix entries are from a commutative ring, the index set is finite, and equality between indices can be decided.

label: Matrix.isHermitian_iff_isSymmetric
slogan: A matrix is Hermitian if and only if the linear map it represents is symmetric, meaning the inner product of the map applied to any two vectors is unchanged when the vectors are swapped. This equivalence holds for matrices over real or complex-like fields with finite dimensions and decidable equality. The linear map is constructed from the matrix using standard basis vectors in a Euclidean space.

label: Matrix.isParabolic_iff_exists
slogan: A 2x2 matrix over a field is parabolic if and only if it can be written as a scalar multiple of the identity matrix plus a nonzero nilpotent matrix that squares to zero. This means the matrix is not diagonalizable and has a repeated eigenvalue of 1 or -1. The condition depends only on the matrix entries and can be checked using basic arithmetic.

label: Matrix.isUnit_iff_isUnit_det
slogan: A square matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant has a multiplicative inverse in the ring; this applies to matrices over commutative rings with finite dimensions and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.kronecker
slogan: The kronecker function takes two matrices and produces a larger matrix by multiplying each element of the first matrix by the entire second matrix, arranging the results in a block structure. The new matrix has rows and columns indexed by pairs from the original matrices' indices, and it requires the element type to support multiplication. This operation is commonly known as the Kronecker product.

label: Matrix.kroneckerMap
slogan: Matrix.kroneckerMap takes two matrices and a function that combines their elements, then builds a new matrix whose entries are the results of applying that function to every pair of elements from the original matrices, arranged in a block structure indexed by pairs of row and column indices.

label: Matrix.kroneckerTMul
slogan: The kroneckerTMul function takes two matrices with entries in modules over a commutative semiring and produces a new block matrix whose entries are the tensor products of the original entries. Each block in the resulting matrix corresponds to the tensor product of an element from the first matrix with an element from the second. The result is a matrix indexed by pairs of indices, with values in the tensor product of the two modules.

label: Matrix.linearIndependent_cols_iff_isUnit
slogan: A square matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if it is invertible, meaning there exists another matrix such that multiplying them gives the identity matrix. This means no column can be expressed as a combination of the others using scalar multiplication and addition, and the matrix must be square with entries from a field. The result applies to finite-dimensional matrices over a field.

label: Matrix.linearIndependent_rows_iff_isUnit
slogan: The rows of a square matrix are linearly independent if and only if the matrix is invertible, meaning there exists another matrix that, when multiplied on either side, gives the identity matrix. This happens exactly when the matrix has a two-sided inverse in the ring of matrices. Invertibility ensures that no nontrivial combination of the rows equals zero.

label: Matrix.map_mul
slogan: If you apply a function to each entry of two matrices and then multiply them, it gives the same result as multiplying the matrices first and then applying the function to each entry of the product, as long as the function preserves addition and multiplication and the matrix dimensions are finite.

label: Matrix.mem_orthogonalGroup_iff
slogan: A square matrix is orthogonal if multiplying it by its transpose gives the identity matrix, and this happens exactly when the matrix preserves distances and angles. The matrix must have entries in a commutative ring, with rows and columns indexed by a finite type that supports decidable equality. The set of such matrices forms a submonoid of the invertible matrices under multiplication.

label: Matrix.mem_orthogonalGroup_iff'
slogan: A matrix is in the orthogonal group if and only if multiplying it by its transpose results in the identity matrix, which means the transpose acts as the inverse of the matrix. This holds for square matrices over a commutative ring with finite dimensions and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.mem_rowStochastic_iff_sum
slogan: A square matrix is row stochastic if and only if all its entries are greater than or equal to zero and the sum of the elements in each row equals one.

label: Matrix.mem_specialOrthogonalGroup_iff
slogan: A square matrix with real number entries is in the special orthogonal group if and only if its transpose is its inverse and its determinant is 1. This means the matrix preserves both lengths and angles (via orthogonality) and does not flip orientation (via determinant 1). The result holds for finite-dimensional matrices over commutative rings where equality of indices can be decided.

label: Matrix.mem_specialUnitaryGroup_iff
slogan: A square matrix is in the special unitary group if and only if its conjugate transpose is its inverse and its determinant equals one, where the matrix entries come from a commutative ring with a conjugation operation and the matrix has finitely many rows and columns with decidable equality.

label: Matrix.minpoly_dvd_charpoly
slogan: The minimal polynomial of a square matrix divides its characteristic polynomial, meaning every root of the minimal polynomial is also a root of the characteristic polynomial. Both polynomials are defined over a field, and this relationship reflects a deep connection between the algebraic structure of the matrix and its eigenvalues.

label: Matrix.mulVec
slogan: Matrix.mulVec describes how a matrix multiplies a vector: for each row of the matrix, it takes the sum of the products of the corresponding entries in that row and the vector, producing a new vector where each entry comes from one such sum. The operation works with any type of data that supports addition and multiplication, and requires the vector's index set to be finite so the sums can be computed. The resulting vector has one entry for each row in the matrix.

label: Matrix.mulVec_add
slogan: Multiplying a matrix by the sum of two vectors gives the same result as multiplying the matrix by each vector separately and then adding the results. This works because the dot product distributes over vector addition, and vectors are added pointwise. The matrix and vectors must be defined over a structure with finite index types and operations that support addition and multiplication, like a semiring.

label: Matrix.mulVec_eq_sum
slogan: Multiplying a matrix by a vector produces a new vector where each entry is the sum of the products of the corresponding row of the matrix and the entries of the vector, summed over all columns. This sum is taken over the entire finite index set of the vector's domain, using the algebraic structure of the underlying type. The operation uses the transpose of the matrix and reverses multiplication order via MulOpposite when computing the result.

label: Matrix.mulVec_injective_iff_isUnit
slogan: A square matrix turns different vectors into different outputs when multiplying them if and only if the matrix has an inverse, meaning there is another matrix that cancels it out when multiplied. This happens exactly when the matrix is square and its determinant is invertible in the underlying field.

label: Matrix.mul_add
slogan: Multiplying a matrix by the sum of two other matrices is the same as multiplying it by each matrix separately and then adding the results. This works when the entries are from a type where multiplication distributes over addition and the number of columns in the first matrix is finite. The equality holds because each entry in the resulting matrix follows the distributive law.

label: Matrix.mul_adjugate
slogan: Multiplying a square matrix by its adjugate gives a diagonal matrix where every diagonal entry is the determinant of the original matrix and all off-diagonal entries are zero, provided the matrix entries come from a commutative ring and the index set is finite.

label: Matrix.mul_apply
slogan: The product of two matrices is computed by taking, for each row i and column k, the sum of the products of corresponding elements from row i of the first matrix and column k of the second matrix, where the sum is over all intermediate indices j. This definition requires that the matrix entries support addition (which is commutative and has a zero) and multiplication, and that the intermediate index type has only finitely many elements. The result at position (i, k) in the product matrix is thus the sum of A[i,j] * B[j,k] for all j.

label: Matrix.mul_assoc
slogan: Matrix multiplication is associative: for any three matrices L, M, and N of compatible dimensions over a non-unital semiring, multiplying L by M and then by N gives the same result as multiplying M by N first and then multiplying L by that product. The entries of the matrices come from a structure where multiplication is associative and distributes over addition, and the index sets for rows and columns are finite. This means the grouping of matrix multiplication operations does not affect the final matrix.

label: Matrix.mul_eq_one_comm
slogan: If two square matrices multiply to give the identity matrix in one order, they also multiply to give the identity in the reverse order, provided the underlying algebraic structure ensures that one-sided inverses are two-sided. This property holds for elements in a monoid with a multiplication operation and an identity element, where left and right inverses coincide.

label: Matrix.mul_inv_rev
slogan: The inverse of the product of two invertible square matrices A and B is the same as the product of their inverses in reverse order: (A * B)^-1 = B^-1 * A^-1. This holds when the matrices have entries in a commutative ring and both matrices are invertible.

label: Matrix.mul_nonsing_inv
slogan: If a square matrix has a determinant that has a multiplicative inverse in the underlying commutative ring, then the matrix itself has an inverse, and multiplying the matrix by this inverse yields the identity matrix. The inverse is given by the adjugate matrix multiplied by the reciprocal of the determinant. This applies to matrices over commutative rings with finite dimensions and decidable equality.

label: Matrix.nonsing_inv_apply
slogan: If a square matrix has an invertible determinant, then its inverse exists and is equal to the adjugate matrix multiplied by the reciprocal of the determinant. This formula gives the explicit form of the inverse in terms of the adjugate and the unit inverse of the determinant. The result holds for matrices over commutative rings where the determinant is a unit.

label: Matrix.of_mem_specialOrthogonalGroup_fin_two_iff
slogan: A 2x2 matrix with real entries is a rotation matrix if and only if it has the form [[a, -b], [b, a]] and a^2 + b^2 = 1, meaning it preserves lengths and orientation in the plane.

label: Matrix.one
slogan: Matrix.one represents the identity matrix for square matrices, where all diagonal entries are 1 and all off-diagonal entries are 0. It exists for any square matrix type where the element type supports a zero, a one, and decidable equality. This matrix acts as the multiplicative identity in matrix multiplication.

label: Matrix.one_apply
slogan: A matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere has the value 1 at position (i, j) if i equals j, and 0 otherwise. This applies to square matrices over any type where equality can be decided and where 0 and 1 are defined. The matrix is built so that each entry is determined by whether its row and column indices are equal.

label: Matrix.one_apply_eq
slogan: The identity matrix has a 1 at position (i, i) when the row and column index are the same, and 0 elsewhere; this result holds for any square matrix over a type with decidable equality and defined zero and one values.

label: Matrix.orthogonalGroup
slogan: Matrix.orthogonalGroup is a group of square matrices where each matrix times its transpose equals the identity matrix, using entries from a commutative ring and indexed by a finite type with decidable equality; it forms a submonoid of invertible matrices under multiplication. This group generalizes real orthogonal matrices and is a special case of the unitary group when the star operation is trivial.

label: Matrix.permMatrixHom
slogan: The function permMatrixHom maps each permutation of a finite type to a corresponding permutation matrix, where each matrix has exactly one 1 in each row and column and 0s elsewhere. It ensures that combining two permutations and then converting to a matrix gives the same result as converting each permutation to a matrix first and then multiplying them. This means the mapping from permutations to matrices preserves the structure of composition.

label: Matrix.permMatrix_one
slogan: The permutation matrix of the identity permutation (which maps every element to itself) is equal to the identity matrix, meaning it has ones on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else. This holds for any type with decidable equality and any ring-like type that has zero and one elements.

label: Matrix.permanent
slogan: The permanent of a square matrix is calculated by summing, over all permutations of the matrix indices, the products of the matrix entries where each row and column is used exactly once, and unlike the determinant, all terms are added without any negative signs. It applies to matrices over a commutative semiring and requires the index type to be finite and decidable. The computation involves taking the sum over all possible ways to pick one element from each row and column such that no two are in the same row or column, multiplying those elements together for each arrangement, and adding up th

label: Matrix.pow_apply_pos_iff_nonempty_path
slogan: For a matrix with nonnegative entries, the entry at position (i, j) in the k-th power of the matrix is positive if and only if there is a path of length k from i to j in the directed graph associated with the matrix.

label: Matrix.rank
slogan: The rank of a matrix is the dimension of the space spanned by its columns, viewed as linear combinations over a commutative ring, and it is computed as the rank of the image of the linear map it represents.

label: Matrix.rank_vecMulVec_le
slogan: The rank of the matrix formed by the outer product of two vectors is at most 1, meaning the resulting matrix has a column space of dimension no greater than 1. This holds for matrices over any commutative ring with finite column index type.

label: Matrix.rowStochastic
slogan: A row stochastic matrix is a square matrix where all entries are nonnegative and each row adds up to 1, meaning that multiplying the matrix by a column vector of all 1s results in the same vector of 1s.

label: Matrix.semiring
slogan: Matrices with entries in a semiring and indexed by a finite type with decidable equality form a semiring, meaning they support addition and multiplication where multiplication distributes over addition, there is a zero matrix and an identity matrix, and multiplying any matrix by the zero matrix gives the zero matrix.

label: Matrix.smul_apply
slogan: When a scalar value multiplies a matrix, the result is a new matrix where each element is the product of the scalar and the corresponding element of the original matrix. This means the operation applies the scalar multiplication entrywise.

label: Matrix.smul_mul
slogan: Multiplying a scalar by a matrix and then multiplying the result with another matrix gives the same result as first multiplying the two matrices and then multiplying the product by the scalar. This holds when the scalar action is compatible with the underlying algebraic structure, ensuring consistent interaction between scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication. The equality a * (M * N) = (a * M) * N is preserved under these conditions.

label: Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup
slogan: The special orthogonal group is the set of square matrices with entries in a commutative ring where the matrix transpose equals the inverse and the determinant is 1, meaning they preserve both distances and orientation. These matrices represent rotations in finite-dimensional space and form a submonoid under matrix multiplication. The definition applies to matrices indexed by finite types with decidable equality.

label: Matrix.specialUnitaryGroup
slogan: The special unitary group is the set of square matrices over a commutative star ring with finite index types and decidable equality, where each matrix has an inverse equal to its conjugate transpose and has determinant exactly one. It is formed by taking the unitary matrices and restricting to those whose determinant is 1, using the kernel of the determinant map. This set forms a submonoid under matrix multiplication.

label: Matrix.submatrix
slogan: Matrix.submatrix takes a matrix and two functions that map new row and column indices to the original matrix's indices, then builds a new matrix by selecting entries from the original matrix at those mapped positions. The result is a smaller matrix made from the chosen rows and columns. Each entry in the new matrix comes directly from the corresponding position in the original.

label: Matrix.symplecticGroup
slogan: The symplectic group consists of square matrices over a commutative ring, indexed by pairs from a finite type, that preserve a symplectic form and form a submonoid under matrix multiplication. These matrices satisfy specific algebraic conditions ensuring they maintain the structure of symplectic geometry. The group includes the identity matrix and is closed under matrix multiplication.

label: Matrix.toBilin
slogan: Matrix.toBilin converts a matrix into a bilinear form by using the matrix to compute a scalar from two vectors via indexed summation, assuming a fixed basis and a finite index set with decidable equality; the operation is linear and invertible, with its inverse being the conversion of a bilinear form back into a matrix.

label: Matrix.toInnerProductSpace
slogan: A positive semi-definite matrix M defines an inner product on vectors by taking the sum of the products of the entries of xᴴ (the conjugate transpose of x), M, and y. This inner product satisfies all the required properties for an inner product space over a real-like field. The resulting space of vectors with this inner product is constructed as an instance of InnerProductSpace.

label: Matrix.toLin_mul
slogan: Converting the product of two matrices to a linear map gives the same result as converting each matrix to a linear map first and then composing those maps. This shows that matrix multiplication aligns with the composition of linear transformations when using fixed bases. The statement holds for finite-dimensional modules over a commutative semiring where basis element equality is decidable.

label: Matrix.toMatrixInnerProductSpace
slogan: A positive semidefinite matrix M defines an inner product on square matrices of the same size by setting the inner product of x and y to be the trace of y times M times the conjugate transpose of x. This construction turns the space of square matrices into an inner product space over a star ring with real-complex-like properties. The inner product is well-defined when the underlying matrix type has finite dimensions and the ring supports conjugation and ordering.

label: Matrix.trace
slogan: The trace of a square matrix is the sum of the elements on its main diagonal, where the matrix has finitely many rows and columns indexed by a finite type, and its entries are elements of a type that supports addition with a zero and commutativity. This sum is computed over all indices using the universal finite set of indices. The trace operation is linear, meaning it preserves addition and scalar multiplication.

label: Matrix.trace_eq_neg_charpoly_nextCoeff
slogan: The trace of a square matrix is equal to the negative of the coefficient of the second-highest power of X in its characteristic polynomial; if the matrix has no entries, the trace is zero. This relationship holds for matrices over any commutative ring. The result connects a basic matrix property (trace) to a specific term in a polynomial derived from the matrix.

label: Matrix.trace_mul_comm
slogan: The trace of the product of two matrices A and B is the same as the trace of the product of B and A, even though matrix multiplication is not commutative. This means that for compatible square matrices, trace(A * B) = trace(B * A), as long as the entries are from a commutative semiring and the index sets are finite.

label: Matrix.transpose
slogan: The transpose of a matrix swaps its rows and columns, so that the element at position (i, j) in the original matrix becomes the element at (j, i) in the transposed matrix. It works for any matrix whose entries are indexed by two types, turning a matrix with m rows and n columns into one with n rows and m columns. This operation is defined by switching the order of the indices when evaluating the matrix's underlying function.

label: Matrix.transpose_mul
slogan: The transpose of the product of two matrices equals the product of their transposes in reverse order, as long as the entries come from a commutative multiplication structure and the inner dimension is finite. This means that (A * B)^T = B^T * A^T holds when multiplying matrices where the shared index type has finitely many elements and the element type supports commutative multiplication. The result relies on the commutativity of the dot product and standard matrix multiplication over finite dimensions.

label: Matrix.transvection
slogan: Matrix.transvection creates a square matrix that is the identity matrix plus a matrix with a single non-zero off-diagonal entry at position (i, j), scaled by a value c. This matrix represents an elementary row operation that adds c times row j to row i. It is used to perform shear transformations in linear algebra while preserving the determinant and invertibility of the matrix.

label: Matrix.unitaryGroup
slogan: The unitaryGroup consists of square matrices over a commutative star ring where each matrix's conjugate transpose is its inverse, meaning multiplying the matrix by its conjugate transpose gives the identity matrix. These matrices form a submonoid under standard matrix multiplication, assuming the matrix size is finite and has decidable equality.

label: Matrix.vandermonde
slogan: Matrix.vandermonde takes a list of n values from a commutative ring and returns an n by n matrix where the entry in row i and column j is the i-th value raised to the power j, using zero-based indexing for both rows and columns through the Fin type.

label: Matrix.vec3_dotProduct
slogan: The dot product of two 3D vectors is found by multiplying their matching components and summing the results: the first components multiplied together, plus the second components multiplied, plus the third components multiplied. This works for any type where multiplication is defined and addition is commutative with a zero element. The result is a single value representing how aligned the two vectors are.

label: Matrix.vecMulVec_eq
slogan: Multiplying a matrix by a vector gives the same result as forming a new matrix where each column is scaled by the corresponding vector entry and then summing those columns. The result is computed using addition and multiplication rules over a type with a single element, ensuring consistency with standard matrix-vector multiplication. This equality holds for any types supporting multiplication and commutative addition.

label: Matroid
slogan: A matroid is a set system where some subsets are labeled independent, the empty set is always independent, any subset of an independent set is also independent, and if one independent set is smaller than another, it can be extended by adding an element from the larger set. This structure generalizes ideas like linear independence in vector spaces and can be defined either by its independent sets or by its maximal independent sets called bases. The exchange property of bases ensures all bases have the same size.

label: Matroid.IsMinor
slogan: A matroid N is a minor of M if N can be obtained by deleting some elements from a contraction of M. This means there are sets C and D such that N equals M contracted by C and then deleted by D. Even though the definition doesn't require C and D to be disjoint or within the ground set, we can always find such sets that are disjoint and contained in M's ground set.

label: Matroid.IsMinor.antisymm
slogan: If one matroid is a minor of another and the second is also a minor of the first, then the two matroids are equal. This means the minor relation is antisymmetric: you can't have two different matroids where each is a minor of the other.

label: Matroid.contract
slogan: The contraction of a matroid M by a set C is a new matroid on the elements of M not in C, where a set is independent if its union with any basis of C is independent in the original matroid. This operation can also be defined as the dual of the deletion of C from the dual of M.

label: Matroid.contract_delete_contract_delete
slogan: When contracting and deleting disjoint sets in a matroid, the order of operations can be rearranged: contracting C and C', then deleting D and D', gives the same result as doing the operations step by step, provided C' and D are disjoint.

label: Maximal
slogan: Maximal P x means that x satisfies property P and no other element y with P is strictly greater than x, using the ≤ relation from the LE typeclass.

label: Measurable
slogan: A function is called measurable if the preimage of every measurable set in the output space is a measurable set in the input space, meaning the function respects the measurable structures on both spaces. This requires both the domain and codomain to have a measurable space structure defined on them.

label: Measurable.add
slogan: If two functions are measurable and addition in their output space is measurable with respect to the product sigma-algebra, then the function formed by adding their outputs pointwise is also measurable. This means that the sum of measurable functions remains measurable when addition itself is a measurable operation. The result depends on the product measurable structure and the measurability of the addition map.

label: Measurable.comp
slogan: If two functions are measurable, meaning they map measurable sets to measurable sets, then their composition is also measurable. This means that applying one measurable function after another still preserves the property that preimages of measurable sets are measurable.

label: Measurable.exists_eq_measurable_comp
slogan: If a function g from X to Z is measurable and depends on X only through another function f from X to Y, then there exists a measurable function h from Y to Z such that g is the composition of h and f. This means g can be factored through f using a measurable function h. The result holds when Z is nonempty and has a standard Borel structure.

label: Measurable.iSup
slogan: If you have a countable family of measurable functions into a space with a suitable order and topology, then the function formed by taking the pointwise supremum (least upper bound) at each point is also measurable. This holds when the codomain is a conditionally complete linear order with the order topology and is second-countable. Measurability is preserved because the structure of the order and the topological properties ensure that preimages of measurable sets remain measurable under the supremum operation.

label: Measurable.measurableEmbedding
slogan: A measurable embedding is an injective measurable function between standard Borel spaces where a set in the domain is measurable if and only if its image is measurable in the codomain, ensuring the measurable structure is fully preserved in both directions.

label: MeasurableSet
slogan: A measurable set is a subset of a given set that is part of a collection which includes all complements and countable unions of its members, forming the foundation for defining measures and integration. This collection must satisfy specific closure properties to ensure consistency in measure theory. The set is considered measurable if it belongs to this structured collection within a measurable space.

label: MeasurableSet.compl
slogan: If a set is measurable, then its complement (the set of all elements not in it) is also measurable. This means the collection of measurable sets is closed under taking complements. It's one of the key properties that defines a measurable space.

label: MeasurableSet.exists_isOpen_diff_lt
slogan: For any measurable set A with finite measure and any positive number ε, there exists an open set U containing A such that the measure of the part of U that is not in A is less than ε, and the measure of U itself is finite. This means measurable sets can be closely approximated from the outside by open sets in terms of their measure.

label: MeasurableSet.iUnion
slogan: If you have a countable collection of sets and each one is measurable in a given measurable space, then their union is also measurable. This means that taking the union of countably many measurable sets results in another measurable set.

label: MeasurableSet.nullMeasurableSet
slogan: A set is null measurable if it is equal to a measurable set except possibly on a subset that has measure zero, meaning it behaves like a measurable set for integration and measure-theoretic purposes. This allows working with sets that are "close enough" to measurable when negligible differences are ignored.

label: MeasurableSet.standardBorel
slogan: In a standard Borel space, any measurable subset inherits the same well-behaved structure, meaning it also forms a standard Borel space when equipped with the induced measurable structure. This ensures that measurable sets in such spaces maintain good properties for use in measure theory and analysis. The result relies on the underlying space having a topology that is separable and completely metrizable.

label: MeasurableSet.univ
slogan: In any measurable space, the set containing all elements of a given type is always measurable. This is because the empty set is measurable, and the complement of the universal set is the empty set. Since measurable sets are closed under complements, the universal set must be measurable.

label: MeasurableSpace
slogan: A measurable space is a set with a specified collection of subsets that includes complements and countable unions of its members, enabling the definition of measures and integration. This structure forms the basis for measure theory and probability. The type MeasurableSpace α represents this structure for a type α.

label: MeasurableSpace.CountablyGenerated
slogan: A measurable space is countably generated if its measurable sets can be built from a countable family of sets using complements and countable unions. This means there is a countable collection of sets such that the smallest sigma-algebra containing them is the entire measurable space. The property combines the structure of a measurable space with the requirement that it is determined by a countable base.

label: MeasurableSpace.CountablySeparated
slogan: A countably separated measurable space is a set with a sigma-algebra such that some countable collection of measurable sets can tell apart any two distinct points. For any two different points, at least one set in this countable family contains one point but not the other. This ensures strong separation using only countably many measurable sets.

label: MeasurableSpace.DynkinSystem.generateFrom_eq
slogan: If a collection of sets is closed under finite intersections, then the smallest sigma-algebra containing it is the same as the smallest Dynkin system that contains it, because that Dynkin system ends up being closed under all finite intersections and thus becomes a sigma-algebra. This means generating measurable sets using countable disjoint unions and complements from a pi-system gives the same result as standard sigma-algebra generation.

label: MeasurableSpace.comap
slogan: Given a function f from a set α to a set β and a measurable space on β, the comap construction defines a measurable space on α by declaring a subset of α to be measurable if its preimage under f is measurable in β. This means the measurable sets in α are precisely those that map into measurable sets in β. It provides a way to pull back measurable structure from the target space to the source space using the function f.

label: MeasurableSpace.generateMeasurableRec
slogan: This function builds a sigma-algebra step by step starting from a collection of sets s, by repeatedly adding the original sets, empty set, complements, and countable unions at each stage, indexed by ordinals. It uses transfinite recursion to ensure all necessary sets are included. By the time the process reaches the first uncountable ordinal, all sets in the generated sigma-algebra are accounted for.

label: MeasurableSpace.measurableSet_top
slogan: In a measurable space, every subset of the space is considered measurable because the structure guarantees that the entire set is included in the collection of measurable sets. This means that for any set, the condition of being measurable is automatically satisfied. The framework ensures that all sets are measurable by the definition of the space itself.

label: MeasurableSpace.measurable_injection_nat_bool_of_countablySeparated
slogan: If a measurable space can distinguish points using a countable collection of measurable sets, then there is an injective measurable function from the natural numbers into the Boolean values, meaning each natural number maps to a unique Boolean value in a way that preserves measurability.

label: MeasureTheory.AECover.integral_tendsto_of_countably_generated
slogan: If a sequence of measurable sets generates a countably generated filter and a function is integrable, then the integrals of the function over these sets converge to the integral over the whole space, provided the function is almost everywhere strongly measurable.

label: MeasureTheory.AEEqFun
slogan: Two functions are considered equivalent if they are equal almost everywhere, meaning the set of points where they differ has measure zero. This equivalence is defined for functions from a measurable space to a topological space, with respect to a given measure. It forms a setoid, allowing one to treat functions as equal when they differ only on negligible sets.

label: MeasureTheory.AEEqFun.tendsto_ae_unique
slogan: If two functions g and h are such that a sequence of functions converges to g almost everywhere and also to h almost everywhere with respect to a nontrivial measure, and the target space is Hausdorff, then g and h must be equal almost everywhere.

label: MeasureTheory.Adapted
slogan: A sequence of functions u is adapted to a filtration f if, for every time i, the function u at i is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra f i. This means that the value of u at each step depends only on the information available up to that step. The term "Adapted" was previously called "StronglyAdapted" before 2026-01-13.

label: MeasureTheory.AddContent.measureCaratheodory
slogan: Given a collection of sets that forms a semiring and an additive content function that is sigma-subadditive, this construction produces a measure defined on a sigma-algebra generated by the Carathéodory condition from the associated outer measure. The resulting measure assigns sizes to sets in a way that extends the original content and satisfies countable additivity. It is built by first forming an outer measure and then restricting to measurable sets.

label: MeasureTheory.Conservative.ae_frequently_mem_of_mem_nhds
slogan: In a conservative dynamical system with a well-behaved topology, almost every point returns to each of its neighborhoods infinitely often as the system evolves.

label: MeasureTheory.Conservative.exists_mem_iterate_mem
slogan: If a function f preserves the structure of a measurable space in a way that no set of positive measure disappears, and if s is a measurable set with positive size, then at least one point in s will come back to s after applying f some nonzero number of times.

label: MeasureTheory.Conservative.measure_mem_forall_ge_image_notMem_eq_zero
slogan: For a conservative dynamical system, almost every point in a measurable set will eventually return to that set after some number of iterations, meaning the set of points that never return after a certain time has measure zero.

label: MeasureTheory.ConvolutionExists.distrib_add
slogan: If the convolution of function f with each of g and g' exists, then the convolution of f with the sum (g + g') equals the sum of the individual convolutions of f with g and f with g'. This means convolution distributes over addition when the required integrability conditions are met.

label: MeasureTheory.Filtration
slogan: A Filtration is a family of sub-sigma-algebras on a measurable space, indexed by a preorder, such that each sigma-algebra is contained in the next as the index increases. It represents a growing collection of information over time in probability theory. The underlying space has a fixed sigma-algebra, and each member of the filtration is a subset of this sigma-algebra that is itself closed under complements and countable unions.

label: MeasureTheory.Filtration.natural
slogan: Given a sequence of functions from a space Ω into topological spaces, the natural filtration is the sequence of the smallest σ-algebras that make each function measurable as you go through the sequence. It is built by taking the preimages of measurable sets under each function and generating the necessary structure step by step. This filtration grows over time, capturing the information revealed by the functions up to each point.

label: MeasureTheory.HasPDF
slogan: A random variable X has a probability density function if the distribution of X can be described relative to another measure μ, meaning the probability of X falling in a set is given by integrating a density against μ, and this relationship is well-defined through absolute continuity and Lebesgue decomposition. This requires the push-forward of the probability measure along X to be absolutely continuous with respect to μ. The measures involved are defined on measurable spaces, and μ is typically the default volume measure unless specified otherwise.

label: MeasureTheory.Integrable
slogan: A function is integrable if it is measurable almost everywhere and the integral of its norm is finite, meaning it doesn't blow up over the space. This requires the function's domain to have a measure and measurable structure, and its codomain to have a topology and a continuous norm. The definition automatically fills in some technical proof requirements during type checking.

label: MeasureTheory.Integrable.fourierInv_fourier_eq
slogan: If a function f is integrable and its Fourier transform is also integrable, then applying the inverse Fourier transform to the Fourier transform of f gives back f at points where f is continuous.

label: MeasureTheory.Integrable.fourier_inversion
slogan: If a function f is integrable on a finite-dimensional real inner product space and its Fourier transform is also integrable, then applying the inverse Fourier transform to the Fourier transform of f recovers the original function f at points where f is continuous.

label: MeasureTheory.Integrable.integrable_convolution
slogan: If two functions are integrable with respect to an s-finite, right-translation-invariant measure on a measurable additive group, and if a continuous bilinear map is given between normed spaces, then their convolution defined using that bilinear map is also integrable with respect to the same measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Integrable.tendsto_ae_condExp
slogan: If g is an integrable real-valued function that is measurable with respect to the smallest sigma-algebra containing all the sigma-algebras in a filtration, then the sequence of conditional expectations of g given each sigma-algebra in the filtration converges almost everywhere to g.

label: MeasureTheory.IsAddFundamentalDomain
slogan: A set is an additive fundamental domain for a group action if it has exactly one point from each orbit under the group's addition, is measurable, and the measure of any set can be found by adding up the measures of its overlaps with the translates of the domain. This means the space can be tiled by shifting the domain using the group, and the measure behaves well under these shifts. It is used to study how groups act on spaces in a way that preserves measure.

label: MeasureTheory.IsProbabilityMeasure
slogan: A probability measure is a way of assigning numbers to sets in a space so that the total number for the whole space is exactly 1, and the numbers follow rules that allow adding up probabilities of disjoint events. It is built on a measurable space, which defines which sets can be measured, and it satisfies properties like non-negativity and countable additivity. This setup is used to model random processes where the entire sample space represents all possible outcomes.

label: MeasureTheory.IsStoppingTime
slogan: A stopping time is a rule for deciding when to stop a process such that at any time i, the decision to stop by then depends only on the information available up to time i. This means the set of outcomes where the stopping time is no later than i must be measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra at time i. The stopping time is formalized as a function from a measurable space Ω into extended time values, where the filtration represents the flow of information.

label: MeasureTheory.IsTightMeasureSet
slogan: A set of measures is called tight if, for every positive number epsilon, there is a compact set such that the measure of the complement of this set is at most epsilon for all measures in the set. This means that all the measures in the set concentrate most of their mass on a common compact set, no matter how small epsilon is. The definition uses filters to express this idea in a more general topological setting.

label: MeasureTheory.L2.innerProductSpace
slogan: The L2 space of measurable functions, where the square of the absolute value has a finite integral, forms an inner product space over a real-like field; this means it has a well-defined inner product that gives rise to a norm, allowing geometric notions like angles and orthogonality. The functions are identified if they are equal almost everywhere, and the space inherits vector space structure with operations defined pointwise. This instance ensures that L2 functions with values in a normed vector space over a real or complex field can be treated as a complete inner product space.

label: MeasureTheory.L2.inner_def
slogan: The inner product of two functions in the L2 space is equal to the integral of the pointwise inner product of those functions with respect to the given measure. This means the overall relationship between two functions is computed by integrating their local relationships at each point. The functions are considered equivalent if they differ only on a set of measure zero.

label: MeasureTheory.LevyProkhorov
slogan: LevyProkhorov is a type synonym used to represent measures, finite measures, or probability measures on a type α when equipping them with the Lévy-Prokhorov distance. It allows treating these measure types as metric spaces using that distance. The type depends on α and resides in the same universe as α.

label: MeasureTheory.LevyProkhorov.eq_convergenceInDistribution
slogan: On a separable metric space, the topology defined by the Lévy-Prokhorov metric on probability measures is the same as the topology of convergence in distribution. This means that a sequence of probability measures converges in the Lévy-Prokhorov metric if and only if it converges in distribution. The result follows by showing that the identity map between the two topologies is continuous in both directions.

label: MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrable
slogan: A function is called locally integrable if, for every point in its domain, there is a neighborhood around that point where the function is measurable and its integral is finite. This depends on the topology (to define neighborhoods), the measurable space (to define measurability), and the measure (to define integration). The function must be well-behaved in small regions everywhere it's defined.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp
slogan: Lp is the space of measurable functions where the p-th power of the absolute value has a finite integral with respect to a given measure, and functions that are equal almost everywhere are treated as the same; it forms a subgroup of equivalence classes of functions under addition.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.SecondCountableTopology
slogan: If a measure is separable, the space E is a second-countable normed abelian group, and p is a real number between 1 and infinity, then the Lp space of functions is second-countable. This means the topology of the Lp space has a countable base. Second-countability implies certain nice properties for the space, like being separable and metrizable.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.fourierTransformₗᵢ
slogan: The Fourier transform on square-integrable functions (L2) is a linear isometry that maps functions to their frequency representations while preserving the inner product structure and norm, and it has an inverse that does the same in reverse. It operates between complex-valued L2 function spaces over finite-dimensional real inner product spaces equipped with the Lebesgue measure. This transformation is fully reversible and maintains completeness and measurability properties.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.inner_fourier_eq
slogan: The inner product of the Fourier transforms of two L2 functions equals the inner product of the original functions, when working over complex inner product spaces and finite-dimensional real vector spaces with appropriate measurability and completeness conditions.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.instCompleteSpace
slogan: The space of measurable functions with finite p-norm, where p is at least 1, is complete: every Cauchy sequence of such functions converges to a limit that is also in the space, under the norm defined by integration with respect to a measure. This means the Lp space is closed under taking limits of sequences that are Cauchy in norm. The result relies on the completeness of the target space and the structure of the underlying measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.instNormedAddCommGroup
slogan: The space of Lp functions, where functions that are equal almost everywhere are treated as the same, forms a commutative group under addition, and the size of a function (its norm) is defined as the p-th root of the integral of the absolute value of the function raised to the p-th power. This norm satisfies basic properties like non-negativity, scalability, and the triangle inequality, and the distance between two functions is the norm of their difference. The zero function has norm zero, and the structure supports a metric that aligns with addition.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.norm_def
slogan: The Lp norm of a function is calculated by taking the integral of the function's absolute value raised to the power p, then taking the p-th root of that integral, with the result being a nonnegative real number or infinity; functions that are equal almost everywhere are treated as identical, and the norm is expressed as a real number when finite.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.norm_fourier_eq
slogan: The norm of the Fourier transform of a square-integrable function is equal to the norm of the function itself. This means the Fourier transform preserves the L2 size of functions. It applies to functions in L2 over a finite-dimensional real inner product space with values in a complex inner product space.

label: MeasureTheory.Lp.simpleFunc.denseRange
slogan: Simple functions that are measurable and take only finitely many values can approximate any function in the Lp space as closely as desired using the Lp norm, meaning their images are densely spread throughout the space. This holds for functions defined on a measure space with values in a normed vector space, when the exponent p is at least 1 and less than infinity. The approximation is understood in terms of the topology induced by the Lp norm, where closeness is measured by integral averages.

label: MeasureTheory.Martingale
slogan: A sequence of functions f indexed by a preorder is a martingale with respect to a filtration F and a measure mu if each f i is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra F i, and for any i <= j, the conditional expectation of f j given F i equals f i almost everywhere with respect to mu.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure
slogan: MeasureTheory.Measure defines a measure as a function that assigns a non-negative number to measurable sets in a given space, requiring that the measure of a countable union of disjoint sets equals the sum of their measures. It depends on a MeasurableSpace structure to specify which sets can be measured, and it generalizes concepts like length, area, volume, and probability. This measure is built on the idea of an outer measure but is restricted to measurable sets and satisfies stronger additivity properties.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.HaveLebesgueDecomposition
slogan: A measure μ has Lebesgue decomposition with respect to another measure ν if μ can be written as the sum of two parts: one that is absolutely continuous with respect to ν (meaning it behaves like a density function relative to ν) and another that is singular with respect to ν (meaning it is concentrated on a set that ν assigns zero measure). This decomposition is unique and always satisfies the additivity property of measures.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.IsComplete
slogan: A measure is complete if every subset of a set with measure zero is also measurable and has measure zero. This ensures no subset of a negligible set is left out of the measurable collection.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.IsHaarMeasure
slogan: A Haar measure is a way of assigning sizes to sets in a topological group so that the size of a set doesn't change when it's shifted by group multiplication, it's finite on compact sets, and every nonempty open set has positive size. It combines group symmetry, topology, and measure theory to allow integration that respects the group structure. Such a measure is defined on a space with both a group operation and a measurable structure compatible with a topology.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.IsMulLeftInvariant
slogan: A MeasureTheory.Measure.IsMulLeftInvariant describes a measure on a set with multiplication, where the measure of any measurable set stays the same when the set is multiplied on the left by any fixed element. In other words, shifting a set using left multiplication does not change its size under this measure. This property is important in areas like harmonic analysis and the study of topological groups.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.IsMulRightInvariant
slogan: A measure is right-invariant if the measure of any measurable set does not change when the set is multiplied on the right by any fixed element of the group. This means that right translations preserve the size assigned by the measure. The concept applies to types equipped with a measurable multiplication operation.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.IsOpenPosMeasure
slogan: A measure on a topological space is such that every nonempty open set has a positive size. This means that if a set contains an open region, it cannot have zero measure. The condition links the geometric idea of openness with the quantitative idea of positive size.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.MutuallySingular
slogan: Two measures are mutually singular if there is a measurable set such that one measure gives it zero mass and the other gives zero mass to its complement, meaning they concentrate on completely separate parts of the space.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.absolutelyContinuous_iff_withDensity_rnDeriv_eq
slogan: If one measure is absolutely continuous with respect to another, then the first measure can be recovered by integrating its Radon-Nikodym derivative against the second measure, provided the measures satisfy a Lebesgue decomposition condition.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_parallelepiped
slogan: The volume of a parallelepiped formed by applying a linear map to the unit cube in a finite-dimensional real vector space is equal to the absolute value of the determinant of that linear map, treated as an extended nonnegative real number. This volume measure is the same as the Haar measure, which is translation-invariant and unique up to scaling. The result shows that the determinant captures how linear transformations scale volumes.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_smul
slogan: Scaling a set by a nonzero real number multiplies its Haar measure by the absolute value of that number raised to the power of the dimension of the space. This means the measure of the scaled set equals the original measure times |r|^n, where r is the scaling factor and n is the dimension. The result applies to any measurable set in a finite-dimensional real vector space.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.condKernel
slogan: Given a finite measure on a product space where the second space is standard Borel and nonempty, the conditional kernel is a measurable assignment of a probability measure on the second space to each point in the first space, such that the original measure equals the product of the marginal on the first space and this kernel.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.conv
slogan: The conv function takes two measures on a space with addition and produces a new measure by combining them through addition: for any set, it integrates the product of the two measures over all pairs of points that add up to elements in that set. It does this by forming the product measure on pairs, then pushing it forward using the addition operation. The space must support measurable addition and have a well-defined product sigma-algebra for this to work.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.count
slogan: The count measure gives each measurable set a size equal to how many elements are in it, counting infinite sets as having infinite size. It is built by adding up Dirac measures, which assign a value of 1 to sets containing a specific point and 0 otherwise. This measure works on any measurable space and follows the standard rules of measures, such as adding up correctly over disjoint sets.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac
slogan: The Dirac measure at a point assigns 1 to any set containing that point and 0 to sets that do not, creating a valid measure on a measurable space. It is built from an outer measure that satisfies Caratheodory's criterion, ensuring proper behavior on measurable sets. This measure models point masses in mathematics and probability.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_of_complexMGF_eq
slogan: If two random variables have the same complex moment-generating function with respect to finite measures, then their induced distributions (the pushforward measures) are equal. This means the complex moment-generating function uniquely determines the distribution of a random variable when the underlying measures are finite.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.finite_of_finite_mconv
slogan: If two measures are finite and defined on a monoid with a suitable measurable structure, then their convolution is also a finite measure. This means that when you combine two measures using the monoid operation, the total size of the resulting measure remains finite. Finiteness here means the measure of the whole space is a finite number, not infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.haarMeasure
slogan: The haarMeasure function assigns a size to measurable sets in a topological group such that the size of a set does not change when it is shifted by any group element. It starts from a measure defined on compact sets that is invariant under group operations and extends it to a full measure on all Borel sets. This measure is nonnegative, countably additive, and respects both the group's algebraic structure and its topology.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.haarMeasure_unique
slogan: On a locally compact topological group, any two regular Borel measures that are invariant under left translations are scalar multiples of each other; if they give the same finite positive measure to a compact set with nonempty interior, then they are exactly the same measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure
slogan: The Hausdorff measure assigns a size to subsets of a metric space in a way that generalizes length, area, and volume, depending on a given dimension d. It is constructed using a method that approximates the size of sets at small scales. This measure is defined for any extended metric space that also has a measurable structure compatible with its topology.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure_smul₀
slogan: Scaling a set by a nonzero factor r in a normed space multiplies its d-dimensional Hausdorff measure by the norm of r raised to the power d. This holds for any non-negative real dimension d and applies to sets in spaces with compatible algebraic and measurable structures. The result reflects how the measure changes under linear scaling.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomposition_of_sigmaFinite
slogan: Any sigma-finite measure can be split into two parts relative to another sigma-finite measure: one part that is absolutely continuous (behaves like a density) and a second part that is singular (concentrated on a set of zero measure). This decomposition is always possible when both measures are sigma-finite.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomposition_spec
slogan: Any measure can be broken into two pieces relative to another measure: one piece that behaves like a scaled version (given by a density function) and another piece that lives entirely on a set where the second measure is zero, and these two pieces together make up the original measure. The density function is measurable, and the singular piece doesn't overlap in support with the second measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.inv
slogan: The inv function takes a measure on a space with an inversion operation and creates a new measure by assigning to each set the measure of its inverse. It uses the map function to push the measure forward through the inversion map. This results in a measure that reflects symmetry under the group's inverse operation.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.isHaarMeasure_eq_of_isProbabilityMeasure
slogan: On a locally compact topological group, if two probability measures are invariant under group translations, then they must be the same measure. This means there can be at most one translation-invariant probability measure on such a group.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.isHaarMeasure_of_isCompact_nonempty_interior
slogan: A measure on a topological group is a Haar measure if it is invariant under left multiplication, assigns finite measure to compact sets, and gives positive measure to nonempty open sets, provided there exists a compact set with nonempty interior that has neither zero nor infinite measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.map
slogan: The map function takes a measure defined on one space and a measurable function to another space, then creates a new measure on the second space by assigning to each measurable set the value of the original measure on its preimage. This new measure, called the pushforward, preserves the structure of the original measure and allows measuring sets in the target space based on how they are reached through the function. It works with extended nonnegative real values, including infinity, and supports standard measure properties like additivity.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.prod
slogan: MeasureTheory.Measure.prod takes two measures defined on measurable spaces and creates a new measure on the product space of pairs, such that the measure of a rectangle (a product of two measurable sets) is the product of their measures. It uses the standard measurable structure on the product space, ensuring that projections and measurable functions behave correctly. This construction allows combining measures from two spaces into one measure that acts on pairs.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.prod_apply
slogan: The product measure of two measures on two spaces assigns to a measurable set in the product space the integral of the measure of its slices, where each slice is taken by fixing a point in the first space and measuring the corresponding section in the second space. For a measurable rectangle, this value equals the product of the two individual measures. This definition ensures the measure is consistent with expected behavior on product sets and uses preimages to maintain measurability.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv
slogan: The rnDeriv function takes two measures on the same measurable space and returns a function from points in the space to extended nonnegative real numbers, representing the rate at which one measure changes relative to the other at each point. If one measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the other, this function acts as a density that recovers the first measure by integrating against the second. When the measures are mutually singular, the function is zero everywhere.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.sum_smul_dirac
slogan: In a countable space where each point can be measured, the total measure of any set is the sum of the individual point masses assigned to it, and this sum matches the original measure when each point's weight is given by the measure of that singleton point. This means adding up scaled Dirac measures (point masses) recovers the full measure. The identity map ensures the pushforward of the sum measure equals the original measure.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.support
slogan: A point x is in the support of a measure μ if every open set containing x has positive measure. This means x is "seen" by the measure in the sense that no neighborhood around x can have zero measure. The support is the set of all such points.

label: MeasureTheory.Measure.withDensity_rnDeriv_eq
slogan: If one measure is absolutely continuous with respect to another, then the first measure can be recovered by integrating the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the first with respect to the second against the second measure. In simpler terms, reweighting the second measure using this derivative function gives back the first measure exactly. This holds when the measures satisfy the conditions for Lebesgue decomposition.

label: MeasureTheory.MeasurePreserving
slogan: A measure-preserving function maps one measurable space to another in a way that keeps the measure of sets unchanged, meaning the size of a set in the output space equals the size of its preimage in the input space. Both spaces must have a defined collection of measurable sets and a measure. This idea is used to study systems where the total amount of "stuff", like probability or volume, stays constant over time.

label: MeasureTheory.MeasurePreserving.exists_mem_iterate_mem
slogan: If a function preserves the measure of sets and the total measure of the space is finite, then for any set with positive measure, there is a point in that set which, after applying the function repeatedly some number of times, returns to the set.

label: MeasureTheory.MeasurePreserving.symm
slogan: If a bijective function between two measurable spaces is measurable in both directions and preserves measure, then its inverse function also preserves measure. This means that when a function pushes forward a measure without changing it, the reverse process using the inverse does the same. The result ensures symmetry in measure preservation for measurable equivalences.

label: MeasureTheory.MeasureSpace
slogan: A measure space is a set where certain subsets are designated as measurable, and a measure function assigns a size (like length or probability) to those subsets in a way that adds up correctly for countable disjoint collections. It combines a measurable space, which defines what can be measured, with a measure, which quantifies the size of measurable sets. This structure supports the rigorous development of integration and probability.

label: MeasureTheory.MemLp
slogan: A function is in Lp space if it is measurable almost everywhere (meaning it matches a measurable function outside a set of measure zero) and the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power p is finite, where the result is taken in the extended non-negative real numbers (including infinity). This depends on a measure, a measurable space, and a topology on the target space. The function's size is measured using the extended Lp norm, which allows infinity as a possible value.

label: MeasureTheory.MemLp.mono_exponent
slogan: If a measurable function belongs to an Lp space with exponent q and the measure of the space is finite, then it also belongs to the Lp space with any smaller exponent p, as long as p is less than or equal to q. This means integrability with a higher exponent implies integrability with any lower exponent in finite measure spaces.

label: MeasureTheory.MemLp.mono_exponent_of_measure_support_ne_top
slogan: If a function is measurable and its values are zero outside a set of finite measure, then being integrable with a higher exponent (q) implies it is also integrable with any lower or equal exponent (p ≤ q). In simpler terms, if a function doesn't spread out too much (finite support) and is Lq-integrable, it's automatically Lp-integrable for smaller p. This shows that integrability gets better (or stays the same) as the exponent decreases, when the function's support has finite measure.

label: MeasureTheory.NoAtoms
slogan: A measure has no atoms if every set with positive size contains a smaller measurable subset with still positive but smaller size, meaning no single point has positive measure on its own. This ensures the measure is spread out rather than concentrated at individual points. It applies to measures on a measurable space and is used to describe continuous-like behavior in integration and probability.

label: MeasureTheory.NullMeasurable
slogan: A function is null measurable if it becomes measurable when ignored on a set of measure zero, meaning it is measurable almost everywhere with respect to a given measure. This allows handling functions that are not fully measurable but behave like measurable ones outside negligible parts of the space. The definition depends on the measurable structures of the domain and codomain, and the measure on the domain.

label: MeasureTheory.NullMeasurable.measurable_of_complete
slogan: If a function is measurable everywhere except possibly on a set of measure zero and the measure includes all subsets of zero-measure sets, then the function is measurable overall. This means the preimage of any measurable set under the function is also measurable. It connects null measurable functions to fully measurable ones when working with complete measures.

label: MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet
slogan: A null measurable set is one that differs from a measurable set by a set of measure zero, meaning it is measurable "up to negligible sets" with respect to a given measure. This allows working with sets and functions that are equivalent almost everywhere, ignoring differences on null sets. It provides a more flexible framework for integration and measure theory where exact equality is less important than equality almost everywhere.

label: MeasureTheory.OuterMeasure.IsCaratheodory
slogan: An outer measure is called Caratheodory if, whenever one set is measurable, the measure of the union of two disjoint sets equals the sum of their individual measures. This condition ensures that the measurable sets form a sigma-algebra and that the outer measure becomes a true measure on that collection. A set is considered measurable in this sense if it splits every other set additively according to the outer measure.

label: MeasureTheory.OuterMeasure.caratheodory
slogan: A set is measurable if it divides every other set into two parts such that the outer measure of the whole is the sum of the measures of the parts; the collection of all such sets forms a measurable space. This measurable space is built using Caratheodory's condition, ensuring closure under complements and countable disjoint unions. The construction starts from an outer measure and produces a valid measurable space structure on the underlying set.

label: MeasureTheory.OuterMeasure.toMeasure
slogan: An outer measure assigns sizes to all subsets of a space, but to get a proper measure, we restrict it to only those sets that split every other set additively, meaning the outer measure of any set equals the sum of the measures of its parts inside and outside a given measurable set. These well-behaved sets form a sigma-algebra, and the resulting measure gives extended nonnegative real values in a way that respects countable additivity for disjoint sets. This process turns an outer measure into a full measure on a measurable space, enabling integration and probability.

label: MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure
slogan: A probability measure is a way of assigning a number between 0 and 1 to sets in a measurable space, such that the entire space has measure 1, representing the total probability. It is built on a measurable space, which defines which subsets can be measured. This structure is used to formalize probability theory in mathematics.

label: MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_iff_forall_integral_tendsto
slogan: A sequence of probability measures converges weakly to a limit measure if and only if the integrals of all bounded continuous real-valued functions with respect to the sequence converge to the integral with respect to the limit measure.

label: MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_iff_tendsto_charFun
slogan: A sequence of probability measures converges weakly to a limit if and only if their characteristic functions converge pointwise to the characteristic function of the limit measure, where each characteristic function is defined as the Fourier transform of the measure using complex exponentials of inner products. This result holds in finite-dimensional real inner product spaces with standard measurability and topological structure. The convergence is expressed in terms of filters, linking topological convergence of measures to convergence of complex-valued functions.

label: MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.exists_compl_positive_negative
slogan: For any signed measure on a measurable space, there exists a measurable set such that the measure is non-negative on that set and non-positive on its complement.

label: MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.exists_isCompl_positive_negative
slogan: For any signed measure, there are two disjoint measurable sets that together make up the whole space, where the measure is non-negative on one set and non-positive on the other.

label: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc
slogan: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc is a function that maps from a measurable space α to a type β, taking only finitely many values and being measurable, meaning preimages of measurable sets in β are measurable in α. It requires α to have a MeasurableSpace structure and outputs values in a type β, combining simplicity and measurability for use in integration theory.

label: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.eapprox
slogan: The function eapprox takes a measurable function from a space to the extended nonnegative real numbers and returns a sequence of simple functions, each taking finitely many values, that increase pointwise toward the original function. These approximating functions are built using rational values embedded into the extended nonnegative reals.
