The construction ensures that for every point in the space, the values of the simple functions eventually get arbitrarily close to the value of the original function.

label: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.integral
slogan: The integral of a simple function is calculated by adding up its values multiplied by the size (measure) of the sets where each value occurs, using real-number scaling in a vector space with a norm. This applies to functions that are measurable and take only finitely many values. The result is an element of the same normed vector space as the function's outputs.

label: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.lintegral
slogan: The lintegral of a simple function is found by taking each value the function outputs, multiplying it by the size (measure) of the set of inputs that map to that value, and adding up all these products. The function must be measurable and only take finitely many values, and the result is a number in the extended non-negative reals (including possibly infinity).

label: MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.posPart_sub_negPart
slogan: For a simple measurable function, subtracting the function that keeps only negative values (and sets positives to zero) from the one that keeps only positive values (and sets negatives to zero) gives back the original function. This works because at each point, the difference between the positive and negative parts of a real number equals the number itself. The result holds pointwise and relies on standard properties of real numbers like order, addition, and subtraction.

label: MeasureTheory.Submartingale
slogan: A submartingale is a sequence of integrable functions indexed by a preorder such that each function in the sequence is measurable with respect to a corresponding sub-sigma-algebra in a filtration, and for any two indices i ≤ j, the value of the function at i is almost everywhere less than or equal to the conditional expectation of the function at j given the information available at i.

label: MeasureTheory.Submartingale.ae_tendsto_limitProcess
slogan: An L¹-bounded submartingale converges almost everywhere to a limit that is measurable with respect to the smallest sigma-algebra containing all the filtrations. The limit function is chosen so that convergence holds for almost all sample points under the given finite measure. If no such limit exists, the process defaults to zero.

label: MeasureTheory.Submartingale.stoppedProcess
slogan: If a process follows a submartingale and you stop it at a stopping time, the resulting stopped process is still a submartingale.

label: MeasureTheory.Supermartingale
slogan: A supermartingale is a sequence of integrable functions indexed by a preorder, adapted to a growing family of sigma-algebras, such that the conditional expectation of a later term given earlier information is almost surely less than or equal to the current term.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInDistribution
slogan: Convergence in distribution means that the probability measures of a sequence of random variables get arbitrarily close to the probability measure of a limiting random variable, in the sense that their expected values converge for all bounded continuous functions. This happens when the underlying index approaches some limit defined by a filter, and all random variables take values in a topological space where open sets are measurable. The random variables are functions from a probability space to a measurable topological space, and the convergence is defined with respect to a given probability

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInDistribution.add_of_tendstoInMeasure_const
slogan: If a sequence of random variables X_n converges in distribution to a random variable Z, and another sequence Y_n converges in measure to a constant c, with each Y_n almost everywhere measurable, then the sum X_n + Y_n converges in distribution to Z + c, provided the underlying space is a second-countable, Borel seminormed topological group and the measure is a probability measure.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInDistribution.continuous_comp
slogan: If a sequence of random variables converges in distribution to a limit and a function is continuous, then applying that function to the sequence results in new random variables that converge in distribution to the function applied to the limit.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInDistribution.prodMk_of_tendstoInMeasure_const
slogan: If a sequence of random variables X_n converges in distribution to a random variable Z, and another sequence Y_n converges in probability to a constant c, then the joint sequence (X_n, Y_n) converges in distribution to (Z, c). This means the limiting behavior of the pair is determined by the limit of X_n and the constant limit of Y_n. Convergence in probability to a constant implies the fluctuations of Y_n become negligible.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInMeasure
slogan: A sequence of functions converges in measure to a limit function if, for any positive tolerance, the size of the set where the sequence differs from the limit by more than that tolerance gets arbitrarily small as the sequence progresses. This means the functions eventually stay close to the limit over nearly the whole space, except possibly on a set of small measure. It is a notion of convergence that is weaker than uniform or pointwise convergence but stronger than convergence in distribution.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInMeasure.exists_seq_tendsto_ae
slogan: If a sequence of functions converges in measure to a limit function, then there is a subsequence that converges almost everywhere to the same limit. This means that outside a set of measure zero, the subsequence approaches the limit function pointwise. The subsequence is chosen such that its indices increase strictly and the convergence holds in the topology of the codomain.

label: MeasureTheory.TendstoInMeasure.tendstoInDistribution
slogan: If a sequence of random variables converges in probability to a limit, then it also converges in distribution to that same limit, provided the variables are almost everywhere measurable and the underlying measure is a probability measure. This holds when the codomain is a second-countable, Borel space with a seminormed group structure. Convergence in distribution means the probability laws of the variables weakly converge to the law of the limit.

label: MeasureTheory.UnifIntegrable
slogan: A sequence of functions is uniformly integrable if, for any small positive number epsilon, there is a corresponding small positive number delta such that whenever a measurable set has measure less than delta, the Lp norm of each function in the sequence over that set is less than epsilon. This means the integrals of the functions over small sets can be made uniformly small across the entire sequence. The concept depends on a measure space, a normed group for the function values, and an extended nonnegative real number p.

label: MeasureTheory.UniformIntegrable
slogan: A family of measurable functions is uniformly integrable if, for some p greater than or equal to 1, the integrals of their p-th powers are uniformly bounded and they are all measurable in a way that respects the measure on the space. This means the functions do not grow too large on sets of positive measure and their sizes, measured by the eLpNorm, stay under a common bound. The condition ensures that no single function in the family can dominate the integral behavior in an uncontrolled way.

label: MeasureTheory.ae
slogan: A set satisfies the "almost everywhere" condition with respect to an outer measure if the points where it fails are contained in a countable union of sets, each having zero measure. This means the property holds everywhere except possibly on a negligible (measure zero) set. The definition uses a filter to capture the idea that a condition holds for all points outside a set that can be ignored in measure theory.

label: MeasureTheory.ae_eq_condExp_of_forall_setIntegral_eq
slogan: If a function g is almost everywhere measurable, integrable on sets of finite measure, and has the same integral as f on every measurable set where the measure is finite, then g is almost everywhere equal to the conditional expectation of f with respect to the given sub-sigma-algebra and measure.

label: MeasureTheory.average
slogan: The average of a function f over a space with respect to a measure μ is the integral of f divided by the total measure of the space, as long as the measure is finite and positive. It gives the mean value of the function in that space using standard integration and vector space operations, with rules extended to handle infinite values where needed. This definition applies to functions mapping into a normed vector space over the real numbers.

label: MeasureTheory.charFun
slogan: The characteristic function of a measure μ on a real inner product space E is a complex-valued function defined for each point t in E by integrating the complex exponential of the inner product of t with points in E, with respect to the measure μ. Specifically, it computes the integral of exp(i * ⟨t, x⟩) dμ(x), where i is the imaginary unit and ⟨t, x⟩ is the inner product of t and x. This function helps analyze measures using tools from Fourier analysis.

label: MeasureTheory.charFun_eq_integral_innerProbChar
slogan: The characteristic function of a measure at a point t is equal to the integral of the function that maps each point x to the complex exponential of the inner product of t and x, with respect to the measure. This function is bounded and continuous, and the integral is taken over the entire space. In simpler terms, it expresses the characteristic function as an average of oscillating complex values weighted by the measure.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp
slogan: The conditional expectation of a function f with respect to a sub-sigma-algebra m under a measure mu, written mu[f|m], is a function that averages f over the measurable sets in m. It is defined as zero if m is not contained in the original sigma-algebra, if mu is not sigma-finite on m, or if f is not integrable. Otherwise, it gives the best approximation of f that is measurable with respect to m.

label: MeasureTheory.condExpL2
slogan: The conditional expectation of an L2 function with respect to a sub-sigma-algebra is the orthogonal projection of that function onto the subspace of functions measurable with respect to the sub-sigma-algebra, using the given measure. It maps square-integrable functions to their best approximation that is measurable with respect to the smaller sigma-algebra. This projection is linear and preserves the integral over sets in the sub-sigma-algebra.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_add
slogan: The conditional expectation of the sum of two integrable functions is equal to the sum of their conditional expectations, almost everywhere with respect to the measure. This holds when both functions map into a complete normed vector space over the reals and are integrable with respect to the given measure. The equality is understood in the almost everywhere sense, meaning it holds except possibly on a set of measure zero.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_condExp_of_le
slogan: If you take the conditional expectation of a function f with respect to a larger sigma-algebra m2, and then take the conditional expectation of that result with respect to a smaller sigma-algebra m1, it's the same as taking the conditional expectation of f directly with respect to m1, almost everywhere under the measure mu. This holds when m1 is contained in m2, and m2 is contained in the base sigma-algebra m0, with mu being sigma-finite on m2.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_indep_eq
slogan: If two sigma-algebras are independent and a function is measurable with respect to one of them, then the conditional expectation of the function given the other sigma-algebra is equal almost everywhere to the integral of the function.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_mono
slogan: If one function is less than or equal to another almost everywhere with respect to a measure, and both are integrable, then the conditional expectation of the first function is less than or equal to the conditional expectation of the second almost everywhere as well. This means the conditional expectation preserves the order of functions under the given conditions. The result holds in a general setting where the functions take values in a complete, normed, ordered vector space.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_mul_of_stronglyMeasurable_left
slogan: If f is a strongly measurable function and both f*g and g are integrable with respect to a measure μ, then the conditional expectation of f*g given a sub-σ-algebra m is almost everywhere equal to f times the conditional expectation of g given m.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_nonneg
slogan: If a function f is almost everywhere non-negative with respect to a measure μ, then its conditional expectation with respect to μ is also almost everywhere non-negative.

label: MeasureTheory.condExp_of_stronglyMeasurable
slogan: If a function f is strongly measurable and integrable with respect to a measure μ, and the σ-algebra m is contained in m₀ with μ being σ-finite when restricted to m, then the conditional expectation of f with respect to m is equal to f itself.

label: MeasureTheory.convolution
slogan: The convolution of two functions f and g with respect to a continuous bilinear map L and a measure μ is defined as the function that, at each point x, gives the integral of L applied to f(t) and g(x - t) with respect to μ over t. It combines f and g in a way that reflects their overlap as one is shifted relative to the other, using L to combine values and μ to weight the integration. This operation is defined for functions on a measurable additive group where the necessary normed and measurable structures are in place.

label: MeasureTheory.convolution_assoc
slogan: Convolution is associative under certain conditions: if the functions involved are almost everywhere strongly measurable, the required convolutions exist almost everywhere, and the norms of the functions satisfy appropriate integrability conditions, then the convolution of f with g, then with k, equals the convolution of f with the convolution of g and k.

label: MeasureTheory.convolution_eq_swap
slogan: The convolution of two functions f and g at a point x, using a bilinear map L and a measure mu, is equal to the integral over t of L applied to f(x - t) and g(t), with respect to mu. This holds when the underlying space is a measurable additive group with a measure that is invariant under addition and negation, and when the functions and spaces involved have appropriate normed and measurability properties. The result shows that the order of the functions in the convolution can be swapped in the integral expression.

label: MeasureTheory.convolution_flip
slogan: The convolution of two functions f and g with respect to a bilinear map L and a measure μ is the same as the convolution of g and f with the flipped bilinear map, meaning the order of functions can be swapped if the map is adjusted accordingly. This holds when the underlying space is a commutative group with a measure that is invariant under addition and negation, and all operations are measurable. The result follows from the symmetry of integration over such a group.

label: MeasureTheory.cylinder
slogan: A cylinder is the set of all functions from an index type ι to dependent types α i such that the restriction of the function to a finite subset s of indices lies in a given set S of functions defined on s. It is formed by taking the preimage of S under the natural projection that restricts functions on ι to functions on s. This construction is used to define measurable sets in product spaces.

label: MeasureTheory.eLpNorm
slogan: eLpNorm computes the size of a measurable function by taking the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value raised to the power p, using extended non-negative real numbers that include infinity; for infinite p, it uses the essential supremum instead. It works within a measure space to account for negligible sets and generalizes the idea of function norms in Lp spaces.

label: MeasureTheory.eLpNormEssSup
slogan: The eLpNormEssSup is a function that computes the essential supremum norm of a measurable function, meaning the smallest number that is greater than or equal to the absolute value of the function almost everywhere, ignoring sets where the measure is zero. It returns a value in the extended nonnegative real numbers, which includes infinity, and is used to measure the largest "significant" size of a function in a measure space. This norm is defined for functions from a measurable space to a type with a norm, using a given measure.

label: MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_add_le
slogan: The extended Lp norm of the sum of two measurable functions is at most the sum of their extended Lp norms, where the norm accounts for infinite values using extended non-negative real numbers. This holds for all p greater than or equal to 1, including infinity, and applies almost everywhere with respect to the measure. It generalizes the triangle inequality to spaces of measurable functions.

label: MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_fderiv_of_eq
slogan: For a continuously differentiable, compactly supported function u from a finite-dimensional normed space E to another finite-dimensional normed space F, the Lp' norm of u is less than or equal to a constant multiple of the Lp norm of its derivative, where p' is defined by 1/p' = 1/p - 1/dim(E) and the constant depends only on E, F, the measure, and p.

label: MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_of_exponent_le
slogan: If p is less than or equal to q and the measure space has finite total measure (like a probability space), then the extended Lp norm of a measurable function is less than or equal to its extended Lq norm. This means that increasing the exponent in the Lp norm does not decrease the norm value. The result holds for functions that are measurable almost everywhere and take values in a space with a continuous norm.

label: MeasureTheory.exists_ne_zero_mem_lattice_of_measure_mul_two_pow_le_measure
slogan: If the volume of a symmetric, compact, convex set in a finite-dimensional real vector space is at least the volume of a fundamental domain of a lattice multiplied by 2 raised to the dimension of the space, then the set must contain a nonzero point from the lattice.

label: MeasureTheory.exists_ne_zero_mem_lattice_of_measure_mul_two_pow_lt_measure
slogan: If a symmetric, convex, measurable set in a finite-dimensional real vector space has measure greater than the measure of a fundamental domain of a lattice multiplied by 2 raised to the dimension of the space, then some nonzero lattice point lies in the set when the set is scaled by a power of two.

label: MeasureTheory.exists_nonempty_inter_of_measure_univ_lt_sum_measure
slogan: If the total measure of the whole space is less than the sum of the measures of a finite collection of measurable sets, then at least two of those sets must overlap; in other words, there exist two distinct sets in the collection whose intersection is not empty. This means the sets cannot all be pairwise disjoint when their combined measure exceeds the measure of the entire space. The result holds for sets that are measurable with respect to a given measure on a measurable space, where measures take values in the extended nonnegative real numbers.

label: MeasureTheory.hasPDF_iff
slogan: A random variable has a probability density function relative to a measure if and only if it is almost everywhere measurable, the pushforward measure of the probability distribution through the variable is absolutely continuous with respect to the target measure, and the pushforward measure admits a Lebesgue decomposition with respect to that target measure.

label: MeasureTheory.inner_condExpL2_left_eq_right
slogan: The inner product of the conditional expectation of a function f with another function g is equal to the inner product of f with the conditional expectation of g, using square-integrable functions and a given measure. This means projecting f onto the space of measurable functions for a sub-sigma-algebra and then taking the inner product with g gives the same result as doing the projection on g first and then taking the inner product with f. The equality holds due to the symmetry of the inner product and the self-adjoint nature of the projection operator.

label: MeasureTheory.integrableOn_Ioi_of_intervalIntegral_norm_bounded
slogan: If a function is integrable on every finite interval from a point a to some b_i, and the integrals of its norm over these intervals are uniformly bounded by a constant, and the b_i tend to infinity, then the function is integrable on the infinite interval (a, ∞). This means the function can be integrated over all real numbers greater than a, provided its size doesn't grow too quickly and it behaves well on large intervals.

label: MeasureTheory.integrable_congr
slogan: If two functions are equal almost everywhere with respect to a measure, then one is integrable if and only if the other is integrable. This means changing a function on a set of measure zero does not affect its integrability.

label: MeasureTheory.integrable_indicator_iff
slogan: The indicator function of a set is integrable if and only if the function is integrable when restricted to that set. This holds when the set is measurable and the measure of the set is finite, ensuring the function's integral is well-defined and bounded. Integrability requires both measurability and a finite total value over the space.

label: MeasureTheory.integrable_norm_iff
slogan: A function is integrable if it is almost everywhere equal to a well-behaved (strongly measurable) function and the integral of its norm is finite; this means the function must be measurable in a strong sense and its size must not grow too large over the space.

label: MeasureTheory.integral
slogan: The integral of a function is defined when the function is measurable and its size has a finite average with respect to a given measure, and it produces a value in the same kind of space the function maps into, such as the real numbers. It is built by first identifying functions that are equal almost everywhere and then using a linear and continuous process to assign a total accumulated value. This works for functions whose outputs can be added and scaled, and where sizes are measured in a consistent way.

label: MeasureTheory.integral2_divergence_prod_of_hasFDerivAt_off_countable
slogan: If a vector field is continuous on a rectangle and differentiable everywhere inside except possibly on a countable set of points, then the double integral of its divergence over the rectangle equals the sum of the line integrals along the edges of the rectangle, representing the total outward flux across the boundary.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_add
slogan: The integral of the sum of two functions equals the sum of their integrals, as long as both functions are integrable over the same measure space. This additivity property holds for functions taking values in a normed vector space, using Bochner integration. It means integration respects addition for functions that are well-behaved in the sense of measure theory.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_condExp
slogan: The integral of the conditional expectation of a function f with respect to a sub-sigma-algebra is equal to the integral of f itself, meaning conditioning does not change the overall average. This holds when the measure is sigma-finite with respect to the smaller sigma-algebra and the function takes values in a complete normed vector space over the reals.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_congr_ae
slogan: If two functions are equal almost everywhere with respect to a measure, then their integrals over that measure are equal. This means that modifying a function on a set of measure zero does not change its integral. The result holds for functions taking values in a normed vector space over the reals.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_convolution
slogan: The integral of the convolution of two integrable functions over a group with respect to a bilinear map equals the bilinear map applied to the integrals of the two functions separately. This holds when the group has compatible measure and topological structure, and the measures involved are invariant and s-finite. The result connects integration with convolution in a linear way.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_of_hasFDerivAt_off_countable
slogan: If a vector field is continuous on a rectangular region and differentiable everywhere except on a countable set, then the integral of its divergence over that region equals the sum of the fluxes through the faces of the boundary. The flux on each face is computed as the difference of integrals of the vector field components at opposite ends of the interval. This extends the divergence theorem to vector fields that are not perfectly smooth.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_prod_Icc_of_hasFDerivAt_of_le
slogan: If a pair of functions from the plane to a normed vector space are continuous on a rectangle and differentiable inside it except possibly on a countable set, and if their derivatives are integrable, then the integral of the sum of the partial derivatives over the rectangle equals the sum of the line integrals of the functions along the boundary of the rectangle, taken in the appropriate directions.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_prod_Icc_of_hasFDerivAt_off_countable_of_le
slogan: The integral of the divergence of a vector function over a rectangle [a, b] x [c, d] equals the sum of the integrals of the function's components along the top and bottom edges minus those on the left and right edges, provided the function is differentiable except on a countable set and continuous on the boundary. This links the total outward flux through the rectangle's edges to the divergence inside the region. It is a 2D version of the divergence theorem for product intervals.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_eq_lintegral_pos_part_sub_lintegral_neg_part
slogan: The integral of a measurable real-valued function with respect to a measure is equal to the integral of its positive part minus the integral of its negative part, where each part is first converted to an extended nonnegative real number, integrated, and then converted back to a real number. This holds when the function is integrable, meaning both parts have finite integrals. The positive and negative parts are handled separately using nonnegative integration before combining them.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_eq_zero_iff_of_nonneg_ae
slogan: If a real-valued function is nonnegative almost everywhere and integrable with respect to a measure, then its integral is zero if and only if the function itself is zero almost everywhere. This means the function can only have a nonzero integral if it is positive on a set of positive measure.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_finset
slogan: The integral of a function over a finite set with respect to a measure equals the sum of the function's values at each point in the set, multiplied by the measure of that point. This holds for functions taking values in a complete normed vector space over the real numbers, provided the function is integrable on the set.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_image_eq_integral_abs_deriv_smul
slogan: The integral of a function g over the image of a set s under a function f equals the integral of g composed with f, multiplied by the absolute value of the derivative of f, provided f is injective and differentiable on s. This formula adjusts the integral to account for how f stretches or shrinks intervals. It is a one-dimensional change of variables rule for integration.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_image_eq_integral_abs_det_fderiv_smul
slogan: When a function f maps a measurable set s in a finite-dimensional real vector space to another space and is injective on s, the integral of a function g over the image of s under f is equal to the integral over s of g composed with f, multiplied by the absolute value of the determinant of f's derivative at each point. This determinant factor accounts for how much the function stretches or shrinks space locally. The result holds for real-valued measures that are translation-invariant, assuming f is differentiable on s and all functions involved are measurable.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_map
slogan: The integral of a function over a space with respect to a pushforward measure is the same as the integral of the composition of that function with the mapping function over the original space with respect to the original measure, as long as the mapping function is almost everywhere measurable. This allows integration to be carried out on a transformed space by instead integrating the composed function on the original space. The result holds under suitable measurability conditions for both the mapping and the integrated function.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_mono
slogan: If one function is less than or equal to another function almost everywhere and both are integrable, then the integral of the first is less than or equal to the integral of the second. This holds for functions taking values in a space with a compatible order, topology, and normed vector structure, integrated over a measure space. The result relies on the functions being measurable and the order being preserved under integration.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_mul_left_eq_self
slogan: The integral of a function after shifting its input by left multiplication by a fixed group element equals the integral of the function itself, when the measure is invariant under such shifts. This holds in a setting where the space has a normed vector structure over the reals, the group operation is measurable, and the function is integrable. Left multiplication preserves both the measure and the integral value.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_nonneg_of_ae
slogan: If a function is greater than or equal to zero almost everywhere with respect to a measure, and it is integrable, then its integral is also greater than or equal to zero. This means that integrating a function that is nonnegative except on a set of measure zero will not produce a negative result. The statement applies to functions taking values in an ordered normed space over the reals.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_prod
slogan: The integral of a function over the product of two measure spaces equals the double integral computed by integrating first with respect to one variable and then the other, provided the function is integrable over the product space. This allows the order of integration to be swapped when the measures are s-finite and the function maps into a normed vector space over the reals.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_prod_mul
slogan: The integral of the product of two functions, one depending only on the first component and the other only on the second, over a product space with s-finite measures equals the product of their individual integrals. This holds when the functions map into a real-like type and are defined on measurable spaces equipped with the product measure. The result connects integration over product spaces with the simpler integrals on each factor space.

label: MeasureTheory.integral_tsum
slogan: The integral of an infinite sum of functions equals the sum of their integrals, provided the functions are measurable, the sum of their norms has finite integral, and the index set is countable. This allows swapping integration and summation for convergent series in normed spaces. The result holds almost everywhere with respect to the measure.

label: MeasureTheory.levyProkhorovDist
slogan: The Lévy-Prokhorov distance between two finite measures is the smallest number r such that, for every measurable set B, the measure of B under one measure is at most the measure of its r-enlargement under the other measure plus r. This distance quantifies how close two measures are by comparing their values on sets and slightly expanded versions of those sets. It is derived from an extended nonnegative real version by converting infinity to a finite real value.

label: MeasureTheory.limsup_measure_closed_le_iff_liminf_measure_open_ge
slogan: For a sequence of probability measures, the limit superior of their measures on any closed set is bounded above by the measure of that set under a candidate limiting measure if and only if the limit inferior of their measures on any open set is bounded below by the measure of that set under the same limiting measure.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral
slogan: The lintegral of a nonnegative measurable function is the smallest number that is at least as large as the integral of every simple function less than or equal to it, using the extended nonnegative real numbers where infinity is allowed. It is defined for functions on a measurable space with a given measure, and it generalizes the idea of summing up areas under curves in a way that works for a wide range of functions. The value is computed as the supremum of integrals of bounded, measurable simple functions that do not exceed the given function.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul
slogan: The integral of a nonnegative measurable function f with respect to a measure mu, after composing with a nonnegative integrable function g, equals the integral over all positive levels t of the measure of the set where f is at least t, multiplied by g(t). This formula expresses the layered structure of the function's values in terms of its level sets. It requires f to be measurable and almost everywhere nonnegative, and g to be integrable on intervals starting at 0.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_lt_mul
slogan: The integral of a nonnegative measurable function f with respect to a measure mu is equal to the integral over t > 0 of the measure of the set where f is greater than t, multiplied by g(t), with respect to t. This holds when f is nonnegative and measurable, and g is nonnegative and integrable on intervals from 0 to t for each t > 0. The result links the integral of f to the sizes of its level sets, using extended nonnegative real numbers to handle infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_congr_ae
slogan: If two non-negative measurable functions are equal almost everywhere with respect to a measure, then their Lebesgue integrals are the same. This means modifying a function on a set of measure zero does not change its integral. The result follows from the fact that the integral depends only on the values of the function outside a negligible set.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_eq_lintegral_meas_le
slogan: The integral of a nonnegative measurable function f over a space with respect to a measure μ is equal to the integral from 0 to infinity of the measure of the set where f is at least t, with respect to t. This means the total integral can be computed by adding up the sizes of the level sets of the function. The result holds for functions that are nonnegative almost everywhere and measurable with respect to the measure.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_eq_lintegral_meas_lt
slogan: The integral of a non-negative measurable function with respect to a measure can be computed as the integral over the positive real numbers of the measure of the set where the function's value is greater than each positive real number. This means the total integral is found by adding up, for each positive threshold, the size of the set where the function exceeds that threshold. The result uses strict inequality (greater than) to define these level sets.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_iSup
slogan: The integral of the limit of an increasing sequence of nonnegative measurable functions is equal to the limit of their integrals. This means that for such sequences, taking the integral and taking the pointwise supremum can be interchanged. The result holds in the extended nonnegative real numbers, where infinity is allowed.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_image_eq_lintegral_abs_det_fderiv_mul
slogan: When a measurable, injective function with a continuously differentiable inverse maps a set in a finite-dimensional real vector space to another space, the integral of a nonnegative extended real-valued function over the image equals the integral over the original set multiplied by the absolute value of the determinant of the derivative of the mapping. This accounts for how the function distorts volumes locally. The measures involved are translation-invariant, and the integrals are taken in the sense of Lebesgue integration for nonnegative functions.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_indicator
slogan: The integral of a function that is nonzero only on a measurable set, with respect to a measure, is the same as the integral of that function restricted to the set. In simpler terms, integrating a function multiplied by an indicator (which is 1 on the set and 0 outside) gives the same result as integrating the function only over the set. This holds for non-negative extended real-valued functions in the context of Lebesgue integration.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_liminf_le
slogan: For a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of the limit inferior of the function values at each point is less than or equal to the limit inferior of the integrals of the functions. The result holds as n goes to infinity, with all integrals computed using the same measure. Function values can be infinite, and the inequality accounts for such cases.

label: MeasureTheory.lintegral_prod
slogan: The integral of a nonnegative measurable function over a product space with respect to the product measure is equal to the double integral computed by first integrating over one variable and then the other. This means you can evaluate a two-dimensional integral as an iterated one-dimensional integral. The result holds when the function is measurable and the measures involved satisfy mild finiteness conditions.

label: MeasureTheory.llr
slogan: The log-likelihood ratio at a point x is the real number obtained by taking the logarithm of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of one measure with respect to another, evaluated at x, and converting the result from an extended non-negative real to a real number. It compares the relative size of two measures locally at x using logarithms. If the derivative is zero or infinite, the ratio may be negative infinity or positive infinity, but is mapped to a real number where possible.

label: MeasureTheory.map_eq_setLIntegral_pdf
slogan: The probability that a random variable X takes values in a measurable set s is equal to the integral of its probability density function over s with respect to a given measure μ, provided the density exists. This means the distribution of X can be computed by integrating its density against μ.

label: MeasureTheory.martingalePart_add_predictablePart
slogan: Any stochastic process indexed by natural numbers can be split into two parts: one that is a martingale and another that is predictable, and when you add these two parts together, you get back the original process.

label: MeasureTheory.martingale_condExp
slogan: Given a function f and a filtration F with a sigma-finite measure mu, the sequence of conditional expectations of f with respect to the sub-sigma-algebras of the filtration forms a martingale with respect to that filtration and measure.

label: MeasureTheory.martingale_iff
slogan: A sequence of functions is a martingale with respect to a filtration and a measure if and only if it is both a submartingale and a supermartingale, meaning the conditional expectation of future values equals the current value almost everywhere.

label: MeasureTheory.maximal_ineq
slogan: For a non-negative submartingale f and any non-negative threshold ε, the measure of the set where the maximum of f up to time n is at least ε, multiplied by ε, is less than or equal to the integral of f at time n over that same set.

label: MeasureTheory.mconv_withDensity_eq_mlconvolution
slogan: The convolution of two measures, each modified by a measurable nonnegative function on a group, equals the measure obtained by convolving those functions and then applying the result as a density to the original measure. This holds when the underlying measure is s-finite and invariant under left multiplication, and the functions involved are measurable. It links the convolution of measures with the convolution of functions in a way that respects integration.

label: MeasureTheory.meas_ge_le_lintegral_div
slogan: For a non-negative measurable function f and a positive constant a, the size of the set where f is at least a is no more than the integral of f divided by a. This gives an upper bound on how large the function can be, based on its average behavior. It is a key inequality in measure theory known as Markov's inequality.

label: MeasureTheory.measureReal_nonneg
slogan: The measure of any set is always at least zero when treated as a real number, since measures represent sizes like length or probability and cannot be negative. This holds even though measures can take infinite values, because the finite ones convert to nonnegative real numbers. The result ensures that the concept of size remains consistent with intuitive expectations.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_diff
slogan: If one measurable set is contained in another and the smaller set has finite measure, then the measure of the set difference (elements in the larger set but not in the smaller) equals the measure of the larger set minus the measure of the smaller set, using extended nonnegative real numbers where subtraction is defined even with infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_empty
slogan: The measure of the empty set is always zero for any outer measure, where measures take values in the extended nonnegative real numbers (including infinity). This means that assigning zero to the empty set is a basic requirement for outer measures in measure theory.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_iUnion
slogan: The measure of a countable union of pairwise disjoint measurable sets equals the sum of the measures of those sets, as long as the measure is countably additive and the sets are part of a measurable space. This means that breaking a set into non-overlapping measurable pieces allows the total measure to be computed by adding up the measures of the pieces. The sum is understood as the limit of partial sums over finite subsets of the index set.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_iUnion_le
slogan: The measure of the union of a countable collection of sets is at most the sum of the measures of those sets, even if the sets overlap. This means overlapping parts are only counted once in the union but could be counted multiple times in the sum, so the union's size is bounded above by the total sum. The result holds for outer measures on any type, with sums defined as the limit of finite approximations.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_limsup_atTop_eq_zero
slogan: If the sum of the measures of a sequence of sets is finite, then the set of points that are in infinitely many of those sets has measure zero. This means that only a negligible number of points appear in infinitely many sets when the total size of the sets is small. The result applies to outer measures and uses the limit superior of the sequence of sets as the index goes to infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_mono
slogan: If one set is a subset of another, then its outer measure is less than or equal to that of the larger set. Outer measures assign sizes to sets using nonnegative real numbers or infinity, and they never decrease when the set gets bigger.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_mono_null
slogan: If a set s is contained in a set t and the outer measure of t is zero, then the outer measure of s must also be zero. This is because outer measures are monotonic, meaning smaller sets can't have larger measure, and zero is the smallest possible measure value.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_ne_zero_iff_nonempty_of_isMulLeftInvariant
slogan: A measure that is invariant under left multiplication in a topological group gives a nonzero value to an open set if and only if the set contains at least one element; thus, only empty sets have measure zero. This applies to regular measures on Borel sets where the measure does not change when the set is shifted by group multiplication on the left. The measure is assumed to be nonzero overall.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_union
slogan: If two measurable sets do not overlap except possibly on a set of measure zero, then the size of their union equals the sum of their sizes, where size is given by a measure that can return finite numbers or infinity. This applies in a setting where sets are part of a measurable space and their sizes follow the rules of measure theory. The measure uses extended non-negative real numbers, including infinity, to assign sizes consistently.

label: MeasureTheory.measure_union_add_inter
slogan: If two sets are measurable, the measure of their union plus the measure of their intersection equals the sum of the measures of the two sets. This means you can compute the total size of two sets by adding their individual sizes and subtracting the size of their overlap. The result holds for measures that take values in the extended non-negative real numbers, including infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.mul_meas_ge_le_integral_of_nonneg
slogan: If a function is nonnegative almost everywhere and integrable, then for any positive number epsilon, the product of epsilon and the measure of the set where the function is at least epsilon is less than or equal to the integral of the function.

label: MeasureTheory.mul_meas_ge_le_lintegral
slogan: For a non-negative measurable function f and a positive constant a, the size of the set where f is at least a, multiplied by a, is less than or equal to the integral of f. This means the integral of f gives an upper bound on how large the function can be on a given set. It is a way to control the measure of sets where f is big using its total integral.

label: MeasureTheory.mul_meas_ge_le_lintegral₀
slogan: For any non-negative measurable function f and a positive constant a, the measure of the set where f is greater than or equal to a is at most the integral of f divided by a. This means the size of the set where f is large is controlled by the average value of f. It is a version of Markov's inequality in measure theory.

label: MeasureTheory.mul_meas_ge_le_pow_eLpNorm
slogan: For a measurable function f, the size of the set where the norm of f is at least a positive value ε is bounded above by the p-th power of the extended Lp norm of f divided by ε raised to the p-th power. This inequality holds for extended nonnegative real numbers and assumes p is finite and nonzero. It provides a way to control how large a function can be on a set using its Lp norm.

label: MeasureTheory.mul_meas_ge_le_pow_eLpNorm'
slogan: For a measurable function f and a positive number a, the measure of the set where the norm of f is at least a is bounded above by the p-th power of the extended Lp norm of f divided by a to the p-th power. This inequality provides a way to control how large a function can be on a set, using its Lp norm. The result applies to functions taking values in a space with a continuous norm and uses extended nonnegative real numbers for the measure and norm.

label: MeasureTheory.mutuallySingular_dirac
slogan: The Dirac measure at a point x is mutually singular to any measure that assigns zero measure to x, meaning there exists a set containing x where the Dirac measure concentrates all its mass and the other measure gives zero mass to the complement of that set. This happens because the Dirac measure only "sees" the point x, while the other measure does not charge that point at all.

label: MeasureTheory.norm_integral_le_integral_norm
slogan: The absolute value of the integral of a function is at most the integral of the absolute value of that function, as long as the function is almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to the given measure. This means that taking the norm after integrating is never larger than integrating the norm pointwise. The result holds for functions taking values in a normed vector space over the reals.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf
slogan: The pdf function gives the probability density of a random variable X with respect to a measure μ, defined as the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the pushforward of the probability measure ℙ by X, relative to μ. It maps each point in the space to a nonnegative extended real number (including infinity). This density describes how the distribution of X compares to the reference measure μ.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.IsUniform
slogan: A random variable X has a uniform distribution on a set s if the probability measure of X is proportional to the restriction of the measure μ to s, scaled by the inverse of μ(s). This means all parts of s have equal probability density according to μ. The condition assumes μ(s) is finite and positive so the scaling makes sense.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.indepFun_iff_pdf_prod_eq_pdf_mul_pdf
slogan: Two random variables are independent if and only if their joint probability density function equals the product of their individual density functions, almost everywhere with respect to the product measure.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.integral_mul_eq_integral
slogan: If a real-valued random variable X has a probability density function f with respect to Lebesgue measure, then the expected value of X is equal to the integral of x times f(x) over the real line. This means the average value of X can be computed by integrating the product of each possible value x and its density f(x). The density f is derived from the probability measure and the random variable's distribution.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.integral_pdf_smul
slogan: The expected value of a function f applied to a random variable X can be computed by integrating f(x) multiplied by the probability density function of X with respect to a measure μ, and this equals the integral of f(X(ω)) over the sample space with respect to the probability measure ℙ. This holds when X has a density relative to μ and f is suitably measurable. The result connects the abstract expectation of f(X) to a concrete integral involving the density of X.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.quasiMeasurePreserving_hasPDF
slogan: If a random variable has a probability density function and is transformed by a function that preserves null sets in a suitable way, then the transformed random variable also has a probability density function, provided the resulting measure can be decomposed relative to the target measure.

label: MeasureTheory.pdf.quasiMeasurePreserving_hasPDF'
slogan: If a random variable X has a probability density function with respect to a measure μ, and g is a measurable function that maps negligible sets to negligible sets when going from μ to another measure ν, then the transformed random variable g(X) also has a probability density function with respect to ν, provided the original measure is s-finite and ν is sigma-finite.

label: MeasureTheory.prob_add_prob_compl
slogan: If a set is measurable in a probability space, the chance of it happening plus the chance of it not happening equals 1. This means the total probability of all possible outcomes is 1, and probabilities of opposite events add up correctly.

label: MeasureTheory.prob_compl_eq_one_sub
slogan: The probability of the complement of a measurable set is one minus the probability of the set itself, as long as the measure is a probability measure (so the whole space has probability 1). This holds for sets in a measurable space where the measure takes nonnegative real values, including infinity, and uses standard arithmetic rules for those values. The set must be measurable, meaning it belongs to a collection closed under complements and countable unions.

label: MeasureTheory.rnDeriv_ae_eq_condExp
slogan: The Radon-Nikodym derivative of the restriction of a signed measure (formed by weighting a measure μ by an integrable function f) with respect to the restriction of μ, is equal almost everywhere to the conditional expectation of f with respect to a sub-sigma-algebra. This holds when the original measure is sigma-finite on the smaller sigma-algebra. The result connects the abstract conditional expectation to a density-like derivative in measure theory.

label: MeasureTheory.setIntegral_mono_set
slogan: If a function is integrable and non-negative almost everywhere on a measurable set, then its integral over any smaller measurable subset is less than or equal to its integral over the larger set, when using the same measure restricted to each set. This means expanding the domain of integration for a non-negative function does not decrease the integral. The result relies on the function mapping into a normed space with a compatible order structure.

label: MeasureTheory.submartingale_iff_expected_stoppedValue_mono
slogan: A process is a submartingale if and only if, for any two bounded stopping times where one is always less than or equal to the other, the expected value of the process at the earlier stopping time is less than or equal to its expected value at the later stopping time. This means that on average, the process tends to increase or stay the same over time when stopped at random times. The process must be adapted and integrable, and the expectation is taken with respect to a finite measure.

label: MeasureTheory.tendstoInMeasure_iff_tendsto_Lp_finite
slogan: A sequence of functions converges to a function g in the Lp norm if and only if the sequence is uniformly integrable and converges to g in measure, assuming the measure is finite and p is a real number between 1 and infinity.

label: MeasureTheory.tendstoInMeasure_of_tendsto_ae
slogan: If a sequence of measurable functions converges to a limit function at almost every point, and the measure of the space is finite, then the sequence also converges in measure to that same limit function. This means that as the functions get closer pointwise almost everywhere, they also get uniformly close in terms of the measure of the sets where they differ. Convergence almost everywhere, combined with measurability and finite measure, implies convergence in measure.

label: MeasureTheory.tendstoInMeasure_of_tendsto_ae_of_measurable_edist
slogan: If a sequence of measurable functions converges to a limit function almost everywhere, and the distance between each function and the limit is measurable, then the sequence also converges in measure. This means that for any positive tolerance, the measure of the set where the functions differ from the limit by more than that tolerance goes to zero as the sequence progresses.

label: MeasureTheory.tendstoInMeasure_of_tendsto_eLpNorm
slogan: If a sequence of measurable functions gets arbitrarily close to a limit function in the Lp norm and the measure space has finite total measure, then the sequence also gets close in measure, meaning the set where the functions differ significantly from the limit has measure tending to zero.

label: MeasureTheory.tendstoUniformlyOn_of_ae_tendsto
slogan: If a sequence of measurable functions converges almost everywhere to a limit function on a set with finite measure, and both the functions and the limit are strongly measurable, then for any given tolerance greater than zero, there exists a subset of arbitrarily small measure such that outside this subset, the sequence converges uniformly to the limit on the rest of the set.

label: MeasureTheory.tendsto_Lp_finite_of_tendstoInMeasure
slogan: If a sequence of uniformly integrable functions converges in measure to a limit function on a finite measure space, and the limit function is in Lp, then the sequence converges to that limit in the Lp norm.

label: MeasureTheory.tendsto_condExpL1_of_dominated_convergence
slogan: If a sequence of measurable functions converges almost everywhere to a limit function and is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function, then the conditional expectations of the sequence converge to the conditional expectation of the limit function in the L1 norm.

label: MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_filter_of_dominated_convergence
slogan: If a sequence of functions converges almost everywhere to a limit function and is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function, then the integrals of the functions converge to the integral of the limit function, with convergence described using filters.

label: MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence
slogan: If a sequence of functions converges almost everywhere to a limit function and each function in the sequence is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function, then the integrals of the functions converge to the integral of the limit function.

label: MeasureTheory.withDensity_eq_iff_of_sigmaFinite
slogan: If a measure is sigma-finite, then two nonnegative measurable functions produce the same weighted measure when used as densities if and only if they are equal almost everywhere with respect to the original measure. This means the resulting measure only depends on the values of the function outside sets of measure zero. The equivalence follows from the fact that integrating functions that are equal almost everywhere gives the same result.

label: Meromorphic.Gamma
slogan: The complex Gamma function is meromorphic over the entire complex plane, meaning it is holomorphic everywhere except at isolated points where it has poles.

label: MeromorphicAt
slogan: A function is meromorphic at a point if, near that point, it is well-behaved and smooth (analytic) everywhere except at isolated locations where it may blow up to infinity (poles), and around those points it can still be described as a ratio of two smooth functions. The function maps between spaces that support both algebraic operations and size measurements, over a field with a meaningful notion of distance. This behavior is local, meaning it only needs to hold in some small region around the point.

label: MeromorphicAt.eventually_eq_zero_or_eventually_ne_zero
slogan: If a function is meromorphic at a point, then near that point, it is either zero everywhere in some neighborhood around the point (excluding possibly the point itself), or it is nonzero everywhere in a deleted neighborhood around the point.

label: MeromorphicOn
slogan: A function is meromorphic on a set if, at every point in that set, it is either complex differentiable (holomorphic) or has a pole, meaning it blows up in a controlled way like the quotient of two holomorphic functions. This applies to functions from a subset of a normed additive group over a nontrivially normed field to a normed vector space, and depends on the local behavior at each point. The idea generalizes the notion of meromorphic functions in complex analysis to more abstract spaces.

label: MeromorphicOn.circleAverage_log_norm
slogan: For a meromorphic function f on a closed disk centered at c with radius R > 0, the average value of log|f| on the boundary circle equals the sum over all zeros and poles u of f inside the disk, each contributing (order at u) * log(R/|c - u|), plus a term (order at c) * log R, plus the log of the absolute value of the leading coefficient of f at c.

label: MeromorphicOn.divisor
slogan: The divisor of a meromorphic function is a function that assigns to each point the order of the function at that point, which is an integer, and assigns zero if the order is infinite or undefined. It is defined so that only points with nonzero values are considered, and these points are locally finite within a given set. The result is a map from points to integers with locally finite support.

label: Metric.Snowflaking
slogan: Metric.Snowflaking creates a new version of a type X where the distance between two points is the original distance raised to the power α, with α being a real number between 0 and 1 (exclusive at 0, inclusive at 1). The new distance function uses the value of each point in the original space and applies the exponent α to scale how distances are measured. This structure contains just one field, the underlying value from the original type.

label: Metric.ball
slogan: Metric.ball returns the set of all points in a pseudometric space that are less than a given distance from a specified center point, using the usual less-than comparison for real numbers. The space allows distinct points to have zero distance, and the ball includes only those points whose distance from the center is strictly less than the given radius. This is defined using the setOf construction based on the distance function and the standard ordering on real numbers.

label: Metric.cauchySeq_iff
slogan: A sequence is Cauchy if and only if for every positive distance ε, there exists a point N in the sequence such that for all indices m and n beyond N, the distance between the terms at m and n is less than ε.

label: Metric.closedBall
slogan: closedBall takes a point x and a real number epsilon in a pseudometric space and returns the set of all points whose distance from x is less than or equal to epsilon. The space allows distinct points to have zero distance, and the distance function satisfies symmetry and the triangle inequality. This set is defined using the standard less-than-or-equal-to relation on real numbers.

label: Metric.continuousAt_iff
slogan: A function between two pseudometric spaces is continuous at a point if and only if for every positive distance epsilon, there is a positive distance delta such that whenever the input is within delta of the point, the output is within epsilon of the function's value at that point.

label: Metric.continuous_iff
slogan: A function between two pseudometric spaces is continuous if and only if, for every point and every positive distance epsilon, there is a positive distance delta such that whenever two points in the domain are within delta of each other, their images under the function are within epsilon of each other.

label: Metric.continuous_infDist_pt
slogan: The function that maps a point to its shortest distance from a given set in a pseudometric space is continuous, meaning small changes in the point's location lead to small changes in the distance. This holds for any set and any space where distance is defined, even if distinct points can be zero distance apart. The continuity is with respect to the standard topology on the real numbers.

label: Metric.diam
slogan: Metric.diam calculates the diameter of a set in a pseudometric space by finding the largest distance between any two points in the set, then converting that distance from an extended nonnegative real number (which could be infinite) to a finite real number, using a default value if the distance is infinite.

label: Metric.hausdorffDist
slogan: The Hausdorff distance between two sets in a space with a pseudometric is the smallest number such that every point in either set is within that distance of some point in the other set; it is calculated using an extended distance measure and then converted to a real number by replacing infinity with a large finite value.

label: Metric.hausdorffEDist
slogan: The hausdorffEDist function measures how far apart two sets are by taking the largest distance from any point in one set to the closest point in the other, then doing the same in reverse, and returning the bigger of the two values. It works in spaces where distances can be infinite or where distinct points might be zero distance apart, and returns a result that is either a nonnegative real number or infinity. The distance is symmetric and uses extended real numbers to handle edge cases like empty sets or unbounded spaces.

label: Metric.infDist
slogan: The function infDist measures the shortest distance from a point to any point in a set, using the distance rule of the space; if the set is empty, it returns infinity converted to a real number. It works in spaces where points can be distinct but still have zero distance, and always returns a regular real number. This value is the infimum of all distances from the point to points in the set.

label: Metric.infDist_zero_of_mem_closure
slogan: If a point is in the closure of a set in a pseudometric space, then the smallest distance from that point to any point in the set is zero. This means there are points in the set that get arbitrarily close to the given point.

label: Metric.isCompact_iff_isClosed_bounded
slogan: In a proper metric space, a set is compact exactly when it is both closed and bounded. This means that a set must contain all its limit points and fit within some finite region to be compact. The equivalence holds because in such spaces, closed balls are themselves compact.

label: Metric.isOpen_iff
slogan: A set in a pseudometric space is open if and only if for every point in the set, there is some positive distance such that all points within that distance from the given point are also in the set. This means a set is open when each of its points has a small ball around it that stays entirely within the set.

label: Metric.mem_nhds_iff
slogan: A set is a neighborhood of a point in a pseudometric space if and only if there is some positive radius such that all points within that distance from the point are contained in the set. This means the set must include an open ball around the point for it to be considered a neighborhood. The radius must be greater than zero, and the ball is defined using the pseudometric.

label: Metric.nhds_basis_ball
slogan: In a pseudometric space, the neighborhoods of any point consist of all sets that contain a ball of positive radius centered at that point; every neighborhood of the point includes such a ball for some small enough radius.

label: Metric.sphere
slogan: Metric.sphere is a function that, given a point and a real number distance, returns the set of all points in a pseudometric space that are exactly that distance away from the given center point. The space allows distinct points to have zero distance, but still uses a symmetric distance function satisfying the triangle inequality. The result is defined using setOf to collect points matching the distance condition.

label: Metric.tendstoUniformlyOn_iff
slogan: A sequence of functions converges uniformly on a set if, for every positive distance ε, there is some point in the sequence beyond which all function values stay within ε of the limit function at every point in the set. This means that the convergence happens at the same rate across the entire set, not depending on the specific point chosen. The condition is equivalent to saying that for each ε > 0, eventually all functions in the sequence are uniformly within ε of the limit function on the set.

label: Metric.tendsto_nhds
slogan: A function approaches a limit at a point in a pseudometric space if, for every positive distance, the function values are eventually within that distance of the limit. This means that as the input gets closer to a point (in terms of the filter), the output gets arbitrarily close to the limit, measured by the metric. Closeness is defined using metric balls around the limit point.

label: Metric.tendsto_nhdsWithin_nhds
slogan: A function f from one metric space to another approaches a limit b at a point a within a subset s if, for every positive distance epsilon, there is a positive distance delta such that whenever a point x in s is within delta of a, the value f(x) is within epsilon of b. This is the standard epsilon-delta condition for convergence, restricted to inputs in the set s. When s is the whole space, this reduces to ordinary convergence at the point.

label: Metric.tendsto_nhds_nhds
slogan: A function between two pseudometric spaces maps points near a given input to points near a given output if and only if, for every positive distance ε around the output, there exists a positive distance δ around the input such that whenever the input points are within δ of the starting point, their images are within ε of the target point. This characterizes limit behavior using the metric notion of distance. The topology induced by the pseudometric allows this ε-δ condition to fully describe convergence.

label: Metric.uniformContinuous_iff
slogan: A function between two pseudometric spaces is uniformly continuous if and only if for every positive number epsilon, there is a positive number delta such that whenever two points in the domain are less than delta apart, their images under the function are less than epsilon apart.

label: MetricSpace
slogan: A MetricSpace is a set where a distance function is defined between any two points, the distance is always zero or positive (positive for distinct points), and it follows symmetry and the triangle inequality; it also has a topology and uniform structure that are compatible with this distance. This structure combines the properties of a pseudo metric space, a topological space, a T1 space (where single points are closed), and a uniform space (which supports uniform concepts like completeness and uniform continuity). The topology and uniform behavior of the space are derived directly from the di

label: MetricSpace.induced
slogan: If f is an injective function from a type α to a metric space β, then α can be made into a metric space by defining the distance between two points in α as the distance between their images in β; this distance is zero if and only if the two points are the same.

label: ModelWithCorners.IsBoundaryPoint
slogan: A point in a manifold is a boundary point if, when mapped through an extended chart, it lands on the edge of the model space. This means the point is on the boundary if its image is in the frontier of the model space's domain. The determination uses the structure of the model and the local chart around the point.

label: ModularForm
slogan: A ModularForm is a holomorphic function from the upper half-plane to the complex numbers that satisfies a certain symmetry condition under the action of a subgroup of 2x2 real invertible matrices and has bounded behavior at infinity, depending on an integer weight parameter. It is defined for a subgroup Gamma of GL(2, R) and an integer k representing the weight. These forms are special cases of slash-invariant functions with additional analytic properties.

label: ModularForm.eta
slogan: The eta function takes a complex number z and returns a complex value defined as q^(1/24) times the infinite product of (1 - q^(n+1)) for n starting at 0, where q is the complex exponential e^(2πiz). This product is computed using a limiting process over finite subsets, ensuring convergence in the complex plane. The function relies on standard complex arithmetic and the periodic nature of exponential terms indexed by natural numbers.

label: Module
slogan: A Module is a structure where elements of a semiring (like natural numbers with addition and multiplication) can scale elements of an additive commutative monoid (like a set with a zero and commutative addition), and this scaling respects both addition and the semiring's multiplication rules. It requires that scaling distributes over addition and follows the semiring's algebraic laws, building on a DistribMulAction by adding these algebraic guarantees. This setup allows for consistent scalar multiplication in algebraic systems that don't necessarily support subtraction.

label: Module.Baer.injective
slogan: If a module allows every linear map from any of its submodules to be extended to a linear map on the whole module, then the module is injective. This means that whenever you have a linear function defined on a smaller part of the module, it can always be extended to the entire module without breaking linearity. The result applies to modules over a ring where such extensions are supported by the algebraic structure.

label: Module.Basis
slogan: A basis of a module is a set of elements that are linearly independent and span the whole module, so every element can be written in exactly one way as a linear combination of basis elements using scalars from a semiring. It generalizes vector space bases to more general algebraic systems where the scalars form a semiring and the module is an additive commutative monoid. The structure supports scalar multiplication and is defined over types representing the index set, scalars, and module elements.

label: Module.Basis.SmithNormalForm
slogan: A Smith normal form provides a way to simplify a matrix over a principal ideal domain so that it becomes diagonal, with each diagonal element dividing the next, using a special basis for the module. This form helps classify finitely generated modules by revealing their structure through invariant factors derived from submodules and linear independence. It applies to modules equipped with scalar multiplication over a commutative ring, where the module operations follow standard algebraic rules.

label: Module.Basis.dualBasis
slogan: Given a finite basis for a module over a commutative semiring, the dualBasis function creates a corresponding basis for the dual module, where each dual basis element returns 1 when applied to its matching original basis vector and 0 for all others. This dual basis is uniquely determined by the original basis and forms a one-to-one linear correspondence with it. The construction requires the basis index type to have decidable equality and to be finite.

label: Module.Basis.exists_basis
slogan: In any vector space over a division ring, there is always a set of vectors that is both linearly independent and spans the whole space, meaning every vector can be expressed uniquely as a combination of these basis vectors using scalar multiplication and addition.

label: Module.Basis.extend
slogan: Given a vector space over a division ring and a linearly independent set of vectors, it is possible to add more vectors to this set so that it becomes a basis for the entire space, meaning the new set is still linearly independent and now spans the whole space. The function provides a way to construct such an extended basis.

label: Module.Basis.exteriorPower
slogan: If M is a module over a commutative ring R with a basis b indexed by a linearly ordered type, then for any natural number n, the n-fold exterior products of elements of b form a basis for the n-th exterior power of M. This basis is indexed by the set of all n-element subsets of the original index set. The resulting basis spans the exterior power as an R-module.

label: Module.Basis.isUnit_det
slogan: If a set of vectors is a basis for a module over a commutative ring, then the determinant of the matrix representing that basis is invertible (has a multiplicative inverse) in the ring. This means the determinant is a unit, ensuring the vectors are linearly independent and span the whole module. The result holds when the basis is finite and the index type has decidable equality.

label: Module.Basis.maximal
slogan: A basis of a module is a linearly independent set that spans the whole module, and it is maximal in the sense that no larger linearly independent set can contain it.

label: Module.Basis.mk
slogan: A family of vectors in a module forms a basis if they are linearly independent and span the whole module, meaning every element can be written uniquely as a linear combination of them; the function mk constructs such a basis by checking these two conditions.

label: Module.Basis.orientation
slogan: For a finite-dimensional vector space over a commutative ring with a chosen basis, the orientation is determined by the sign of the determinant: bases are grouped into two classes (positive or negative) based on whether the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix lies in the same positive-scaling class as the original basis, giving a consistent idea of "handedness".

label: Module.Basis.orientation_comp_linearEquiv_eq_iff_det_pos
slogan: Two bases have the same orientation after applying a linear equivalence if and only if the determinant of that linear equivalence is positive. This means the transformation preserves the relative direction of the basis vectors exactly when its determinant is greater than zero. The result relies on the ordered ring structure and the behavior of determinants under linear isomorphisms.

label: Module.Basis.toMatrix
slogan: Given a basis for a module over a commutative semiring, the toMatrix function creates a matrix where each column contains the coordinates of a basis vector expressed in terms of another basis, allowing basis conversion through matrix multiplication. This matrix represents how the two bases are related by writing each vector of one basis as a linear combination of the vectors in the other. The construction uses the module's algebraic structure and relies on coordinate representations having only finitely many nonzero entries.

label: Module.Basis.toMatrix_mul_toMatrix
slogan: Multiplying the matrix that changes from one basis to a second by the matrix that changes from the second basis to a third gives the same result as the matrix that changes directly from the first basis to the third, provided the middle basis is finite; when the third basis is the same as the first, this product is the identity matrix.

label: Module.Dual
slogan: The dual of a module M over a semiring R is the set of all functions from M to R that preserve addition and scalar multiplication. These functions, called linear functionals, take elements of the module and return scalars in a way that respects the module's algebraic structure. This dual space itself forms a module under pointwise addition and scalar multiplication.

label: Module.Dual.eval
slogan: The dual evaluation map sends a module element and a linear functional to the scalar obtained by applying the functional to the element, and it does so in a way that is linear in both arguments. It is defined for modules over a commutative semiring, where the dual space consists of all linear maps from the module to the semiring. This evaluation operation preserves addition and scalar multiplication in each argument separately.

label: Module.Dual.finrank_ker_add_one_of_ne_zero
slogan: If a linear function from a finite-dimensional vector space to its field is not the zero function, then the dimension of the set of vectors it sends to zero is exactly one less than the dimension of the whole space.

label: Module.Dual.instIsReflecive
slogan: A module is reflexive if the natural map sending each element to its corresponding evaluation function in the double dual is an isomorphism, meaning the module is structurally identical to its double dual. This declaration states that if a module M over a commutative semiring R is reflexive, then its dual module — the space of linear maps from M to R — is also reflexive. The result follows from the existence of a natural isomorphism between a reflexive module and its double dual, which extends to the dual space via the inverse of the evaluation equivalence.

label: Module.Dual.transpose
slogan: Module.Dual.transpose turns a linear map from one module to another into a linear map between their dual spaces by precomposing with the original map, so that a linear functional on the target module gets sent to a linear functional on the source module. The result is always linear and respects scalar multiplication. This operation is defined using the natural pairing of a module with its dual and preserves the module structure over the base semiring.

label: Module.Dual.transpose_apply
slogan: The transpose of a linear map u from module M to module M' turns a linear function on M' into a linear function on M by composing it with u.
