slogan: The greatest common divisor of the mth and nth Fibonacci numbers is the same as the Fibonacci number located at the position given by the greatest common divisor of m and n. For instance, if m is 6 and n is 9, their greatest common divisor is 3, so the GCD of the 6th and 9th Fibonacci numbers equals the 3rd Fibonacci number. This relationship holds for all natural numbers m and n.

label: Nat.fib_succ_eq_succ_sum
slogan: The (n+1)th Fibonacci number is equal to the sum of all Fibonacci numbers from the 0th up to the (n-1)th, plus 1. This means each Fibonacci number can be expressed as the total of all the earlier ones in the sequence, adjusted by adding one.

label: Nat.fib_succ_eq_sum_choose
slogan: The (n+1)-th Fibonacci number equals the sum of binomial coefficients "k choose i" for all pairs (k, i) such that k + i = n. This means each Fibonacci number can be computed by adding up entries along the anti-diagonal of Pascal's triangle. The identity connects the Fibonacci sequence directly to combinations.

label: Nat.find
slogan: Nat.find takes a condition on natural numbers that can be checked for each number, and returns the smallest number that satisfies the condition, given that at least one such number exists.

label: Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq
slogan: For any natural number n and any positive integers q and a, if a and q share no common divisors other than 1, then there exists a prime number p larger than n such that p leaves the same remainder as a when divided by q.

label: Nat.gcd_comm
slogan: The greatest common divisor of two natural numbers m and n is the same regardless of the order, so m.gcd n equals n.gcd m.

label: Nat.gcd_eq_gcd_ab
slogan: For any two natural numbers m and n, there are integers a and b such that the greatest common divisor of m and n can be written as a times m plus b times n. This means the gcd can always be expressed as a linear combination of the two numbers. The values a and b are computed by specific functions called gcdA and gcdB.

label: Nat.gcd_mul_lcm
slogan: The product of the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple of two natural numbers equals the product of those two numbers. For any two natural numbers m and n, multiplying their gcd and lcm together gives the same result as multiplying m and n directly. This holds even when one or both of the numbers are zero.

label: Nat.gcd_rec
slogan: The greatest common divisor of two natural numbers m and n is the same as the greatest common divisor of the remainder of n divided by m and m itself. This is the recursive step of the Euclidean algorithm, used to compute the GCD efficiently. If m is zero, the GCD is simply n.

label: Nat.greatestFib
slogan: Given a natural number n, Nat.greatestFib returns the largest number k such that the k-th Fibonacci number is less than or equal to n.

label: Nat.infinite_setOf_prime
slogan: The set of all prime numbers is infinite because there is no largest prime; for any natural number, there exists a prime number larger than it. This means the collection of primes never ends and cannot be fully listed in a finite set.

label: Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_and_eq_mod
slogan: For any positive integer q and any integer a that is coprime to q, there are infinitely many prime numbers that leave a remainder of a when divided by q.

label: Nat.instCommMonoid
slogan: The natural numbers support multiplication that is associative, commutative, and has 1 as the identity element, meaning n * m equals m * n, n * 1 equals n, and (n * m) * k equals n * (m * k) for all natural numbers n, m, and k.

label: Nat.instCommSemiring
slogan: The natural numbers (0, 1, 2, ...) have addition and multiplication operations that are both commutative and associative, with 0 as the additive identity and 1 as the multiplicative identity, and they follow standard arithmetic rules where multiplication distributes over addition and any number times zero is zero.

label: Nat.instLinearOrder
slogan: The declaration sets up a standard linear ordering for natural numbers, ensuring that any two numbers can be compared using less than, equal to, or greater than, with consistent and total ordering rules. It guarantees that for any two natural numbers, one is always less than or equal to the other, and supports operations like finding the maximum. This allows natural numbers to be used in contexts requiring a fully ordered set, such as sorting or comparisons.

label: Nat.iterate
slogan: Nat.iterate takes a function op from a type α to itself, a natural number n, and a starting value x of type α, and returns the result of applying op to x exactly n times. When n is 0, it returns x unchanged. This allows repeated application of a function in a structured way.

label: Nat.land
slogan: Computes the bitwise AND of two natural numbers, returning a new natural number where each bit is set to 1 only if the corresponding bits in both input numbers are 1. This operation is typically written using the &&& operator. It is implemented using a general helper function for bitwise operations on natural numbers.

label: Nat.le_induction
slogan: If a property is true for a natural number m and stays true when moving from any number n to n + 1, then it is true for all natural numbers greater than or equal to m. This principle lets you prove statements for all numbers starting at a given point by repeatedly stepping forward. It uses the fact that each number is less than or equal to the next one.

label: Nat.length_digits
slogan: The number of digits of a natural number n in base b (where b is greater than 1) is equal to the floor of the logarithm of n in base b, plus one. This count matches the length of the list obtained by breaking n into its base-b digits. The formula holds for all non-zero natural numbers n.

label: Nat.log2
slogan: Nat.log2 is a function that takes a natural number n and returns the largest integer less than or equal to the base-two logarithm of n, or zero if n is zero or one. It effectively counts how many times you can divide n by 2 before it drops below 2. For example, numbers from 4 to 7 return 2, and 8 returns 3.

label: Nat.lt_wfRel
slogan: The declaration states that the less-than relation on natural numbers is well-founded, meaning there are no infinite descending sequences of natural numbers where each number is smaller than the previous one. This ensures that recursive functions based on decreasing natural numbers will always terminate. In other words, you can't keep finding smaller and smaller natural numbers forever, since you'll eventually reach zero.

label: Nat.minFac
slogan: Nat.minFac is a function that takes a natural number and returns its smallest prime factor, returning 2 for 0 and 1 for 1. It works by testing divisors starting from 2 upward, using a helper function that stops when a divisor is found or the number is confirmed prime. The process is guaranteed to end because divisibility is decidable and the search space is limited by the number's size.

label: Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum
slogan: Every natural number is congruent to the sum of its decimal digits modulo 9. For example, the number 123 is congruent to 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 modulo 9. This means the remainder when dividing a number by 9 is the same as the remainder when dividing the sum of its digits by 9.

label: Nat.mul
slogan: Nat.mul is a function that takes two natural numbers and returns their product, typically used with the * operator. It is implemented efficiently in the system but logically defined as repeated addition. The function works with arbitrarily large natural numbers.

label: Nat.mul_eq_zero
slogan: The product of two natural numbers is zero if and only if at least one of them is zero.

label: Nat.multichoose
slogan: Nat.multichoose n k counts the number of ways to choose k elements from a set of n elements when repetition is allowed and order does not matter, and it equals the binomial coefficient (n + k - 1) choose k.

label: Nat.multichoose_eq
slogan: The number of ways to choose k elements from a multiset of size n, allowing repetition, is equal to the number of ways to choose k elements from a set of size n + k - 1 without repetition. This is expressed as n.multichoose k = (n + k - 1).choose k.

label: Nat.multinomial
slogan: The multinomial coefficient counts the number of distinct strings that can be formed using symbols from a finite set, where each symbol appears a specified number of times. It is calculated as the factorial of the total number of symbols divided by the product of the factorials of the counts of each symbol.

label: Nat.multiplicative_factorization
slogan: Every nonzero natural number can be broken down into prime factors, and this breakdown is unique. The theorem states that for any function f that respects multiplication of coprime numbers (i.e., f(x*y) = f(x)*f(y) when x and y share no common prime factors) and maps 1 to 1, the value of f at any nonzero n is determined by multiplying the values of f at the prime powers in n's factorization. This product is taken over the prime powers in the unique factorization of n, using the exponents from the prime factorization.

label: Nat.nthRoot
slogan: Nat.nthRoot is a function that takes two natural numbers, n and k, and returns the largest natural number m such that m raised to the power of k is less than or equal to n. It computes the integer part of the k-th root of n.

label: Nat.ofDigits_eq_foldr
slogan: The value of a list of digits in a given base is the same as starting from zero and repeatedly multiplying by the base and adding the next digit, processing digits from right to left, where each digit is converted to the target type using natural number casting. This holds for any base and list of digits in a type that supports semiring operations.

label: Nat.ofDigits_eq_sum_mapIdx
slogan: The value of a number made from a list of digits in base b equals the sum of each digit multiplied by the corresponding power of b, where the exponent is the digit's position in the list, starting from 0 on the right. This means you can compute the number by going through each digit with its index, multiplying the digit by b raised to that index, and adding up all the results.

label: Nat.perfect_iff_sum_divisors_eq_two_mul
slogan: A natural number is perfect exactly when the sum of all its divisors equals twice the number. This means adding up every number that divides it (including 1 and itself) gives a total of two times the original number. For example, 6 is perfect because its divisors 1, 2, 3, and 6 add up to 12, which is 2 * 6.

label: Nat.perfect_iff_sum_properDivisors
slogan: A natural number is perfect exactly when the sum of its divisors that are less than it equals the number itself.

label: Nat.pow_totient_mod
slogan: If x and n are positive integers greater than 1 and share no common divisor other than 1, then raising x to any power k and taking the remainder modulo n gives the same result as raising x to the power of (k modulo the number of integers up to n that are coprime to n) and then taking the remainder modulo n.

label: Nat.primeCounting
slogan: The prime counting function counts how many prime numbers are less than or equal to a given natural number n. It is denoted by π(n) when using the scoped prime notation. Unlike the related function primeCounting', which counts primes strictly less than n, this one includes n if it is prime.

label: Nat.primeFactorsList_unique
slogan: The prime factorization of a natural number is unique: any list of prime numbers that multiplies to the number must contain the same primes with the same frequencies, just possibly in a different order.

label: Nat.prime_iff_fac_equiv_neg_one
slogan: For any natural number n greater than 1, n is prime if and only if (n-1)! leaves a remainder of -1 when divided by n. This means the factorial of one less than n is congruent to -1 modulo n exactly when n is a prime number.

label: Nat.prime_two
slogan: The number 2 is prime because it is greater than 1 and its only divisors are 1 and 2.

label: Nat.rfind
slogan: Nat.rfind takes a partial function p from natural numbers to booleans and returns the smallest natural number n for which p n is defined and true, assuming p k is defined and false for all k less than n; the result is a partial value that may not exist if no such n is found.

label: Nat.set_induction
slogan: If a set of natural numbers contains 0 and also contains the next number (k + 1) whenever it contains any number k, then that set contains every natural number.

label: Nat.sq_add_sq_mul
slogan: If two natural numbers can each be written as the sum of two squares, then their product can also be written as the sum of two squares.

label: Nat.sqrt
slogan: The Nat.sqrt function computes the integer square root of a natural number n, returning the largest natural number whose square is less than or equal to n. It uses Newton's method for the calculation and is implemented efficiently at runtime. The result is always a natural number.

label: Nat.stirlingFirst
slogan: Nat.stirlingFirst n k gives the number of ways to arrange n elements into exactly k cycles, where each cycle is a permutation of a subset of the elements and no two cycles share elements.

label: Nat.stirlingSecond
slogan: Nat.stirlingSecond n k counts how many ways you can split a set of n elements into k non-empty groups, where the order of the groups doesn't matter.

label: Nat.strong_induction_on
slogan: If a property holds for a natural number n whenever it holds for all smaller numbers, then that property holds for every natural number. This is strong induction, which allows assuming the property for all predecessors, not just the immediate one. The less-than relation for natural numbers is used to define "smaller".

label: Nat.sub_eq_zero_iff_le
slogan: Subtracting one natural number from another results in zero if and only if the first number is less than or equal to the second.

label: Nat.succ_eq_add_one
slogan: The successor of any natural number n is equal to n plus one. In other words, adding one to a number gives the next number in the sequence. The expression n + 1 is preferred over writing the successor directly.

label: Nat.succ_injective
slogan: If two natural numbers have the same successor, then the numbers must be equal. This means that adding one to each number produces the same result only when the original numbers are the same.

label: Nat.succ_mul_choose_eq
slogan: Multiplying (n + 1) by the number of ways to choose k elements from n elements equals the number of ways to choose (k + 1) elements from (n + 1) elements, multiplied by (k + 1).

label: Nat.succ_ne_zero
slogan: The successor of any natural number is never equal to zero. In other words, adding one to a natural number always results in a nonzero value.

label: Nat.sum_Icc_choose
slogan: The sum of the binomial coefficients "m choose k" for all m from k to n is equal to (n + 1) choose (k + 1). This identity holds for all natural numbers n and k. It describes how sums of combinations over a range relate to a single combination value.

label: Nat.sum_four_squares
slogan: Every natural number can be expressed as the sum of four integer squares.

label: Nat.sum_range_choose
slogan: The sum of all binomial coefficients "n choose k" for k ranging from 0 to n equals 2^n. This means the total number of subsets of a set with n elements is 2^n. The equation uses standard natural number arithmetic.

label: Nat.sum_totient
slogan: For any positive natural number n, adding up the values of Euler's totient function for each divisor of n gives n itself. The totient function counts how many numbers from 1 to a given number are coprime to it, and summing these counts over all divisors of n results in the original number n.

label: Nat.sum_zeckendorf_fib
slogan: Every natural number equals the sum of the Fibonacci numbers corresponding to the indices in its Zeckendorf representation.

label: Nat.superFactorial
slogan: Nat.superFactorial is a function that, given a natural number n, computes the product of the factorials of all numbers from 1 up to n. It returns 1 when n is 0. For instance, for n = 4, it multiplies 1! * 2! * 3! * 4! to get 288.

label: Nat.totient
slogan: Nat.totient n counts how many whole numbers from 0 up to n-1 have no common divisors with n except 1. It does this by checking each number in that range to see if it is coprime with n, then adds up how many pass the test. The result is a whole number representing that count.

label: Nat.totient_eq_card_coprime
slogan: The number of integers from 0 to n-1 that share no common divisors with n other than 1 is exactly the value of Euler's totient function for n. This count is found by checking each number in that range for coprimality with n and then counting how many pass. The result equals the totient of n.

label: Nat.totient_eq_mul_prod_factors
slogan: The totient of a natural number n is calculated by multiplying n by the product of (1 - 1/p) for each distinct prime p that divides n. This formula adjusts n by the proportion of numbers not divisible by each of its prime factors. It provides a way to compute how many positive integers up to n are coprime to n using the prime factors of n.

label: Nat.totient_eq_prod_factorization
slogan: The totient of a nonzero natural number n is calculated by taking each prime factor p of n, raising p to the power of one less than its exponent in n's prime factorization, multiplying that by (p minus 1), and then multiplying all these values together. This formula uses the unique prime factorization of n to compute how many numbers from 1 to n-1 are coprime to n. The result is the product of terms of the form (p - 1) * p^(k - 1) for each prime power p^k dividing n.

label: Nat.totient_even
slogan: For any natural number n greater than 2, the number of positive integers less than or equal to n that share no common factors with n other than 1 is always even. This count is given by Euler's totient function, and the result states that this value is divisible by 2 for all n > 2.

label: Nat.totient_gcd_mul_totient_mul
slogan: For any two natural numbers a and b, the product of the totient of their gcd and the totient of their product equals the product of their totients multiplied by their gcd. This identity links the totient function, multiplication, and greatest common divisor in a single equation. It shows how the totient of a product relates to the totients of the numbers and their shared factors.

label: Nat.totient_lt
slogan: For any natural number n greater than 1, the count of numbers from 1 to n-1 that share no common divisors with n (other than 1) is always less than n. This count, called Euler's totient function, is positive but strictly smaller than n because at least one number in that range shares a common factor with n. For example, 0 is never counted since it is not coprime with n when n > 1.

label: Nat.totient_mul
slogan: If two natural numbers have no common factors other than 1, then the number of positive integers up to their product that are coprime to it equals the product of the numbers of integers coprime to each factor separately.

label: Nat.totient_prime
slogan: If p is a prime number, then there are exactly p - 1 positive integers less than p that share no common divisors with p other than 1. This means the count of numbers from 1 to p - 1 that are coprime to p is p - 1.

label: Nat.totient_prime_pow
slogan: If p is a prime number and n is a positive natural number, then the count of numbers from 1 to p^n that share no common factors with p^n is equal to p^(n-1) multiplied by (p - 1).

label: Nat.zeckendorfEquiv
slogan: Every natural number can be uniquely represented as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers (starting from F_2), and this correspondence is a one-to-one match between natural numbers and lists of indices that satisfy the Zeckendorf conditions. The function converting a number to its Zeckendorf representation and the function recovering the number from such a list are inverses of each other. This equivalence ensures both existence and uniqueness of the representation.

label: Nat.zero_le
slogan: For any natural number n, zero is less than or equal to n. This means every natural number is non-negative. The comparison uses the standard less-than-or-equal-to relation on natural numbers.

label: NoZeroDivisors
slogan: A type has no zero divisors if multiplying two nonzero elements never results in zero; that is, whenever a * b = 0, at least one of a or b must be zero. This assumes the type supports multiplication and has a zero element. It is different from but related to cancellation properties for nonzero multipliers.

label: NonUnitalNonAssocRing
slogan: A NonUnitalNonAssocRing is a set with operations of addition, subtraction, zero, and multiplication such that addition is commutative and invertible, multiplication does not need to be associative or have an identity, and multiplication distributes over addition from both sides. It is similar to a ring but without requiring a multiplicative unit or associativity of multiplication. This structure combines a commutative group under addition with a general multiplication that respects distributivity.

label: NonUnitalStarAlgHom.norm_apply_le
slogan: A homomorphism between complex C*-algebras without unit that preserves the star operation and algebraic structure does not increase the norm of elements, meaning the norm of the image is less than or equal to the norm of the input.

label: NonUnitalStarAlgHom.norm_map
slogan: A norm-preserving map between complex C*-algebras without units, which is injective and respects the algebraic and star operations, must preserve the norm of every element. That is, the norm of the image of any element under such a map equals the norm of the element itself. This means injective star algebra homomorphisms between non-unital C*-algebras are automatically isometric.

label: NonUnitalStarSubalgebra.nonUnitalCStarAlgebra
slogan: If a subset of a non-unital C*-algebra is closed under addition, multiplication, negation, and the star operation, and it inherits the norm and complex scalar multiplication from the larger algebra, then this subset is itself a non-unital C*-algebra, meaning it satisfies the C*-identity and is complete under the norm.

label: NonemptyInterval
slogan: A nonempty closed interval in an ordered type consists of two endpoints, where the first is less than or equal to the second, representing all elements between them inclusive. It is defined as a pair of values from the ordered type, ensuring the interval is not empty. This structure can be converted to the set of elements it contains.

label: Norm
slogan: A norm is a function that measures the size of elements in a type E, returning a non-negative real number and satisfying properties like absolute scalability and the triangle inequality. It generalizes the idea of length in vector or group structures. Here, E refers to a real number, indicating the norm maps into the real numbers.

label: Normal
slogan: A normal field extension is one where any irreducible polynomial over the base field that has at least one root in the extension splits completely into linear factors within that extension. It applies to fields F and K where K is an algebra over F, and all elements of K are algebraic over F. The real numbers may serve as the base field F in some cases.

label: NormalSpace
slogan: A normal space is a type of topological space where, given any two disjoint closed sets, there are disjoint open sets that contain them. The space must already be a topological space, and closed sets are defined as complements of open sets. This property ensures a strong level of separation between closed parts of the space.

label: NormalSpace.instCompletelyRegularSpace
slogan: In a topological space where any two disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open sets (normal space) and where topologically indistinguishable points are equal (R0 space), it is always possible to find a continuous real-valued function that maps any point to 0 and any disjoint closed set to 1, making the space completely regular.

label: NormalSpace.of_compactSpace_r1Space
slogan: A compact space where any two distinguishable points can be separated by open sets is also a space where any two disjoint closed sets can be separated by open sets. This is because closed sets in a compact space are compact, and in such a space, disjoint compact sets can be separated. Therefore, the space meets the definition of normality.

label: NormedAddCommGroup
slogan: A NormedAddCommGroup is a type where elements can be added and subtracted in a way that is commutative and associative, with a zero element and additive inverses, and where each element has a non-negative size (called a norm) that scales with multiplication by real numbers and satisfies the triangle inequality; this norm defines a distance between elements, making the type into a metric space.

label: NormedAddCommGroup.summable_imp_tendsto_iff_completeSpace
slogan: In a normed additive group, every series whose terms have convergent absolute values will converge to a limit in the space if and only if the space is complete. This means the space contains all necessary limit points for such series to converge. Completeness ensures no gaps exist where limits should be.

label: NormedAlgebra
slogan: A NormedAlgebra is a ring with a scalar multiplication operation over a normed field, where the ring and scalar operations work well together, and the norm respects both multiplication and scaling. It combines algebraic structure with size measurements in a way that ensures consistency across operations. The scalars come from a normed field, and the ring itself has a norm that behaves properly with addition, multiplication, and scalar scaling.

label: NormedSpace
slogan: A NormedSpace is a module over a normed field where every vector has a size (norm), and scaling a vector multiplies its norm by the absolute value of the scalar. It combines vector addition, scalar multiplication, and a well-behaved notion of length. This structure allows consistent algebraic operations and geometric size measurements.

label: NormedSpace.exp_analytic
slogan: The exponential function in a complete normed algebra over a field like the real or complex numbers can be expressed as a convergent power series around any point, and this series converges everywhere. This means the function is smooth and locally representable by a power series at every point in the space. The infinite radius of convergence ensures no restrictions on where the series works.

label: NormedSpace.exp_eq_tsum
slogan: The exponential of an element in a normed space is the sum of the series where each term is the element raised to the n-th power and divided by n factorial, and this sum converges no matter the order of addition. The series uses standard algebraic operations and the topology of the space to define the limit of its partial sums. This holds in a complete topological algebra over a field of characteristic zero with continuous operations.

label: NormedSpace.inclusionInDoubleDual
slogan: The function inclusionInDoubleDual takes a vector from a normed space and maps it to a continuous linear functional on the dual space by evaluating each functional at that vector; this map is linear and does not change the norm of the vector. It provides a way to embed the original space into its double dual while preserving both vector space operations and distances.

label: NormedSpace.inclusionInDoubleDualLi
slogan: The function inclusionInDoubleDualLi takes each element of a normed space E over a field 𝕜 and maps it to the double dual space by sending the element to a continuous linear functional that evaluates dual elements at that point. This mapping is linear, preserves the norm, and is continuous, meaning the size of the element in E is exactly the same as the size of its image in the double dual. The result is a linear isometry from E into its double dual.

label: NormedSpace.normalize
slogan: Given a vector x in a real normed space, normalize x scales x to have length 1 if x is nonzero, keeping its direction; if x is zero, then normalize x returns zero.

label: NumberField.AdeleRing
slogan: The NumberField.AdeleRing combines all the local completions of a number field—both at finite primes and infinite embeddings—into a single topological ring, using the ring of integers of the field and its fraction field. It includes the finite adeles, built from completions at prime ideals, and the infinite adeles, built from real and complex embeddings, allowing global arithmetic properties to be studied locally everywhere at once. This structure supports advanced analysis and number theory over global fields.

label: NumberField.FinitePlace
slogan: NumberField.FinitePlace represents a way to measure the size of elements in a number field based on divisibility by a nonzero prime ideal in its ring of integers, using a valuation that counts the exponent of the prime in the element's factorization and extends this to the whole field; it corresponds to non-archimedean absolute values, unlike infinite places which come from real or complex embeddings.

label: NumberField.InfinitePlace
slogan: An infinite place of a number field K is a way to measure the size of elements in K by mapping them into the real or complex numbers and using the standard absolute value; these mappings come from field embeddings and capture how elements grow large in magnitude. The type NumberField.InfinitePlace K represents all such infinite places of K. It depends on K being a field and uses the normed structures of the real and complex numbers.

label: NumberField.InfinitePlace.card_add_two_mul_card_eq_rank
slogan: The number of real embeddings of a number field, plus twice the number of complex embeddings, equals the dimension of the field as a vector space over the rational numbers. This dimension is a natural number that counts the number of independent generators needed to span the field using rational coefficients. The equation connects the field's algebraic structure with its behavior under embeddings into the real and complex numbers.

label: NumberField.IsTotallyComplex
slogan: A number field is totally complex if it cannot be embedded into the real numbers in a way that respects its algebraic operations, meaning all of its embeddings into the complex numbers land outside the reals. This means the field has no real-valued representations and only complex ones. It is a property used to classify number fields based on how they sit inside the complex numbers.

label: NumberField.IsTotallyReal
slogan: A number field K is totally real if every way of embedding it into the complex numbers results in real numbers only. This means all elements of K are mapped to real values under any such embedding. The property IsTotallyReal holds for those number fields K where this condition is true.

label: NumberField.RingOfIntegers
slogan: The ring of integers of a number field consists of all elements in the field that are roots of monic polynomials with integer coefficients, and this set forms a subring that includes the ordinary integers and is closed under addition and multiplication.

label: NumberField.RingOfIntegers.basis
slogan: The ring of integers of a number field has a finite basis over the integers, meaning every element in it can be written uniquely as a combination of basis elements using integer coefficients. This function returns a specific basis chosen using the module structure of the ring of integers over the integers. The basis allows for constructive manipulation of elements in the ring as linear combinations with integer scalars.

label: NumberField.RingOfIntegers.instFintypeClassGroup
slogan: The ring of integers in a number field has only finitely many ideal classes, meaning the collection of invertible fractional ideals modulo principal ideals forms a finite set. This finiteness comes from the structure of the number field and the existence of a suitable absolute value. As a result, the class group, which measures how far the ring is from having unique factorization, is always finite.

label: NumberField.Units.exist_unique_eq_mul_prod
slogan: In a number field, every unit can be expressed in exactly one way as a root of unity times a product of fundamental units raised to integer powers.

label: NumberField.Units.regulator
slogan: The regulator of a number field is a positive real number that measures the "size" of the unit group in the field, based on the logarithmic embedding of units into a real vector space. It is defined as the covolume of the lattice formed by the image of the units under this embedding, modulo roots of unity. This value plays a key role in understanding the arithmetic structure of the number field.

label: NumberField.Units.unitLattice_rank
slogan: The unit group of a number field has a rank equal to the number of real embeddings plus half the number of complex embeddings minus one, and this rank is the dimension of the lattice formed by taking logarithms of the absolute values of units at all infinite places. This lattice is a discrete subgroup of a real vector space and represents the multiplicative structure of units modulo roots of unity. The result follows from Dirichlet's Unit Theorem and shows how many independent units of infinite order exist.

label: NumberField.classNumber
slogan: The class number of a number field is the size of the group formed by grouping the invertible fractional ideals of its ring of integers into equivalence classes, where two ideals are equivalent if one becomes the other when multiplied by a principal ideal; this number is always a finite natural number and reflects how much unique factorization fails in the ring of integers.

label: NumberField.classNumber_eq_one_iff
slogan: The class number of a number field is 1 if and only if every nonzero ideal in its ring of integers can be generated by a single element, meaning the ring is a principal ideal ring. This condition ensures that ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals, with no obstruction to unique factorization. In this case, the ring of integers has the simplest possible ideal structure.

label: NumberField.dedekindZeta
slogan: The Dedekind zeta function of a number field takes a complex number s and returns the sum of the reciprocals of the norms of all nonzero integral ideals raised to the power s, where the norm of an ideal is the size of the quotient ring. It is defined as an L-series using the number of integral ideals of each norm n. If the series does not converge absolutely, the function returns zero.

label: NumberField.discr
slogan: The discriminant of a number field is the integer that measures the squared volume of the fundamental domain of its ring of integers, using an integer basis. It is computed as the determinant of the trace matrix of the basis elements' pairwise products. This value gives information about the arithmetic structure of the field.

label: NumberField.tendsto_sub_one_mul_dedekindZeta_nhdsGT
slogan: As the complex variable s approaches 1 from values greater than 1, the product of (s - 1) and the Dedekind zeta function of a number field K tends to a specific limit equal to the residue of the zeta function at s = 1, which is related to important arithmetic invariants of K.

label: ODE.picard
slogan: The Picard iteration is a method for constructing approximate solutions to ordinary differential equations; given a function f, an initial time t0, an initial value x0, and a path a, it produces a new function that refines a by integrating f along a over time intervals around t0. If this new function matches a near t0, then a satisfies the differential equation defined by f with the given initial condition.

label: ODE_solution_unique
slogan: If two functions both satisfy the same ordinary differential equation x' = v(t, x) with the right-hand side v being Lipschitz continuous in x, and they start at the same initial point at time t = a, then the functions are equal everywhere on the interval [a, b].

label: ODE_solution_unique_univ
slogan: If two functions both satisfy the same ordinary differential equation, where the right-hand side is Lipschitz continuous, and they start at the same initial point, then the functions are identical everywhere.

label: OnePoint
slogan: OnePoint X adds a single extra point to the space X, creating a new space that includes all points of X plus one additional point. This construction is used to form a compactification of X by adding a single point at infinity. The resulting space has a topology that makes it compact under certain conditions.

label: OpenSubgroup.isClosed
slogan: In a topological group, if a subgroup is open (contains a neighborhood around each of its points), then it is also closed (its complement is open). This happens because the group operations are continuous and the openness of the subgroup forces its complement to be a union of open sets. As a result, the subgroup is both open and closed in the topology.

label: Or.resolve_left
slogan: If a or b is true and a is not true, then b must be true.

label: Order.Frame
slogan: A Frame is a structure that has a complete lattice with arbitrary meets and joins, an implication operation, and a complement, satisfying the infinite distributive law where taking a meet distributes over any join. It combines logical operations like implication and negation with set-like operations in a general ordered setting. This allows modeling both logical reasoning and set theory in a unified algebraic form.

label: Order.Ideal
slogan: An Ideal is a downward-closed set in a type with a less-than-or-equal-to relation, meaning if an element is in the set and another element is smaller, then that smaller element is also in the set. It is based on the idea of a lower set and requires the type to support a comparison operation (≤). This structure is used to represent special subsets in ordered types.

label: Order.Ideal.IsMaximal
slogan: An ideal is maximal if it is not the whole set and there is no other proper ideal that contains it, meaning it is as large as possible without being everything. It is a coatom in the lattice of proper ideals, so any ideal strictly containing it must be the entire set. This requires the type to have a less-than-or-equal-to relation and the ideal to be downward-closed and proper.

label: Order.Ideal.IsPrime
slogan: An ideal I is prime if whenever a and b are elements such that a ∧ b is in I, then at least one of a or b is in I, and I is not the entire set. This means the complement of I is closed under finite meets and upward closure, forming a filter. The ideal must also be proper, meaning it is not equal to the whole preorder.

label: Order.Ideal.IsPrime.isMaximal
slogan: In a Boolean algebra, every prime ideal is also a maximal ideal, meaning there are no strictly larger proper ideals containing it.

label: Order.IsOfFiniteCharacter
slogan: A family of sets F has finite character if a set X belongs to F exactly when every finite subset of X also belongs to F. This means membership in F depends only on finite subsets. The property holds for any type of elements and uses standard subset relations between sets.

label: Order.IsOfFiniteCharacter.exists_maximal
slogan: If a collection of sets has the property that a set belongs to it whenever all its finite parts do, and the collection is not empty, then there is a set in the collection that cannot be made larger without losing this property.

label: Order.PFilter
slogan: A filter on a preorder P is a nonempty subset of P that is downward directed (any two elements have a common lower bound in the subset) and upward closed (if an element is in the subset and another element is greater than or equal to it, then the larger element is also in the subset).

label: Order.cof
slogan: The cofinality of a cardinal is the smallest size of a set of smaller cardinals whose union reaches up to the given cardinal. It measures how many smaller steps are needed to approach the cardinal. This function computes that minimal size for a given order relation.

label: Order.cof_nat
slogan: The cofinality of the natural numbers is countable, meaning the smallest way to reach the entire set of natural numbers as a union of smaller sets requires countably many such sets. This is expressed by saying the cofinality of the natural numbers equals aleph0, the cardinality of the natural numbers themselves.

label: Order.iso_of_countable_dense
slogan: Any two nonempty, countable, densely ordered linear orders without a smallest or largest element can be matched in a way that preserves their order. This means there exists an order isomorphism between them. The result is known as Cantor's isomorphism theorem.

label: Order.succ
slogan: Order.succ is a function that, given an element in a type with a preorder and a successor structure, returns the smallest element strictly greater than the given element, if such a next element exists. It relies on the type having both a <= and < relation (preorder) and a well-defined notion of "next element" (SuccOrder). The function maps an element to its immediate successor in the order.

label: OrderBot
slogan: A type with a partial order (≤) and a smallest element 'bot' such that bot is less than or equal to every element in the type. This structure combines the ordering relation with the existence of a minimum value. It is used to model ordered sets that have a bottom element.

label: OrderDual
slogan: OrderDual takes a type and creates a new version where the order is flipped, so smaller becomes larger and larger becomes smaller. It reverses the meaning of ≤ so that a ≤ b in the original becomes b ≤ a in the dual. This allows reasoning about reversed order structures using the same type.

label: OrderIso
slogan: OrderIso is a type that represents a one-to-one correspondence between two ordered types, where both the function and its inverse preserve the order: x ≤ y if and only if f(x) ≤ f(y). It means the two types have the same order structure. This isomorphism is defined for types equipped with a ≤ relation.

label: OrderTopology
slogan: OrderTopology is a property that a type has when it supports both a preorder (with ≤ and <) and a topology, and the open sets in the topology are consistent with the order structure. This compatibility ensures that topological concepts like convergence and continuity work well with the ordering, as they do in familiar spaces like the real numbers. It connects the algebraic idea of ordering with the geometric idea of nearness in a coherent way.

label: OrderTopology.completelyNormalSpace
slogan: In a topological space where the topology comes from a linear order, any two separated sets can be surrounded by non-overlapping open sets, ensuring that the space and all its subspaces have strong separation properties. This means that disjoint closed sets in any subspace can always be separated by disjoint open sets. The result holds when the topology is compatible with the order structure of the set.

label: Ordinal
slogan: An ordinal represents the shape of a well-ordered set, capturing how its elements are ordered without caring about what the elements actually are. Two well-ordered sets have the same ordinal if their elements can be matched in a way that preserves the order. The type Ordinal contains all such order types and allows comparisons and operations based on their inherent ordering.

label: Ordinal.CNF
slogan: The Cantor normal form of an ordinal o in base b is a list of pairs (exponent, coefficient) that represents o as a sum of terms like b^u * v, listed in decreasing order of exponents. For b = 0 or b = 1, it returns [(0, o)] when o is not zero. This form breaks down any ordinal into its base-b exponential components, similar to writing a number in scientific notation using powers of b.

label: Ordinal.IsInitial
slogan: An ordinal is called initial if no smaller ordinal has the same number of elements, meaning there is no one-to-one correspondence between it and any ordinal below it. It is the smallest ordinal of its size.

label: Ordinal.add
slogan: Ordinal.add defines addition of two ordinal numbers by combining their well-ordered sets into a disjoint union and ordering the result lexicographically, where elements of the first set come before those of the second, producing a new ordinal that represents the total order. This operation respects the structure of ordinals as order types and ensures the sum of two well-ordered sets remains well-ordered. The addition is based on the idea that equivalent well-ordered sets yield equivalent sums, preserving order isomorphism.

label: Ordinal.bddAbove_of_small
slogan: Any set of ordinals that is indexed by a small type has an upper bound, meaning there is some ordinal that is greater than or equal to every ordinal in the set. This is because the ordinals are well-ordered and suprema exist for small collections. The result ensures that such families cannot be unbounded above.

label: Ordinal.bot_eq_zero
slogan: The smallest ordinal number is zero, meaning the empty well-ordered set has order type zero. This zero is the least element in the ordering of all ordinals.

label: Ordinal.card
slogan: Ordinal.card is a function that takes an ordinal and returns a cardinal number representing its size, such that two ordinals have the same cardinal if there is a bijection between them. It ensures that the assignment respects the equivalence relations on ordinals and cardinals by using quotient maps. This allows the size of a well-ordered set to be defined without depending on its specific elements or ordering.

label: Ordinal.cof
slogan: The cofinality of an ordinal is the smallest cardinality of a set of smaller ordinals that can reach arbitrarily high within the ordinal through some function. In other words, it measures the shortest unbounded sequence that can climb up the ordinal. This value is defined as a cardinal number and reflects how difficult it is to "approach the top" of the ordinal.

label: Ordinal.cof_eq_aleph0_of_isSuccLimit
slogan: If an ordinal is not the smallest and has no immediate predecessor, and is less than the first uncountable ordinal, then its cofinality is aleph0, meaning it can be reached by a countable sequence but not by any finite sequence.

label: Ordinal.cof_omega
slogan: The cofinality of the smallest infinite ordinal, omega, is omega itself, meaning the shortest unbounded sequence of natural numbers leading up to omega has the same length as the natural numbers. This holds for any ordinal that is a successor-limit, where no single element immediately precedes it and it is not the smallest ordinal.

label: Ordinal.cof_type
slogan: The cofinality of an ordinal is the smallest ordinal that can be mapped into it so that every element of the original ordinal is eventually exceeded by the map. This measures how far the ordinal is from being reachable by a smaller, unbounded sequence. It is defined using the order type of the converse of a well-founded relation to ensure minimality.

label: Ordinal.cof_zero
slogan: The cofinality of the ordinal zero is zero, meaning no sequence of smaller ordinals can approach it because there are no elements to build such a sequence. This reflects that zero is the smallest ordinal and has no predecessors.

label: Ordinal.epsilon
slogan: The epsilon function maps each ordinal to the corresponding fixed point of the function that raises omega to the power of that ordinal, meaning it lists ordinals where omega raised to the ordinal equals the ordinal itself. It is equivalent to the first level of the Veblen hierarchy beyond exponentiation. For example, epsilon zero is the smallest ordinal such that omega raised to it equals it.

label: Ordinal.epsilon_zero_eq_nfp
slogan: Epsilon zero is the smallest ordinal that cannot be reached by repeatedly raising omega to the power of smaller ordinals, and it equals the least fixed point obtained by iterating the function that maps an ordinal a to omega raised to the power a, starting from zero. This fixed point is found by taking the supremum of the sequence 0, omega^0, omega^(omega^0), and so on.

label: Ordinal.exists_isFundamentalSeq
slogan: Every ordinal has a strictly increasing sequence of smaller ordinals that approaches it and whose range is cofinal in it. This sequence is called a fundamental sequence, and it is defined on the set of ordinals less than the cofinality of the given ordinal. Given an ordinal o and a proof that a equals the cofinality of o, such a sequence exists.

label: Ordinal.induction
slogan: To prove a property holds for all ordinals, it is enough to show that if the property holds for every ordinal smaller than a given one, then it also holds for that ordinal. This works because there are no infinite descending sequences of ordinals, making induction valid on the less-than relation.

label: Ordinal.instLinearOrder
slogan: Ordinals can always be compared: for any two ordinals, one is less than, equal to, or greater than the other, and this comparison is based on a decidable ordering. This means the usual rules of ordering apply fully across all ordinals. The structure builds on the fact that ordinals already support a partial order and that both the less-than and equality relations between them can be decided algorithmically.

label: Ordinal.instPow
slogan: Ordinal exponentiation is defined so that one ordinal can be raised to the power of another, using recursion that handles limit ordinals by taking the supremum over all smaller exponents. This fits with the usual ordinal arithmetic and extends how powers work beyond natural numbers. The operation is built using the structure of ordinals as a linearly ordered type with zero and a well-founded less-than relation.

label: Ordinal.isEquivalent
slogan: Two well-ordered sets are equivalent if there's a one-to-one, order-preserving map between them, and this equivalence is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. The relation forms a setoid on the type of well orders, meaning it respects composition and inversion of order isomorphisms. This equivalence captures the idea that two well-ordered sets have the same "order shape" or structure.

label: Ordinal.isPrincipal_add_iff_add_lt_ne_self
slogan: An ordinal a is principal under addition if and only if the sum of any two ordinals less than a is never equal to a. This means a cannot be expressed as the sum of two smaller ordinals. The property holds precisely when the set of ordinals below a is closed under addition.

label: Ordinal.isSuccLimit_iff
slogan: An ordinal is a successor-limit if it is not the smallest ordinal and has no immediate predecessor. This means it is neither zero nor directly after another ordinal. The statement says that an ordinal is a successor-limit if and only if it is not zero and no ordinal immediately comes before it.

label: Ordinal.le_omega_self
slogan: Every ordinal is less than or equal to omega, the smallest infinite ordinal. This means no ordinal can be larger than omega in the standard ordering. The result follows from the fact that ordinals are linearly ordered and well-founded.

label: Ordinal.leftDistribClass
slogan: For any ordinals a, b, and c, multiplying a by the sum of b and c is the same as adding the products a times b and a times c. This means ordinal multiplication distributes over addition when the multiplication is on the left. The system recognizes this property by marking ordinals as an instance of a left-distributive algebraic structure.

label: Ordinal.lt_wf
slogan: The relation "less than" on ordinal numbers has no infinite descending sequences, meaning you can't keep finding smaller and smaller ordinals forever. This property ensures that induction and recursion based on ordinals are logically valid.

label: Ordinal.monoid
slogan: Ordinal numbers support a multiplication operation that is associative and has a multiplicative identity (one), forming a monoid structure. This allows for consistent repeated multiplication of ordinals where the grouping of operations does not affect the result.

label: Ordinal.not_bddAbove_fp
slogan: For any normal ordinal function, there is no upper limit to its fixed points: given any ordinal, there is always a larger one that the function maps to itself. This means the fixed points extend indefinitely through the ordinals. A normal function is one that is strictly increasing and continuous in the ordinal sense.

label: Ordinal.omega
slogan: Ordinal.omega is the smallest infinite ordinal, representing the order of the natural numbers and coming after all finite ordinals. It is the first limit ordinal with no immediate predecessor and is used as the starting point for building larger infinite ordinals. This ordinal describes an infinite, well-ordered sequence that continues without bound.

label: Ordinal.omega0
slogan: Ordinal.omega0 is the smallest infinite ordinal, representing the order of the natural numbers in their usual sequence. It comes after all finite ordinals and corresponds to the idea of counting without end. This ordinal is defined in a way that allows it to be used across different universe levels while preserving its structure.

label: Ordinal.omega0_le_of_isSuccLimit
slogan: The smallest infinite ordinal, omega0, is less than or equal to any ordinal that has no immediate predecessor and is not the smallest. Such ordinals are larger than all natural numbers, and since omega0 is the supremum of the natural numbers, it must be less than or equal to them.

label: Ordinal.ord_cof_eq
slogan: The cofinality of a well-ordered set is the smallest ordinal that can be mapped into it in a way that the image is unbounded. This means there exists a subset of the original order that has no upper bound and whose order type equals the cofinality. In simple terms, it's the shortest length of an increasing sequence that eventually goes past any given element.

label: Ordinal.type
slogan: The type Ordinal assigns a unique ordinal number to every well-ordered set, based on its order structure, so that two sets get the same ordinal if they are order-isomorphic. It uses well-founded, transitive, and trichotomous relations to define valid orderings. Each ordinal acts as a canonical representative for all well-ordered sets of the same shape.

label: Ordinal.type_eq
slogan: If two well-ordered sets have the same ordinal number, then there exists an order-preserving bijection between them, meaning they have the same order structure. This equivalence is based on the idea that ordinals classify well-ordered sets up to order isomorphism. The statement asserts that equal ordinal types imply the existence of such an isomorphism.

label: Ordinal.type_fintype
slogan: The order type of any finite totally ordered set is the same as the natural number representing how many elements are in the set, when that number is converted into an ordinal. This means a well-ordered set with n elements has the ordinal n. It connects the size of finite sets with their order structure in a natural way.

label: Ordinal.type_nat_lt
slogan: The order type of the natural numbers with the usual less-than relation is equal to omega0, the smallest infinite ordinal. This means the natural numbers form a well-ordered set whose structure is the canonical example of an infinite countable order.

label: Ordinal.zero_or_succ_or_isSuccLimit
slogan: Every ordinal is either zero, the successor of some other ordinal, or a limit ordinal that has no immediate predecessor.

label: Ordnode.Balanced
slogan: Balanced t means that for every node in the tree t, the sizes of the left and right subtrees are roughly equal according to a fixed balance condition, ensuring the tree remains efficiently organized. This balance is checked using the sizes of subtrees and a predefined tolerance. The tree must maintain this property at all levels to be considered balanced.

label: Orientation.areaForm
slogan: The areaForm is a function that takes two vectors in a 2-dimensional real inner product space and returns a real number representing the signed area of the parallelogram they form, with the sign determined by the orientation of the space. It is an antisymmetric bilinear map, meaning the area changes sign when the order of the vectors is swapped. This form is defined relative to a chosen orientation of the plane.

label: Orientation.eq_or_eq_neg
slogan: If two orientations of a finite-dimensional vector space over an ordered field are defined using bases with the same number of elements, then the orientations must either be identical or negatives of each other, meaning there can be at most two distinct orientations for the space.

label: OrthogonalFamily.norm_sum
slogan: If you add together a finite number of vectors that are mutually orthogonal (each pair has an inner product of zero), then the square of the norm of the sum equals the sum of the squares of the norms of the individual vectors. This happens because the cross terms in the inner product expansion cancel out, leaving only the contributions from each vector's own norm. The result holds in any inner product space over a field like the real or complex numbers.

label: Orthonormal
slogan: A set of vectors is orthonormal if each vector has length 1 and any two different vectors are perpendicular, meaning their inner product is zero. This is defined in a vector space with an inner product that induces a norm. The function checks this condition for a given family of vectors indexed by some type.

label: Orthonormal.sum_inner_products_le
slogan: If you have a finite set of orthonormal vectors in an inner product space, then for any vector x, the sum of the squares of the inner products of x with each of these orthonormal vectors is less than or equal to the square of the norm of x.

label: Orthonormal.tsum_inner_products_le
slogan: In an inner product space, for any orthonormal set of vectors and any given vector x, the sum of the squares of the inner products between the orthonormal vectors and x is at most the square of the norm of x, even when summing over infinitely many vectors using the limit of finite partial sums.

label: OrthonormalBasis.sum_rankOne_eq_id
slogan: In a finite-dimensional inner product space, if you have an orthonormal basis, then adding up the projections onto each basis vector (where each projection maps a vector to its component in that basis direction) gives back the original vector; this sum of rank-one projection operators is exactly the identity map.

label: OrthonormalBasis.sum_repr
slogan: In a finite-dimensional inner product space, any vector can be written as a sum of its projections onto each orthonormal basis vector, where each term is the inner product of the vector with a basis element multiplied by that basis element, and this sum equals the original vector.

label: OrthonormalBasis.sum_repr'
slogan: In a finite-dimensional inner product space with a finite orthonormal basis, every vector can be written as the sum of its projections onto each basis vector, where each term in the sum is the inner product of the vector with a basis element multiplied by that basis element. The sum includes all basis vectors indexed by a finite set. This representation exactly reconstructs the original vector.

label: OrthonormalBasis.sum_sq_norm_inner_left
slogan: In a finite-dimensional inner product space with a real or complex orthonormal basis, the sum of the squares of the absolute values of the inner products of a vector with each basis vector equals the square of the vector's norm. This means the total energy of a vector can be computed by adding up the squared projections onto each basis direction. The result relies on the basis being both orthogonal and normalized.

label: OrthonormalBasis.tensorProduct
slogan: Given two orthonormal bases in inner product spaces over a real-like field, their tensor product forms a new orthonormal basis for the tensor product space, with index set being the Cartesian product of the original index sets.

label: OrthonormalBasis.toMatrix_orthonormalBasis_mem_orthogonal
slogan: If you have two orthonormal bases in a finite-dimensional real inner product space, then the change-of-basis matrix from one to the other is an orthogonal matrix, meaning its transpose equals its inverse and it preserves lengths and angles. This matrix satisfies the condition that multiplying it by its transpose gives the identity matrix, so it belongs to the group of orthogonal matrices over the real numbers. The result holds because orthonormal bases ensure that the matrix columns are unit vectors and mutually perpendicular.

label: Oscillation.eq_zero_iff_continuousAt
slogan: The oscillation of a function at a point is zero exactly when the function is continuous at that point, meaning there is no abrupt change in the function's values near the point. This happens when the function's output stays close to its value at the point as the input gets close to it.

label: PFun.Dom
slogan: The domain of a partial function from type α to type β is the set of inputs in α for which the function is defined. It is represented as a set of elements where the partial function returns a value. This is computed by collecting all elements of α that map to a defined result in β.

label: PFun.dom_coe
slogan: When a total function is converted to a partial function, its domain is the set of all possible inputs, meaning it is defined everywhere.

label: PFun.graph
slogan: The graph of a partial function f is the set of all pairs (x, y) such that f is defined at x and maps x to y. It consists of input-output pairs where the input is in the domain of f and the output is the corresponding value of f at that input. This set is formed by collecting all (x, f x) for which f x has a value.

label: PFun.graph'
slogan: The graph of a partial function f from type α to type β is the set of pairs (x, y) such that f is defined at x and the value of f at x is y. It represents the relation where x and y are connected exactly when f produces y from x. This relation is built using the set of all such input-output pairs for which the function is defined.

label: PMF
slogan: A PMF (probability mass function) is a function from a type α to the non-negative extended real numbers (including infinity) such that the sum of all its values equals 1. It represents a discrete probability distribution where each value indicates the probability of a specific outcome.

label: PMF.bernoulli
slogan: A Bernoulli probability distribution assigns a probability p (between 0 and 1) to the outcome true, and the remaining probability (1 - p) to false, forming a valid discrete probability distribution over Boolean values.

label: PMF.toMeasure_apply
slogan: The measure associated with a probability mass function p assigns to any measurable set s the sum of the probabilities p(x) for all elements x in s, where elements not in s contribute zero. This sum is taken over the entire type and equals the total probability mass contained in the set.

label: PMF.uniformOfFinset
slogan: The uniformOfFinset function creates a probability distribution where each element in a nonempty finite set has an equal chance of being selected, and all probabilities add up to 1. It assigns the same positive probability to every element in the set, and zero probability to everything outside the set. This is done by dividing 1 by the number of elements in the set to get each individual probability.

label: PMF.uniformOfFintype
slogan: The uniformOfFintype function creates a probability distribution where every element in a finite, non-empty type has an equal probability of being selected, with each probability equal to 1 divided by the total number of elements in the type. It ensures the probabilities sum to 1, assigning the same value to each element. This represents a discrete uniform distribution over all elements of the type.

label: PNat.instCancelCommMonoid
slogan: The positive natural numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) form a structure where multiplication is associative, commutative, and has 1 as the identity, and where you can cancel a common factor from both sides of an equation: if a * b = a * c, then b = c.

label: PSet.ofNat
slogan: PSet.ofNat takes a natural number n and returns the corresponding von Neumann ordinal as a pre-set, where each ordinal is represented as the set of all smaller ordinals. The function builds finite ordinals in the context of ZFC set theory using the PSet type. For example, 0 is the empty set, 1 contains 0, 2 contains 0 and 1, and so on.

label: Padic
slogan: The p-adic numbers are built by completing the rational numbers using a special size function called the p-adic norm, where p is a prime number, so that numbers are considered close when their difference is divisible by a high power of p. This process fills in gaps among the rationals, creating a complete number system where all Cauchy sequences converge under the p-adic norm. The resulting system extends the rationals into a field with well-defined addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, preserving arithmetic while using p-adic size instead of the usual absolute value.

label: Padic.denseRange_ratCast
slogan: For any prime number p, every p-adic number can be approximated as closely as desired by rational numbers, since the image of the rationals under the cast to p-adic numbers is dense in the p-adic topology.

label: Padic.instCompleteSpace
slogan: The p-adic numbers form a complete space, meaning every Cauchy sequence of p-adic numbers converges to a p-adic number. This holds for any prime p and ensures that sequences getting arbitrarily close under the p-adic metric have a limit within the same system.

label: Padic.nonarchimedean
slogan: For any prime number p, the p-adic absolute value of the sum of two p-adic numbers is at most the larger of their p-adic absolute values. This means that adding two p-adic numbers cannot result in a larger norm than the largest norm of the two numbers. The property reflects the ultrametric nature of p-adic arithmetic, where distances behave differently than in standard real arithmetic.

label: Padic.norm_eq_zpow_neg_valuation
slogan: For a prime number p and a nonzero rational number x, the p-adic norm of x is equal to p raised to the negative of the p-adic valuation of x.

label: Padic.valuation
slogan: The p-adic valuation of a rational number measures how many times a given prime p divides the number, with positive values when p divides the numerator and negative when it divides the denominator. It is extended to p-adic numbers by looking at the eventual constant valuation of Cauchy sequences of rationals under the p-adic norm. The function assigns to each nonzero p-adic number an integer representing this limiting exponent of p.

label: PadicComplex
slogan: PadicComplex(p) creates a complete, normed field for a given prime number p by completing the algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers using a uniform structure based on their norm. This field contains all roots of polynomials with p-adic coefficients and all limits of Cauchy sequences under the p-adic norm. It is the p-adic analog of the complex numbers, combining algebraic closure and topological completeness.

label: PadicComplex.isAlgClosed
slogan: For any prime number p, the field of p-adic complex numbers, formed by completing the algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers, is algebraically closed, meaning every nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in this field has a root in it. This follows from the fact that the algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers is densely embedded in its completion and that polynomials over the algebraic closure split completely in the completed field.

label: PadicInt
slogan: PadicInt p is the type of p-adic integers, which are p-adic numbers whose p-adic norm is less than or equal to 1, where p is a prime number. It is defined for any natural number p that is prime, and forms a subset of the p-adic numbers. These integers form a ring under addition and multiplication within the p-adic number system.

label: PadicInt.adicCompletionIntegersEquiv
slogan: For a prime number p, the ring of p-adic integers is the same as the completion of the integers using the p-adic metric, meaning it includes all limits of Cauchy sequences of integers under this metric. This equivalence respects both the ring operations and the topology of convergence. Each p-adic integer can be expressed as a power series in p with coefficients between 0 and p-1.

label: PadicInt.compactSpace
slogan: For any prime number p, the set of p-adic integers is compact, meaning every sequence has a convergent subsequence and the space is closed and bounded in a topological sense. This follows from the fact that the p-adic integers form a complete space where all Cauchy sequences converge, and the entire set can be covered by finitely many small regions of any given size. Compactness here is equivalent to being both complete and totally bounded.

label: PadicInt.hasSum_mahler
slogan: For any continuous function f from the p-adic integers to a p-adic Banach space E, the infinite sum of scaled Mahler basis functions—using coefficients derived from repeated forward differences of f at 0—converges to f. The convergence is in the topology of uniform convergence, relying on the completeness and ultrametric structure of E. This expansion allows representing continuous p-adic functions as series similar to polynomial expansions.

label: PadicInt.ideal_eq_span_pow_p
slogan: Every nonzero ideal in the ring of p-adic integers is the set of all multiples of some power of p, where p is a prime number.

label: PadicInt.instIsDiscreteValuationRing
slogan: The ring of p-adic integers is a discrete valuation ring when p is a prime number, meaning every nonzero ideal in the ring is generated by a power of p and there is a unique maximal ideal. This holds because p is irreducible and every nonzero p-adic integer can be expressed as a unit times a power of p, with units being exactly those elements not divisible by p.

label: PadicInt.isFractionRing
slogan: The p-adic integers form a ring that consists of fractions where the denominators are not divisible by a fixed prime p, and this ring is the localization of the integers at the set of integers not divisible by p. This means the p-adic integers can be understood as the result of allowing division by all integers that are not multiples of p. The structure satisfies the universal property of a fraction ring over this localized subring of the integers.

label: PadicInt.isUnit_den
slogan: A p-adic integer is invertible if and only if its denominator, when written in lowest terms, is not divisible by the prime p. This means the element has a multiplicative inverse in the p-adic integers exactly when the denominator of its rational form shares no factor of p. The result links invertibility in the p-adic integers to the simple arithmetic condition of p not dividing the denominator.

label: PadicInt.isUnit_iff
slogan: A p-adic integer is invertible (has a multiplicative inverse in the ring of p-adic integers) if and only if its p-adic norm is exactly 1, which happens precisely when it is not divisible by the prime p.

label: PadicInt.ker_toZModPow
slogan: The kernel of the ring homomorphism from p-adic integers to integers modulo p^n is the set of p-adic integers divisible by p^n. This means a p-adic integer maps to zero modulo p^n exactly when it is a multiple of p^n. The kernel is thus the ideal generated by p^n in the ring of p-adic integers.

label: PadicInt.lift
slogan: PadicInt.lift is a function that maps elements from a ring R into the ring of p-adic integers, provided there is a consistent family of ring homomorphisms from R to the integers modulo p^n for each n, and p is a prime number. It constructs this map by ensuring all these homomorphisms align properly across different powers of p, preserving addition and multiplication. The result is a ring homomorphism that respects the structure of both R and the p-adic integers.

label: PartialFun
slogan: PartialFun is a category where objects are types and morphisms are partial functions between them, meaning functions that are defined only on some subset of their input type.

label: PartialHomeomorph
slogan: A partial homeomorphism is a continuous bijection between open subsets of two topological spaces, with a continuous inverse. It acts like a homeomorphism but only on restricted open parts of the spaces. This structure is used to study local symmetries in topology where continuity and openness are preserved.

label: PartialOrder
slogan: A partial order is a way of comparing elements in a set where every element is less than or equal to itself, the relation is transitive, and if two elements are mutually less than or equal to each other, they must be equal. It builds on a preorder by adding this last condition, known as antisymmetry. This structure is defined for a type α and includes both ≤ and < relations that work together consistently.

label: PartitionOfUnity
slogan: A partition of unity is a family of continuous, nonnegative real-valued functions on a topological space where, at every point, the sum of the function values is one, and the supports of the functions are locally finite and each lie within some set of a given open cover. It exists for normal topological spaces and allows global functions to be built from local data. The space is covered by open sets, and each function in the partition is tied to one of these sets.

label: Partrec.dom_re
slogan: If a partial function is computable, then the set of inputs for which it is defined is recursively enumerable.

label: Path
slogan: A Path is a continuous function from the interval [0, 1] to a topological space, where the function's continuity is defined using the subspace topology on [0, 1] and the topology on the target space. It connects two points x and y in that space, meaning the function starts at x (when t=0) and ends at y (when t=1). The path is built from a ContinuousMap, ensuring the function respects the topological structure.

label: Path.Homotopic.equivalence
slogan: Path homotopy is an equivalence relation because it is reflexive (every path is homotopic to itself), symmetric (if one path can be continuously deformed into another, the reverse is true), and transitive (if a first path deforms into a second and the second into a third, then the first can be deformed into the third).

label: Path.Homotopic.trans_assoc
slogan: For any three paths p, q, and r that connect four points in sequence, the path formed by first combining p and q and then combining the result with r is homotopic to the path formed by first combining q and r and then combining p with that result. This means that path concatenation is associative up to homotopy.

label: Path.Homotopy
slogan: A Path.Homotopy is a continuous deformation between two paths that start and end at the same points, where the deformation keeps the endpoints fixed throughout. It is a special case of a homotopy relative to a subset, specifically relative to the set {0, 1} in the unit interval. The homotopy itself is a continuous map from the unit square [0,1] x [0,1] to a topological space, transforming one path into another over time.

label: Path.trans
slogan: Path.trans takes two continuous paths where the end of the first matches the start of the second and returns a new continuous path that goes from the start of the first to the end of the second, by traversing each path in sequence over the interval [0,1].

label: PathConnectedSpace
slogan: A path-connected space is a type of topological space where, for any two points, there is a continuous path between them using a function from the interval [0,1] to the space. The space must have a topology defined on it so that continuity makes sense. This property means the space is "all one piece" in a strong sense.

label: PathConnectedSpace.connectedSpace
slogan: If a topological space has the property that any two points can be joined by a continuous path, then the space is connected, meaning it cannot be divided into two disjoint nonempty open sets. This result shows that path-connectedness implies connectedness in such spaces.

label: Pell.IsFundamental.eq_zpow_or_neg_zpow
slogan: Every solution to the Pell equation x^2 - d*y^2 = 1 can be expressed as either a positive or negative integer power of a fundamental solution, up to sign.

label: Pell.Solution₁
slogan: Pell.Solution₁ d is the type of integer solutions (x, y) to the equation x^2 - d*y^2 = 1, where d is an integer. These solutions correspond to elements of the ring Z[sqrt(d)] with norm equal to 1. The structure supports operations from algebraic types like monoids and commutative rings.

label: Pell.exists_of_not_isSquare
slogan: If d is a positive integer that is not a perfect square, then there are integers x and y, with y nonzero, such that x squared minus d times y squared equals 1.

label: Perfect.exists_nat_bool_injection
slogan: There exists an injective, continuous function from the natural numbers into a nonempty perfect subset C of a complete metric space, such that all function values lie within C. This means infinitely many distinct points in C can be mapped to in a structured, one-to-one way. The result uses the topological properties of perfect and complete spaces to ensure such a mapping exists.

label: PerfectField.ofFinite
slogan: Every finite field is perfect, meaning that in a field with only finitely many elements, every element has a p-th root where p is the characteristic of the field, and all irreducible polynomials over it have distinct roots. This happens because finite fields have prime characteristic and no nonzero nilpotent elements, making the Frobenius map (which raises elements to the p-th power) surjective. As a result, such fields satisfy the condition of being perfect.

label: PerfectRing.ofFiniteOfIsReduced
slogan: A finite commutative ring with identity and no nonzero nilpotent elements, in prime characteristic p, is perfect because the Frobenius map (raising elements to the p-th power) is injective and thus surjective due to finiteness. This means every element has a p-th root, making the ring perfect.

label: PerfectSpace.not_isolated
slogan: In a perfect topological space, no point is isolated, meaning every point has other points arbitrarily close to it. Specifically, for any point x, every neighborhood around x contains points different from x. This is expressed by saying the filter of neighborhoods of x, restricted to the space without x, is nontrivial.

label: PerfectlyNormalSpace
slogan: A perfectly normal space is a topological space where any two disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open sets, and every closed set can be written as the intersection of a countable number of open sets. It is a stronger version of a normal space with extra structure on how closed sets are formed. This property ensures very fine control over separating parts of the space.

label: PeriodPair.derivWeierstrassP_sq
slogan: The square of the derivative of the Weierstrass elliptic function ℘ at a point z is equal to 4 times the cube of ℘(z), minus g₂ times ℘(z), minus g₃, provided z is not in the lattice generated by the period pair. The constants g₂ and g₃ depend on the period pair. This equation holds for complex numbers z where the function is defined.

label: PeriodPair.g₂
slogan: The value g2 is defined as 60 times the sum of the reciprocals of the fourth powers of all nonzero elements in a lattice generated by two complex numbers that are not real multiples of each other.
