This sum is computed using the Eisenstein series G4 associated with the lattice. The result is a complex number that serves as an invariant of the lattice.

label: PeriodPair.lattice
slogan: The lattice generated by a pair of complex numbers that are linearly independent over the real numbers, consisting of all integer linear combinations of these two periods. This set forms a subgroup of the complex numbers under addition. It is structured as a Z-submodule of the complex plane.

label: PeriodPair.meromorphic_weierstrassP
slogan: The Weierstrass P function associated with a pair of complex numbers that are linearly independent over the real numbers is meromorphic, meaning it is holomorphic everywhere except at isolated points (the lattice points), where it has poles. This function is doubly periodic with respect to the lattice generated by the pair. The result confirms that the function fits the general definition of a meromorphic function in complex analysis.

label: PeriodPair.weierstrassP
slogan: The Weierstrass P function takes a pair of complex numbers that are linearly independent over the real numbers, forming a lattice, and returns a complex-valued function defined on the complex plane. This function is doubly periodic with respect to the lattice and is given by a sum over all nonzero lattice points involving inverse square terms. It is used in the study of elliptic functions and has poles at the lattice points.

label: Pi.Lex.linearOrder
slogan: Functions are ordered lexicographically by comparing their values at the first input where they differ, using the order of the output types, and this ordering is total and strict, meaning any two functions can be compared and one will always be less than, equal to, or greater than the other.

label: Pi.add_apply
slogan: For any two functions f and g, the sum f + g evaluated at a point i is equal to f(i) + g(i), meaning addition of functions is defined pointwise by adding their values at each input. This works when each output type supports addition.

label: Pi.compactSpace
slogan: The product of any collection of compact topological spaces is also compact when given the product topology, meaning that if all the individual spaces in the product are compact, then the space of all functions from the index type to the respective spaces is compact as well. This is a general form of Tychonoff's theorem. It relies on the product topology, where open sets are defined using finite constraints across the components.

label: Pi.complete
slogan: The product of a family of complete uniform spaces, when given the product uniformity, is also a complete uniform space. This means that any Cauchy filter in the product space converges to some point in the space. Convergence in the product is determined by convergence in each component space.

label: Pi.monoid
slogan: If each part of a collection of types has a multiplication with an identity and associativity, then the set of functions into these types also has a multiplication that is associative and has an identity, where multiplication is done point by point. This means that multiplying two functions results in a new function whose value at each point is the product of the values at that point, and there is a constant function that acts as the identity. The whole structure satisfies the rules of a monoid.

label: Pi.norm_def
slogan: The norm of a function defined on a finite type, taking values in a family of seminormed additive groups, is the largest norm among its values, where each component's norm is measured in its respective group and the maximum is taken over all indices. This maximum is computed as a non-negative real number and then converted to a real number. The finiteness of the index type ensures that the maximum exists and is well-defined.

label: Pi.ring
slogan: If you have a collection of rings, then the set of functions into these rings forms a ring where you add, subtract, and multiply by doing the operation at each point separately. This structure inherits the ring properties from the individual rings, building on the fact that the functions already form an additive group and a semiring under pointwise operations. The operations are defined so that the result at each index behaves just like the original ring at that index.

label: Pi.topologicalSpace
slogan: Pi.topologicalSpace gives a product of topological spaces a topology where a set is open if it can be built from unions and finite intersections of sets that are open in the individual spaces when projected down. This topology is the coarsest one making all projection maps continuous. It uses the infimum of topologies to define the smallest topology that includes all the preimages of open sets from each component space.

label: Pi.zero_apply
slogan: The zero function from any type A to a family of types with zero elements sends every input to the zero of its corresponding output type. In other words, applying the zero function at any point gives zero in that component. This relies on each output type having a designated zero element.

label: PiLp.completeSpace
slogan: The space PiLp, made up of functions taking values in a family of normed spaces and having finite lp norm, is complete, meaning every Cauchy sequence in this space converges to a limit that is also in the space, provided each component space is complete. The norm uses extended nonnegative real numbers (including infinity) to allow for unbounded values. This result follows from the fact that the product of complete spaces with the product uniform structure is itself complete.

label: PiLp.instDist
slogan: PiLp.instDist defines a distance between two elements in a product space made from multiple normed spaces, where the distance is calculated by summing the p-th powers of their component-wise distances and then taking the p-th root. This works when the number of components is finite, using real number arithmetic, and the result is always a non-negative real number. The structure supports p-norm style metrics for finite collections of spaces.

label: PiTensorProduct.lift
slogan: Given a multilinear map from a family of R-modules to another R-module E, there is a unique linear map from the tensor product of those modules to E that agrees with the original multilinear map when composed with the canonical multilinear map into the tensor product. This establishes a one-to-one correspondence between multilinear maps and linear maps out of the tensor product. The construction respects the module structure over a commutative semiring R.

label: PointDerivation
slogan: A PointDerivation is a linear operation that takes smooth functions defined near a point on a manifold and returns values in a module, acting like a directional derivative by satisfying the product rule. It is defined using the structure of smooth maps on manifolds modeled over normed vector spaces and depends on a chosen base point. The smoothness class can be finite or infinite, and the derivation respects this regularity.

label: PolishSpace
slogan: A Polish space is a topological space whose topology can be defined by a complete metric and which has a countable base for its open sets. It combines the properties of being second-countable and completely metrizable.

label: Polygon
slogan: A polygon with n vertices in a space P is defined as a way to assign each of the n vertices (numbered 0 to n-1) to a point in P. The structure uses Fin n to index the vertices, ensuring there are exactly n of them. This means a polygon is essentially a list of n points in P, where the order matters and the shape is formed by connecting consecutive points.

label: Polynomial
slogan: A polynomial is built from variables and coefficients where the coefficients are elements of a semiring, meaning they support addition and multiplication with familiar arithmetic properties like distributivity and the existence of zero and one. The type Polynomial R represents all polynomials with coefficients from the semiring R. Operations like addition and multiplication of polynomials are supported and produce new polynomials of the same type.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_complex_cos
slogan: The n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, when evaluated at the cosine of a complex number θ, gives the cosine of n times θ. This holds for any integer n and complex number θ. The result connects polynomial evaluation with trigonometric scaling.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_derivative_eq_U
slogan: The derivative of the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind is equal to n times the (n-1)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind, where n is an integer and the polynomials are defined over a commutative ring.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_eq_U_sub_X_mul_U
slogan: For any integer n and commutative ring R, the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind equals the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind minus the product of the variable X and the (n-1)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_mul
slogan: The (m * n)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind is equal to the composition of the m-th Chebyshev polynomial with the n-th Chebyshev polynomial, for any integers m and n and over any commutative ring R.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_mul_T
slogan: For any commutative ring R and integers m and k, twice the product of the m-th and k-th Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind equals the sum of the (m+k)-th and (m-k)-th Chebyshev polynomials.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_real_cos
slogan: For any real number θ and integer n, the value of the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind at cos(θ) equals cos(n*θ). This means evaluating the polynomial at the cosine of an angle gives the cosine of the angle multiplied by n. The result connects polynomial evaluation with trigonometric scaling of angles.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.T_real_cosh
slogan: The n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, when evaluated at the hyperbolic cosine of a real number θ, gives the hyperbolic cosine of n times θ. In other words, plugging cosh(θ) into the polynomial T_n returns cosh(n*θ). This holds for any real number θ and any integer n.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.U
slogan: U n is a polynomial that represents the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind, defined for any commutative ring R and taking integer n as input. It is constructed recursively, using the relation U(n) = 2*x*U(n-1) - U(n-2), starting from U(0) = 1 and U(1) = 2*x. These polynomials are used to approximate functions and solve differential equations in mathematical applications.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.U_real_cos
slogan: For any real number θ and integer n, the value of the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind at cos(θ) multiplied by sin(θ) equals sin((n + 1) * θ).

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.abs_eval_T_real_le_one
slogan: For any integer n and real number x between -1 and 1 inclusive, the absolute value of the nth Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind evaluated at x is less than or equal to 1.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.chebyshevTsequence
slogan: The ChebyshevTsequence is a sequence of polynomials over a commutative ring R where each polynomial in the sequence has degree equal to its index, starting from degree 0, and the polynomials satisfy the recurrence relation of Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind; it is defined only for rings where 2 is not zero and the ring is a domain. Each polynomial in the sequence is constructed so that its degree matches its position in the list, and the sequence is built using integer coefficients cast into the ring R. This sequence captures the standard Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind as elem

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.integral_eq_sumZeroes
slogan: The integral of a polynomial of degree less than 2n over the interval [-1, 1], weighted by 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), equals pi times the average of the polynomial's values at the points cos((2i + 1)pi/(2n)) for i from 0 to n-1.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.integral_eval_T_real_mul_eval_T_real_measureT_of_ne
slogan: The integral of the product of two different Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind, evaluated over the real numbers and weighted by 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), is zero. This holds when the polynomials are of different degrees. The result reflects the orthogonality property of Chebyshev polynomials with respect to this weighted measure.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.isExtrOn_T_real_iff
slogan: The real values of x between -1 and 1 where the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind reaches a maximum or minimum are exactly those points x that equal the cosine of (k times pi divided by n), for some integer k from 0 to n, provided n is not zero.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.leadingCoeff_eq_iff_of_forall_abs_le_one
slogan: Among all polynomials of degree at most n (with n at least 2) that do not exceed absolute value 1 on the interval [-1, 1], the only one with leading coefficient equal to 2^(n-1) is the nth Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. Conversely, if such a polynomial equals the nth Chebyshev polynomial, its leading coefficient must be 2^(n-1). This characterizes the Chebyshev polynomial as the unique extremal case under these boundedness and degree conditions.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.leadingCoeff_le_of_forall_abs_le_one
slogan: If a polynomial with real coefficients has degree at most n and its absolute value is at most 1 for all inputs between -1 and 1, then the absolute value of its leading coefficient is at most 2 raised to the power of (n - 1).

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.node
slogan: For natural numbers n and i where n is not zero and i is at most n, the function node n i returns the value cos(pi * i / n), which represents one of the points in the interval [-1, 1] where the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind reaches its extreme values.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.rootMultiplicity_T_real
slogan: The theorem states that for any natural numbers n and k where k is less than n, the cosine of (2k + 1)π/(2n) is a simple root (with multiplicity 1) of the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind over the real numbers.

label: Polynomial.Chebyshev.roots_T_real
slogan: The real roots of the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind are exactly the numbers cos((2*k + 1)*pi/(2*n)) for k = 0, 1, ..., n-1. These values are computed by applying the cosine function to specific angles that divide the interval [0, pi] into equal parts. The set of roots is finite and contains exactly n distinct values, each corresponding to one of these angles.

label: Polynomial.Gal
slogan: The Galois group of a polynomial is the set of all symmetries (automorphisms) of its splitting field that leave the base field unchanged, and these symmetries permute the roots of the polynomial. It is formed using the algebraic structure of the splitting field as an extension of the base field. This group captures how the roots relate to each other under these symmetries.

label: Polynomial.Gal.galActionHom
slogan: The galActionHom function maps each automorphism in the Galois group of a polynomial to a permutation of the polynomial's roots in an extension field, provided the polynomial splits in that field. It ensures that combining automorphisms corresponds to composing permutations, using the algebraic embedding of the base field into the extension. This gives a precise way to view Galois group elements as symmetries acting on roots.

label: Polynomial.Gal.galActionHom_bijective_of_prime_degree
slogan: If a polynomial with rational coefficients has prime degree, is irreducible, and has exactly two more complex roots than real ones, then the mapping from its Galois group to the permutations of its roots is bijective—meaning every permutation of the roots comes from a unique symmetry in the Galois group.

label: Polynomial.Gal.galAction_isPretransitive
slogan: If a polynomial is irreducible and all its roots are in a field extension, then the Galois group permutes the roots in such a way that any root can be mapped to any other root by some automorphism in the group. This transitive action depends on the polynomial being irreducible and the extension containing all roots. The result asserts that the Galois group acts transitively on the distinct roots of the polynomial.

label: Polynomial.IsEisensteinAt
slogan: A polynomial is Eisenstein at a prime ideal if its constant term is not divisible by the square of the ideal, all intermediate coefficients are divisible by the ideal, and the leading coefficient is not divisible by the ideal; this guarantees the polynomial can't be factored over the ring. The condition applies to polynomials whose coefficients come from a commutative semiring.

label: Polynomial.IsEisensteinAt.irreducible
slogan: If a polynomial has integer-like coefficients and there is a prime number that divides all coefficients except the leading one, does not divide the leading coefficient, and whose square does not divide the constant term, then the polynomial cannot be factored into simpler polynomials over the ring, provided the ring has no zero divisors and the polynomial's coefficients share no common factor.

label: Polynomial.IsRoot.norm_lt_cauchyBound
slogan: If a polynomial has a root in a normed division ring, then the norm of that root is strictly less than the polynomial's Cauchy bound, which is computed from its coefficients. This gives an upper estimate for how large the absolute value of any root can be. The bound helps locate all roots within a known range.

label: Polynomial.Monic
slogan: A polynomial is called monic if the coefficient of its highest-degree term is 1, provided the polynomial is not zero. This definition works for polynomials with coefficients in any semiring, where basic arithmetic rules hold. The leading coefficient is determined by looking at the term with the highest power that has a non-zero coefficient.

label: Polynomial.Splits.eq_prod_roots
slogan: If a polynomial can be broken down into linear factors over a commutative ring that is an integral domain, then the polynomial is equal to its leading coefficient times the product of (X - r) for each root r, where each root appears as many times as its multiplicity.

label: Polynomial.SplittingField
slogan: Polynomial.SplittingField creates a new field from a given polynomial by adding all its roots so that the polynomial can be written as a product of linear factors. This extended field contains the original field and is built by successively adjoining roots until the polynomial splits completely. The result is a minimal field where the polynomial has all its roots and factors fully.

label: Polynomial.abc
slogan: For three nonzero polynomials a, b and c over a field that are pairwise coprime and satisfy a + b + c = 0, the degree of each polynomial plus one is at most the degree of the product of all distinct irreducible factors of a*b*c, unless all three polynomials are constant (i.e., their derivatives are zero).

label: Polynomial.aeval_conj
slogan: For any polynomial with real coefficients and any element x in a real clifford-like algebra, evaluating the polynomial at the conjugate of x gives the conjugate of the polynomial evaluated at x. This is because conjugation respects the algebra structure and commutes with polynomial evaluation. The result follows from conjugation being an algebra automorphism that preserves real scalars and is its own inverse.

label: Polynomial.as_sum_range
slogan: Any polynomial can be written as the sum of its terms from degree 0 up to its natural degree, where each term is the coefficient at that degree times the corresponding power of X. Higher-degree terms do not appear because their coefficients are zero. This sum uses only the powers of X that actually contribute to the polynomial.

label: Polynomial.as_sum_support
slogan: A polynomial equals the sum of its nonzero terms, where each term is a coefficient times a power of the variable and only powers with nonzero coefficients are included. The sum uses standard addition and multiplication rules in any system where these operations follow basic algebraic laws, such as natural numbers or more general semirings. This means the polynomial is fully described by adding up just its active terms, with no contribution from zero coefficients.

label: Polynomial.basisMonomials
slogan: The set of monomials (like 1, x, x^2, x^3, etc.) forms a basis for all polynomials over a semiring, meaning every polynomial can be uniquely written as a sum of these monomials multiplied by coefficients from the semiring. This basis is constructed using the fact that polynomials correspond exactly to finitely supported functions from natural numbers to coefficients. The correspondence preserves algebraic structure, ensuring addition and scalar multiplication behave correctly.

label: Polynomial.bernoulli
slogan: The bernoulli function takes a natural number n and returns the n-th Bernoulli polynomial with rational coefficients, built using binomial coefficients and Bernoulli numbers. Each polynomial is formed by summing terms that combine binomial coefficients with Bernoulli numbers scaled by powers of the variable. The coefficients come from the rational numbers, and the construction relies on standard polynomial operations.

label: Polynomial.card_roots
slogan: A nonzero polynomial over an integral domain has at most as many roots as its degree, counting each root as many times as it appears. The total number of roots, including duplicates, is finite and cannot exceed the polynomial's degree. This assumes that equality of elements can be decided and relies on the fact that polynomials over domains cannot vanish at more points than their degree allows.

label: Polynomial.card_roots'
slogan: The number of roots of a nonzero polynomial over an integral domain, counting multiplicities, is at most the degree of the polynomial, where the degree is the highest power of the variable with a nonzero coefficient; this count is always a natural number and the zero polynomial is considered to have no roots.

label: Polynomial.coeff
slogan: Polynomial.coeff takes a polynomial and a natural number, then returns the coefficient of the term with that power in the polynomial. The polynomial is treated as a function from natural numbers to a semiring, where only finitely many values are nonzero. This function gives direct access to the individual coefficients that make up the polynomial.

label: Polynomial.coeff_eq_esymm_roots_of_card
slogan: For a polynomial over a commutative ring with no zero divisors, if the number of roots (counting multiplicities) equals the degree of the polynomial, then the coefficient of the term of degree k is the leading coefficient multiplied by (-1) raised to the power of (degree minus k), times the (degree minus k)-th elementary symmetric sum of the roots. This means the coefficients can be computed directly from the roots using symmetric combinations. The formula holds when the polynomial splits completely into linear factors.

label: Polynomial.coeff_mul
slogan: The coefficient of x^n in the product of two polynomials is found by adding up all products of coefficients from the two polynomials where the powers of x in each term add up to n. This sum is taken over all pairs of natural numbers (i, j) such that i + j = n, and only finitely many of these products are nonzero. The result follows from how multiplication is defined in polynomials over a semiring.

label: Polynomial.comp
slogan: Polynomial.comp takes two polynomials, p and q, and produces a new polynomial by replacing the variable in p with the polynomial q. The operation uses the algebraic structure of the coefficient semiring to compute the resulting polynomial's coefficients. It relies on standard polynomial evaluation and substitution rules, supported by the semiring properties of the coefficients.

label: Polynomial.cyclotomic
slogan: The cyclotomic function takes a natural number n and a ring R, and returns a polynomial over R whose roots are the primitive n-th roots of unity. It is computed by dividing x^n - 1 by the product of all cyclotomic polynomials of proper divisors of n, resulting in a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This polynomial captures the algebraic structure of complex numbers that generate all n-th roots of unity without repetition.

label: Polynomial.degree
slogan: The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent of any term with a nonzero coefficient, or negative infinity if the polynomial is zero; it is calculated by taking the largest exponent from the set of exponents with nonzero coefficients, using a number system that includes a special value for negative infinity; this works for polynomials whose coefficients are from any semiring, using standard ordering of natural numbers extended to include a bottom element.

label: Polynomial.degree_monomial
slogan: The degree of a monomial a * X^n is n when a is a nonzero element in a semiring; if a is zero, the degree is undefined and represented as negative infinity. This means the highest power of X with a nonzero coefficient determines the degree. The result depends only on the exponent of the nonzero term.

label: Polynomial.deriv_gaussian_eq_hermite_mul_gaussian
slogan: The nth derivative of the function that maps y to exp(-(y^2 / 2)) evaluated at x equals (-1)^n times the value of the nth probabilist's Hermite polynomial evaluated at x, multiplied by exp(-(x^2 / 2)).

label: Polynomial.derivative
slogan: The derivative of a polynomial is found by multiplying each coefficient by its term's exponent and reducing the exponent by one, following the usual power rule. This operation works on polynomials over any semiring and behaves linearly with respect to addition and scalar multiplication. The result is a new polynomial whose degree is one less than the original, provided the original had degree at least one.

label: Polynomial.dickson_one_one_eq_chebyshev_C
slogan: The nth Dickson polynomial of the first kind with parameter 1 over a commutative ring R is equal to the nth rescaled Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind over R, where the rescaling means C_n(2x) = 2T_n(x). This identity holds for all natural numbers n and any commutative ring R. Both polynomials satisfy the same recurrence relation and initial conditions, leading to their equality.

label: Polynomial.discr
slogan: The discriminant of a polynomial is calculated using the resultant of the polynomial and its derivative, scaled by the leading coefficient and the degree, and it equals zero if and only if the polynomial has a repeated root. It is defined for polynomials over any commutative ring and uses the natural number degree and matrix determinant in its computation. The value lies in the same ring as the polynomial's coefficients.

label: Polynomial.div
slogan: Polynomial.div computes the quotient when dividing one polynomial by another over a field, requiring the divisor to be monic (leading coefficient 1). It returns a polynomial result such that the original polynomial equals the quotient times the divisor plus a remainder, where the remainder has a smaller degree than the divisor or is zero. This operation uses the algebraic structure of polynomials and the field properties of the coefficients to ensure correct division.

label: Polynomial.div_modByMonic_unique
slogan: When dividing a polynomial f by a monic polynomial g, there is only one correct quotient q and remainder r such that f = g * q + r and the degree of r is less than the degree of g.

label: Polynomial.div_tendsto_atTop_leadingCoeff_div_of_degree_eq
slogan: As x approaches infinity, the ratio of two polynomials of the same degree evaluated at x approaches the ratio of their leading coefficients.

label: Polynomial.dvd_iff_isRoot
slogan: A polynomial has (x - a) as a factor if and only if substituting a into the polynomial gives zero. This means the polynomial is divisible by (x - a) exactly when a is a root. The result holds in any commutative ring.

label: Polynomial.eq_zero_of_degree_lt_of_eval_finset_eq_zero
slogan: If a polynomial with coefficients in an integral domain evaluates to zero at more points than its degree, then the polynomial must be the zero polynomial. Specifically, if a polynomial f vanishes on a finite set s of points and the degree of f is less than the number of points in s, then f is identically zero.

label: Polynomial.factorial_mul_shiftedLegendre_eq
slogan: The nth shifted Legendre polynomial multiplied by n factorial equals the nth derivative of the polynomial x^n * (1 - x)^n. This formula gives a way to compute shifted Legendre polynomials using derivatives of a simple polynomial expression. It is similar to Rodrigues' formula used in classical orthogonal polynomial theory.

label: Polynomial.funext
slogan: If two polynomials with coefficients in an infinite integral domain produce the same value when evaluated at every point in that domain, then the polynomials are exactly the same.

label: Polynomial.fwdDiff_iter_degree_eq_factorial
slogan: Applying the forward difference operator repeatedly to a polynomial, using step size 1 and iterating as many times as the polynomial's degree, results in a constant function whose value is the leading coefficient of the polynomial multiplied by the factorial of its degree.

label: Polynomial.hermite
slogan: Polynomial.hermite is a function that takes a natural number n and returns the n-th probabilist's Hermite polynomial, expressed as a polynomial with integer coefficients. These polynomials are defined recursively and involve derivatives and multiplication by X, using standard polynomial operations over the integers. The result is always an element of the polynomial ring with integer coefficients.

label: Polynomial.hermite_eq_deriv_gaussian
slogan: The nth Hermite polynomial evaluated at a real number x equals (-1)^n times the nth derivative of the function exp(-y^2 / 2), evaluated at y = x, divided by exp(-x^2 / 2). This relates Hermite polynomials to repeated derivatives of the Gaussian function. The formula shows how the polynomial arises from differentiating a Gaussian and normalizing by the Gaussian itself.

label: Polynomial.instEuclideanDomain
slogan: Polynomials with coefficients in a field can be divided to give a quotient and a remainder, where the remainder is either zero or has a smaller degree than the divisor. This division works because the degree of a polynomial acts as a size measure, using a special value for the zero polynomial that behaves like negative infinity. The setup ensures that polynomial arithmetic follows predictable rules, including unique factorization and standard operations like addition and multiplication.

label: Polynomial.instMul
slogan: Polynomial.instMul provides a way to multiply two polynomials by combining their coefficients using the underlying semiring's addition and multiplication, following the standard rules of polynomial multiplication. It ensures that the product of two polynomials is another polynomial with finitely many nonzero terms. This allows the use of the * operator for polynomials in a way that matches familiar algebraic expressions.

label: Polynomial.irreducible_of_eisenstein_criterion
slogan: A polynomial with coefficients in a commutative ring that is an integral domain is irreducible if there is a prime ideal such that the prime divides all coefficients except the leading one, does not divide the leading coefficient, and the square of the prime does not divide the constant term, provided the polynomial is primitive and has positive degree.

label: Polynomial.isEquivalent_atTop_lead
slogan: For large values of x, the polynomial behaves like its leading term, meaning the polynomial's value is approximately the leading coefficient multiplied by x raised to the degree of the polynomial.

label: Polynomial.isNoetherianRing
slogan: If a commutative ring has the property that all its ideals are finitely generated, then the ring of polynomials over that ring also has the same property—every ideal in the polynomial ring is finitely generated.

label: Polynomial.leadingCoeff
slogan: The leading coefficient of a polynomial is the number multiplying the highest power of the variable that has a non-zero coefficient; if all coefficients are zero, the leading coefficient is zero. It is found by evaluating the polynomial's coefficient function at the position given by its natural degree. This value belongs to the same semiring as the polynomial's coefficients.

label: Polynomial.modByMonic_X_sub_C_eq_C_eval
slogan: When you divide a polynomial p by (X - a), the remainder is the constant polynomial whose value is p evaluated at a. This works for polynomials over any commutative ring. The theorem links polynomial division by linear terms directly to function evaluation.

label: Polynomial.modByMonic_add_div
slogan: When you divide a polynomial p by a monic polynomial q, the remainder plus the quotient times q equals the original polynomial p. This means p can be written as (p /ₘ q) * q + (p %ₘ q). The result holds for polynomials over any ring.

label: Polynomial.mod_X_sub_C_eq_C_eval
slogan: When you divide a polynomial p by (X - a), the remainder is the constant polynomial whose value is p evaluated at a. This means plugging a into the polynomial gives the same result as the remainder of the division. The rule works for polynomials over any field because (X - a) is monic and division by monic polynomials behaves well.

label: Polynomial.natDegree_eq_one
slogan: A polynomial has degree 1 if and only if it can be written as a * X + b, where a and b are elements of the coefficient ring, and a is not zero. This means the polynomial is linear with a nonzero leading coefficient.

label: Polynomial.one_lt_rootMultiplicity_iff_isRoot
slogan: A root of a polynomial has multiplicity greater than one if and only if the polynomial and its derivative both evaluate to zero at that root. This means the root is shared between the polynomial and its first derivative. The result holds for nonzero polynomials over a field.

label: Polynomial.quadratic_dvd_of_aeval_eq_zero_im_ne_zero
slogan: If a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root that is not a real number, then the polynomial is divisible by the quadratic polynomial x^2 - 2*Re(z)*x + |z|^2, where z is the complex root.

label: Polynomial.resultant
slogan: The resultant of two polynomials is calculated as the determinant of their Sylvester matrix, which is built from the coefficients of the polynomials and used to check if they have a common root. It is defined over a commutative ring, using the natural degrees of the polynomials by default, and may accept optional degree parameters. The matrix is constructed using finite index types like Fin, and the determinant is computed using standard properties of permutations and signs.

label: Polynomial.ringKrullDim_le
slogan: The Krull dimension of the polynomial ring over a commutative ring R is at most twice the Krull dimension of R plus one. This means that the length of the longest chain of prime ideals in the polynomial ring R[x] does not exceed 2 * dim(R) + 1.

label: Polynomial.ringKrullDim_of_isNoetherianRing
slogan: If a commutative ring R is Noetherian, then the Krull dimension of the polynomial ring R[X] is exactly one more than the Krull dimension of R.

label: Polynomial.rootMultiplicity
slogan: The root multiplicity of a polynomial p at a value a is the highest number n such that (x - a)^n divides p, found by checking successive powers until one no longer divides p. If p is zero at a, the multiplicity is zero. This works because division by (x - a) is decidable when the polynomial ring has decidable equality.

label: Polynomial.rootSet_derivative_subset_convexHull_rootSet
slogan: If a polynomial has complex coefficients and is not constant, then all of its derivative's roots lie within the convex hull of the original polynomial's roots. This means every root of the derivative can be expressed as a weighted average of the roots of the polynomial. The result holds for nonconstant polynomials over the complex numbers.

label: Polynomial.roots_countP_pos_le_signVariations
slogan: The number of positive roots of a polynomial with coefficients in an ordered ring is less than or equal to the number of sign changes in the sequence of its nonzero coefficients. Each root is counted as many times as its multiplicity. This result is known as Descartes' Rule of Signs.

label: Polynomial.shiftedLegendre
slogan: shiftedLegendre n is a polynomial with integer coefficients, defined for each natural number n as the sum from k = 0 to n of (-1)^k times (n choose k) times (n + k choose n) times x^k. It is used in combinatorics and the study of orthogonal polynomials. The result is always a polynomial in x with integer coefficients.

label: Polynomial.sum_range_pow_eq_bernoulli_sub
slogan: For natural numbers n and p, the sum of k^p for k from 0 to n-1, multiplied by (p+1), equals the value of the (p+1)-th Bernoulli polynomial evaluated at n, minus the (p+1)-th Bernoulli number.

label: Polynomial.sylvester
slogan: Polynomial.sylvester takes two polynomials f and g with coefficients in a semiring R and positive integers m and n, then constructs an (m+n) by (m+n) matrix whose entries are coefficients of f and g arranged in a block pattern: the first n rows contain shifted copies of f's coefficients, and the last m rows contain shifted copies of g's coefficients. The determinant of this matrix gives the resultant, which is zero if and only if the two polynomials have a common root. This matrix is built using index arithmetic on finite sets and relies on standard polynomial coefficient extraction.

label: Polynomial.uniqueFactorizationMonoid
slogan: Polynomials with coefficients in a commutative ring that already has unique factorization also form a unique factorization structure, meaning every such polynomial can be broken down into irreducible factors in a way that is essentially unique. This guarantees that factorizations are finite and well-behaved, similar to how integers factor uniquely into primes. The result relies on the polynomial ring having properties like well-founded divisibility and greatest common divisors.

label: Polynomial.wronskian
slogan: The Wronskian of two polynomials a and b is defined as the polynomial ab' - a'b, where a' and b' are the derivatives of a and b respectively. It is computed using standard polynomial multiplication and subtraction. This operation takes two polynomials over a commutative ring and returns another polynomial over the same ring.

label: PontryaginDual
slogan: The Pontryagin dual of a monoid A with a topology is the set of all continuous functions from A to the unit circle (complex numbers of size 1) that also preserve the multiplicative structure. These functions form a group under pointwise multiplication. The dual inherits a natural topology from the compact-open setup, though that detail is not stated in the definition itself.

label: PositiveLinearMap
slogan: A PositiveLinearMap is a function between two ordered modules that acts like a linear map—preserving addition, scalar multiplication, and zero—while also sending elements that are greater than or equal to zero to elements that are likewise non-negative. It respects both the algebraic operations and the order structure of the spaces it maps between. This means if one element is at least as large as another in the input space, the same relationship holds for their outputs.

label: PositiveLinearMap.GNS
slogan: Given a positive linear functional on a non-unital C*-algebra, the GNS construction produces a Hilbert space by completing a pre-inner product space derived from the functional. This space is built by first defining a sesquilinear form on the algebra and then taking the completion of the resulting quotient space. The output is a complete inner product space where the algebra acts via bounded operators.

label: PositiveLinearMap.gnsStarAlgHom
slogan: Given a positive linear functional f on a unital C*-algebra A, this construction produces a unital star-homomorphism from A into the algebra of bounded operators on the Hilbert space obtained via the GNS construction for f.

label: PowerSeries.coeff
slogan: PowerSeries.coeff extracts the coefficient of x^n from a power series over a semiring R, returning the element of R that multiplies the nth power of the variable. It treats the power series as a function from natural numbers to R, where each input n maps to the corresponding coefficient. This function is linear, meaning it preserves addition and scalar multiplication.

label: PowerSeries.coeff_mul
slogan: The coefficient of the product of two power series at index n is the sum of products of coefficients from each series, where the indices of the multiplied terms add up to n. This sum is taken over all pairs of natural numbers that sum to n, ensuring a well-defined result. Each term in the sum comes from one term in the first series and one in the second, whose degrees combine to match the target index.

label: PowerSeries.exp_unique_of_derivative_eq_self
slogan: If a power series has a derivative equal to itself and its constant term is 1, then it must be the exponential power series, where each coefficient is 1/n!. The conditions uniquely determine all coefficients through a recursive relation. This holds in any commutative ring with scalar multiplication by rational numbers and no additive torsion.

label: PowerSeries.inv
slogan: The inverse of a power series over a field is another power series that, when multiplied by the original, gives the constant series 1; this inverse exists only if the constant term of the original series is nonzero. The function computes this inverse formally, using the fact that nonzero elements in a field have reciprocals. It is defined recursively, relying on the invertibility of the constant coefficient.

label: PowerSeries.order
slogan: The order of a power series is the highest natural number n such that the series is divisible by X^n, represented as a value in the extended natural numbers (including infinity). If the series is zero, its order is infinity; otherwise, it is the smallest n where the coefficient of X^n is nonzero.

label: PreInnerProductSpace.Core
slogan: A PreInnerProductSpace.Core is a framework for spaces where vectors can be added and scaled by numbers from a real-like system, and an inner product operation lets you compute a scalar value representing angles and lengths, following rules like linearity and symmetry. It requires the space to support addition with inverses, scalar multiplication, and a base type that behaves like the real numbers. This structure forms the foundation for defining geometric concepts in vector spaces.

label: PreirreducibleSpace.preconnectedSpace
slogan: A preirrereducible space is one where any two nonempty open sets must overlap, and this implies the space is preconnected, meaning it cannot be divided into two disjoint nonempty open sets. The entire space remains in one piece under the topology. This result follows from the fact that overlapping open sets prevent any clean separation.

label: Preord
slogan: Preord is a type of structures for sets with a reflexive and transitive "less than or equal to" relation, allowing for order-like behavior without requiring that a ≤ b and b ≤ a imply a = b. It is used to define the category of preorders, where maps between objects preserve the preorder. Each Preord lives in a higher universe level due to its type structure.

label: Preorder.smallCategory
slogan: For any type with a preorder, you can form a small category where the objects are elements of the type and there is exactly one morphism from a to b if a ≤ b, and none otherwise; the category is small because both objects and morphisms form sets.

label: PresentedGroup
slogan: PresentedGroup takes a set of generators and a set of relations between words formed from those generators, then constructs a group by starting with all possible combinations of generators and their inverses (the free group) and imposing the given relations as equalities. It does this by forming a quotient of the free group by the smallest normal subgroup containing the relations. The result is a group where the specified relations hold among the generators.

label: PresentedGroup.equivPresentedGroup
slogan: If two sets of generators are in bijection and the corresponding free groups have related relations via that bijection, then the groups presented by those generators and relations are isomorphic. Specifically, applying a bijection between generator sets transforms the relations in a way that preserves the structure of the presented group. The resulting groups are isomorphic through a map induced by the generator bijection.

label: PresentedMonoid
slogan: PresentedMonoid creates a new monoid from a set of generators (elements of type α) and a set of relations between words (lists) built from those generators, by taking the free monoid on α and quotienting it by the smallest congruence relation that includes the given relations. This means it forms a monoid where the specified relations hold, and all monoid operations respect those equalities. The result is a monoid defined by generators and the equations they satisfy.

label: Prime
slogan: A prime element in a commutative monoid with zero is a non-unit element that, whenever it divides a product of two elements, it must divide at least one of them.

label: PrimeSpectrum.compactSpace
slogan: The prime spectrum of a commutative semiring, with the Zariski topology, is compact, meaning every open cover has a finite subcover. This is because any collection of closed sets with the finite intersection property (every finite subcollection has nonempty intersection) also has nonempty total intersection. The key algebraic reason is that if the unit ideal is contained in a join of ideals, it is already contained in a finite subjoin.

label: PrimeSpectrum.isIrreducible_iff_vanishingIdeal_isPrime
slogan: A subset of the prime spectrum is irreducible in the Zariski topology if and only if its vanishing ideal is a prime ideal. This means the set cannot be written as the union of two smaller nonempty closed sets exactly when the ideal it defines has the property that whenever a product of two elements is in the ideal, at least one of the elements must already be in it. The result connects a topological property (irreducibility) with an algebraic property (primeness of ideals).

label: PrimeSpectrum.isIrreducible_zeroLocus_iff
slogan: A closed set in the prime spectrum of a commutative semiring is irreducible if and only if it is the set of all prime ideals that contain a fixed prime ideal. This happens exactly when the ideal defining the set, after taking its radical, is a prime ideal. The result connects the geometric idea of irreducibility with the algebraic condition of being prime.

label: PrimeSpectrum.zariskiTopology
slogan: The declaration sets up a topology on the set of prime ideals of a commutative ring by defining which collections of prime ideals are closed sets, where a closed set consists of all prime ideals that contain a fixed ideal. The closed sets are built using the rule that the zero locus of an ideal I is the set of prime ideals containing I, with the whole space closed (as primes containing the zero ideal) and the empty set closed (as primes containing the unit ideal). Finite unions and arbitrary intersections of such closed sets are also closed, forming the Zariski topology.

label: PrimeSpectrum.zeroLocus_vanishingIdeal_eq_closure
slogan: In the prime spectrum of a commutative ring, the set of prime ideals that contain all elements of a given ideal is exactly the same as the closure of the set of those prime ideals; this means taking the smallest closed set containing the prime ideals that include the ideal gives the same result as looking at where the ideal vanishes.

label: Primrec.nat_iterate
slogan: If f, g, and h are primitive recursive functions where f gives a number of iterations, g gives an initial value, and h updates the value at each step, then the function that applies h repeatedly f(a) times starting from g(a) is also primitive recursive.

label: Primrec.nat_le
slogan: The relation that checks whether one natural number is less than or equal to another is primitive recursive. This means there is an algorithm that can compute, in a basic and finite way, whether x ≤ y holds for any two natural numbers x and y. The result is given as a boolean value, and the function computing it uses only primitive recursive operations.

label: Primrec.nat_strong_rec
slogan: If a function f from α and natural numbers to σ can be defined such that each value f a n is computed by a primitive recursive function g that combines a and the list of prior values f a 0 through f a (n-1), then f itself is primitive recursive. The function g must be primitive recursive in both of its arguments and must correctly produce the next value in the sequence as long as all previous values have been computed. This allows defining functions recursively on natural numbers using primitive recursive operations.

label: Primrec.succ
slogan: The successor function, which adds one to any natural number, is primitive recursive, meaning it is part of the basic set of computable functions that can be built using simple rules like composition and recursion. This function is inherently computable within the formal system of primitive recursion.

label: PrimrecPred.and
slogan: If two predicates p and q on a type α are primitive recursive, meaning their truth values can be computed using basic arithmetic operations and primitive recursion after encoding inputs as natural numbers, then the predicate that checks whether both p and q are true for a given input is also primitive recursive. This is because the boolean AND of two computable truth values can itself be computed by a primitive recursive function. The result follows from the fact that the composition of primitive recursive functions, including the function for logical AND, remains primitive recursive.

label: PrimrecPred.or
slogan: If two predicates p and q on a type α are primitive recursive, meaning their truth can be decided by simple computable operations, then the predicate that checks whether p a or q a holds for any input a is also primitive recursive. This relies on the ability to encode elements of α as natural numbers and on the primitive recursiveness of the logical OR operation on boolean values.

label: PrimrecRel.comp
slogan: If a relation R between elements of types β and γ is primitive recursive, and functions f and g from type α to β and γ respectively are also primitive recursive, then the property of R holding between f(a) and g(a) for any a in α is itself a primitive recursive predicate on α. This means applying primitive recursive functions to inputs before checking a primitive recursive relation results in another primitive recursive condition.

label: PrincipalIdealRing.isMaximal_of_irreducible
slogan: In a principal ideal ring, if an element cannot be factored into non-unit elements, then the set of all its multiples forms an ideal that is maximal—meaning no other proper ideal contains it except the whole ring.

label: PrincipalIdealRing.to_uniqueFactorizationMonoid
slogan: Every principal ideal ring that is also a domain allows each nonzero non-unit element to be factored uniquely into irreducibles, up to order and units, because such rings are Noetherian and satisfy the conditions for unique factorization.

label: PrincipalSeg.ofElement
slogan: Given a type and a relation on it, along with an element of that type, PrincipalSeg.ofElement produces the set of all elements strictly less than the given element, restricted to those elements under the same relation, forming a principal initial segment as a subtype.

label: ProbabilityTheory.CondIndepFun
slogan: Two functions are conditionally independent given a sigma-algebra if the measurable structures they generate are conditionally independent with respect to that sigma-algebra and a given finite measure. The measurable structure generated by a function is formed by pulling back the target space's measurable sets. This definition uses the notation X ⟂ᵢ[Z, hZ; μ] Y to express that X and Y are conditionally independent given Z under measure μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.CondIndepSet
slogan: Two sets are conditionally independent given a sub-sigma-algebra if, almost everywhere, the conditional probability of their intersection equals the product of their individual conditional probabilities. This means that knowing whether one set occurs does not change the likelihood of the other, when conditioning on the given information. The definition applies to sets in a standard Borel space with a finite measure and a measurable structure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasGaussianLaw.iIndepFun_of_covariance_eq_zero
slogan: If a finite collection of real-valued random variables are jointly Gaussian and each pair has zero covariance, then the variables are independent.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasGaussianLaw.indepFun_of_covariance_eq_zero
slogan: If two random variables X and Y are jointly Gaussian and their covariance is zero, then X and Y are independent. This means that knowing the value of one variable gives no information about the other. Zero covariance implies independence in the special case of Gaussian distributions.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasIndepIncrements
slogan: A stochastic process X has independent increments if, for any increasing sequence of times t1 ≤ t2 ≤ ... ≤ tn, the differences between successive values of X (like X(t2) - X(t1), X(t3) - X(t2), etc.) are independent random variables. This means the change in the process over non-overlapping time intervals does not influence each other. An alternative way to define this uses sequences that eventually stop changing, focusing on the independence of the increments at each step.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw
slogan: HasLaw X μ P means that the random variable X, mapping from a space Ω to a space 𝓧, has distribution μ when probabilities are computed using the measure P, which happens exactly when the pushforward of P by X equals μ; it also requires X to be almost everywhere measurable with respect to P. This condition ensures that X behaves well with respect to transformations and operations involving independent functions. The measure P is taken by default if not explicitly provided.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasSubgaussianMGF.measure_sum_ge_le_of_iIndepFun
slogan: If a finite collection of independent random variables each have sub-Gaussian moment-generating functions with certain parameters, then the probability that their sum exceeds a given non-negative value ε is bounded above by the exponential of minus ε squared divided by twice the sum of those parameters.

label: ProbabilityTheory.HasSubgaussianMGF.measure_sum_range_ge_le_of_iIndepFun
slogan: If you have a sequence of independent random variables, each with a sub-Gaussian moment-generating function bounded by a constant c, then the probability that their sum over n terms exceeds a value ε is at most exp(-ε² / (2 * n * c)). This bound decreases exponentially as ε increases, reflecting the concentration of the sum around zero. The result is a form of Hoeffding's inequality for sub-Gaussian variables.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IdentDistrib
slogan: Two functions are identically distributed if they map their respective measure spaces into the same distribution on a common measurable space, meaning the measures of the preimages of any measurable set are equal. This requires both functions to be almost everywhere measurable so that their image measures are well-defined. The definition compares functions across potentially different measure spaces using their induced measures.

label: ProbabilityTheory.Indep
slogan: Two sigma-algebras on the same space are independent with respect to a given measure if the probability of the intersection of any two measurable sets (one from each sigma-algebra) equals the product of their individual probabilities. This means the measure of the overlap between sets from the two structures factors into the product of their individual measures. Independence here captures the idea that the occurrence of events in one sigma-algebra does not affect the likelihood of events in the other.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun
slogan: Two functions are independent if the sigma-algebras they generate are independent with respect to a given measure; this means that the probability of events defined by one function does not affect the probability of events defined by the other. The generated sigma-algebra for a function is formed by pulling back the measurable sets of its codomain. Independence is denoted f ⟂ᵢ[μ] g, where μ is the measure on the underlying space.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.covariance_eq_zero
slogan: If two real-valued random variables are independent and each has a finite second moment (meaning their squares have finite expected values), then their covariance is zero. This means that independent random variables do not linearly influence each other on average.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.integral_mul_eq_mul_integral
slogan: If two independent functions are almost everywhere strongly measurable, then the integral of their product equals the product of their integrals. This holds for functions taking values in a real-like space and defined on a measure space. Independence means the functions do not influence each other's behavior probabilistically.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.map_add_eq_map_conv_map₀
slogan: If two independent, almost everywhere measurable functions f and g map from a probability space to a measurable additive monoid, then the distribution of their sum f + g is equal to the convolution of the distributions of f and g, provided the underlying measure is finite.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.map_mul_eq_map_mconv_map
slogan: If two measurable functions f and g from a probability space to a measurable monoid are independent, then the distribution of their product is the convolution of their individual distributions. This means the pushforward measure of the product function equals the convolution of the pushforward measures of f and g. The result holds when the underlying measure is finite and the monoid operation is measurable.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.pdf_add_eq_lconvolution_pdf
slogan: If two independent random variables X and Y have probability density functions with respect to a left-invariant measure μ on an additive group, then the density of their sum X + Y is equal almost everywhere to the left convolution of their individual densities with respect to μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.pdf_mul_eq_mlconvolution_pdf
slogan: If two independent random variables X and Y take values in a measurable group G and have probability density functions with respect to a left-invariant measure μ, then the density of their product X * Y is equal almost everywhere to the convolution of their individual densities with respect to μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.process_indepFun_process
slogan: Two stochastic processes are independent if, for any finite selection of indices, the random variables from the first process at those indices are independent of the random variables from the second process at any finite selection of its indices. This means the joint behavior of any finite parts of the two processes does not influence the other. The result holds under the assumption that the underlying measure is a probability measure or zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun.variance_sum
slogan: The variance of a sum of finitely many pairwise independent random variables equals the sum of their individual variances, provided each variable has finite second moment.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IndepSet
slogan: Two sets are independent if the probability of their intersection equals the product of their individual probabilities, based on the measurable sets they generate (like the empty set, the whole space, each set, and their complements). This definition relies on a given measure and the measurable space structure that treats each set and its complement as the basic measurable sets. Independence here means no influence between the occurrence of the two sets under the given probability measure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IsAEKolmogorovProcess
slogan: A stochastic process X is said to be almost everywhere a Kolmogorov process if it has a modification that satisfies the Kolmogorov continuity condition, meaning the process behaves like a continuous process almost surely under the given probability measure. This involves bounds on the p-th moment of increments of the process, controlled by a power q of the distance in the index set, up to a constant M. The property holds almost everywhere with respect to the measure P on the sample space.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IsGaussianProcess
slogan: A function X that maps time points and random outcomes to a real vector space is called a Gaussian process if, for any finite set of time points, the joint distribution of the values at those points follows a multivariate normal distribution. This means every finite collection of outputs behaves like a Gaussian random vector under the given probability measure. The setup requires the space of outcomes to be measurable, the vector space to support addition and scalar multiplication, and the process to be measurable and topological.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IsKolmogorovProcess
slogan: A stochastic process X mapping from an index set T and a probability space Ω to a space E satisfies the Kolmogorov condition if, for any two indices s and t, the distance between X(s) and X(t) raised to power p has an expected value bounded by a constant M times the distance between s and t raised to power q, and the pair (X(s), X(t)) is measurable with respect to the Borel sets of E×E.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IsMarkovKernel
slogan: A Markov kernel is a function that assigns to each point in one measurable space a probability measure on another measurable space, such that for every measurable set, the resulting function on the first space is measurable. Each measure it produces must assign total size 1 to the whole space, making it a probability measure. This ensures the kernel models probabilistic transitions where outcomes are uncertain but probabilities add up to 1.

label: ProbabilityTheory.IsUniform
slogan: The statement IsUniform H X μ means that the random variable X has a distribution which is uniformly spread over the set H, so every point in H has equal probability under the measure μ. It does not require H to be finite or non-empty, or X to be measurable, though in typical use those conditions would hold. The definition works even if H is infinite, in which case the statement would simply be false.

label: ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.Invariant
slogan: A measure μ is invariant under a kernel κ if applying κ to μ and then taking the resulting measure gives back μ itself. In other words, the distribution μ remains unchanged after being transformed by the kernel κ. This means that for every measurable set, the expected measure after one step according to κ is the same as the original measure under μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.IsIrreducible
slogan: A kernel κ from a space α to itself is called φ-irreducible if, for any point a in α and any measurable set A that has positive measure under φ, there is some number of steps n such that starting from a, the n-step transition probability given by κ^n assigns positive probability to reaching A. This means the process described by the kernel can eventually get to any sufficiently large part of the space, given enough steps.

label: ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.IsReversible
slogan: A Markov kernel κ is reversible with respect to a measure π if, for any two measurable sets A and B, the total probability mass moving from A to B under κ weighted by π equals the mass moving from B to A. This means the process looks the same forwards and backwards in time when started according to π. Reversibility captures a kind of symmetry in the transition behavior of the system.

label: ProbabilityTheory.ae_eq_integral_of_variance_eq_zero
slogan: If a random variable has zero variance, then it is almost surely equal to its expected value. This means the variable takes on a single constant value with probability one. The result assumes the variable is square-integrable and the measure is finite.

label: ProbabilityTheory.analyticOn_complexMGF
slogan: The complex moment-generating function of a real-valued random variable is analytic at all points in the complex plane where the real part lies within the interior of the set of values for which the exponential of the variable is integrable. This means the function can be expressed as a convergent power series around each such point. The region of analyticity forms a vertical strip in the complex plane determined by the integrability of exp(t * X) with respect to the given measure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.bayesRisk
slogan: The Bayes risk is the smallest possible average loss achievable by any estimator, when averaging over all possible parameter values and data outcomes using a given prior distribution and data-generating process. It is computed as the infimum of the average risks across all estimators, where average risk combines the loss function, the probability kernel for data given parameters, and the prior measure on parameters. The result is a single extended nonnegative real number representing the best possible expected performance.

label: ProbabilityTheory.beta
slogan: The beta function takes two real numbers, alpha and beta, and returns a real number that acts as the normalizing constant for the beta distribution. It is defined using the gamma function, where beta(alpha, beta) equals gamma(alpha) times gamma(beta) divided by gamma(alpha + beta). This ensures the total area under the beta distribution curve is 1.

label: ProbabilityTheory.betaPDF
slogan: The betaPDF function returns the value of the beta distribution's probability density at a point x, using shape parameters alpha and beta, with the result as a nonnegative real number or infinity. It is defined as (1 / B(α,β)) * x^(α-1) * (1-x)^(β-1) when x is between 0 and 1, and zero otherwise, where B(α,β) is the beta function. The output is expressed in extended nonnegative reals, meaning it can include positive infinity but not negative values.

label: ProbabilityTheory.betaPDFReal
slogan: The betaPDFReal function calculates the probability density at a point x for a beta distribution with shape parameters alpha and beta. It returns (1 / beta(alpha, beta)) * x^(alpha - 1) * (1 - x)^(beta - 1) if x is between 0 and 1, and 0 otherwise. The beta function in the denominator ensures the total area under the curve is 1.

label: ProbabilityTheory.binomial
slogan: The binomial distribution with parameters n and p is a probability measure on the natural numbers that gives the likelihood of getting each possible number of successes in n independent trials, where each trial has success probability p. It is defined using the measure theory framework, where probabilities are assigned to sets of outcomes in a mathematically rigorous way. The parameter p is restricted to be between 0 and 1, inclusive.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cauchyPDFReal
slogan: The cauchyPDFReal function returns the value of the Cauchy probability density function at a point x, given a location parameter x₀ and a scale parameter γ, using the formula 1 / (π * γ * (1 + ((x - x₀) / γ)²)). The parameters x₀ and x are real numbers, and γ is a non-negative real number. This function describes the shape of the Cauchy distribution's probability curve.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cdf
slogan: The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of a probability measure on the real numbers is a function that, for each real number x, gives the measure of the set of all values less than or equal to x. It is defined as a Stieltjes function, meaning it is increasing and right-continuous. For a probability measure μ, the value of the cdf at x equals the measure of the interval (-∞, x].

label: ProbabilityTheory.cdf_expMeasure_eq
slogan: The cumulative distribution function of the exponential distribution with rate r > 0 is 1 - exp(-r * x) when x is non-negative, and 0 otherwise.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cdf_gammaMeasure_eq_integral
slogan: The cumulative distribution function of the gamma distribution with shape parameter a and rate parameter r at a point x equals the integral of the gamma probability density function from negative infinity up to x. This holds for positive values of a and r, and the integral is taken over the interval of all real numbers less than or equal to x.

label: ProbabilityTheory.centralMoment
slogan: The central moment of a real-valued random variable X of order p is the expected value of (X minus its mean) raised to the power p, computed with respect to a given probability measure. It measures the average deviation of the random variable from its mean, raised to a power, and is used to describe the shape of the distribution. This quantity is defined using integration with respect to a measure on a measurable space.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cgf
slogan: The cumulant-generating function of a real random variable X is defined as the natural logarithm of the expected value of exp(t*X), where t is a real number and the expectation is taken with respect to a given measure. It is only defined when the expected value of exp(t*X) is positive. This function is closely related to the moment-generating function, but uses the logarithm to transform it.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cgf_gaussianReal
slogan: The cumulant-generating function of a normally distributed real random variable with mean μ and variance v is the function that maps each real number t to μ times t plus half of v times t squared. This function is the natural logarithm of the moment-generating function of the Gaussian distribution.

label: ProbabilityTheory.charFun_gaussianReal
slogan: The characteristic function of a Gaussian distribution with mean mu and variance v is the function that maps a real number t to the complex exponential of (t times mu times i minus v times t squared over 2), where i is the imaginary unit.

label: ProbabilityTheory.compProd_posterior_eq_map_swap
slogan: When you combine a measure μ on a space Ω and a kernel κ that gives a measure on 𝓧 for each point in Ω, the joint distribution on Ω × 𝓧 can be reversed by using the posterior kernel: the result of first sampling from μ and then from κ, and swapping the order of the outcomes, is the same as mapping the swapped pairs through the joint distribution defined by μ and κ. This means the posterior kernel effectively encodes the conditional distribution of the original input given the output, in a way that matches the reversed joint distribution.

label: ProbabilityTheory.complexMGF
slogan: The complexMGF function takes a real-valued random variable X, a measure μ representing the probability distribution, and a complex number z, then computes the expected value of the complex exponential of z times X. This is done by integrating exp(z * X) with respect to the measure μ over the sample space. It extends the concept of the moment-generating function to complex arguments.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cond
slogan: The conditional probability of an event A given event B is calculated by dividing the probability of A and B both happening by the probability of B, but only when the probability of B is not zero. This is done using a measure that is limited to the outcomes where B occurs, and then scaled appropriately. The result is a new measure that represents how likely events are under the condition that B has happened.

label: ProbabilityTheory.condDistrib
slogan: condDistrib Y X μ is a function that, for almost every value of X, gives a probability measure describing the distribution of Y given that X has that value, and it satisfies the property that integrating a function against this conditional distribution gives the same result as the conditional expectation of that function given X.

label: ProbabilityTheory.condExpKernel
slogan: The condExpKernel is a function that, for each point in a space, gives a probability measure describing how the conditional expectation behaves given a sub-sigma-algebra. It ensures that integrating a function against this measure at a point equals the conditional expectation of the function almost everywhere. This kernel is built using a conditional distribution and adjusted via a measurable transformation to align with the right sigma-algebra structure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.condExp_ae_eq_integral_condExpKernel
slogan: The conditional expectation of a function f with respect to a sigma-algebra m is almost everywhere equal to the integral of f with respect to a special probability measure that depends on each point and is associated with m. This probability measure is given by the condExpKernel, which encodes how expectations condition on the smaller sigma-algebra. The equality holds almost everywhere with respect to the original measure mu.

label: ProbabilityTheory.condVar_ae_eq_condExp_sq_sub_sq_condExp
slogan: The conditional variance of a real-valued function X with respect to a sub-sigma-algebra m and measure μ is almost everywhere equal to the conditional expectation of X squared minus the square of the conditional expectation of X, where all conditional expectations are taken with respect to μ and m. This holds when m is a sub-sigma-algebra of the original measurable space, μ is a finite measure, and X is square-integrable. The equality holds except possibly on a set of measure zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cond_apply
slogan: The conditional probability of event t given event s is found by dividing the probability of both s and t occurring by the probability of s, as long as s has nonzero probability. This is done by restricting the measure to outcomes in s and scaling so that the total measure of s becomes 1. The result gives the likelihood of t within the context where only outcomes in s are considered.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cond_eq_inv_mul_cond_mul
slogan: If the probability of event s is not zero, then the conditional probability of t given s equals the probability of the intersection of s and t divided by the probability of s, which can be rewritten as the inverse of the probability of s multiplied by the probability of the intersection. This relationship holds when both events are measurable and the measure of the whole space is finite. It formally links conditional probability with joint probability using basic arithmetic on non-negative real numbers.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cond_eq_zero
slogan: If the probability of an event s is zero or infinite, then the conditional probability measure given s is the zero measure, meaning no event can have positive probability when conditioned on s. This reflects the idea that conditioning on an impossible or negligible event leads to a degenerate probability measure. The result holds because restricting a measure to a set of measure zero yields the zero measure, and scaling by infinity does not change that outcome.

label: ProbabilityTheory.cond_isProbabilityMeasure
slogan: If you start with a probability measure and condition on a measurable set that has positive, finite measure, the resulting conditional probability is also a probability measure, meaning it assigns total measure 1 to the whole space and follows the standard rules of probability.

label: ProbabilityTheory.covariance
slogan: The covariance of two real-valued random variables X and Y is defined as the expected value of the product of their deviations from their respective means, computed as an integral with respect to a given probability measure. It measures how much the variables change together on average. The result is a real number that can be positive, negative, or zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.covarianceBilin
slogan: The covarianceBilin function takes a probability measure on a real inner product space and returns a continuous bilinear form that computes the covariance between vectors, defined as the expected value of the inner products of deviations from the mean. It generalizes the concept of covariance to infinite-dimensional spaces in a way that respects the topology and linear structure. If the second moment is not finite, the covariance is set to zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.covarianceBilin_comm
slogan: The covariance of two vectors with respect to a given probability measure on a real inner product space is symmetric, meaning the order of the vectors does not affect the result. This symmetry holds for the bilinear form defined by the expected inner product of deviations from the mean. If the second moments are not finite, the covariance is taken to be zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.covarianceBilin_map
slogan: The covariance of two vectors with respect to the pushforward of a finite measure under a continuous linear map equals the covariance of their preimages under the adjoint of that map, computed with respect to the original measure, provided the identity function is square-integrable. This result relates how linear transformations affect the covariance structure of a probability measure on inner product spaces. It holds in complete, second-countable real inner product spaces with Borel measures.

label: ProbabilityTheory.covariance_eq_sub
slogan: The covariance of two real-valued random variables X and Y with respect to a probability measure μ is equal to the integral of their product minus the product of their individual integrals, all with respect to μ. This formula holds when both X and Y are square-integrable, meaning their squares have finite integrals under μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.exp_cgf
slogan: The exponential of the cumulant-generating function of a random variable X at a point t is equal to the moment-generating function of X at t, provided the exponential of t times X is integrable and the measure is nonzero. This means the moment-generating function can be expressed as the exponential of the logarithm of the expected value of exp(t*X).

label: ProbabilityTheory.gammaPDFReal
slogan: The gammaPDFReal function computes the probability density at a point x for the gamma distribution with shape parameter a and rate parameter r, using real number arithmetic. It combines exponentiation, multiplication, division, and the gamma function to evaluate the density formula. The result is a real number representing the height of the probability density function at x.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianPDFReal
slogan: The gaussianPDFReal function returns the value of the Gaussian (normal) distribution's probability density at a point x, given a mean μ and a variance v, where v is a non-negative real number. It computes this using the standard formula involving the square root of 2π times the variance, the exponential of negative (x minus μ) squared over twice the variance, and basic real number operations like division and multiplication. The constants pi and the exponential function are defined as usual in real arithmetic.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal
slogan: The gaussianReal function creates a probability measure on the real numbers that represents a normal (Gaussian) distribution with a given mean μ and variance v, where v is non-negative. This measure assigns probabilities to intervals on the real line according to the Gaussian probability density function.
