It is constructed by taking the standard Lebesgue measure on the reals and reweighting it using the Gaussian density function.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_add_gaussianReal_of_indepFun
slogan: If two independent random variables each follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution with means m1 and m2 and variances v1 and v2, then their sum is also normally distributed with mean m1 + m2 and variance v1 + v2.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_const_mul
slogan: If a random variable X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance v, then multiplying X by a constant c results in a new random variable that follows a normal distribution with mean c*μ and variance c^2*v.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_div_const
slogan: If a real random variable X follows a Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance v, then dividing X by a constant c results in a new random variable that follows a Gaussian distribution with mean μ/c and variance v/c².

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_map_continuousLinearMap
slogan: Applying a continuous linear function L to a Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance v results in a new Gaussian distribution whose mean is L(μ) and whose variance is (L(1))² times v.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_map_linearMap
slogan: Applying a linear function L to a Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance v results in a new Gaussian distribution whose mean is L(μ) and whose variance is (L(1))² times v.

label: ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal_zero_var
slogan: A Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance 0 is equal to the Dirac measure at μ, meaning all the probability is concentrated at the single point μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.hasSubgaussianMGF_of_mem_Icc_of_integral_eq_zero
slogan: If a random variable X has average value zero and is almost surely between two real numbers a and b, then its moment-generating function is bounded by that of a sub-Gaussian random variable with parameter ((b - a)/2)^2. This means the probability that X takes large values decreases at least as fast as a Gaussian distribution with that variance. The result holds under a probability measure and requires X to be measurable and integrable.

label: ProbabilityTheory.iIndep
slogan: A collection of sigma-algebras indexed by a type is independent with respect to a measure if, for any finite number of indices, the measure of the intersection of measurable sets from each sigma-algebra equals the product of their individual measures. This means that the occurrence of events in different sigma-algebras does not affect each other probabilistically. The definition formalizes the standard notion of independence of multiple sigma-algebras under a given probability measure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.iIndepFun.hasGaussianLaw
slogan: If a finite family of random variables are independent and each has a Gaussian distribution, then the entire family together has a joint Gaussian distribution.

label: ProbabilityTheory.indepFun_iff_map_prod_eq_prod_map_map
slogan: Two functions f and g are independent with respect to a finite measure μ if and only if the distribution of the pair (f(ω), g(ω)) is the same as the product of the distributions of f and g separately. This means that the joint behavior of f and g matches what you would expect if they had no influence on each other. The result holds when f and g are almost everywhere measurable.

label: ProbabilityTheory.indepSet_iff_measure_inter_eq_mul
slogan: Two measurable sets are independent with respect to a probability measure if and only if the probability of their intersection equals the product of their individual probabilities.

label: ProbabilityTheory.integrableExpSet
slogan: For a real-valued function X defined on a measure space with measure μ, the set integrableExpSet consists of all real numbers t such that the function exp(t * X) is integrable with respect to μ.

label: ProbabilityTheory.integral_condVar_add_variance_condExp
slogan: The total variance of a random variable is equal to the average of its conditional variance plus the variance of its conditional expectation, when working with a probability measure and square-integrable random variables.

label: ProbabilityTheory.isPosSemidef_covarianceBilin
slogan: The covariance bilinear form associated with a probability measure on a real inner product space is always positive semidefinite, meaning that the covariance of any vector with itself is non-negative. This reflects the fact that variance is never negative in probability theory. The result holds even in infinite-dimensional spaces under appropriate measurability and topological conditions.

label: ProbabilityTheory.isProjectiveLimit_map
slogan: The law of a stochastic process is the unique measure on the space of all paths such that, for any finite set of time points, the distribution of the process at those times matches the pushforward of this measure under the projection. This measure is the projective limit of the finite-dimensional distributions of the process. It exists and is consistent when the process is almost everywhere measurable with respect to the underlying probability measure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.isProjectiveMeasureFamily_map_restrict
slogan: The finite-dimensional distributions of a stochastic process form a consistent family of measures, meaning that the distribution on any larger finite set of time points pushes forward to the distribution on any smaller subset under the natural projection. This consistency holds when each component of the process is almost everywhere measurable with respect to the underlying probability measure. As a result, these distributions satisfy the conditions of a projective measure family.

label: ProbabilityTheory.iteratedDeriv_mgf
slogan: For any real number t inside the interval where the exponential of t times the random variable X is integrable, the n-th derivative of the moment-generating function of X at t equals the expected value of X raised to the power n times the exponential of t times X. This holds for natural numbers n and is expressed as an integral with respect to the measure μ. The result connects the derivatives of the moment-generating function directly to the moments of the random variable weighted by the exponential function.

label: ProbabilityTheory.meas_ge_le_variance_div_sq
slogan: The probability that a real-valued random variable deviates from its mean by at least a positive constant c is at most the variance of the variable divided by the square of c. This holds for random variables that are square-integrable with respect to a finite measure. The result is expressed using the extended nonnegative real numbers, with negative values clamped to zero.

label: ProbabilityTheory.measure_ge_le_exp_cgf
slogan: For a real random variable X and a threshold ε, the probability that X is at least ε is bounded above by the exponential of (-t*ε plus the cumulant-generating function of X at t), for any non-negative t where the moment-generating function exists. This bound is derived using exponential tail estimates and properties of integrable functions. It gives a way to control large deviation probabilities using the moment-generating behavior of X.

label: ProbabilityTheory.measure_ge_le_exp_mul_mgf
slogan: For a real random variable X and a probability measure mu, the probability that X is at least epsilon is bounded above by the exponential of -t times epsilon multiplied by the moment-generating function of X evaluated at t, provided t is non-negative and the exponential moment is finite. This gives an upper bound on tail probabilities using the moment-generating function. It is a general form of the Chernoff bound for the upper tail.

label: ProbabilityTheory.measure_zero_or_one_of_measurableSet_limsup_atTop
slogan: If a sequence of sigma-algebras is independent, then any event that belongs to the tail sigma-algebra (formed by taking the limit superior at infinity) has probability either 0 or 1. This means that tail events for independent processes are almost surely determined.

label: ProbabilityTheory.memLp_id_gaussianReal
slogan: All moments of a real Gaussian distribution are finite, meaning the identity function has a finite Lp norm for any finite p with respect to the Gaussian measure on the real line.

label: ProbabilityTheory.mgf
slogan: The moment-generating function of a real-valued random variable X is defined as the expected value of exp(t*X), where t is a real number and the expectation is taken with respect to a given probability measure. It maps each real t to the integral of exp(t*X) over the sample space. This function helps characterize the distribution of X through its moments.

label: ProbabilityTheory.mgf_gaussianReal
slogan: The moment-generating function of a real-valued random variable that follows a Gaussian (normal) distribution with mean μ and variance v is the function that maps each real number t to the exponential of (μ times t plus half of v times t squared). This means the expected value of exp(t*X) for such a random variable X is exp(μ*t + v*t^2/2).

label: ProbabilityTheory.moment
slogan: The moment of a real random variable X raised to a natural number power p is defined as the expected value of X^p with respect to a given probability measure μ. It is computed as the integral of (X(ω))^p over the sample space Ω with respect to the measure μ. This quantity captures the average magnitude of the random variable raised to the p-th power.

label: ProbabilityTheory.monotone_cdf
slogan: The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of a probability measure on the real numbers is an increasing function: if one number is less than or equal to another, then the probability of being less than or equal to the first is less than or equal to the probability of being less than or equal to the second.

label: ProbabilityTheory.setBernoulli
slogan: The setBernoulli function creates a probability measure on sets of elements where each element in a given set u is included independently with probability p, and elements not in u are never included. It models a product of independent Bernoulli trials restricted to a specific subset of the space. The measure assigns probabilities to subsets by multiplying the individual probabilities for each element in u.

label: ProbabilityTheory.strong_law_ae
slogan: If X n is a sequence of pairwise independent, identically distributed random variables with finite mean, taking values in a complete normed real vector space, then the average of the first n variables converges almost surely to the expected value of X 0 as n goes to infinity.

label: ProbabilityTheory.strong_law_ae_real
slogan: If X n is a sequence of pairwise independent, identically distributed, integrable real-valued random variables, then the average of the first n terms, (X 0 + X 1 + ... + X (n-1)) / n, converges almost surely to the expected value of X 0 as n goes to infinity.

label: ProbabilityTheory.sum_meas_smul_cond_fiber
slogan: The sum of the measure of each set where a measurable function takes a specific value, scaled by the conditional measure on that set, equals the original measure of the whole space when the function has finitely many values and the sets are disjoint. This identity holds because the preimages of the function values form a partition of the space, and the measure is additive over disjoint measurable sets. It connects weighted sums of restricted measures to the total measure under finite, measurable partitions.

label: ProbabilityTheory.tendstoInDistribution_inv_sqrt_mul_sum
slogan: If you have a sequence of independent, identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, then the scaled average (multiplied by 1 over the square root of n) converges in distribution to a standard normal (Gaussian) random variable as n goes to infinity.

label: ProbabilityTheory.tendstoInDistribution_inv_sqrt_mul_sum_sub
slogan: If you have a sequence of independent, identically distributed random variables with mean μ and finite variance v, then the scaled average (sqrt(n)⁻¹ times the sum of the first n variables minus n*μ) gets closer and closer in distribution to a normal random variable with mean 0 and variance v as n increases.

label: ProbabilityTheory.tendsto_charFun_inv_sqrt_mul_pow
slogan: As n grows large, the characteristic function of the scaled sum of n independent copies of a real-valued random variable X with mean 0 and variance 1, evaluated at t/sqrt(n), converges to the complex exponential of -t squared over 2, which is the characteristic function of a standard normal distribution.

label: ProbabilityTheory.tendsto_choose_mul_pow_of_tendsto_mul_atTop
slogan: If the product of n and p(n) approaches a real number r as n grows large, then the probability of getting exactly k successes in n Bernoulli trials with success probability p(n) approaches (exp(-r) * r^k) / k!. This describes how the binomial distribution converges to the Poisson distribution under certain conditions.

label: ProbabilityTheory.uniformOn
slogan: The uniformOn function creates a probability measure where every element in a finite, non-empty set has the same chance of being selected, and the total probability of the whole set is 1. It works only on measurable spaces and requires the set to have a finite number of elements. This measure is built by scaling the counting measure so that the sum of probabilities equals 1.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_add
slogan: The variance of the sum of two square-integrable random variables X and Y with respect to a finite measure is equal to the sum of their individual variances plus twice their covariance. This holds when both functions are measurable and their second moments are finite. The result expresses how the variability of the sum depends on both individual variations and their joint behavior.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_const_mul
slogan: The variance of a random variable scaled by a constant is equal to the variance of the original variable multiplied by the square of that constant. This means scaling a random variable by a factor increases its variance by the square of that factor.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_eq_sub
slogan: The variance of a real-valued random variable is equal to the expected value of its square minus the square of its expected value, with both integrals taken with respect to a probability measure. This holds for functions that are square-integrable, meaning the integral of the square of the function is finite. The result is a real number measuring how much the values of the function spread out from the mean.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_le_sq_of_bounded
slogan: If a random variable X takes values between a and b almost surely, then its variance is at most ((b - a)/2)^2. This means the spread of X cannot exceed a fixed bound determined by the interval [a, b]. The result holds for any probability space and measurable real-valued function X.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_nonneg
slogan: The variance of a real-valued random variable with respect to a given measure is always greater than or equal to zero. This means squared deviations from the mean, when averaged, cannot be negative. The result follows because variance is defined using a nonnegative integral and conversion from extended nonnegative reals to reals preserves nonnegativity.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_sub
slogan: The variance of the difference between two random variables X and Y is equal to the variance of X minus twice their covariance plus the variance of Y, provided both variables have finite second moments and the measure is finite.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_sum
slogan: The variance of the sum of a finite number of real-valued random variables is equal to the sum of all pairwise covariances between those variables, where each variable has a finite second moment with respect to a given finite measure.

label: ProbabilityTheory.variance_zero
slogan: The variance of the constant zero random variable is zero, regardless of the underlying probability space and measure. This follows because the expected value of zero is zero, and the average squared deviation from the mean is therefore zero. In plain terms, if a random variable always takes the value zero, it has no variability.

label: Prod
slogan: Prod is a type that represents pairs of values, where the first value has type α and the second has type β. It is written as α × β and can be nested to represent tuples with more than two elements. In code, the symbol × is typically spelled as Prod in names.

label: Prod.Lex.instIsWellFounded
slogan: If two relations are well-founded, then the lexicographic order on pairs formed by comparing the first components and then the second when the first are equal is also well-founded. This means recursive definitions and inductions over such pairs are valid. The result ensures that any decreasing sequence of pairs must eventually terminate.

label: Prod.Lex.instLinearOrder
slogan: If two types have a linear order, then pairs of elements from these types can be compared using dictionary-style (lexicographic) ordering, where the first elements are compared first, and the second elements are used to break ties, resulting in a total order on the pairs.

label: Prod.ext_iff
slogan: Two pairs are equal if and only if their first components are equal and their second components are equal.

label: Prod.instCommRing
slogan: If R and S are both commutative rings, then the set of pairs (r, s) where r is in R and s is in S forms a commutative ring by performing addition, subtraction, and multiplication separately on each component.

label: Prod.instGroup
slogan: If G and H are groups, then the set of pairs (g, h) where g is in G and h is in H forms a group by performing operations like multiplication and inversion on each component separately. The identity element is the pair of the identities from G and H, and the product of two pairs is obtained by multiplying their corresponding components. This group structure is defined directly on the Cartesian product type G × H.

label: Prod.instLattice
slogan: If two types each have a lattice structure (with operations for least upper bound and greatest lower bound), then the type of pairs from these two types also forms a lattice, where the operations are applied separately to each component of the pair.

label: Prod.instLieGroup
slogan: If two spaces each have a smooth structure and a group operation that fit together nicely (making them Lie groups), then their product space also has a smooth structure and a group operation defined component by component, and this product is also a Lie group. The smooth structure on the product comes from combining the individual smooth structures, and the group operation multiplies pairs element-wise. This works for spaces modeled over a normed field with appropriate topological and geometric properties.

label: Prod.instMonoid
slogan: If two types each have a multiplication and a unit element that satisfy the monoid properties, then the type of pairs formed from them also forms a monoid by multiplying each component separately and using the pair of units as the identity.

label: Prod.instPartialOrder
slogan: If two types each have a partial order, then pairs of elements from these types can be ordered by comparing both components separately: one pair is less than or equal to another if the first component is less than or equal in the first type and the second component is less than or equal in the second type. This defines a partial order on the product type using the existing partial orders on the individual types.

label: Prod.instRing
slogan: If two types each have a ring structure, then the set of pairs made from one element of each type also forms a ring, where operations like addition and multiplication are performed separately on each component of the pair.

label: Prod.metricSpaceMax
slogan: The Prod.metricSpaceMax declaration gives the product of two metric spaces a metric structure by defining the distance between two pairs as the maximum of the distances in each component. This makes the product space into a metric space where the topology matches the usual product topology. It relies on the fact that the max-based metric induces the same open sets as the product of the original topologies.

label: Prod.t2Space
slogan: If two topological spaces are Hausdorff (where distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets), then their product space with the product topology is also Hausdorff, meaning any two distinct pairs of points can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.

label: ProfiniteGrp
slogan: A ProfiniteGrp is a group with a topology that is compact, totally disconnected, and has a basis of clopen sets, meaning it can be expressed as an inverse limit of finite discrete groups. It combines algebraic group structure with a topological structure where group operations are continuous. Such groups commonly appear in Galois theory and number theory.

label: ProjectiveSpectrum
slogan: The projective spectrum of a graded commutative ring consists of all prime ideals that are homogeneous and do not contain the irrelevant ideal, which is the ideal generated by all elements of positive degree. It is constructed from a ring graded by the natural numbers, where each component is a submodule and multiplication respects the grading. This structure forms the basis for defining a topological space used in algebraic geometry.

label: ProjectiveSpectrum.vanishingIdeal
slogan: The vanishing ideal of a set t of points in the projective spectrum of a graded ring A is the set of all homogeneous elements of A that vanish (evaluate to zero) at every point in t, where each point is a homogeneous prime ideal; it is formed by taking the intersection of all such prime ideals in t. This ideal captures the algebraic functions that are zero across the entire set t.

label: ProjectiveSpectrum.zariskiTopology
slogan: The ProjectiveSpectrum.zariskiTopology defines a topology on the set of homogeneous prime ideals in a graded ring, where the closed sets are those ideals that contain a given set of homogeneous elements. This topology is constructed by specifying which subsets are closed, based on the vanishing of elements in the ring. It provides the foundation for studying geometric properties of projective algebraic varieties.

label: Projectivization
slogan: The projectivization of a vector space V over a division ring K is the set of all lines through the origin in V, where two nonzero vectors are considered the same if one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other. It is denoted ℙ K V and is formed by taking the nonzero vectors of V and identifying those that are related by scalar multiplication. This construction captures the idea of treating directions in the vector space as points in a new space, ignoring magnitude.

label: Projectivization.Subspace.span
slogan: The span of a set of points in projective space is the smallest projective subspace containing those points, formed by including all points that come from adding representative vectors and their scalar multiples. This subspace maintains the structure of the underlying vector space when projected into projective space. It is built by closing the set under vector addition and scalar multiplication, ensuring that sums of nonzero vectors that remain nonzero produce points in the subspace.

label: Projectivization.card_of_finrank
slogan: If V is a finite-dimensional vector space of dimension n over a finite field k, then the number of points in the projectivization of V is the sum of the powers of the size of k from k^0 up to k^(n-1).

label: Projectivization.equivSubmodule
slogan: The projectivization of a vector space V over a division ring K is equivalent to the set of all one-dimensional subspaces of V. Each point in the projectivization corresponds to a unique line through the origin in V. This equivalence matches each equivalence class of nonzero vectors under scalar multiplication with the subspace they span.

label: Projectivization.finite_of_finite
slogan: If a vector space V over a finite field k has only finitely many elements, then the projective space of V (denoted ℙ k V) also has finitely many elements.

label: Projectivization.generalLinearGroup_smul_def
slogan: When an invertible linear map acts on a projective space, the action is defined by applying the corresponding linear equivalence to the underlying vector space and then mapping the result into the projective space. This action sends each line through the origin to the line obtained by transforming it with the invertible map. The operation is well-defined because invertible linear maps preserve the structure of lines through the origin.

label: Projectivization.instMulAction
slogan: If a group acts linearly on a vector space V over a division ring K, then it also acts on the projective space of V, which consists of all lines through the origin in V. This action is well-defined because linear maps send lines through the origin to other such lines. The group action respects the structure of the projective space.

label: Projectivization.map
slogan: If there is an injective semilinear map between two vector spaces over division rings, then this map induces a well-defined function between their projective spaces, sending lines through the origin in one space to lines through the origin in the other.

label: Projectivization.mk
slogan: Given a nonzero vector v in a vector space V over a division ring K, Projectivization.mk produces the corresponding point in the projective space P(K,V) by identifying v with all its nonzero scalar multiples. This construction forms an element of the projectivization, which is the space of all lines through the origin in V.

label: Projectivization.rep
slogan: Given a point in the projectivization of a vector space over a division ring, Projectivization.rep selects a nonzero vector from the original vector space that represents this point, by picking a member of the equivalence class corresponding to it.

label: ProperCone.dual_dual_flip
slogan: The double dual of a proper cone, when using a continuous perfect pairing between two topological vector spaces, is equal to the original cone. This means that taking the dual of a proper cone twice returns the same cone you started with. The result holds in real locally convex spaces with appropriate continuity and algebraic structure.

label: ProperCone.hyperplane_separation
slogan: If a compact convex set K does not intersect a closed convex cone C that contains no lines through the origin, then there exists a continuous linear functional f such that f is nonnegative on C and strictly negative on every point of K. This means you can separate the cone and the set using a hyperplane defined by f. The result is a geometric form of Farkas' lemma and a stronger version of the Hahn-Banach separation theorem for cones.

label: ProperCone.hyperplane_separation_point
slogan: If a point is not in a closed, pointed cone in a locally convex topological vector space, then there exists a continuous linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone and negative at that point.

label: ProperSMul
slogan: A group action is proper if the map sending a pair (g, x) to the pair (x, g.x) is a proper map, meaning the preimage of a compact set is compact; this involves topological spaces and a continuous group action. The condition ensures the action behaves well with respect to convergence and compactness. It combines topology and algebra by requiring both the group and the space it acts on to be topological, with a compatible group structure and action.

label: ProperSpace
slogan: A proper space is a kind of space where distances are defined between points (with possible zero distance between different points), and every closed ball (the set of points within a fixed distance from a center) is compact. This means sequences in such balls have convergent subsequences, combining metric and strong topological behavior. It builds on the structure of a pseudometric space by adding compactness of closed balls.

label: PseudoMetricSpace
slogan: A PseudoMetricSpace is a set where every pair of points has a defined distance, distances are symmetric, and the triangle inequality holds, but two different points can be zero distance apart. It provides a topology, uniform structure, and notion of bounded sets all derived from the distance function. Unlike a full metric space, it does not require that distinct points have positive distance.

label: PythagoreanTriple
slogan: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three integers a, b, and c where a squared plus b squared equals c squared, using normal integer arithmetic.

label: PythagoreanTriple.IsPrimitiveClassified
slogan: A Pythagorean triple is primitive if the three integers have no common divisor larger than 1, and all such primitive triples can be uniquely generated using two coprime integers where one is even and the other is odd.

label: PythagoreanTriple.classification
slogan: Every Pythagorean triple of integers (x, y, z) that satisfies x^2 + y^2 = z^2 can be written as multiples of expressions involving two integers m and n, where x and y are k times (m^2 - n^2) and 2mn in some order, and z is plus or minus k times (m^2 + n^2), for some integer k, with m and n coprime and not both odd.

label: PythagoreanTriple.classified
slogan: All primitive Pythagorean triples (sets of three integers x, y, z such that x^2 + y^2 = z^2 and gcd(x, y, z) = 1) can be generated using two integers m and n where m > n, m and n are coprime, and one is even while the other is odd; the triple takes the form (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) up to the order of x and y.

label: PythagoreanTriple.coprime_classification
slogan: A Pythagorean triple of integers x, y, z satisfying x*x + y*y = z*z and having no common divisor greater than 1 can be written using two coprime integers m and n, one even and one odd with m > n > 0, such that the triple is (m*m - n*n, 2*m*n, m*m + n*n) or (2*m*n, m*m - n*n, m*m + n*n), up to signs and order.

label: PythagoreanTriple.even_odd_of_coprime
slogan: If a, b, and c are integers such that a^2 + b^2 = c^2 and the greatest common divisor of a and b is 1, then one of a or b must be even and the other must be odd.

label: PythagoreanTriple.isPrimitiveClassified_of_coprime
slogan: If three integers satisfy a^2 + b^2 = c^2 and the first two have no common divisor other than 1, then the triple is primitive and can be generated uniquely from two coprime integers where one is even and the other is odd.

label: PythagoreanTriple.mul
slogan: If three integers a, b and c satisfy a*a + b*b = c*c, then multiplying each of them by the same integer k gives another set of integers k*a, k*b and k*c that also satisfy (k*a)*(k*a) + (k*b)*(k*b) = (k*c)*(k*c).

label: PythagoreanTriple.normalize
slogan: Any primitive Pythagorean triple (a, b, c) where a^2 + b^2 = c^2 can be generated uniquely using two coprime integers m and n of opposite parity with m > n > 0, resulting in the triple (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) or (2mn, m^2 - n^2, m^2 + n^2). The given Lean theorem states that dividing each element of a Pythagorean triple by the greatest common divisor of the first two elements yields another Pythagorean triple, effectively reducing it to its simplest form.

label: QuadraticForm
slogan: A quadratic form is a function from a module over a commutative semiring to the semiring, satisfying specific algebraic properties related to scaling and addition. It generalizes the idea of expressions like x^2 or ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 in linear algebra. The structure requires the module to have a commutative addition with zero and the semiring to support multiplication and addition that behave nicely together.

label: QuadraticForm.equivalent_of_isAlgClosed
slogan: Over an algebraically closed field where 2 is invertible, any two nondegenerate quadratic forms on a finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent, meaning one can be transformed into the other by a change of basis. Nondegenerate means the associated bilinear form has no nontrivial kernel. This equivalence holds regardless of the specific form, as long as both are nondegenerate.

label: QuadraticForm.equivalent_weightedSumSquares_of_isAlgClosed
slogan: Over an algebraically closed field where 2 is invertible, any nondegenerate quadratic form can be transformed into a sum of squares through a change of basis. This means the quadratic form behaves like the standard sum of squared variables after applying a suitable linear isomorphism. The result holds for finite-dimensional vector spaces over such fields.

label: QuadraticMap
slogan: A QuadraticMap is a function between two modules over a commutative semiring that respects scalar multiplication by squaring the scalar and has an associated symmetric, bilinear polar form. It generalizes the idea of a quadratic form by allowing the target to be a module rather than the base ring. Such a map can be constructed using the polar form method when the underlying structure supports it.

label: QuadraticMap.Anisotropic
slogan: A quadratic map is called anisotropic if the only vector that maps to zero is the zero vector itself.

label: QuadraticMap.Equivalent
slogan: Two quadratic forms over a ring R are considered equivalent if there is a linear isomorphism between their domains that preserves the quadratic structure, meaning one form can be transformed into the other via this map. This relation depends on the existence of a bijective linear map that respects the underlying module and ring structures. The equivalence captures when two quadratic forms have the same algebraic shape up to a change of basis.

label: QuadraticMap.IsometryEquiv
slogan: An isometric equivalence between two quadratic spaces over a ring is a bijective linear map that preserves the quadratic forms, meaning the value of the form is unchanged when vectors are mapped from one space to the other. It requires the spaces to be modules over a commutative semiring, with addition and scalar multiplication respected by the map. The equivalence ensures the structure defined by the quadratic map is maintained in both directions.

label: QuadraticMap.polarBilin
slogan: Given a quadratic map Q between modules over a commutative ring, the function polarBilin produces a bilinear map that captures the symmetric interaction between two vectors, derived from the polarization of Q. This bilinear map is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed. It is constructed using the polar function associated with Q and satisfies both additivity and scalar multiplication properties in each argument.

label: Quandle
slogan: A quandle is a set with a binary operation x ◃ y that satisfies self-distributivity and has the property that each element is fixed by its own associated automorphism, meaning x ◃ x = x. It extends a rack by requiring this idempotent-like behavior. The operation still allows invertible actions, as in a rack.

label: QuasiErgodic.ae_empty_or_univ₀
slogan: For a quasi-ergodic transformation, any set that is almost invariant under the map must either have nearly zero measure or be nearly the entire space, when measured with respect to a given measure.

label: QuasiSober
slogan: A quasi-sober space is a topological space where every nonempty closed set that cannot be written as the union of two smaller closed sets has a point whose closure is exactly that set. This means each such closed set is the closure of some single point, called a generic point. The condition connects topological structure to geometric ideas common in algebraic geometry.

label: QuasispectrumRestricts.isSelfAdjoint
slogan: If a normal element in a C*-algebra has its complex quasispectrum contained in the real numbers, then the element is selfadjoint. This means that whenever such an element's spectral values are all real, the element equals its own adjoint. The condition is checked using the real part map on complex numbers as a continuous linear functional.

label: Quaternion
slogan: A quaternion is a four-dimensional number made up of one real part and three imaginary parts, defined for any type that has a zero, a one, and supports negation. It uses standard algebraic operations to enable arithmetic like addition and multiplication. The structure relies on basic building blocks: having a zero value, a unit value, and the ability to negate.

label: Quaternion.instInv
slogan: Quaternion.instInv provides a way to compute the inverse of a quaternion a using the notation a^-1, defined as the conjugate of a divided by the squared norm of a, for any quaternion over a field. This allows division by nonzero quaternions in algebraic computations. The instance ensures that the inverse notation works correctly when the underlying type supports field operations.

label: Quaternion.instStarRing
slogan: The quaternions over a commutative ring form a star ring, meaning they have a conjugation operation that flips the sign of the imaginary parts (i, j, k) while keeping the real part the same, and this operation works properly with addition and multiplication. This structure comes from the general star ring structure of quaternion algebras.

label: Quaternion.normSq
slogan: The normSq function takes a quaternion and returns the sum of the squares of its components, which is the same as multiplying the quaternion by its conjugate to get a real number. This result is always non-negative and equals the square of the quaternion's magnitude. For a real number treated as a quaternion, normSq gives the square of that number.

label: QuaternionAlgebra
slogan: The QuaternionAlgebra structure creates a four-dimensional algebra over a ring R using three imaginary units i, j, and k, where i^2 = a, j^2 = b, and ij = k = -ji for given elements a, b, c in R. It supports addition, multiplication, and scalar operations consistent with quaternion arithmetic. This allows quaternions to be defined and manipulated in a general algebraic context over any ring.

label: QuaternionGroup
slogan: The quaternion group QuaternionGroup n is a group of order 4n defined by two generators a and x, where a raised to 2n equals 1, x squared equals a to the n, and conjugating a by x gives the inverse of a. Elements of the group are written as a i for powers of a and xa i for x times a power of a. This group is defined for any natural number n.

label: Quiver
slogan: A quiver is a directed graph that allows multiple directed edges between the same pair of vertices and permits self-loops, with edges having a specific direction from one vertex to another. It generalizes a digraph by not limiting the number of edges between vertices. When a quiver is "thin," it means there is at most one edge from any vertex to another, making it similar to a standard directed graph.

label: Quiver.Arborescence
slogan: A quiver is called an arborescence if there is exactly one directed path from a fixed starting vertex to every other vertex in the graph. This means the structure resembles a tree with all edges pointing away from the root. The property depends on the quiver having a designated default vertex and unique paths to all others.

label: Quiver.IsThin
slogan: A quiver is thin if there is no more than one edge from any given vertex to any other vertex, meaning multiple edges between the same pair of vertices are not allowed. This makes the quiver behave like a simple directed graph.

label: Quiver.Path
slogan: A path in a quiver is a sequence of directed edges that connect a chain of vertices, where each edge points from one vertex to the next. It starts at a given vertex and follows edges in order to reach a final vertex. The type describes all possible paths from a starting vertex to any other vertex in the quiver.

label: Quiver.reverse
slogan: A quiver with a reverse operation includes a function that, given any directed edge from vertex A to vertex B, produces a corresponding edge from B to A. This ensures the quiver is symmetric, meaning every edge has a reverse counterpart. The structure supports multiple edges and loops, and the reverse function allows traversal in both directions between any connected vertices.

label: Quotient
slogan: Quotient creates a new type where elements of a base type are grouped into equivalence classes based on a given equivalence relation from a Setoid. Functions on this new type must treat equivalent elements the same way, and any two elements related by the equivalence relation are considered equal in the quotient. Elements are added to the quotient using Quotient.mk, functions are defined using Quotient.lift, and proofs about the quotient can be done by assuming all elements come from Quotient.mk.

label: Quotient.instConnectedSpace
slogan: If a topological space is connected and you form a quotient space by identifying points under an equivalence relation, then the resulting quotient space is also connected, as long as the quotient map is continuous and surjective. This is because the quotient topology ensures continuity, and continuous images of connected spaces remain connected. The declaration asserts that any quotient of a connected space remains connected under these conditions.

label: Quotient.lift
slogan: Quotient.lift lets you define a function on a quotient type by providing a function on the original type and a proof that it gives the same result for equivalent elements. The resulting function takes a quotient value and returns a value in the target type, consistent with the original function. It ensures computations on equivalence classes are well-defined.

label: Quotient.map
slogan: Quotient.map takes a function from one type to another and lifts it to a function between their quotient types, as long as the function maps equivalent elements to equivalent elements. It ensures the lifted function is well-defined by preserving the equivalence relations given by the Setoids on both types. The result is a function that works on equivalence classes rather than individual elements.

label: Quotient.mk
slogan: Quotient.mk takes a value and a setoid (a type with an equivalence relation) and puts the value into a new type where equivalent elements are treated as equal. The resulting quotient type ensures that any operation on it must respect the given equivalence relation. This version requires the setoid to be provided explicitly, unlike Quotient.mk' which infers it.

label: QuotientAddGroup.quotientKerEquivRange
slogan: For any homomorphism between two additive groups, the quotient of the domain by the kernel is isomorphic to the image of the homomorphism, meaning each coset in the quotient corresponds uniquely to an element in the image. The isomorphism maps a coset to the value of the homomorphism on any representative of that coset. This establishes a one-to-one correspondence that preserves addition.

label: QuotientGroup.Quotient.group
slogan: If N is a normal subgroup of a group G, then the set of cosets of N in G forms a group under the operation (aN)(bN) = (ab)N, where the identity element is N itself and the inverse of aN is (a^-1)N. This group is called the quotient group G/N. The operation is well-defined because N is normal, and the natural map sending each element of G to its coset in G/N is surjective.

label: QuotientGroup.comapMk'OrderIso
slogan: The function QuotientGroup.comapMk'OrderIso sets up a one-to-one correspondence between subgroups of the quotient group G/N and subgroups of G that contain the normal subgroup N, where the correspondence preserves the order of inclusion. It uses the preimage under the quotient map to link subgroups in the quotient back to subgroups in the original group. This bijection ensures that larger subgroups in the quotient correspond to larger subgroups in G containing N.

label: QuotientGroup.con_ker_eq_conKer
slogan: The equivalence relation where two group elements are considered the same if they map to the same value under a homomorphism is identical to the equivalence relation defined by multiplying with elements from the kernel subgroup. This means grouping elements by their behavior under the homomorphism is the same as grouping them by whether their ratio lies in the kernel. The two ways of forming the quotient group—via the kernel as a subgroup or via the homomorphism's fibers—yield the same result.

label: QuotientGroup.instIsTopologicalGroup
slogan: If a group has a topology where multiplication and taking inverses are continuous, and you form a quotient by a normal subgroup, then the quotient group automatically gets a topology where multiplication and inverses are also continuous. This topology is defined so that the quotient map is both continuous and open, ensuring the algebraic and topological structures are compatible. The result is that the quotient group is a topological group in a natural way.

label: QuotientGroup.instT2Space
slogan: If G is a topological group and H is a closed subgroup of G, then the quotient space G/H (the set of left cosets of H in G) with the quotient topology is Hausdorff (i.e., distinct cosets can be separated by disjoint open sets).

label: QuotientGroup.instTopologicalSpace
slogan: The quotient group G/N is given a topology where a set is open if and only if its preimage in G is open, using the subgroup N to define the equivalence classes. This makes the quotient map from G to G/N continuous and ensures the topology respects the group structure. The result is a topological space on the quotient that is compatible with the original group and its topology.

label: QuotientGroup.isOpenQuotientMap_mk
slogan: The map sending each element of a topological group to its coset in the quotient group sends open sets to open sets, as long as the group's multiplication is continuous. This means the quotient topology on the group of cosets is well-behaved with respect to openness. The result holds for any subgroup of the group.

label: QuotientGroup.leftRel
slogan: QuotientGroup.leftRel defines an equivalence relation on a group by saying two elements are equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by left-multiplying with an element from a fixed subgroup. This relation groups elements into left cosets of the subgroup, forming the basis for constructing the quotient group. The subgroup's closure under multiplication and inverses ensures the relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

label: QuotientGroup.mk
slogan: QuotientGroup.mk takes an element of a group and maps it to its corresponding coset in the quotient group formed by dividing the group by a subgroup. The quotient group consists of sets of elements that differ by an element of the subgroup, with the group operation defined by multiplying representatives. This construction works because the subgroup is closed under multiplication and inverses, ensuring the cosets form a well-defined group.

label: QuotientGroup.quotientInfEquivProdNormalQuotient
slogan: If H is a subgroup and N is a normal subgroup of a group G, then the quotient of H by the part of N that lies in H is isomorphic to the quotient of the subgroup generated by H and N by N itself, and this isomorphism respects the group operation.

label: QuotientGroup.quotientKerEquivOfSurjective
slogan: If a group homomorphism maps every element in its domain to some element in the codomain (surjective), then the quotient group formed by dividing the domain by the kernel of the homomorphism is isomorphic to the codomain, with the isomorphism preserving the group operation.

label: QuotientGroup.quotientKerEquivRange
slogan: For any group homomorphism, the quotient of the domain by the kernel is equivalent to the image of the homomorphism, meaning each coset in the quotient corresponds uniquely to an element in the image. This equivalence is a bijective map that preserves the group operation. It is built by showing the natural map from the quotient to the image is both one-to-one and onto.

label: QuotientGroup.quotientQuotientEquivQuotient
slogan: If N is a normal subgroup of G and M is a normal subgroup of G containing N, then the quotient of the group G/N by the subgroup M/N is isomorphic to the quotient group G/M. This means that modding out G by N and then by M/N gives the same result as directly modding out G by M. The isomorphism respects the group structure and is built using the natural maps between these quotient groups.

label: R0Space
slogan: An R0Space is a type of topological space where any two distinct points can be distinguished by their neighborhoods, meaning if two points are different, at least one has an open set around it that doesn't contain the other. This ensures no two points have exactly the same neighborhoods. It is a separation condition weaker than Hausdorff but stronger than T0.

label: R1Space
slogan: A space is R1 if any two points that the topology can distinguish have separate open neighborhoods around them. This means that whenever two points are not topologically indistinguishable, there are disjoint open sets containing each. The property is defined for any type equipped with a topology.

label: R1Space.quasiSober
slogan: In a T0 topological space where any two topologically distinguishable points have disjoint neighborhoods (R1 space), every nonempty irreducible closed set contains a point whose closure is the whole set (quasi-sober). This means that the ability to separate points with disjoint open sets ensures that irreducible closed subsets have a dense point. So, R1 spaces automatically satisfy the condition that irreducible closed sets come with a generic point.

label: R1Space.t2Space_iff_t0Space
slogan: A topological space is Hausdorff (T2) if and only if it is both T0 (distinct points can be distinguished by open sets) and R1 (topologically distinguishable points can be separated by disjoint neighborhoods). The R1 condition alone ensures that points with different closures can be separated, and when combined with T0, this guarantees that all distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets. Thus, being R1 and T0 together is equivalent to being Hausdorff.

label: RKHS
slogan: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) is a Hilbert space of functions where each point evaluation map is continuous, meaning the value of a function at any point can be reliably determined by the inner product structure of the space. It involves a space H of functions defined on a set X, taking values in another Hilbert space V, with a compatible inner product and norm structure over a real-like scalar type 𝕜. The RKHS class captures this setup in a way that supports functional analysis and machine learning applications.

label: Rat
slogan: Rat represents rational numbers using a pair of integers, where the number is expressed as a numerator divided by a denominator. The denominator is always positive, and the numerator and denominator have no common factors other than 1.

label: Rat.AbsoluteValue.equiv_real_or_padic
slogan: Every nontrivial absolute value on the rational numbers is equivalent to either the standard real absolute value or a p-adic absolute value for some prime p.

label: Rat.denseRange_cast
slogan: The rational numbers, when mapped into a topologically ordered field where addition and order behave nicely and every element can be surpassed by adding a smaller one enough times, end up being densely spread throughout that field. This means every element in the field is either a rational or can be approximated as closely as desired by one. The mapping preserves the arithmetic structure of the rationals while ensuring their image comes arbitrarily close to any point in the space.

label: Rat.finite_rat_abs_sub_lt_one_div_den_sq
slogan: For any fixed rational number, there are only finitely many other rational numbers such that the absolute difference between them is less than the reciprocal of the square of the denominator of the approximating rational.

label: Rat.instDenumerable
slogan: The rational numbers can be systematically listed in a sequence that matches each one to a unique natural number, meaning they are countably infinite. This is possible because every rational number can be uniquely represented as a fraction of two integers in lowest terms, and such pairs can be effectively encoded into natural numbers. Since the set of rationals is infinite and each can be encoded, they form a denumerable set.

label: Rat.instField
slogan: The rational numbers form a field, meaning they support addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero), with all the usual algebraic properties like commutativity and distributivity. Every nonzero rational number has a reciprocal, and operations behave as expected. Natural and integer numbers can be converted into rationals in a standard way, allowing consistent arithmetic across number types.

label: Rat.instTotallyDisconnectedSpace
slogan: The rational numbers, with their standard topology, form a totally disconnected space, meaning the only connected subsets are single points or empty sets. This follows from the fact that between any two distinct rationals, there exists an irrational number, allowing the space to be split into disjoint open sets around any subset. As a result, no interval of rational numbers can be connected.

label: Rat.isFractionRing
slogan: The rational numbers (Rat) are constructed as fractions of integers (Int), where every nonzero integer has a multiplicative inverse in the rationals. Each rational number can be written as a reduced fraction of an integer numerator and a nonzero natural number denominator, with the numerator and denominator having no common factors other than 1. This construction ensures that arithmetic operations on rationals match the expected behavior of fraction addition and multiplication.

label: Rat.numberField
slogan: The rational numbers, with their usual addition and multiplication, form a number field because they are a field of characteristic zero and have finite dimension when considered as a vector space over themselves. This means every rational number can be expressed using a finite basis, and all standard arithmetic operations behave as expected. The instance confirms that the structure of the rationals meets the algebraic requirements to be called a number field.

label: RatFunc
slogan: RatFunc is a type that represents rational functions—ratios of polynomials—over a commutative ring K that has no zero divisors, meaning it behaves like a field in terms of cancellation. It constructs these rational functions by formally allowing division of polynomials, where the denominator is not zero, using a process similar to creating fractions from integers. The structure supports standard operations like addition and multiplication of rational functions and includes a natural way to view polynomials as rational functions via embedding.

label: RatFunc.eval
slogan: RatFunc.eval takes a ring homomorphism, a value for the variable, and a rational function, then evaluates the function by separately computing the numerator and denominator polynomials at that value using the homomorphism on coefficients, and dividing the results in the target field as long as the denominator is not zero. It uses the normalized numerator and denominator forms to ensure the result is well-defined. This extends polynomial evaluation to rational functions in a consistent way.

label: RatFunc.finrank_eq_max_natDegree
slogan: The degree of the field extension from the base field K to the field generated by a rational function f over K equals the maximum of the degrees of the numerator and denominator polynomials of f. This means the dimension of the larger field as a vector space over K is determined by the higher degree between the top and bottom polynomial of f.

label: RatFunc.intDegree
slogan: intDegree x is the degree of a rational function x, calculated as the natural degree of its numerator minus the natural degree of its denominator, with the special case that the degree of zero is defined to be zero. The result is always an integer.

label: RatFunc.mk
slogan: RatFunc.mk takes two polynomials, a numerator and a non-zero denominator, and constructs a rational function as their fraction, provided the coefficient ring is a commutative ring with no zero divisors. It uses the general method of forming fractions of a ring by treating polynomials as elements of a ring where nonzero elements can serve as valid denominators. The result is a well-defined element of the field of rational functions that supports standard operations like addition and multiplication.

label: RatFunc.numDenom
slogan: Given a rational function over a field, this function returns a simplified numerator and denominator as polynomials that have no common factors, with the denominator scaled to be monic (its leading coefficient is 1), as long as the denominator is not zero.

label: Real
slogan: Real is the type representing all real numbers, constructed from rational numbers (Rat) by including every limit of Cauchy sequences of rationals, which ensures there are no gaps in the number line.

label: Real.Gamma
slogan: Real.Gamma(s) is a function that takes a real number s and returns the value of the gamma function at s, which generalizes the factorial to real numbers, but is not defined for zero or negative integers because it goes to infinity there. It works by taking the complex gamma function and applying it only to real number inputs. The function relies on converting real numbers into complex numbers using Complex.ofReal when needed.

label: Real.Gamma_eq_integral
slogan: For any positive real number s, the gamma function at s equals the integral from 0 to infinity of (e to the power of -x) times (x to the power of s minus 1) dx. This integral definition holds for all positive real inputs and gives a concrete way to compute gamma values using standard calculus. The result ties the gamma function directly to an improper integral involving exponential decay and power growth.

label: Real.Gamma_mul_add_mul_le_rpow_Gamma_mul_rpow_Gamma
slogan: For positive real numbers s and t, and positive weights a and b that add up to 1, the gamma function evaluated at the weighted average a*s + b*t is less than or equal to the weighted geometric mean of the gamma values at s and t, raised to the powers a and b respectively.

label: Real.Gamma_one_half_eq
slogan: The gamma function evaluated at 1/2 equals the square root of pi. This means that a special mathematical function called the gamma function, when given the input one-half, gives the same value as the square root of pi. This result is closely related to the total area under the bell curve defined by e^(-x^2) over all real numbers.

label: Real.Lp_add_le
slogan: For any finite set of points, and for two real-valued functions f and g defined on that set, the p-th root of the sum of |f(i) + g(i)|^p over the set is less than or equal to the sum of the p-th roots of the sums of |f(i)|^p and |g(i)|^p, provided p is at least 1. This is the triangle inequality for Lp norms in the context of finite sums. It means the size of the sum of two functions is no larger than the sum of their sizes when measured in the Lp sense.

label: Real.Wallis.tendsto_W_nhds_pi_div_two
slogan: The sequence formed by multiplying ratios of consecutive even and odd numbers, like (2/1)*(2/3)*(4/3)*(4/5)*..., gets closer and closer to pi/2 as more terms are included. This means the limit of this sequence as the number of terms goes to infinity is pi divided by two.

label: Real.add_one_le_exp
slogan: For any real number x, the value of x + 1 is always less than or equal to the exponential of x, or in symbols: x + 1 <= exp(x). This inequality holds for all real numbers, regardless of sign or magnitude.

label: Real.arccos_eq_pi_div_two_sub_arcsin
slogan: The arccosine of any real number between -1 and 1 is equal to pi divided by two minus the arcsine of that number. This means you can find the inverse cosine of a value by subtracting its inverse sine from pi/2. The identity connects the inverse trigonometric functions arcsin and arccos using simple arithmetic and the constant pi.

label: Real.arctan_inv_of_pos
slogan: If x is a positive real number, then the arctangent of 1/x equals pi/2 minus the arctangent of x. This equation connects the arctangent of a positive number with the arctangent of its reciprocal using pi. The identity holds only when x is greater than zero.

label: Real.artanh_eq_half_log
slogan: The inverse hyperbolic tangent of a real number x between -1 and 1 is equal to half the natural logarithm of (1 + x) divided by (1 - x). This formula expresses artanh in terms of the logarithm function. It is valid only when x is in the closed interval from -1 to 1.

label: Real.ball_eq_Ioo
slogan: The open ball of radius r centered at a point x on the real line consists of all points strictly between x - r and x + r. This means a real number is within distance r of x if and only if it lies in the open interval (x - r, x + r). The equality between the metric ball and the open interval reflects how distance and order define the same sets on the real numbers.

label: Real.binEntropy
slogan: The binary entropy function calculates a measure of uncertainty for a random event with two outcomes, where one outcome has probability p and the other has probability 1-p. It is computed as -p * log(p) - (1-p) * log(1-p), using the natural logarithm. The result is a real number that represents the entropy in bits when p is between 0 and 1.

label: Real.binEntropy_le_log_two
slogan: The binary entropy of a probability p is always less than or equal to the natural logarithm of 2. This maximum value is reached when p is exactly 0.5, meaning both outcomes are equally likely. For all other values of p, the entropy is strictly less than log(2).

label: Real.binEntropy_two_inv
slogan: The binary entropy of 0.5 is equal to the natural logarithm of 2. This means that when an event has two equally likely outcomes, the amount of uncertainty or information it produces is exactly log(2). The value 2⁻¹ represents 1/2, and the entropy is calculated using the natural logarithm.

label: Real.binEntropy_zero
slogan: The binary entropy of 0 is 0, meaning that if one outcome of a two-result event has zero probability, the uncertainty (or information content) of the event is zero. This follows from the definition of binary entropy using logarithms, where the term involving log(0) does not contribute because it is multiplied by zero.

label: Real.coe_fib_eq
slogan: The nth Fibonacci number, when converted to a real number, equals the difference between the nth powers of the golden ratio and its conjugate, divided by the square root of 5.

label: Real.continuousOn_log
slogan: The logarithm function is continuous for all positive real numbers, meaning that if you change the input slightly, the output also changes only slightly, as long as the input stays greater than zero.

label: Real.continuous_exp
slogan: The real exponential function is continuous, meaning that if you change the input by a small amount, the output also changes by only a small amount. This is because the real exponential function is the restriction of the continuous complex exponential function to real numbers. Continuity here means that open sets in the output have open preimages in the input under the standard real number topology.

label: Real.continuous_sin
slogan: The sine function on real numbers is continuous, meaning small changes in the input result in small changes in the output. This is because the real sine function is defined using the complex sine function, which is continuous, and the embedding of real numbers into complex numbers is also continuous. Since the composition of continuous functions is continuous, the real sine function is continuous.

label: Real.convexOn_log_Gamma
slogan: The logarithm of the Gamma function is convex for all positive real numbers, meaning that for any two points x and y greater than 0, the value of log(Gamma) at any point between x and y lies below or on the straight line connecting log(Gamma(x)) and log(Gamma(y)). This property holds across the entire domain where x > 0.

label: Real.cos
slogan: The Real.cos function calculates the cosine of a real number by first converting it to a complex number with zero imaginary part, then applying the complex cosine function defined as (exp(i*z) + exp(-i*z)) / 2. This approach ensures the real cosine matches the complex cosine when restricted to real inputs.

label: Real.cosh_eq_tsum
slogan: The hyperbolic cosine of a real number r equals the infinite sum of terms r raised to the power 2n, divided by the factorial of 2n, for all natural numbers n starting from 0.

label: Real.cosh_le_exp_half_sq
slogan: For any real number x, the hyperbolic cosine of x is less than or equal to the exponential of half of x squared.

label: Real.cosh_sq_sub_sinh_sq
slogan: For any real number x, the square of the hyperbolic cosine of x minus the square of the hyperbolic sine of x equals 1.

label: Real.deriv_Gamma_nat
slogan: The derivative of the Gamma function at a positive integer n+1 equals n factorial multiplied by the quantity (harmonic number n minus the Euler-Mascheroni constant), where the harmonic number is the sum of reciprocals from 1 to n.

label: Real.deriv_exp
slogan: The derivative of the exponential function exp(x) with respect to x is equal to exp(x) for all real numbers x. This means the rate at which exp(x) changes at any point is exactly the value of exp(x) at that point. The result follows from the fact that the exponential function is differentiable everywhere on the real line.

label: Real.deriv_log
slogan: The derivative of the natural logarithm function at any positive real number x is 1/x. This means the slope of the tangent line to the log function at x > 0 is exactly the reciprocal of x. The logarithm is not differentiable at zero or negative numbers because it is not defined there.

label: Real.deriv_sin
slogan: The derivative of the sine function at any real number x is equal to the cosine of x. This means the rate at which sin(x) changes with respect to x is given by cos(x). The result holds because sine and cosine are well-defined for real numbers and satisfy the necessary conditions for differentiability.

label: Real.digits
slogan: Real.digits takes a real number x between 0 (inclusive) and 1 (exclusive) and a base b (a positive natural number), then returns a function that gives the nth digit of x in base b, where each digit is a natural number from 0 to b-1.

label: Real.dist_0_eq_abs
slogan: The distance from any real number to zero is the same as the absolute value of that number.

label: Real.dist_eq
slogan: The distance between two real numbers is the absolute value of their difference, meaning it measures how far apart they are regardless of direction. This uses standard subtraction and absolute value operations defined for real numbers. The real numbers support this distance function because they have both arithmetic and order structure.

label: Real.eq_Gamma_of_log_convex
slogan: If a function f is positive on the positive real numbers, its logarithm is convex, it satisfies f(x+1) = x * f(x) for all x > 0, and f(1) = 1, then f must be equal to the Gamma function for all positive real numbers.

label: Real.equivCauchy
slogan: Real.equivCauchy sets up a one-to-one correspondence between real numbers and equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers, where two sequences are considered equivalent if the absolute value of their difference approaches zero. This construction builds the real numbers by completing the rationals using limits of Cauchy sequences.

label: Real.eulerMascheroniConstant
slogan: The Euler-Mascheroni constant gamma is defined as the limit of the sequence (harmonic number n minus the natural logarithm of n+1) as n approaches infinity. It is a real number that represents the difference between the harmonic series and the logarithm function in the limit.

label: Real.exists_convs_eq_rat
slogan: If a rational number q is close enough to a real number xi such that the absolute difference |xi - q| is less than 1 divided by twice the square of q's denominator, then q must appear as one of the convergents in the continued fraction expansion of xi.

label: Real.exists_extension_norm_eq
slogan: If a linear function is defined on a subspace of a real normed vector space and is bounded by a constant, then there exists a linear function on the whole space that agrees with the original function on the subspace and has the same norm.

label: Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le
slogan: For any real number and any positive natural number n, there exist integers j and k such that k is between 1 and n, and the absolute value of (k times the real number minus j) is at most 1 divided by (n+1).

label: Real.exists_isLUB
slogan: Every nonempty set of real numbers that has an upper bound has a least upper bound. This means there is always a smallest real number that is greater than or equal to every number in the set. This property is known as the completeness of the real numbers.

label: Real.exists_isMinOn_Gamma_Ioi
slogan: There is a real number between 1 and 2 where the Gamma function reaches its smallest value on the interval (0, infinity). This means the Gamma function has a minimum point in that range. The result guarantees the existence of such a minimizing point.

label: Real.exists_rat_eq_convergent
slogan: If a rational number q is sufficiently close to a real number ξ such that the absolute difference |ξ - q| is less than 1 divided by twice the square of q's denominator, then q must appear as one of the convergents in the continued fraction expansion of ξ.

label: Real.exp
slogan: The real exponential function takes a real number and returns its exponential value, computed as a real number. It is defined by restricting the complex exponential function to real inputs, using the fact that real numbers can be embedded in the complex numbers by setting the imaginary part to zero. The result is consistent with the infinite series sum of x^n / n! for real x.

label: Real.exp_add
slogan: The exponential of the sum of two real numbers equals the product of their exponentials: exp(a + b) = exp(a) * exp(b) for any real numbers a and b. This property is derived from the more general rule for complex numbers but applies specifically to real values. The real exponential function is defined as the restriction of the complex exponential to real inputs.

label: Real.exp_bound
slogan: For any real number x with absolute value at most 1, the difference between the exponential of x and the sum of the first n terms of its Taylor series (from m=0 to n-1) is bounded above by |x|^n times (n+1)/(n! * n), where n is a positive integer. This bound shows how closely the partial sum approximates the exponential function. The error decreases rapidly as n increases due to the factorial in the denominator.

label: Real.exp_log
slogan: For any positive real number x, taking the natural logarithm of x and then applying the exponential function gives back x. This means the exponential function undoes the logarithm when x is greater than zero.

label: Real.exp_one_near_20
slogan: The number e (the base of the natural logarithm) is very close to the fraction 363916618873 / 133877442384, and the absolute difference between e and this fraction is less than or equal to 1 divided by 10^20. This means e is approximately 2.71828... and this specific rational number approximates it with extremely high precision. The bound comes from analyzing the Taylor series expansion of the exponential function at 1.

label: Real.exp_pos
slogan: For any real number x, the value of e^x is always greater than zero. This means the exponential function never produces zero or negative results when given a real input. The result follows from the definition of the exponential function and properties of real numbers.

label: Real.fourierIntegral
slogan: Real.fourierIntegral refers to the Fourier transform as a function from type E to type F, where F is treated as an output parameter determined by the type class instance. It is used to express the Fourier transform in a notation-friendly way without requiring additional structure like linearity. The transform is defined through the FourierTransform type class, which allows F to be inferred from E.

label: Real.fourierIntegral_eq
slogan: The Fourier transform of a function f from a finite-dimensional real inner product space V to a complex normed space E is given by integrating f(v) multiplied by a complex exponential factor involving the inner product of v and w, over all points v in V. The exponential factor uses the standard 2π convention and rotates around the unit circle in the complex plane. This formula holds when V has a Borel measurable structure and finite dimension.

label: Real.fourierInv_eq_fourier_comp_neg
slogan: The inverse Fourier transform of a function f is the same as the Fourier transform of the function obtained by negating the input of f. In other words, flipping the sign of the variable in the original function gives the same result as taking the inverse Fourier transform. This holds for functions from a finite-dimensional real inner product space to a complex normed vector space, under suitable measurability conditions.

label: Real.fourier_deriv
slogan: The Fourier transform of the derivative of a function is equal to the Fourier transform of the original function multiplied by 2 * pi * i * x, where i is the imaginary unit and x is the frequency variable. This holds for functions that are differentiable and whose derivatives are integrable.

label: Real.fourier_iteratedDeriv
slogan: The Fourier transform of the n-th derivative of a function f is equal to the Fourier transform of f multiplied by (2 * pi * i * x) raised to the power n, provided f is n times continuously differentiable and all its derivatives up to order n are integrable.

label: Real.fourier_mul_convolution_eq
slogan: The Fourier transform of the convolution of two functions equals the product of their Fourier transforms. This holds for functions that are integrable and continuous on a finite-dimensional real inner product space, with values in a complete normed ring over the complex numbers. The convolution uses a continuous bilinear map, and the result is stated pointwise for each frequency ξ.

label: Real.geom_goldenRatio_isSol_fibRec
slogan: The sequence defined by raising the golden ratio φ to successive powers (i.e., φ^n) satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence relation, meaning each term is the sum of the two previous terms. This holds because the golden ratio is a root of the characteristic equation of the Fibonacci sequence. The result applies in any algebraic structure where addition and multiplication are well-defined and commutative.

label: Real.geom_mean_le_arith_mean
slogan: For a finite set of nonnegative real numbers, the weighted geometric mean is always less than or equal to the weighted arithmetic mean, with positive weights ensuring the total weight is greater than zero.

label: Real.geom_mean_le_arith_mean_weighted
slogan: For a list of nonnegative real numbers and corresponding nonnegative weights that add up to one, the product of each number raised to its weight is less than or equal to the sum of each number multiplied by its weight. This means the weighted geometric mean does not exceed the weighted arithmetic mean. The result holds as long as all numbers and weights are nonnegative and the weights sum to one.

label: Real.goldenRatio
slogan: The golden ratio is defined as the real number (1 + the square root of 5) divided by 2. It is a specific positive real number approximately equal to 1.618.

label: Real.goldenRatio_mul_fib_succ_add_fib
slogan: Multiplying the golden ratio by the (n+1)th Fibonacci number and adding the nth Fibonacci number gives the (n+1)th power of the golden ratio. This holds for all natural numbers n. The Fibonacci numbers are treated as real numbers in this context.

label: Real.goldenRatio_pow_sub_goldenRatio_pow
slogan: The golden ratio, approximately 1.618, has the property that raising it to the power of n+2 and subtracting the power of n+1 gives the same result as raising it to the power of n, for any natural number n.

label: Real.goldenRatio_sq
slogan: The square of the golden ratio, which is (1 + sqrt(5))/2, equals the golden ratio plus one.

label: Real.harm_mean_le_geom_mean
slogan: For a nonempty finite collection of positive real numbers, the ratio of the sum of weights to the sum of weighted reciprocals is less than or equal to the weighted geometric mean of the numbers raised to the power of the reciprocal of the total weight.

label: Real.hasDerivAt_exp
slogan: The exponential function on real numbers is differentiable at every point, and its derivative is the same as the function itself — so the slope of e^x at any point x is just e^x. This follows from the fact that the complex exponential is differentiable everywhere and the real exponential is the restriction of the complex one. The real derivative is obtained by taking the real part of the complex derivative and applying the embedding of reals into complexes.

label: Real.hasDerivAt_log
slogan: The derivative of the natural logarithm function at any nonzero real number x is 1/x. This means the slope of the tangent line to the log curve at x is exactly the reciprocal of x. The result is valid for positive real numbers, where the logarithm is defined.

label: Real.hasDerivAt_sigmoid
slogan: The derivative of the sigmoid function at any real number x is equal to the value of the sigmoid function at x multiplied by one minus that value. This means the rate of change of the sigmoid function at a point depends only on the function's value at that point. The result holds for all real inputs.

label: Real.hasDerivAt_sin
slogan: The derivative of the sine function at any real number x is equal to the cosine of x. This means that the rate at which sin(x) changes as x changes is given by cos(x). The result is based on the fact that sine is strictly differentiable and its derivative matches the cosine function.

label: Real.hasPDF_iff
slogan: A random variable has a probability density function if and only if it is almost everywhere measurable and its distribution assigns zero probability to any set that has zero volume. This means the probability measure pushed forward by the random variable is absolutely continuous with respect to the standard volume measure.

label: Real.hasStrictDerivAt_const_rpow
slogan: The derivative of the function that maps x to a^x, where a is a positive constant, is equal to a^x times the natural logarithm of a. This holds for all real numbers x and describes how the exponential function changes at any point. The result is based on strict differentiability, meaning the function's behavior near each point closely matches its linear approximation.

label: Real.hasSum_log_one_add_inv
slogan: The sum of the terms 2 * (1 / (2 * k + 1)) * (1 / (2 * a + 1))^(2 * k + 1) for natural numbers k equals the natural logarithm of (1 + 1/a), provided a is a positive real number. This provides a series expansion for log(1 + 1/a) in terms of powers of 1/(2 * a + 1). The result connects an infinite sum involving rational functions and powers to a logarithmic expression.

label: Real.hasSum_log_sub_log_of_abs_lt_one
slogan: If the absolute value of a real number x is less than 1, then the difference log(1 + x) - log(1 - x) equals the sum of the infinite series 2 * x^(2k+1) / (2k+1) for all non-negative integers k.
