label: SetRel.exists_graph_eq_iff
slogan: There is a function whose graph equals a given set of pairs if and only if every input has exactly one output paired with it in that set.

label: SetRel.inv
slogan: The inverse of a relation swaps the order of each pair of related elements, so that if a is related to b in the original, then b is related to a in the inverse; this is done by applying the swap function to each pair and taking the preimage under that swap. The result is a new relation where the roles of the input and output elements are reversed. This operation converts a relation from type A to B into a relation from B to A.

label: Setoid
slogan: A setoid is a type equipped with an equivalence relation, which is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. This equivalence relation is used to group elements into equivalence classes when forming a quotient type. The quotient type treats equivalent elements as equal and allows defining functions and proofs that respect this equivalence.

label: Setoid.IsPartition
slogan: A collection c of subsets of a type a is a partition if the empty set is not in c, and every element of a belongs to exactly one subset in c.

label: Setoid.Partition.completeLattice
slogan: The collection of all partitions of a type α, where each partition is a set of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets that cover α, forms a complete lattice under the refinement order. This means any family of partitions has both a finest common coarsening and a coarsest common refinement. The lattice structure is derived from the known complete lattice of equivalence relations via a one-to-one correspondence that preserves order.

label: Setoid.Partition.orderIso
slogan: There is a one-to-one correspondence between equivalence relations on a type α and partitions of α into non-overlapping, non-empty subsets, and this correspondence preserves the structure of ordering between them.

label: Setoid.classes
slogan: Returns the set of all equivalence classes induced by an equivalence relation on a type. Each equivalence class is a set of elements that are related to each other. The result is a collection of these classes as subsets of the original type.

label: Setoid.eqvGen_eq
slogan: The equivalence relation generated by a given relation r is the smallest equivalence relation that includes r, meaning two elements are related in this generated relation if and only if they can be connected by a chain of steps using r along with reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. This generated relation is defined as the greatest lower bound (infimum) of all equivalence relations that contain r.

label: Setoid.isPartition_classes
slogan: For any equivalence relation on a type, the collection of its equivalence classes forms a partition of the type, meaning every element belongs to exactly one equivalence class and no class is empty.

label: Setoid.ker
slogan: Given a function f from type a to type b and an equivalence relation on b, two elements of a are considered equivalent under the kernel setoid if their images under f are equivalent in b. This creates an equivalence relation on a by pulling back the relation from b through the function f. The result is a setoid structure on a where elements are equivalent whenever f maps them to equivalent values in b.

label: Setoid.ker_def
slogan: Two elements in the domain of a function are considered equivalent if the function maps them to equal values in the codomain. This equivalence relation on the domain is defined by comparing outputs of the function. The kernel setoid captures this idea by equating inputs whenever their outputs are the same.

label: Setoid.liftEquiv
slogan: If a function from type a to type b respects the equivalence relation defined by a setoid on a, then there is a unique well-defined function from the quotient type (a modulo the equivalence) to b that maps each equivalence class to the function's value on any representative, and this correspondence is bijective with the set of all such compatible functions.

label: Setoid.mem_classes
slogan: For any element y in a type with an equivalence relation, the set of all elements related to y is one of the equivalence classes in the partition defined by that relation.

label: Setoid.quotientEquivClasses
slogan: The quotient of a type by an equivalence relation is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of all equivalence classes formed by that relation. This means that each element in the quotient corresponds uniquely to an equivalence class, and vice versa. The mapping between them is bijective and preserves equality.

label: Setoid.quotientQuotientEquivQuotient
slogan: If you quotient a type by an equivalence relation and then quotient the result by a coarser relation that respects the first, it's the same as quotienting the original type by the coarser relation directly. The equivalence between these two quotients preserves the structure of the relations. This means step-by-step collapsing of elements gives the same result as doing it all in one step.

label: SheafOfModules
slogan: A sheaf of modules is a presheaf of modules where the underlying presheaf of abelian groups satisfies the sheaf condition, meaning that local data can be glued together uniquely when it agrees on overlaps. It is defined over a Grothendieck topology and takes values in modules over a sheaf of rings. This structure ensures compatibility between the algebraic module operations and the topological gluing conditions.

label: SheafOfModules.IsFiniteType
slogan: A sheaf of modules is of finite type if, around every point, its sections can be generated by a finite number of elements. This means that locally, the module structure is not too large or complicated. The condition is expressed in terms of covering families and behavior under sheafification.

label: Sigma
slogan: Sigma represents pairs where the first element has type α and the second element has a type that depends on the value of the first; it is used to form dependent pairs written as Σ a : α, β a. The resulting type belongs to the universe level equal to the maximum of the universes of α and β. This structure generalizes Cartesian products by allowing the type of the second component to vary with the first.

label: SigmaCompactSpace
slogan: A sigma compact space is a topological space that can be covered by a countable collection of compact sets, each of which is closed in the topology. This means there exists a sequence of compact subsets such that every point in the space lies in at least one of them. The space must already have a topology defined, and the union of these compact sets equals the whole space.

label: SignType.sign
slogan: The sign function takes a value from any type that supports comparison and has zero, one, and negation, and returns -1 if the value is negative, 0 if it is zero, and 1 if it is positive. It maps elements into the sign type (-1, 0, or 1) in a way that preserves the order of the original values. The function is defined so that comparisons between signs match the expected ordering: negative is less than zero, and zero is less than positive.

label: SimpContFract.determinant
slogan: For a simple continued fraction over a field, the expression A_n * B_(n+1) - B_n * A_(n+1) equals (-1) raised to the power of n+1, as long as the fraction has not terminated at step n. Here, A_n and B_n are the numerator and denominator of the nth convergent, respectively.

label: SimpleGraph
slogan: A simple graph consists of a set of vertices and a relation that specifies which pairs of vertices are connected by an edge, with no vertex connected to itself and at most one edge between any two vertices. The edge set is the collection of all unordered pairs of adjacent vertices.

label: SimpleGraph.CliqueFree.card_edgeFinset_le
slogan: In a finite simple graph with n vertices that has no clique of size r+1, the number of edges is at most (n^2 - (n mod r)^2) * (r-1) / (2*r) plus the number of ways to choose 2 elements from (n mod r).

label: SimpleGraph.Colorable
slogan: A graph is colorable with at most n colors if there exists a way to assign one of n colors to each vertex such that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

label: SimpleGraph.Coloring
slogan: An α-coloring of a simple graph G is a way of assigning colors (from a set α) to the vertices of G so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color, which is equivalent to mapping the graph G into a complete graph on α where every pair of distinct vertices is connected. This mapping must preserve adjacency, meaning connected vertices in G are sent to different vertices in the complete graph. Such a coloring ensures that connected vertices always have different colors.

label: SimpleGraph.Coloring.colorClass
slogan: The color class of a given color is the set of vertices that are assigned that color in a proper graph coloring. It consists of all vertices mapped to a specific color by the coloring function.

label: SimpleGraph.Connected
slogan: A graph is considered connected if it has at least one vertex and there is a path between any two vertices. This means the graph consists of exactly one connected component. The notation h u v can be used directly to express that vertices u and v are connected by a path.

label: SimpleGraph.Connected.exists_isTree_le
slogan: Every connected graph has a subgraph that is a tree and includes all the vertices of the original graph. This subgraph keeps the graph connected while removing any cycles. Such a tree is called a spanning tree.

label: SimpleGraph.EdgeLabeling
slogan: An edge labeling of a simple graph assigns a label from a type K to each edge of the graph, where edges are unordered pairs of vertices. This labeling does not require that adjacent edges have different labels. The structure simply associates each edge in the graph with a value from the label type.

label: SimpleGraph.Hom
slogan: A graph homomorphism is a function between the vertex sets of two simple graphs that maps adjacent vertices to adjacent vertices. The notation G →g G' denotes the type of such homomorphisms from graph G to graph G'. It is defined for any two simple graphs over arbitrary vertex types V and W.

label: SimpleGraph.IsAcyclic
slogan: A graph is called acyclic if it contains no cycles, meaning there is no path that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating any edge. This property applies to simple graphs, which have undirected edges, no self-loops, and at most one edge between any pair of vertices. Being acyclic means the graph is a forest, where each connected component is a tree.

label: SimpleGraph.IsBipartite
slogan: A simple graph is bipartite if its vertices can be divided into two groups such that no two vertices within the same group are connected by an edge. This is equivalent to saying the graph can be colored using only two colors so that no adjacent vertices have the same color.

label: SimpleGraph.IsBipartiteWith
slogan: A graph G is bipartite with sets s and t if s and t are disjoint and every edge in G connects a vertex in s to a vertex in t. This means no edge connects two vertices within s or two within t. The relation defining adjacency in G must only hold between vertices from different sets.

label: SimpleGraph.IsClique
slogan: A clique in a simple graph is a set of vertices where every two different vertices are connected by an edge. This means that for any two vertices in the set, there is an edge between them in the graph. The condition is expressed by checking that the adjacency relation holds pairwise on the set.

label: SimpleGraph.IsClique.card_le_chromaticNumber
slogan: In any simple graph, the number of vertices in a clique is at most the chromatic number of the graph. This means you need at least as many colors to color the graph as there are vertices in the largest clique.

label: SimpleGraph.IsContained
slogan: A graph A is contained in a graph B if there is a way to map A to a subgraph of B such that the structure (adjacency of vertices) is preserved. This means A can be found inside B, possibly with vertices and edges of B not used. The mapping must respect the adjacency relationships present in A.

label: SimpleGraph.IsEdgeConnected
slogan: A graph is k-edge-connected if, for any two vertices, there is still a path between them even after removing fewer than k edges. This means the graph stays connected unless at least k edges are removed. The property depends on the graph's structure and the number k.

label: SimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree
slogan: A simple graph is regular of degree d if it has finite neighborhoods at each vertex and every vertex has exactly d neighbors. This means all vertices in the graph have the same number of adjacent vertices, equal to d. The graph must be locally finite, so no vertex has infinitely many neighbors.

label: SimpleGraph.IsTree
slogan: A tree is a graph that has no cycles and where every pair of vertices is connected by some path, with the graph containing at least one vertex. It combines the properties of being acyclic and connected.

label: SimpleGraph.IsTree.exists_vert_degree_one_of_nontrivial
slogan: A tree with more than one vertex has at least one vertex that is connected to exactly one other vertex.

label: SimpleGraph.IsTree.isBipartite
slogan: Every tree (a connected graph with no cycles) can be colored using just two colors such that no two adjacent vertices share the same color, meaning all trees are bipartite.

label: SimpleGraph.IsVertexCover
slogan: A set of vertices c is a vertex cover of a simple graph G if every edge in G touches at least one vertex in c.

label: SimpleGraph.Iso
slogan: A graph isomorphism is a one-to-one correspondence between the vertices of two graphs that preserves edges, meaning two vertices are connected in one graph if and only if their corresponding vertices are connected in the other. The notation G ≃g G' denotes the type of such isomorphisms between graphs G and G'. It is defined for simple graphs, which have no self-loops or multiple edges between the same pair of vertices.

label: SimpleGraph.Reachable
slogan: Two vertices in a simple graph are considered reachable from one another if there exists a path of adjacent vertices connecting them. This means you can get from one vertex to the other by following edges in the graph. Reachability includes the possibility of staying at the same vertex (reflexivity) and chaining together multiple steps (transitivity).

label: SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsMatching
slogan: A subgraph M of a simple graph G is a matching if each vertex in M is connected to exactly one edge in M. Vertices that are part of such edges are called matched or saturated. This means no vertex in the subgraph touches more than one edge, and every vertex in the subgraph touches exactly one.

label: SimpleGraph.UnitDistEmbedding
slogan: A unit-distance embedding of a graph into a metric space is a way of placing the graph's vertices as points in the space so that any two connected vertices are exactly distance 1 apart. The embedding must also be injective, meaning no two distinct vertices map to the same point. This structure combines a graph, a metric space, and an injective function with the unit-distance condition.

label: SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle
slogan: A cycle at a vertex u is a closed walk starting and ending at u, with no repeated edges and no repeated vertices except u, which appears exactly twice.

label: SimpleGraph.Walk.IsEulerian
slogan: A walk in a simple graph is Eulerian if it traverses every edge exactly once. Such a walk must start and end at specific vertices, and when it also forms a closed loop, it is called an Eulerian circuit. The property depends on the graph having decidable equality for its vertices and edges being represented as unordered pairs.

label: SimpleGraph.Walk.IsHamiltonian
slogan: A Hamiltonian path is a walk in a graph that visits every vertex exactly once, starting from one vertex and ending at another. The walk is defined by the list of vertices it passes through, and being Hamiltonian means each vertex in the graph appears exactly once in that list. While the definition does not require the walk to be simple (i.e., edge-non-repeating), adding the condition that it is a valid path ensures no repeated edges.

label: SimpleGraph.Walk.IsHamiltonianCycle
slogan: A Hamiltonian cycle is a closed path in a simple graph that starts and ends at the same vertex, visits every vertex exactly once (except the starting/ending vertex, which appears twice), and uses no repeated edges. It is a special kind of cycle that covers all vertices of the graph. The property checks whether a given closed walk in a graph meets this condition.

label: SimpleGraph.Walk.IsPath
slogan: A path is a sequence of vertices in a simple graph that starts at one vertex and ends at another, where each consecutive pair of vertices is connected by an edge and no vertex appears more than once. This means the sequence does not revisit any vertex along the way. The property of being a path depends only on having no duplicate vertices in the walk.

label: SimpleGraph.adjMatrix
slogan: The adjMatrix function creates a matrix where each entry is 1 if the corresponding pair of vertices are connected in the graph, and 0 otherwise, using elements from a given type that supports zero and one. The matrix is indexed by the graph's vertices, and the relation of adjacency must be decidable. This matrix is built over a type that has zero and one values defined.

label: SimpleGraph.binomialRandom
slogan: SimpleGraph.binomialRandom defines a probability measure on the set of all simple graphs with a given vertex type V, where each possible edge is included independently with probability p. The measure is built using independent Bernoulli trials for each unordered pair of vertices, treating edges as elements of Sym2 V. This models a random graph where every edge appears with the same fixed probability p between 0 and 1.

label: SimpleGraph.boxProd
slogan: The box product of two simple graphs G and H creates a new graph whose vertices are pairs (a, b) where a is a vertex from G and b is a vertex from H. Two pairs are connected if either their first components are adjacent in G and their second components are the same, or their second components are adjacent in H and their first components are the same.

label: SimpleGraph.card_edgeFinset_top_eq_card_choose_two
slogan: The number of edges in a complete graph with n vertices is equal to the number of ways to choose 2 vertices from n, which is n*(n-1)/2. This means every pair of distinct vertices is connected by exactly one edge. The total count of such pairs is given by the binomial coefficient "n choose 2".

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber
slogan: The chromatic number of a graph is the smallest number of colors needed to color the vertices so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color, or infinity if no such finite number exists. It is represented as a natural number or infinity using the extended natural numbers (ℕ∞). If the graph can be colored with finitely many colors, converting this value to a natural number gives the usual chromatic number.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_cycleGraph_of_odd
slogan: The chromatic number of an odd cycle graph with at least 3 vertices is 3, meaning it requires exactly 3 colors to color the vertices so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_eq_iff_colorable_not_colorable
slogan: A graph needs exactly n + 1 colors to be properly colored if and only if it can be colored with n + 1 colors but cannot be colored with only n colors.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_eq_one_iff
slogan: A graph has chromatic number 1 if and only if it has no edges and has at least one vertex. This means all vertices can be colored the same because no two are connected.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_card
slogan: The chromatic number of a finite graph is at most the total number of its vertices, because each vertex can be assigned a unique color to ensure no two adjacent vertices share the same color. This means the minimum number of colors needed to properly color the graph cannot exceed the size of the vertex set.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_two_iff_isBipartite
slogan: A graph can be colored with at most two colors so that no adjacent vertices share the same color if and only if it is bipartite. A bipartite graph is one whose vertices can be divided into two groups such that no two vertices within the same group are connected. This means the graph has no odd-length cycles.

label: SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_top
slogan: The chromatic number of a complete graph on a finite set of vertices equals the total number of vertices, because every vertex must be assigned a different color.

label: SimpleGraph.circulantGraph
slogan: The circulant graph over an additive group G with a set of jumps s is a simple graph where each vertex g in G is connected to g + s for every s in the set s, forming edges based on group addition. It is constructed using a symmetric relation that ensures no self-loops and undirected edges. This graph models connections in a cyclic or rotational structure defined by the group and jump set.

label: SimpleGraph.cliqueNum
slogan: The clique number of a graph G is the largest number of vertices that are all directly connected to each other. It measures the size of the biggest complete subgraph in G.

label: SimpleGraph.cliqueNum_le_chromaticNumber
slogan: In any simple graph, the size of the largest group of vertices that are all directly connected to each other is at most the minimum number of colors needed to color the graph so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

label: SimpleGraph.completeGraph
slogan: The complete graph on a type V is a simple graph where every pair of distinct vertices is connected by an edge. It is defined such that any two different vertices are adjacent, with no self-loops or multiple edges. This graph represents the maximum possible connectivity for a simple graph on V.

label: SimpleGraph.cycleGraph
slogan: The cycle graph on n vertices is a simple graph where the vertices are the numbers 0 through n-1, and each vertex i is connected to the vertices i+1 and i-1 modulo n, forming a single cycle that includes all vertices. It is constructed using the circulant graph construction with jumps of plus and minus one in the additive group of integers modulo n. This graph represents a regular polygon where each corner is connected to its two nearest neighbors.

label: SimpleGraph.degMatrix
slogan: The degMatrix function creates a square matrix where each diagonal entry corresponds to the number of edges connected to a vertex in a simple graph, and all off-diagonal entries are zero. The matrix is built using the degrees of the vertices, with entries in a type that supports addition and has a notion of natural numbers. This requires the vertex type to be finite and equality between vertices to be decidable.

label: SimpleGraph.degree
slogan: The degree of a vertex v in a simple graph G is the number of vertices directly connected to v. It is calculated as the size of the finite set of neighbors of v, provided that the set of neighbors is finite. This value is always a natural number.

label: SimpleGraph.dist
slogan: The distance between two vertices in a simple graph is the length of the shortest walk connecting them, or 0 if no walk exists. This value is always a natural number, even when the vertices are unreachable from each other. It is derived from the extended distance by converting infinity to 0.

label: SimpleGraph.edgeFinset
slogan: The edgeFinset function converts the set of edges in a simple graph into a finite set (Finset), provided the edge set is finite. It takes a graph G with vertex type V and returns its edges as a Finset of unordered pairs of vertices (Sym2 V). This is useful for performing finite set operations on the edges of a graph.

label: SimpleGraph.edgeSet
slogan: G.edgeSet is the set of all unordered pairs of vertices that are adjacent in the graph G, where each pair represents an edge. It is defined such that an unordered pair (v, w) is in G.edgeSet exactly when vertices v and w are adjacent according to G.Adj. This allows edges to be conveniently accessed using dot notation.

label: SimpleGraph.emptyGraph
slogan: The empty graph on a vertex type V is a simple graph with no edges, meaning no two vertices are connected. It is the smallest possible graph in the Boolean algebra of all simple graphs on V.

label: SimpleGraph.exists_bijective_of_forall_ncard_le
slogan: If a simple graph is bipartite with parts p1 and p2, and every subset of p1 has at most as many vertices as its set of neighbors in p2, then there exists a bijective function from p1 to p2 such that each vertex in p1 is adjacent to its image in p2.

label: SimpleGraph.extremalNumber
slogan: The extremal number for a natural number n and a graph H is the largest number of edges possible in a graph with n vertices that does not contain any subgraph isomorphic to H. If every graph on n vertices must contain H, then the extremal number is zero.

label: SimpleGraph.hasse
slogan: The Hasse diagram of a preorder is defined as a simple graph where vertices are elements of the type and edges connect pairs of elements that are related by the covering relation (one element is strictly greater than another with no element in between). This graph only includes edges for direct coverings, not general order relations. The covering relation ensures no element is connected to itself.

label: SimpleGraph.incMatrix
slogan: The incMatrix of a simple graph G over a type R is a matrix where each entry (a, e) is 1 if vertex a is incident to edge e, and 0 otherwise; the matrix has rows indexed by vertices and columns indexed by unordered pairs of vertices (edges). This requires R to have zero and one elements, and equality and adjacency must be decidable.

label: SimpleGraph.indepNum
slogan: The independence number of a graph G is the largest number of vertices that can be chosen so that no two are connected by an edge. It is defined as the supremum of the sizes of all independent sets in the graph. This value is always a natural number.

label: SimpleGraph.isAcyclic_iff_path_unique
slogan: A simple graph has no cycles if and only if there is exactly one path between any two vertices. In such a graph, any two vertices are connected by at most one unique path. If multiple paths exist between some pair of vertices, the graph must contain a cycle.

label: SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_exists_isBipartiteWith
slogan: A simple graph is bipartite if and only if its vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets such that every edge connects a vertex from one set to a vertex from the other. This means there are no edges within the same set. The graph being bipartite is equivalent to the existence of such a pair of sets.

label: SimpleGraph.isExtremal_top_free_turanGraph
slogan: Among all graphs with a given finite number of vertices that do not contain a complete subgraph of a certain size, the Turán graph has the maximum possible number of edges. Specifically, the Turán graph for avoiding cliques of size equal to the number of vertices is extremal, meaning it achieves the highest edge count while satisfying the restriction. This holds when the vertex set has more than one element.

label: SimpleGraph.isMaximalIndepSet_iff
slogan: A set of vertices in a graph is a maximal independent set if it is independent (no two vertices are adjacent) and no larger independent set contains it; this means any independent set that includes it must be equal to it.

label: SimpleGraph.isTree_iff_connected_and_card
slogan: A simple graph is a tree if and only if it is connected and the number of edges plus one equals the number of vertices.

label: SimpleGraph.isTree_iff_existsUnique_path
slogan: A simple graph is a tree if and only if there is at least one vertex and between every pair of vertices, there exists exactly one path that connects them without repeating any vertices.

label: SimpleGraph.isTuranMaximal_iff_nonempty_iso_turanGraph
slogan: A simple graph with n vertices that has the maximum possible number of edges without containing a clique of size r+1 must be isomorphic to the Turán graph on n vertices with r parts. This means the Turán graph is the only graph (up to isomorphism) that achieves the largest edge count while avoiding (r+1)-cliques. The theorem states that being Turán-maximal is equivalent to being isomorphic to this specific Turán graph.

label: SimpleGraph.lapMatrix
slogan: The Laplacian matrix of a graph G over a ring R is defined as the difference between the degree matrix D and the adjacency matrix A of G, where D is a diagonal matrix with vertex degrees and A has 1s for adjacent vertex pairs and 0s otherwise. This matrix is indexed by the graph's vertices and takes values in R. The graph must have a finite vertex set with decidable equality and edge relation, and R must support addition, subtraction, and contain 0 and 1.

label: SimpleGraph.lineGraph
slogan: The line graph of a simple graph G is a new graph where each vertex represents an edge from G, and two vertices are connected if their corresponding edges in G share a common endpoint.

label: SimpleGraph.maxDegree_lt_card_verts
slogan: In a finite, nonempty graph where edges are determined by a decidable relation, the highest number of edges connected to any single vertex is less than the total number of vertices in the graph.

label: SimpleGraph.neighborSet
slogan: G.neighborSet v returns the set of all vertices connected directly to vertex v in the graph G.

label: SimpleGraph.partitionable_iff_colorable
slogan: A graph can be divided into n independent sets (with no edges within any set) if and only if it can be colored using n colors such that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

label: SimpleGraph.pathGraph
slogan: The path graph on n vertices is a simple graph where the vertices are the numbers 0 through n-1, and each vertex is connected only to the next one in sequence, forming a straight path. It is built using the natural ordering of the finite set of numbers less than n. This graph represents the covering relation of the partial order on these numbers.

label: SimpleGraph.sum_degrees_eq_twice_card_edges
slogan: In a finite simple graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges. Each edge contributes to the degree of two vertices, so it is counted twice in the total sum of degrees. This result is known as the handshaking lemma.

label: SimpleGraph.sum_degrees_support_eq_twice_card_edges
slogan: The sum of the degrees of all vertices that are part of at least one edge equals twice the number of edges in the graph.

label: SimpleGraph.turanDensity
slogan: The Turán density of a simple graph H is the limiting value of the ratio of the maximum number of edges in an H-free graph on n vertices to the total number of possible edges on n vertices, as n grows large. This limit always exists and is a real number between 0 and 1. It measures how dense a graph can become without containing a copy of H.

label: SimpleGraph.turanGraph
slogan: The turanGraph function creates a simple graph with n vertices, structured to have as many edges as possible without forming a clique of size r+1. It uses numbers from 0 to n-1 as vertices and connects them in a way that avoids complete subgraphs of r+1 nodes. This graph is a standard example in extremal graph theory for maximizing edges under clique restrictions.

label: SimpleGraph.tutte
slogan: A graph has a perfect matching if and only if, for every subset of vertices, removing that subset leaves at most as many odd-sized connected components as the number of removed vertices. This condition ensures the graph can be fully paired up without leftovers. The theorem uses the absence of a "Tutte violator" — a subset that would break this rule — to confirm the existence of such a matching.

label: SimpleGraph.vertexCoverNum
slogan: The vertex cover number of a simple graph G is the smallest number of vertices needed to touch every edge, where the count can be a natural number or infinity. It is defined as the infimum of the sizes of all vertex covers of G, with sizes measured as extended natural numbers.

label: SimplyConnectedSpace
slogan: A simply connected space is a topological space where any two points can be connected by a path, and every loop can be continuously shrunk to a point, meaning there are no holes. This is equivalent to saying its fundamental groupoid has only one unique path (up to equivalence) between any two points, and no nontrivial loops. In simpler terms, the space is path-connected and has trivial fundamental group.

label: SimplyConnectedSpace.instPathConnectedSpace
slogan: A simply connected space is always path-connected, meaning that for any two points in the space, there exists a continuous path between them. This follows from the fact that a simply connected space has exactly one homotopy class of paths between any two points. The result is derived from the equivalence between simply connected spaces and those having unique path homotopy classes.

label: SimplyConnectedSpace.ofContractible
slogan: If a topological space is contractible, meaning it can be continuously shrunk to a point, then it is simply connected, meaning all loops in the space can be continuously contracted to a point. This is because being contractible implies the space has the same connectivity properties as a single point.

label: SmoothPartitionOfUnity
slogan: A smooth partition of unity on a set s is a collection of infinitely differentiable, nonnegative functions such that at each point in s, their values add up to exactly one, while their total sum at any point never exceeds one, and only finitely many functions are nonzero in a neighborhood of any point. These functions are defined on a manifold modeled on a normed real vector space, with smoothness ensured by the structure of the space. The set s is typically the entire space unless specified otherwise.

label: SmoothPartitionOfUnity.IsSubordinate
slogan: A smooth partition of unity is subordinate to a family of sets U i if, for each i, the closure of the set where the function f i is nonzero is contained within U i.

label: SmoothPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate
slogan: On a smooth manifold that is also a paracompact and Hausdorff space, for any closed subset and any open cover of that subset, there exists a smooth partition of unity indexed by the same set as the cover, such that each function in the partition has its support contained in one of the open sets of the cover.

label: SpectralSpace
slogan: A spectral space is a topological space that is compact, T0, has a basis of compact open sets closed under finite intersections, every nonempty irreducible closed set has a generic point, and the intersection of any two quasi-compact open sets is quasi-compact. It combines compactness, separation, and algebraic-like structure on open sets. Such spaces often arise in algebraic geometry and logic.

label: StandardBorelSpace
slogan: A StandardBorelSpace is a measurable space that can be matched with the Borel sets of a Polish space, meaning it has a nice structure for doing measure theory and probability. It ensures the measurable sets come from a topology that is second-countable and completely metrizable. This compatibility allows the use of powerful tools from analysis and descriptive set theory.

label: StandardBorelSpace.prod
slogan: If two spaces each have a well-behaved measurable structure known as standard Borel, then the space of pairs formed by taking one element from each also has the same kind of well-behaved structure. This result holds because the product of the underlying Polish spaces (complete, separable metric spaces) remains Polish, and the measurable sets in the product match the expected Borel structure. The construction ensures that standard Borel properties are preserved when forming product spaces.

label: StandardSubspace
slogan: A standard subspace S of a complex inner product space H is a closed real subspace such that S and iS (the set of elements multiplied by the imaginary unit) intersect only at zero and together span the entire space. This means S contains no nonzero elements that are purely imaginary multiples of each other and that every element in H can be written as the sum of an element in S and one in iS. The structure combines algebraic, topological, and geometric conditions on subspaces of complex vector spaces with an inner product.

label: StarAlgEquiv
slogan: A StarAlgEquiv is a bijective function between two star algebras that preserves addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and the star operation. It ensures that the structure and involution are maintained, meaning f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b), f(a * b) = f(a) * f(b), f(r * a) = r * f(a), and f(star(a)) = star(f(a)). This makes it an isomorphism respecting both algebra and star operations.

label: StarAlgHom
slogan: A StarAlgHom is a function between two algebras that preserves addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and the star operation (like complex conjugation). It works over a base commutative semiring R and ensures the function respects both algebra structure and the involution. This means it is both an algebra homomorphism and star-preserving.

label: StarConvex
slogan: A set is star-convex if there is a fixed point in the set such that, for every other point in the set, the straight line segment from the fixed point to that point (using scalar multiples from 0 to 1) stays entirely within the set. This relies on a structure where scalars form a semiring with a partial order, and the space is a commutative monoid with a scalar multiplication action. The condition ensures convexity-like behavior relative to one chosen base point.

label: StarModule
slogan: A StarModule is a type where elements can be multiplied by scalars and also have a star operation (like complex conjugation), and applying the star to a scaled element is the same as scaling the starred element with the starred scalar. This means star commutes with scalar multiplication in a specific way. It applies to structures like complex vector spaces with conjugate-linearity.

label: StarSubalgebra.cstarAlgebra
slogan: A StarSubalgebra is a subset of a C*-algebra that is closed under addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and the star operation, and when it is also topologically closed, it forms a C*-algebra in its own right using the same norm and operations as the larger algebra.

label: StarSubalgebra.to_cstarRing
slogan: A StarSubalgebra is a subset of an algebra that is closed under addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and the star operation, and when it inherits the norm from the larger space, it satisfies the C*-identity, making it a C*-ring. This means the subalgebra has all the structure needed to be a complete normed *-algebra with the C* property. The instance shows that any such subalgebra naturally carries the structure of a CStarRing.

label: StieltjesFunction.measure
slogan: Given a non-decreasing function on a linearly ordered topological space, this construction produces a Borel measure by first defining an outer measure from the function's jumps over intervals and then restricting it to measurable sets. The measure of an interval [a, b) is the difference in the function's value at b and a. This measure is defined on all Borel sets and matches the intuitive size of intervals based on the function.

label: StieltjesFunction.outer
slogan: Given a function that assigns lengths to half-open intervals on a linearly ordered topological space, the outer measure is built by covering arbitrary subsets with such intervals and taking the smallest possible sum of lengths. This outer measure is defined for all subsets and satisfies countable subadditivity. It extends the interval lengths in a consistent way using the order and topology of the space.

label: Stirling.factorial_isEquivalent_stirling
slogan: The factorial of a natural number n grows similarly to the expression sqrt(2 * pi * n) * (n / e)^n as n gets very large, meaning their ratio gets closer and closer to 1. This is a precise way of saying that the factorial function is well-approximated by this formula for large values of n.

label: Stirling.le_factorial_stirling
slogan: For any natural number n, n factorial is at least the square root of 2 times pi times n, multiplied by (n divided by e) to the power of n.

label: Stirling.le_log_factorial_stirling
slogan: For any positive natural number n, the logarithm of n factorial is at least as big as n times the log of n minus n, plus half the log of n, plus half the log of 2 times pi. This gives a lower bound for log(n!) based on Stirling's approximation. The bound becomes tighter as n increases.

label: Stirling.stirlingSeq
slogan: stirlingSeq is a function that takes a natural number n and returns a real number approximation of n factorial using Stirling's formula, which involves multiplying the square root of 2 * pi * n by (n/e)^n. It automatically converts natural numbers to reals when needed and uses real exponentiation and square roots. This approximation becomes more accurate as n gets larger.

label: StoneCech
slogan: The StoneCech operation takes a topological space and produces a compact Hausdorff space by first extending the space using ultrafilters and then applying a quotient to ensure the Hausdorff property. Continuous functions from the original space to any compact Hausdorff space can be uniquely extended to the StoneCech compactification. This makes the StoneCech space a universal compactification for the given space.

label: Stream'
slogan: Stream' is a type that represents an infinite sequence of values of a given type, where elements are computed only when needed. It allows handling infinite data efficiently by generating values on demand. The type takes another type as input and produces a type representing its infinite streams.

label: StrictConvex
slogan: A set is strictly convex if, for any two different points in the set, every point on the line segment between them (excluding the endpoints) lies inside the interior of the set. This means the set contains no line segments on its boundary. The definition uses a scalar multiplication structure, a topology, and a semiring to define combinations of points along line segments.

label: StrictConvex.extremePoints_eq_diff_interior
slogan: For a strictly convex set in a real normed space, the extreme points are exactly those points that are in the set but not in its interior. This means a point is extreme if it lies on the boundary and cannot be inside any open line segment between two points of the set. Thus, the set of extreme points equals the set minus its interior.

label: StrictConvexSpace.extremePoints_closedBall_eq_sphere
slogan: In a strictly convex real normed space with more than one point, the extreme points of a closed ball (the points that don't lie on any nontrivial line segment inside the ball) are exactly the points on the sphere (those at distance exactly equal to the radius from the center).

label: StrictMono
slogan: StrictMono is a property of a function between two preordered types, saying that if one input is strictly less than another, then the output for the first input is also strictly less than the output for the second. It ensures the function preserves strict order in a consistent way.

label: StrictMono.orderIsoOfSurjective
slogan: A strictly increasing function that maps every element of one linearly ordered set to another preordered set, covering all elements in the target, creates a one-to-one correspondence that preserves the order both ways, and this correspondence is an order isomorphism.

label: StrictMonoOn.orderIso
slogan: A strictly increasing function on a subset of a linearly ordered set sets up a one-to-one correspondence between that subset and its image, where the order of elements is preserved so that one element is less than another if and only if their images are in the same order.

label: StrongDual.polar
slogan: The polar of a set in a topological module consists of all continuous linear functionals that, when applied to elements of the set, yield values whose absolute values are at most 1. This construction uses the pairing between the module and its strong dual, where the dual space carries the topology of uniform convergence on bounded sets. It is a tool for studying duality, convexity, and topological properties in functional analysis over normed rings.

label: StructureGroupoid
slogan: A structure groupoid is a set of invertible, continuous maps between open parts of a topological space that includes the identity maps, and is closed under composing maps, inverting them, and restricting them to smaller open sets. These maps must preserve the topology, meaning both the map and its inverse are continuous. It provides a way to define consistent geometric structures on manifolds by specifying which coordinate changes are allowed.

label: StructureGroupoid.maximalAtlas
slogan: The maximal atlas for a structure groupoid on a manifold is the set of all open partial homeomorphisms from the manifold to a model space such that, on every small enough open set, the transition maps between charts are included in the given groupoid. It collects all charts that are compatible with the geometric structure enforced by the groupoid, forming the largest possible consistent collection of such charts.

label: Subalgebra
slogan: A Subalgebra is a subset of an algebra that includes zero and one, is closed under addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication, and maintains the same algebraic structure as the larger algebra. It must also be compatible with the map that embeds the base ring into the algebra. This means it acts like a smaller algebra inside a larger one, preserving all necessary operations and identities.

label: Subalgebra.SeparatesPoints
slogan: A subalgebra of continuous functions separates points if, for any two different points in the space, there is a continuous function in the subalgebra that takes different values at those points, meaning the functions can distinguish between all pairs of points.

label: Subgroup
slogan: A subgroup is a subset of a group that includes the identity element, is closed under the group's operation (so combining any two elements in the subset stays in the subset), and contains the inverse of each of its elements. This means the subset itself forms a group using the same operation as the larger group.

label: Subgroup.Normal
slogan: A normal subgroup is a subgroup H of a group G such that for every element g in G, the set gH (multiplying H by g on the left) is the same as the set Hg (multiplying H by g on the right). This condition allows the collection of cosets (shifts of H) to form a group under multiplication, called the quotient group. Normal subgroups are exactly those subgroups for which this quotient construction works.

label: Subgroup.card_subgroup_dvd_card
slogan: In a finite group, the number of elements in any subgroup divides the total number of elements in the group. For example, if a group has 12 elements, any subgroup must have a size that is a divisor of 12, such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12. This is known as Lagrange's theorem.

label: Subgroup.center
slogan: The center of a group G is the set of elements that commute with every other element in G, meaning for any element x in the center and any element y in G, x * y equals y * x. This set includes the identity, is closed under multiplication and taking inverses, and thus forms a subgroup of G. It is defined for any type G that has a group structure with associative multiplication, an identity, and inverses.

label: Subgroup.closure
slogan: The closure of a subset of a group is the smallest subgroup that contains all elements of the subset, along with their inverses and all products formed from them. It is built by including every element needed to satisfy the group operations and is uniquely determined by the subset. This closure is always a subgroup and can be thought of as the intersection of all subgroups containing the given set.

label: Subgroup.connectedComponentOfOne
slogan: The connected component of the identity element in a topological group is the largest set containing the identity that cannot be split into separate open pieces, and this set is itself a subgroup because it is closed under multiplication and taking inverses. It is formed using the topology of the space and the group operations, relying on continuity of multiplication and inversion. This subgroup consists of all elements that are in the same connected piece as the identity.

label: Subgroup.equivSMul
slogan: When a group acts on another group by multiplication in a way that respects the group structure, multiplying all elements of a subgroup by a fixed element produces another subgroup, and this operation gives a one-to-one correspondence between the original subgroup and the new one, preserving the group operation.

label: Subgroup.exists_right_complement'_of_coprime
slogan: If a normal subgroup H of a group G has an order that shares no common factors with its index in G (other than 1), then there exists another subgroup K such that every element of G can be uniquely written as a product of an element of H and an element of K, and H and K share only the identity element.

label: Subgroup.groupEquivQuotientProdSubgroup
slogan: There is a one-to-one match between elements of a group and pairs made up of a coset of a subgroup and an element of that subgroup. Each group element corresponds uniquely to a combination of a coset and a representative difference from that coset. This lets the group be broken down into parts based on the subgroup and its cosets.

label: Subgroup.index_mul_card
slogan: In a finite group, the total number of elements equals the number of elements in a subgroup multiplied by how many copies of that subgroup fit inside the whole group.

label: Subgroup.isClosed_of_discrete
slogan: In a Hausdorff topological group, any subgroup that has the discrete topology—where each point is isolated—is a closed set. This means if the relative topology on the subgroup makes every point open, then the subgroup contains all its limit points in the ambient group. The result connects discreteness in topology with closure properties in topological groups.

label: Subgroup.isCyclic
slogan: A subgroup is cyclic if all its elements can be written as powers of a single element from the group. This means there exists some element g such that every member of the subgroup is g raised to some integer power, positive, negative, or zero. The subgroup formed by all such powers of g is called the zpowers of g, and if a subgroup equals this set, it is cyclic.

label: Subgroup.isNilpotent
slogan: Any subgroup of a nilpotent group is also nilpotent, because the process of taking commutators eventually leads to the trivial subgroup in both the original group and its subgroup. This happens since the commutator structure of the subgroup is inherited from the larger group.

label: Subgroup.is_normal_topologicalClosure
slogan: The closure of a normal subgroup in a topological group, when equipped with the topology, is still a normal subgroup. This is because conjugation is continuous in topological groups, and continuous functions preserve closure under group operations. Thus, the closed set obtained by taking the closure remains invariant under conjugation.

label: Subgroup.le_zpowers_iff
slogan: A subgroup is contained in the cyclic subgroup generated by powers of an element g if and only if it is itself generated by some power of g.

label: Subgroup.relIndex_mul_index
slogan: If K is a subgroup of H and H is a subgroup of G, then the number of cosets of K in G equals the number of cosets of H in G multiplied by the number of cosets of K in H. This holds for both finite and infinite groups by using cardinal numbers to represent sizes.

label: Subgroup.toCommGroup
slogan: If a subgroup consists of elements that all commute with each other, then that subgroup can be given the structure of a commutative group. This is done by treating the subgroup as a subtype of the original group and defining the group operations on it. The instance Subgroup.toCommGroup provides this commutative group structure when the elements of the subgroup satisfy the required commutativity condition.

label: Subgroup.topologicalClosure
slogan: The topological closure of a subgroup in a topological group is the smallest closed set containing that subgroup, and it still satisfies the group properties: it includes the identity, is closed under multiplication, and contains inverses of all its elements. Because the group operations are continuous, this closure itself forms a subgroup. It combines the algebraic structure of the subgroup with the topological notion of closure.

label: Subgroup.zpowers
slogan: The zpowers of an element g in a group are the set of all integer powers of g, including g raised to positive, negative, and zero exponents. This set forms a subgroup because it contains the identity element, is closed under the group operation, and includes the inverse of each of its elements. It is defined as the range of the function that maps each integer n to g raised to the power n.

label: Sublattice
slogan: A sublattice is a subset of a lattice that is closed under the meet (inf) and join (sup) operations, so combining any two elements in the subset using these operations gives another element that is still in the subset. It uses the same meet and join operations as the original lattice.

label: Submodule
slogan: A submodule is a subset of a module that includes zero and stays closed under addition and scalar multiplication, meaning adding two elements in the subset or multiplying an element by a scalar keeps the result in the subset. It must support the operations of a semiring acting on an additive commutative monoid. This structure combines the properties of an additive submonoid and a substructure closed under scalar multiplication.

label: Submodule.ClosedComplemented.of_finiteDimensional
slogan: In a finite-dimensional normed vector space over a complete normed field, every closed subspace has a closed complementary subspace, and there exists a continuous linear projection onto that subspace.

label: Submodule.IsLattice
slogan: A submodule M of a module V over a ring R is called a lattice if it is finitely generated and its elements can combine using scalars from a larger ring A to produce every element of V. The ring A is typically the fraction field of R, and the structure ensures compatibility between scalar multiplication by R and A. This definition uses an output parameter for A to help Lean infer types correctly during type class resolution.

label: Submodule.IsOrtho
slogan: Two submodules are orthogonal if every vector in one has an inner product of zero with every vector in the other, meaning they are perpendicular. This is defined by saying one submodule is contained in the orthogonal complement of the other, where the orthogonal complement consists of all vectors that have zero inner product with each vector in the original submodule. The definition relies on the structure of submodules and the properties of the inner product space.

label: Submodule.LinearDisjoint
slogan: Two submodules are linearly disjoint if the only way to write zero as a sum of one element from each submodule is when both elements are zero, meaning their intersection contains only zero and they do not otherwise overlap.

label: Submodule.Quotient.completeSpace
slogan: If a normed module is complete and you take a quotient by one of its submodules, then the resulting quotient space is also complete, meaning every Cauchy sequence in the quotient converges to a point in the quotient. This happens because the original space's norm and completeness carry over to the quotient structure. The submodule must be compatible with the module's operations, and the quotient inherits both the algebraic and topological properties.

label: Submodule.basisOfPid
slogan: Every submodule of a free module with finite basis over a principal ideal domain has a basis indexed by a finite set of natural numbers, meaning it is freely generated by a linearly independent set of elements. The function returns both the size of this basis and the basis itself as a structured object. This works because modules over PIDs have strong structure theorems ensuring the existence of such bases.

label: Submodule.comapMkQRelIso
slogan: The function Submodule.comapMkQRelIso sets up a one-to-one match between submodules of the quotient module M/p and submodules of M that contain p. Each submodule in the quotient corresponds to a unique submodule in M that includes all elements of p, and this correspondence respects subset inclusion and module operations. This means taking preimages under the quotient map gives a structure-preserving bijection between these two collections of submodules.

label: Submodule.dualAnnihilator
slogan: The dual annihilator of a submodule W consists of all linear functionals that send every element of W to zero. It forms a submodule of the dual space, which is the space of all linear maps from the original module to the ring. This construction identifies the functionals that vanish on W, linking submodules to their corresponding kernels in the dual space.

label: Submodule.dualAnnihilator_sup_eq
slogan: The set of linear functionals that vanish on the sum of two submodules is exactly the set of functionals that vanish on each submodule individually. In other words, a functional kills the sum U + V if and only if it kills both U and V. This means the annihilator of the sum equals the intersection of the annihilators.

label: Submodule.dualQuotEquivDualAnnihilator
slogan: The dual of the quotient of a module by a submodule consists of all linear functionals on the original module that vanish on the submodule, and this correspondence is a natural isomorphism. Every such functional on the quotient space is uniquely determined by a functional on the whole module that sends elements of the submodule to zero. This isomorphism is formed by composing functionals with the projection map from the module to its quotient.

label: Submodule.eq_bot_of_le_smul_of_le_jacobson_bot
slogan: If a finitely generated submodule is contained in its scalar multiple by an ideal that lies within the Jacobson radical of the ring, then the submodule must be the zero submodule. This means the only such submodule satisfying this containment condition is the trivial one.

label: Submodule.eq_smul_of_le_smul_of_le_jacobson
slogan: If a finitely generated submodule N is contained in the product of an ideal I and itself, and I is inside the Jacobson radical of another ideal J, then N must equal J times N; in particular, if J is the whole ring, this forces N to be zero.

label: Submodule.finrank_le
slogan: If a module has a finite basis, then any submodule inside it also has a finite basis, and the number of basis vectors in the submodule is less than or equal to the number in the whole module.

label: Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank
slogan: For a finite-dimensional module over a ring, the dimension of a submodule plus the dimension of the quotient space equals the dimension of the whole module. This means splitting a module into a submodule and its quotient preserves total dimension. Dimensions are treated as natural numbers added in the usual way.

label: Submodule.finrank_sup_add_finrank_inf_eq
slogan: For two submodules of a finite-dimensional vector space, the sum of their dimensions is equal to the dimension of their sum plus the dimension of their intersection.

label: Submodule.instIsModularLattice
slogan: The collection of all submodules of a module forms a lattice where the sum and intersection of submodules follow the modular law: if one submodule is contained in another, then adding it to the intersection of two others gives the same result as intersecting the sums. This lattice structure is built using the module's addition and scalar multiplication, with inclusion defining the order. Meet is intersection, join is sum, and the modular identity holds due to the algebraic properties of submodules.

label: Submodule.isCompl_orthogonal_of_hasOrthogonalProjection
slogan: If a submodule has an orthogonal projection in a real-like inner product space, then the submodule and its orthogonal complement intersect only at zero and together span the whole space, meaning every vector can be written uniquely as a sum of one vector from the submodule and one from its orthogonal complement.

label: Submodule.isLasker
slogan: In a Noetherian module over a commutative ring, every submodule can be expressed as an intersection of finitely many primary submodules. This means that submodules in such well-behaved algebraic structures can always be broken down into simpler, primary components. The result generalizes the idea of factoring ideals to more general module settings.

label: Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right
slogan: A vector v is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by a single vector u if and only if the inner product of u and v is zero. This means v is perpendicular to u when their inner product vanishes. The result holds in inner product spaces over star rings with appropriate algebraic structure.

label: Submodule.orthogonal
slogan: The orthogonal complement of a submodule K in an inner product space is the set of all vectors that are perpendicular to every vector in K, meaning their inner product with each vector in K is zero. This set itself forms a submodule. It is defined using the inner product's properties like linearity and the fact that only the zero vector has zero length.

label: Submodule.orthogonalProjection
slogan: Given a vector in an inner product space and a closed subspace, the orthogonal projection sends the vector to the nearest point in the subspace, and the difference between the original vector and its projection is perpendicular to every vector in the subspace.

label: Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal_eq_closure
slogan: In an inner product space where the space is complete, the set of all vectors perpendicular to the vectors that are perpendicular to a given submodule equals the closure of that submodule. This means double orthogonality recovers the smallest closed set containing the submodule. The result depends on the inner product and the completeness of the space.

label: Submodule.quotientQuotientEquivQuotient
slogan: If S and T are submodules of a module M with S contained in T, then the quotient of the quotient module (M/S) by the image of T in M/S is isomorphic to the direct quotient M/T. This isomorphism respects the module structure over the ring R, meaning it preserves addition and scalar multiplication. It provides a natural way to simplify a double quotient into a single quotient.

label: Submodule.reflection
slogan: Submodule.reflection defines a function that flips a vector over a given submodule in an inner product space by using the orthogonal projection. The reflection is calculated by taking the original vector and subtracting twice its component that lies in the direction perpendicular to the submodule. This operation is a linear and norm-preserving transformation that maps the space onto itself.

label: Submodule.reflection_inv
slogan: Reflecting a vector across a submodule in an inner product space is an invertible operation, and the inverse of the reflection is the reflection itself, so applying it twice gives back the original vector. This reflection is a linear isometry, meaning it preserves distances and the vector space structure, and it works for real-like scalar types when orthogonal projections onto the submodule exist.

label: Submodule.reflection_involutive
slogan: Reflecting a vector across a submodule twice brings it back to itself, as long as the submodule has an orthogonal projection. The reflection flips the part of the vector perpendicular to the submodule, and doing it again reverses the flip. This operation preserves distances and linearity.

label: Submodule.span
slogan: The span of a set in a module is the smallest submodule containing that set, made by taking all linear combinations of the set's elements using scalars from the semiring. It can also be defined as the intersection of all submodules that include the set, ensuring it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

label: Submodule.starProjection_minimal
slogan: The distance from a vector y to its projection onto a complete, nonempty submodule U is the smallest possible distance from y to any point in U. This minimum distance is equal to the infimum of the distances from y to all points in U. The projection achieves this minimum because the difference between y and its projection is orthogonal to every vector in U.

label: Submodule.sup_orthogonal_of_hasOrthogonalProjection
slogan: If a submodule has a well-defined orthogonal projection in an inner product space, then the sum of the submodule and its orthogonal complement equals the entire space. This means every vector in the space can be written as the sum of one vector from the submodule and one from its orthogonal complement. The result depends on the existence of unique closest points in the submodule for any vector in the space.

label: Submodule.toAffineSubspace
slogan: Given a submodule of a module over a ring, the toAffineSubspace operation produces an affine subspace by treating the submodule as a flat subset that may not include the origin; this affine subspace consists of all points that can be reached by translating elements of the submodule by a fixed vector, and it remains closed under combinations where the coefficients sum to one.

label: Submonoid
slogan: A submonoid is a subset of a type that includes the multiplicative identity (one) and is closed under multiplication, meaning multiplying any two elements in the subset gives another element in the subset. It requires the underlying type to have a multiplication operation and a one element that acts as an identity. This structure allows the subset to form a monoid with the same operations as the original type.

label: Subring
slogan: A subring is a subset of a ring that includes zero and one, is closed under addition, multiplication, and additive inverses, and inherits the ring structure from the larger set. It is both an additive subgroup and a subsemiring. This means it supports all the basic arithmetic operations and forms a ring on its own using the same operations as the original.

label: Subring.center
slogan: The center of a subring consists of all elements that commute with every element in the subring under multiplication, meaning the order of multiplication does not matter. This set forms a subring itself, containing the multiplicative identity and closed under addition, multiplication, and negation. It is defined using the general concept of the center applied to the multiplicative structure of the subring.

label: Subsemigroup
slogan: A Subsemigroup is a subset of a type that has a multiplication operation, where multiplying any two elements in the subset gives a result that is also in the subset. It requires the type to support multiplication via the Mul typeclass. This is used to work with multiplicative structures in algebra.

label: Subtype.countable
slogan: If a type has countably many elements, then any subset of that type—defined by a specific condition on its elements—is also countable. This is because the mapping from the subset to the original type is one-to-one, and a one-to-one image of a countable set is countable.

label: Subtype.partialOrder
slogan: If a type has a partial order and you take a subset of its elements defined by a condition, then that subset also has a partial order where elements are compared using the original ordering. This induced order on the subset is defined by comparing elements through their inclusion into the original type. The ordering works because the inclusion map is injective, ensuring distinct elements in the subset remain distinguishable.

label: Summable
slogan: A function is summable if the sums of its values over larger and larger finite subsets get arbitrarily close to some value in a topological space where addition is commutative and continuous. This means the infinite sum can be defined as the limit of these finite sums, using a specific way of growing the subsets. The sum, written as tsum, exists and equals that limit when the function is summable.

label: Summable.norm
slogan: If the sum of the sizes (norms) of a sequence of vectors in a finite-dimensional real vector space converges, then the sum of the vectors themselves converges to a well-defined limit in that space.

label: Summable.of_norm
slogan: If the sum of the absolute values of a function's outputs converges, and the space is complete (meaning all Cauchy sequences converge), then the function itself can be summed over an infinite set and the sum will converge. This applies to functions taking values in a complete normed abelian group. The convergence of the sum is guaranteed by the behavior of the norms and the completeness of the space.

label: Summable.tendsto_atTop_zero
slogan: If a sequence of elements in a topological abelian group can be summed to a well-defined limit, then the individual terms of the sequence must eventually get and stay arbitrarily close to zero. This means that for any neighborhood around zero, all but finitely many terms of the sequence lie inside that neighborhood. The result holds because, in the natural numbers, being eventually in every large set (atTop) is the same as being outside only finitely many elements (cofinite).

label: Summable.tsum_mul_tsum_eq_tsum_sum_antidiagonal
slogan: If two sequences of numbers can be summed to finite values, then the product of their total sums equals the sum of all products of pairs of terms where the indices add up to the same number, grouped by those index sums. This holds in a setting where addition and multiplication are continuous and behave well with limits. The result rigorously links the multiplication of infinite series to summing over diagonal slices of index pairs.

label: Summable.tsum_prod
slogan: If a function defined on a product of two index sets is summable in a complete uniform additive group, then the total sum over all pairs equals the iterated sum where you first sum over one index, then the other. This means summing f(b, c) over all b and c can be done by summing over b first and then c, or vice versa. The result holds in spaces where addition is well-behaved and limits of partial sums exist.

label: SupIrred
slogan: A sup-irreducible element is one that is not the least upper bound of any set of smaller elements, and it is not the smallest element in the order.

label: SupPrime.supIrred
slogan: If an element is sup-prime in a semilattice with a supremum operation, then it is also sup-irreducible, meaning it cannot be expressed as the join of two strictly smaller elements.

label: Sylow
slogan: A Sylow p-subgroup of a finite group G is a subgroup whose order is the largest power of a prime p that divides the order of G. These subgroups are guaranteed to exist for every prime p dividing the group's order, and they help in understanding the structure of finite groups. The declaration defines a type representing such Sylow subgroups within the framework of group theory.

label: Sylow.card_dvd_index
slogan: In a finite group, the number of Sylow p-subgroups divides the index of any Sylow p-subgroup, meaning this count is a factor of how many times the subgroup fits inside the whole group, when p is a prime dividing the group's order.

label: Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity
slogan: In a finite group, the size of any Sylow p-subgroup is the highest power of the prime p that divides the group's order, and this power is given by the exponent of p in the prime factorization of the group's size.

label: Sylow.conj_eq_normalizer_conj_of_mem
slogan: If two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate and an element of one is contained in the other, then the conjugation can be achieved using an element from the normalizer of their intersection. This means the transformation between the subgroups respects the symmetry of their common part. The result applies in finite groups where the subgroup order is a power of a prime p.

label: Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime
slogan: If a finite group has a size that is divisible by a power of a prime number p^k, then the group must have a subgroup whose size is exactly p^k. This applies to any prime p and any exponent k where p^k divides the total number of elements in the group.

label: Sylow.isPretransitive_of_finite
slogan: If G is a finite group and p is a prime number, then any two Sylow p-subgroups of G are conjugate to each other via an element of G. This means the group action of conjugation by G permutes the Sylow p-subgroups transitively. The result relies on the finiteness of G and basic properties of prime numbers.

label: Sylow.nonempty
slogan: For any prime number p and any finite group G, there is always at least one subgroup of G whose size is the largest power of p that divides the order of G. This subgroup is called a Sylow p-subgroup, and the result guarantees its existence without showing how to build it.

label: Sylow.normal_of_subsingleton
slogan: If a Sylow subgroup is the only one of its kind in the group (meaning there can be at most one such subgroup for a given prime), then it is a normal subgroup. This is because having only one Sylow subgroup forces it to be invariant under all automorphisms (making it characteristic), and characteristic subgroups are always normal.

label: Sylow.normalizer_sup_eq_top
slogan: If a subgroup is contained in a Sylow p-subgroup of a normal subgroup N, then the normalizer of that subgroup, when combined with N, generates the entire group. This means no proper subgroup can contain both N and the normalizer unless it is the whole group. It shows how Sylow subgroups and normalizers interact to control group structure.

label: Sylow.normalizer_sup_eq_top'
slogan: If a Sylow p-subgroup P is contained in a normal subgroup N of a group G, then the normalizer of P in G together with N generates the whole group G. This means that any element of G can be expressed as a combination of elements from N and elements that normalize P. The result helps determine when a Sylow subgroup is normal by examining how its normalizer interacts with other subgroups.

label: Sylow.stabilizer_eq_normalizer
slogan: In a group, the set of elements that leave a Sylow subgroup unchanged when conjugating it is exactly the same as the set of elements that normalize that subgroup. This means stabilizing the subgroup under conjugation is equivalent to being in its normalizer. The equality follows directly from the definitions of stabilizer and normalizer in group actions.

label: Sym
slogan: Sym takes a type and a natural number n, and represents the collection of unordered n-tuples of elements from that type, where rearranging the elements doesn't change the tuple. It is based on multisets, ensuring that two tuples are the same if they contain the same elements regardless of order. For pairs, it ensures (a, b) is treated exactly the same as (b, a).

label: Sym.card_sym_eq_choose
slogan: The number of ways to choose k elements from a finite set of size n, where order doesn't matter and repetition is allowed, is equal to the binomial coefficient (n + k - 1) choose k. This count depends only on the size of the set and the number of elements to choose. It is known as the stars and bars formula.

label: Sym.card_sym_eq_multichoose
slogan: For a finite set with n elements, the number of ways to choose k elements where order does not matter and repetitions are allowed is equal to the multichoose of n and k. This count is the same regardless of the specific elements in the set, only depending on how many there are.

label: Symmetric
slogan: A relation r is symmetric if whenever r is true for elements a and b, it is also true for b and a. This means that the order of the elements does not matter for the relation. The definition applies to any type α and any relation r from α to α returning a proposition.

label: SymmetricAlgebra
slogan: The symmetric algebra of a module M over a commutative semiring R is constructed by taking the tensor algebra of M and imposing the relation that elements of M commute with each other. This results in an algebra where the order of multiplication of elements from M does not matter. It is a way of building a commutative algebra from M that supports linear operations over R.

label: SymmetricPower
slogan: The symmetric power of a module M over a commutative semiring R, indexed by a type ι, is the space of tensors of degree ι modulo the equivalence relation that identifies two tensors if one can be obtained from the other by permuting the indices. It is constructed as a quotient of the tensor product of copies of M indexed by ι. This object inherits a module structure over R and supports linear combinations that respect symmetry under index permutations.

label: T0Space
slogan: A T0Space is a topological space where for any two different points, there is an open set that contains one point but not the other. This means no two distinct points have the same collection of neighborhoods, so each point can be distinguished from the others by the open sets it belongs to.

label: T1Space
slogan: A T1Space is a topological space where every set containing just one point is closed, meaning its complement is an open set. This property builds on the existing structure of open and closed sets defined by a topology. In such a space, for any point, the set containing only that point is considered closed.

label: T25Space
slogan: A T25 space is a topological space where every point and disjoint closed set can be separated by disjoint open sets, and one of those open sets must belong to a neighborhood base defined using filters. This condition is stronger than regularity but weaker than complete regularity. It relies on the concepts of topological spaces and filters to formalize local separation properties.

label: T25Space.t2Space
slogan: A T25 space is a topological space where points and disjoint closed sets can be separated by open neighborhoods, using a filter-based definition of neighborhoods, and this property ensures the space is also Hausdorff (T2), meaning any two distinct points have non-overlapping neighborhoods.

label: T2Space
slogan: A T2Space is a topological space where any two different points can each be contained in an open set that does not overlap with the other, meaning they can be separated by non-overlapping neighborhoods. This condition is known as the Hausdorff property. It requires both the structure of a topological space and the logical requirement that this separation holds for every pair of distinct points.

label: T2Space.r1Space
slogan: In a Hausdorff space, any two different points can be separated by non-overlapping open sets, and this property ensures that the space also satisfies the weaker R1 condition, where topologically distinguishable points can be separated by disjoint neighborhoods.

label: T2Space.t1Space
