This means the space has a basis of mutually perpendicular unit vectors that can approximate any element arbitrarily well. Such a basis allows the space to be represented as a sequence space of square-summable functions.

label: exists_increasing_or_nonincreasing_subseq
slogan: Every sequence of elements in a type with a transitive relation has a subsequence that is either entirely increasing or entirely non-increasing with respect to that relation.

label: exists_integral_inj_algHom_of_fg
slogan: For any finitely generated algebra A over a field k, there is some number s and an injective algebra homomorphism from the polynomial ring k[X0, ..., X(s-1)] into A such that every element of A is integral over the image of that polynomial ring.

label: exists_isMIntegralCurveAt_of_contMDiffAt
slogan: For a continuously differentiable vector field on a smooth manifold, there exists a curve passing through a given point at a given time that follows the direction of the vector field in a neighborhood of that point, provided the point is in the interior and the model space is complete. The curve starts at the specified point and matches the vector field's direction in local coordinates around that point. This guarantees local solutions to the flow defined by the vector field.

label: exists_isTranscendenceBasis
slogan: In any algebra over a commutative ring where the scalar action is faithful, there exists a set of algebraically independent elements such that every element of the algebra can be expressed as a combination of these using polynomial operations. This set forms a transcendence basis for the algebra. Such a basis always exists under these conditions.

label: exists_le_isAssociatedPrime_of_isNoetherianRing
slogan: In a Noetherian ring, for any nonzero element of a module, there exists a prime ideal that is the annihilator of that element and contains the annihilator of the element. This prime ideal is an associated prime of the module.

label: exists_lt_ack_of_nat_primrec
slogan: If a function f from natural numbers to natural numbers is primitive recursive, then there is some natural number m such that f(n) is less than ack(m, n) for every natural number n.

label: exists_maximal_of_chains_bounded
slogan: In any partially ordered set where every chain has an upper bound, there exists a chain that cannot be made larger without breaking the chain property, meaning no other comparable element can be added to it. This maximal chain is as large as possible while maintaining the condition that all its elements are ordered. The result ensures such a maximal chain exists if the ordering is transitive and every chain is bounded above.

label: exists_mem_Icc_isFixedPt
slogan: If a continuous function maps a closed interval [a, b] into itself and the space is densely ordered with the order topology, then there is some point c in [a, b] such that f(c) = c. This means the function has at least one fixed point in the interval. The result relies on the interval being connected and the function preserving order-related continuity.

label: exists_mem_Icc_isFixedPt_of_mapsTo
slogan: If a continuous function maps a closed interval [a, b] into itself, then there is some point c in [a, b] such that f(c) = c, meaning c is unchanged by the function. This result applies to linearly ordered spaces where between any two points there is another, and relies on the interval being closed and the function being continuous on it.

label: exists_norm_eq_iInf_of_complete_convex
slogan: In a complete and convex subset of a real inner product space, for any given point, there is a point in the subset that is closest to it, meaning the distance from the given point to this closest point equals the greatest lower bound of all possible distances to points in the subset.

label: exists_open_convex_of_notMem
slogan: If a point is not in a closed convex set in a locally convex topological vector space over an ordered field, then there is an open convex set containing the point that does not intersect the original set.

label: exists_orthonormalBasis
slogan: In a finite-dimensional real inner product space, there is always a basis where each vector has length 1 and any two different vectors are perpendicular to each other, and this basis spans the whole space.

label: exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card
slogan: In any finite group, there is an element whose order is a prime number that divides the total size of the group.

label: exists_ratio_hasDerivAt_eq_ratio_slope
slogan: If two functions are continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on the open interval inside, then there is some point between the endpoints where the ratio of their derivatives equals the ratio of their overall changes across the interval.

label: exists_taylor_mean_remainder_bound
slogan: If a function f is n+1 times continuously differentiable on the interval [a, b], then there exists a constant C such that the difference between f(x) and its nth degree Taylor polynomial at a is bounded by C * (x - a)^(n+1) for all x in [a, b].

label: exists_wellOrder
slogan: Every set can be arranged in a total order such that every non-empty subset has a smallest element, and this is done by mapping the set into the cardinal numbers with an injective function and using their natural order. The resulting order relation is well-founded, meaning there are no infinite descending chains. This guarantees the existence of a well-ordering for any set.

label: extDeriv
slogan: The exterior derivative of a differential form is defined as a sum over each input vector, where for each term, the derivative of the form is taken with respect to that vector while omitting it from the arguments, multiplied by a sign factor of (-1)^i. This operation extends a differential form of degree n to one of degree n+1 in a way that captures how the form changes across the space. It is computed using the Fréchet derivative and alternating summation over all positions in the input.

label: extDeriv_apply
slogan: The exterior derivative of a differential form at a point is computed by summing the directional derivatives of the form with respect to each vector, where each term is weighted by (-1) raised to the index of the omitted vector. This calculation involves removing one vector at a time from the input tuple and applying the derivative to the remaining tuple. The result is a new multilinear map that takes one more vector than the original form.

label: extDeriv_extDeriv
slogan: The exterior derivative of a sufficiently smooth differential form, when taken twice, always results in zero. This means that applying the exterior derivative operation to a form and then applying it again yields the zero form. The form must be at least twice continuously differentiable for this to hold.

label: extDeriv_pullback
slogan: The exterior derivative of a differential form pulled back by a smooth map is the same as pulling back the exterior derivative of the form. In other words, taking the exterior derivative and then applying a change of variables (via a smooth function) gives the same result as first changing variables and then taking the exterior derivative. This holds when the form and the map are sufficiently smooth.

label: extend_partialOrder
slogan: Any partial order on a set can be expanded to a total order on that set, so that every pair of elements can be compared without contradicting the original order.

label: exteriorPower.finrank_eq
slogan: If a module M over a nontrivial commutative ring R has finite rank r, then the dimension of the n-th exterior power of M over R is equal to the binomial coefficient "r choose n". This means the number of linearly independent n-vectors in the exterior power is the same as the number of ways to choose n elements from a set of size r. The result holds when M is finitely generated and free, with a well-defined rank.

label: fderiv_comp
slogan: The derivative of the composition of two functions at a point is the composition of their derivatives at that point, provided both functions are differentiable there. This means the rate of change of the composite function is found by applying the derivative of the outer function after the derivative of the inner function. The result is a continuous linear map that approximates the composite function near the point.

label: fderiv_mul
slogan: The derivative of the product of two functions at a point is the first function's value times the derivative of the second, plus the second function's value times the derivative of the first, provided both functions are differentiable at that point and their outputs lie in a space with a normed algebra structure over a nontrivially normed field. This product rule applies in the setting of normed vector spaces and yields a continuous linear map as the derivative of the product.

label: fderiv_pi
slogan: The derivative of a function that maps into a finite product of normed spaces is the product of the derivatives of its components, as long as each component function is differentiable at the point. This means the best linear approximation of the function at that point is built by combining the best linear approximations of each part. The result applies to functions over a nontrivially normed field and uses the standard product space structure.

label: fermatLastTheoremFor_iff_int
slogan: Fermat's Last Theorem is true for a given exponent n if and only if there are no positive integers a, b, and c such that a^n + b^n = c^n, where the numbers are considered within the set of integers. This means the theorem's validity for integers is equivalent to the non-existence of such solutions in that domain. The statement applies to natural number exponents greater than 2.

label: fermatLastTheoremFor_iff_rat
slogan: Fermat's Last Theorem for exponent n is true for rational numbers if and only if it is true for integers, meaning that the equation x^n + y^n = z^n has no solutions in positive rational numbers when n is greater than 2, just as it has no solutions in positive integers.

label: fermatLastTheoremFour
slogan: There are no positive integers a, b, c such that a^4 + b^4 = c^4. This means that the sum of two fourth powers of positive whole numbers can never equal another fourth power. It is a specific instance of Fermat's Last Theorem for the case when the exponent is 4.

label: fermatLastTheoremThree
slogan: There are no positive whole numbers a, b, and c such that a cubed plus b cubed equals c cubed. This means the equation a^3 + b^3 = c^3 has no solutions in positive integers.

label: forall_liouvilleWith_iff
slogan: A real number can be approximated by rational numbers a/b (with b > 1) better than any fixed power of 1/b if and only if it is a Liouville number. This means that being Liouville is equivalent to satisfying the Liouville approximation condition for every real exponent.

label: fourierBasis
slogan: fourierBasis is a family of complex exponential functions indexed by integers, forming a complete orthonormal basis for the space of square-integrable complex functions on the circle with period T, such that every function in this space can be uniquely represented as a convergent sum of these exponentials. This basis provides an isometric isomorphism between the function space and the sequence space of square-summable complex sequences indexed by integers. Each basis function corresponds to a character of the circle group, given by n ↦ exp(2πi n x / T).

label: fourierCoeff
slogan: The fourierCoeff function computes the n-th Fourier coefficient of a function defined on a circle of period T, by integrating the product of the function with a complex exponential wave of frequency -n over one period. The result is a value in a complex normed vector space where the function takes its values. The integral uses a normalized measure so that the total length of the circle is 1.

label: fourierIntegral_gaussian
slogan: The integral of exp(i * t * x) * exp(-b * x^2) over all real numbers x equals (pi / b)^(1/2) * exp(-t^2 / (4 * b)), provided the real part of the complex number b is positive.

label: fourierSubalgebra_closure_eq_top
slogan: The set of continuous complex-valued functions on a circle of period T, built from combinations of exponential functions like exp(2πi n x / T) for integers n, is dense in the space of all such continuous functions. This means any continuous function on the circle can be uniformly approximated by sums and products of these exponentials. The result holds because these functions separate points and form a closed algebra under the necessary operations.

label: fourier_gaussian_innerProductSpace
slogan: The Fourier transform of a complex exponential function involving a Gaussian in a finite-dimensional real inner product space is another Gaussian function, scaled by a factor involving pi and the complex parameter b, and evaluated at the transformed frequency variable. The result holds when the real part of b is positive and the space has a measurable structure compatible with its topology. The formula expresses how Gaussian functions are essentially preserved under Fourier transformation, up to scaling and squaring of norms.

label: fourier_gaussian_pi
slogan: The Fourier transform of the function that maps x to exp(-pi * b * x^2) is equal to the function that maps t to (1 / sqrt(b)) * exp(-pi * t^2 / b), provided that the real part of the complex number b is positive.

label: fourier_neg
slogan: The value of the Fourier function at -n is the complex conjugate of its value at n, for any integer n and point on the circle of period T. This means flipping the sign of the frequency reverses the phase of the corresponding complex exponential. The result holds in the context of continuous maps from the additive circle to the complex numbers.

label: frontier
slogan: The frontier of a set in a topological space is the collection of points that are in the closure of the set but not in its interior. It is calculated as the set difference between the closure and the interior. These points lie on the boundary, neither fully inside nor fully outside the set.

label: funext
slogan: If two functions produce equal outputs for every input, then the functions themselves are equal. This means equality of functions is determined by their behavior, not their definitions.

label: funext_iff
slogan: Two functions f and g are equal if and only if f(x) equals g(x) for every input x.

label: fwdDiff
slogan: The forward difference operator computes the difference between the value of a function at a point shifted by h and its value at the original point, defined as f(n + h) - f(n). It applies to functions from a commutative monoid M to a commutative group G, where addition and subtraction are well-behaved. The operator is parameterized by a step size h and a function f.

label: fwdDiff_iter_eq_sum_shift
slogan: The n-th forward difference of a function f at a point y, with step size h, equals the sum over k from 0 to n of (-1) raised to the power (n - k), multiplied by the binomial coefficient "n choose k", multiplied by the value of f at y + k*h.

label: gauge
slogan: The gauge function takes a set and a point in a real vector space and returns the smallest positive number such that scaling the set by this number includes the point; if no such number exists, it returns infinity. It uses scalar multiplication and the ordering of real numbers to compute this value as the infimum of all positive scalars that make the scaled set contain the point.

label: gaugeSeminorm
slogan: The gauge seminorm is a function that assigns to each point in a real vector space the smallest non-negative number such that scaling a given balanced, convex, and absorbing set by that number contains the point. It satisfies the properties of a seminorm: it is absolutely homogeneous and subadditive. This means scaling a vector scales its gauge value by the absolute value of the scalar, and the gauge of the sum of two vectors is at most the sum of their gauge values.

label: gcd_greatest_associated
slogan: If d divides both a and b, and every other common divisor of a and b also divides d, then d is associated with the greatest common divisor of a and b, meaning d and gcd(a, b) differ only by a unit factor.

label: ge_iff_le
slogan: The statement x >= y is true if and only if y <= x, meaning "greater than or equal" is defined as the reverse of "less than or equal" for any type with a <= relation.

label: gelfandStarTransform
slogan: The Gelfand transform is a one-to-one correspondence between a commutative unital C*-algebra over the complex numbers and the algebra of continuous complex-valued functions on its character space. This correspondence preserves addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and the star operation. It means every element of the algebra can be uniquely represented as a continuous function on the space of its characters.

label: gelfandTransform_bijective
slogan: The Gelfand transform maps elements of a commutative C*-algebra over the complex numbers to continuous functions on its character space, and this mapping is both one-to-one and onto. This means every continuous function on the character space corresponds to exactly one element of the algebra. As a result, the algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of continuous functions on its character space.

label: geom_sum_eq
slogan: For any element x not equal to 1 in a division ring, the sum 1 + x + x^2 + ... + x^(n-1) equals (x^n - 1) / (x - 1).

label: geometric_hahn_banach_closed_point
slogan: In a locally convex space, if a point is not in a closed convex set, then there is a continuous linear function that gives the point a higher value than every point in the set.

label: geometric_hahn_banach_compact_closed
slogan: If two sets in a topological vector space do not overlap, one is compact and the other is closed, and both are convex, then there exists a continuous linear function and two real numbers such that the function's values on the first set are all less than the first number, and its values on the second set are all greater than the second number, with the first number less than the second.

label: geometric_hahn_banach_open
slogan: If two convex sets in a real topological vector space do not overlap and one of them is open, then there is a continuous linear function that assigns strictly smaller values to points in one set than to points in the other, with a clear gap between their value ranges.

label: gradient
slogan: The gradient of a function f at a point x is the vector that represents the direction and rate of fastest increase of f, if such a vector exists; otherwise, it is zero. It is defined in spaces with an inner product and completeness, where the function can be approximated near x by a linear expression involving the gradient. The gradient exists when the function's change near x is well-approximated by the inner product of the gradient and small displacements from x.

label: groupCohomology.cocycles
slogan: The groupCohomology.cocycles are functions from a group to a module that satisfy a specific condition: they are mapped to zero by a differential operator, meaning they are cycles in a cochain complex. These functions are part of a structure built from group actions on modules over a commutative ring, where the cohomology framework uses a sequence of maps with the property that applying the differential twice gives zero. The cocycles form a module over the ring, capturing the algebraic essence of solutions to the cycle condition in group cohomology.

label: groupCohomology.exists_div_of_norm_eq_one
slogan: If L/K is a finite cyclic Galois extension and an element x in L has norm 1, then there exists a nonzero element y in L such that x equals y divided by the image of y under the generator of the Galois group.

label: groupCohomology.exists_mul_galRestrict_of_norm_eq_one
slogan: If L/K is a finite cyclic Galois extension and η is an element in a certain integral closure B with norm 1 (when viewed in L), then there exists a nonzero element ε in B such that multiplying η by the Galois generator applied to ε gives back ε.

label: groupHomology
slogan: Group homology is defined for a group G and a module M over a commutative ring R by constructing a chain complex from inhomogeneous chains, where each term is built from tuples of group elements tensored with the module, and boundary maps are set so that boundaries of boundaries vanish. The homology at each degree measures how far the complex is from being exact, computed as cycles modulo boundaries in the category of R-modules. This gives a sequence of R-modules that capture algebraic invariants of the group action on the module.

label: hammingDist
slogan: The Hamming distance counts how many positions differ between two functions that map from a finite index set to a family of types, each with decidable equality; it returns the number of indices where the functions have unequal values.

label: harmonic
slogan: The harmonic function takes a natural number n and returns the nth harmonic number, which is the sum of the reciprocals 1/1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n as a rational number. It computes this sum over the finite set of integers from 1 to n. Each reciprocal is formed by casting the natural number to a rational and taking its inverse.

label: hasDerivAt_abs
slogan: The absolute value function |x| has a derivative at every nonzero real number x, and the derivative is 1 if x is positive and -1 if x is negative. This means the slope of |x| is constant on each side of zero. The derivative does not exist at zero because the function has a sharp corner there.

label: hasDerivAt_abs_rpow
slogan: For any real number x and real exponent p greater than 1, the derivative of the function that maps x to the absolute value of x raised to the power p is equal to p times the absolute value of x raised to the power (p minus 2), times x.

label: hasDerivAt_iff_isLittleO
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if and only if the difference between the function's values and its linear approximation near that point becomes negligible compared to the distance from the point, meaning the error shrinks faster than the distance as you get close. This is stated using limits and norms in spaces over a field with a nontrivial absolute value. The linear approximation uses scalar multiplication in a normed vector space.

label: hasDerivAt_iff_tendsto
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if and only if the ratio of the error in the linear approximation to the size of the input change approaches zero as the input change gets arbitrarily close to zero, using norms to measure size in a vector space over a nontrivially normed field.

label: hasDerivAt_iff_tendsto_slope
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if and only if the limit of its difference quotient (the slope between that point and nearby points) approaches the derivative value as the input gets closer to the point, where "closer" means within the neighborhood around the point excluding the point itself. This limit is expressed using filters, specifically the neighborhood filter restricted to the complement of the point. The function and its derivative take values in a normed vector space over a nontrivially normed field.

label: hasDerivAt_iff_tendsto_slope_zero
slogan: A function has a derivative at a point if and only if the limit of its difference quotient, as the input approaches that point, equals the derivative; this limit is defined using filters, focusing on the behavior of the function near the point while excluding the point itself.

label: hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le
slogan: If a function depends on a parameter and is differentiable at a point, and its derivative is bounded by an integrable function nearby, then the integral of the function with respect to that parameter is also differentiable at the point, and the derivative of the integral equals the integral of the derivative. This allows swapping differentiation and integration when the derivative is controlled by a sufficiently nice (integrable) bound. The result holds under mild measurability and integrability conditions on the function and its derivative.

label: hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_lip
slogan: If a function depends on a parameter and is integrable, and its rate of change with respect to that parameter is bounded by an integrable function while behaving in a Lipschitz way near a point, then the derivative of the integral with respect to the parameter equals the integral of the derivative at that point. This allows swapping differentiation and integration when the function's variation is suitably controlled. The result holds almost everywhere with respect to the given measure.

label: hasFDerivAt_iff_isLittleO
slogan: A function has a Fréchet derivative at a point if and only if the error between the function's actual change and the change predicted by a continuous linear map becomes negligible compared to the size of the input change as you approach that point, meaning the ratio of the error to the input change goes to zero. This condition is expressed using little-o notation with respect to the neighborhood filter around the point. The derivative is such a linear map that provides this locally accurate approximation.

label: hasFDerivAt_of_tendstoUniformly
slogan: If a sequence of functions converges pointwise to a limit function and their derivatives converge uniformly to a limit, then the derivative of the limit function equals the limit of the derivatives at a point. This allows interchanging the order of taking limits and derivatives under uniform convergence of the derivatives. The result holds in normed vector spaces over fields like the real or complex numbers.

label: hasFDerivWithinAt_closure_of_tendsto_fderiv
slogan: If a function is differentiable on an open, convex set and its derivative approaches a limit as it gets close to a point in the closure of that set, and the function is continuous at that point relative to the closure, then the function has a derivative at the point equal to the limiting value, with the derivative defined relative to the closure of the set.

label: hasGradientAt_iff_isLittleO
slogan: A function f has gradient f' at point x if and only if the difference between f(x') and its linear approximation f(x) + inner product of f' and (x' - x) becomes negligible compared to the distance between x' and x, as x' approaches x. This means the error in the approximation goes to zero faster than the distance to x. The result holds in complete inner product spaces over real-like scalars.

label: hasSum_coe_mul_geometric_of_norm_lt_one
slogan: If the size of a number r is less than 1, then the infinite sum of n times r to the power n, starting from n = 0, converges to r divided by (1 - r) squared. This holds in any algebraic system with division and a notion of size where limits can be defined. The result is computed using standard addition, multiplication, and division operations.

label: hasSum_fourier_series_L2
slogan: The Fourier series of a square-integrable complex-valued function on the circle of period T converges to the function itself when convergence is measured in the L2 norm, meaning the integral of the squared difference between the function and its Fourier series tends to zero.

label: hasSum_fourier_series_of_summable
slogan: If the Fourier coefficients of a continuous periodic function f are absolutely summable, then the Fourier series built from these coefficients converges uniformly to f.

label: hasSum_geometric_of_lt_one
slogan: If a real number r is between 0 and 1, the sum of all its powers (1 + r + r^2 + r^3 + ...) converges to 1 / (1 - r). This means the total of the infinite series gets arbitrarily close to that value as more terms are added. The result applies to standard real numbers with usual arithmetic and limits.

label: hasSum_sq_fourierCoeff
slogan: For a square-integrable complex-valued function on a circle of period T, the sum of the squares of the absolute values of its Fourier coefficients equals the integral of the square of the absolute value of the function over the circle, using the normalized Haar measure.

label: hasSum_zeta_two
slogan: The sum of the reciprocals of the squares of the natural numbers equals pi squared divided by six.

label: hensels_lemma
slogan: If a polynomial has coefficients in a commutative semiring over the p-adic integers and its value at a point a is sufficiently small compared to the square of its derivative at a, then there is a unique nearby root z close to a where the polynomial evaluates to zero, the distance from z to a is smaller than the norm of the derivative at a, and the derivative at z has the same norm as at a.

label: himp_eq_top_iff
slogan: In a generalized Heyting algebra, the implication a => b equals the top element if and only if a is less than or equal to b. This means the implication is true (top) precisely when the premise a does not exceed the conclusion b. The result relies on the algebraic properties of implication and the top element in such structures.

label: iff_iff_implies_and_implies
slogan: A logical equivalence between two propositions a and b is true exactly when both a implies b and b implies a are true. This means a if and only if b is the same as saying a implies b and b implies a. The conjunction of the two implications is equivalent to the biconditional.

label: imp_and
slogan: For any type α and propositions b and c, the statement "for all a in α, both b and c are true" is equivalent to saying "for all a in α, b is true" and "for all a in α, c is true". This means a universal claim over a conjunction can be split into separate universal claims. The logical and between two universally quantified statements holds when each quantified statement holds on its own.

label: imp_iff_not_or
slogan: If it's possible to determine whether a proposition a is true or false, then the statement "a implies b" is logically equivalent to "either a is false or b is true". This means proving "a implies b" amounts to showing that either a does not hold or b holds.

label: inf_eq_left
slogan: The greatest lower bound of two elements a and b is equal to a if and only if a is less than or equal to b. This means a is below or equal to b exactly when combining a and b using the inf operation gives back a. The result depends on the properties of the inf operation and the partial order structure.

label: inf_iSup_eq
slogan: In a complete Boolean algebra, the meet of an element with the join of a family of elements equals the join of the meets of that element with each member of the family. This means you can distribute a meet over an arbitrary join. The equality holds because of the algebra's distributive and complement properties.

label: inf_sup_left
slogan: In a distributive lattice, the meet of an element with the join of two others is equal to the join of the meet of the element with each of the other two, showing that meet distributes over join from the left. This means a ⊓ (b ⊔ c) is the same as (a ⊓ b) ⊔ (a ⊓ c) for any elements a, b, and c. The equality holds because the lattice satisfies the distributive property.

label: inf_sup_self
slogan: If a value a is less than or equal to the least upper bound of a and b, then the greatest lower bound of a and the least upper bound of a and b is just a. This holds in any lattice, where every pair of elements has both a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

label: inner_add_right
slogan: The inner product of a vector x with the sum of two vectors y and z is equal to the sum of the inner products of x with y and x with z. This means the inner product is additive in the second argument for all vectors in an inner product space.

label: inner_conj_symm
slogan: In an inner product space, the inner product of vector x with vector y is the complex conjugate of the inner product of y with x. This means the order of vectors in the inner product affects the result only by conjugation. For real vector spaces, swapping the order does not change the value.

label: inner_eq_sum_norm_sq_div_four
slogan: In an inner product space, the inner product of two vectors x and y can be calculated as one-fourth of the difference between the squared norm of x plus y and the squared norm of x minus y, plus a similar difference involving multiplication by the imaginary unit, all divided by 4. This formula works for any vectors x and y in the space. It allows computing the inner product using only vector addition, subtraction, and the norm.

label: inner_gradient_left
slogan: If a function from a complete inner product space to a real-like field is differentiable at a point, then the directional derivative in the direction of any vector equals the inner product of the gradient and that vector. This means the gradient vector captures the rate of change of the function in all directions via the inner product. The result follows from how the derivative and gradient are defined in terms of linear approximation.

label: inner_map_polarization
slogan: The inner product of T(y) and x can be calculated using a combination of inner products involving sums and differences of x and y, scaled by the imaginary unit i and divided by 4. This formula works for complex inner product spaces and relies on linearity of the map T. It expresses the inner product in terms of values of the form inner(T(z), z), showing how the inner product can be recovered from quadratic-like expressions.

label: inner_mul_inner_self_le
slogan: The absolute value of the inner product of two vectors, multiplied by itself, is less than or equal to the product of the real parts of the inner products of each vector with itself. This inequality holds for any pair of vectors in an inner product space over a real-like type. It is a general form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

label: inner_self_eq_norm_mul_norm
slogan: The inner product of a vector with itself is equal to the square of its norm. This means that measuring the vector's size using the inner product gives the same result as squaring its length. The value is always a non-negative real number.

label: inner_self_eq_norm_sq
slogan: For any vector x in an inner product space, the real part of the inner product of x with itself equals the square of the norm of x. This holds because the norm is defined in terms of the inner product, and the space follows the algebraic rules of real-like numbers. The result is consistent with how lengths and angles are measured in vector spaces.

label: inner_sub_sub_self
slogan: The inner product of the difference (x - y) with itself equals the inner product of x with x, minus the inner product of x with y, minus the inner product of y with x, plus the inner product of y with y. This identity holds for any vectors x and y in an inner product space over a real-like field. It generalizes the algebraic expansion of the squared norm of a difference.

label: instBooleanAlgebraSubtypeIsIdempotentElem
slogan: The set of elements in a commutative ring that satisfy a * a = a (idempotent elements) can be given the structure of a Boolean algebra, meaning they support logical-like operations such as AND (meet), OR (join), and NOT (complement) that behave like those in classical logic or set theory. This structure includes a smallest element (false or empty set) and a largest element (true or full set), and the operations distribute over each other. As a result, these idempotent elements act like truth values under Boolean logic.

label: instCStarAlgebraContinuousLinearMapComplexIdOfCompleteSpace
slogan: If E is a complete complex inner product space, then the space of continuous linear operators from E to itself forms a C*-algebra using the operator norm and adjoint operation.

label: instIsCyclicUnitsOfFinite
slogan: If a finite commutative ring has no zero divisors, then its group of invertible elements under multiplication is cyclic, meaning all nonzero elements can be generated by powers of a single element.

label: instIsZLatticeRealSpan
slogan: The integer linear combinations of a finite basis in a real normed vector space form a discrete subgroup that is closed under addition and integer scaling, and this subgroup is a Z-lattice within the space. This lattice consists of all finite sums of basis vectors multiplied by integers, and it inherits the normed structure of the ambient space. The result holds because the basis spans the space over the reals and its integer span is finitely generated and discrete.

label: instRegularSpaceOfWeaklyLocallyCompactSpaceOfR1Space
slogan: A topological space where every point has a compact neighborhood and any two distinguishable points can be separated by disjoint open sets will also allow any point and a disjoint closed set to be separated by disjoint open sets, making it a regular space. This follows from properties of neighborhood filters and compactness. The declaration asserts that such a space satisfies the conditions to be regular.

label: instTopologicalSpaceProd
slogan: The product of two topological spaces X and Y is given a topology, called the product topology, which is the coarsest topology that makes the projection maps from X × Y to X and to Y continuous. This topology is generated by taking all sets of the form U × V, where U is open in X and V is open in Y, and forming the smallest topology containing these "open boxes". As a result, the product space X × Y becomes a topological space in a natural way.

label: instTopologicalSpaceQuotient
slogan: This declaration equips a quotient type with a topology by defining the open sets in the quotient as those whose preimages under the quotient map are open in the original space. The resulting topology is the coarsest one that makes the quotient map continuous and respects the equivalence relation. It ensures that the quotient space inherits a topological structure in a natural way.

label: instTopologicalSpaceSubtype
slogan: A subset of a topological space gets a natural topology where a set is open if it comes from intersecting an open set of the original space with the subset. This is the smallest topology that makes the inclusion map continuous. The subset, defined by a condition on elements, automatically has this topological structure.

label: intCyclicMulEquiv
slogan: If a group is infinite and generated by a single element, then it is isomorphic to the integers under addition, with the isomorphism sending each integer n to the nth power of the generator. The function intCyclicMulEquiv provides this isomorphism by mapping the multiplicative version of the integers to the group.

label: integralClosure
slogan: The integral closure of a subring R in an algebra A is the set of all elements in A that satisfy a monic polynomial with coefficients in R. This set includes all elements of R (via the algebra map) and is closed under addition and multiplication, containing 0 and 1. It forms a subalgebra of A consisting exactly of the elements that are integral over R.

label: integral_Ioi_rpow_of_lt
slogan: The integral from a positive number c to infinity of the function t raised to a power a is equal to -c^(a+1)/(a+1), provided that a is less than -1 and c is positive. This means the improper integral converges when the exponent causes the function to decay sufficiently fast. The result is expressed in terms of real-valued integration over an unbounded interval.

label: integral_gaussian
slogan: The integral of the function e^(-b * x^2) with respect to x over all real numbers equals the square root of (pi divided by b), for any positive real number b. This formula gives the exact area under the Gaussian curve, which is widely used in probability and analysis. The result holds for positive values of b and relies on properties of integration and square roots in real analysis.

label: integral_gaussian_complex
slogan: The integral of the function exp(-b * x^2) with respect to x over all real numbers is equal to the square root of (pi / b), provided that the real part of the complex number b is positive. This generalizes the standard Gaussian integral to complex scaling factors. The result is expressed using real pi and complex exponentiation.

label: integral_inv
slogan: The integral of 1/x from a to b equals the natural log of the absolute value of b divided by a, as long as the interval between a and b does not include zero. This is because the derivative of the logarithm function is 1/x, and the function 1/x is continuous wherever x is not zero. The result follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the logarithm function.

label: integral_inv_of_neg
slogan: The integral of 1/x from a to b equals the natural logarithm of the absolute value of b divided by the absolute value of a, when both a and b are negative real numbers and the interval between them does not include zero. This result follows from the fact that the derivative of log|x| is 1/x for nonzero x. The expression uses standard division and reciprocal notation for real numbers.

label: integral_log
slogan: The integral of the natural logarithm function from a to b is equal to b times the log of b minus a times the log of a minus b plus a, for any positive real numbers a and b. This formula follows from standard calculus rules for integrating the log function. The result holds whether a is less than, equal to, or greater than b, due to properties of definite integrals.

label: integral_one_div
slogan: The integral of 1/x from a to b, where a and b are positive real numbers and the interval between them does not include zero, equals the natural logarithm of b minus the natural logarithm of a. This is based on the fact that the derivative of the natural logarithm function is 1/x, and it applies to standard integration over real intervals. The result is expressed using basic algebraic and analytic structures on the real numbers.

label: integral_one_div_of_pos
slogan: The integral of 1/x from a positive real number a to another positive real number b equals the natural logarithm of the ratio b/a. This result uses standard integration on the real line with the usual measure and applies only when both a and b are greater than zero. It shows that the area under the curve 1/x between two positive points is given by the log of their quotient.

label: integral_one_div_one_add_sq
slogan: The integral from a to b of 1 divided by (1 plus x squared) with respect to x equals the difference between the arctangent of b and the arctangent of a. This means the area under the curve of that function over an interval is given by the change in the arctangent function at the endpoints.

label: integral_sqrt_one_sub_sq
slogan: The integral from -1 to 1 of the square root of (1 minus x squared) equals pi divided by 2. This represents the area under the curve of a semicircle of radius 1, which is half the area of a full circle. The function sqrt(1 - x^2) is continuous on the interval [-1, 1], allowing the integral to be computed using standard techniques.

label: interior
slogan: The interior of a set is the biggest open set that fits inside it, made by combining all the open sets that are contained within the given set. It uses the union of every open subset of the set to form this largest open subset.

label: intermediate_value_Icc
slogan: If a function is continuous on a closed interval [a, b] in an ordered space where the order and topology are well-behaved, then the function takes every value between f(a) and f(b) at some point in that interval. This means the range of the function over [a, b] includes all values from f(a) to f(b), inclusive. The result depends on the interval being unbroken (preconnected) and the function preserving continuity.

label: intermediate_value_Ioo
slogan: If a continuous function on a closed interval takes two values, then it must hit every value in between those two values at some point within the open interval between the endpoints.

label: intermediate_value_univ
slogan: If a continuous function on a space that is in one piece (preconnected) maps into a linearly ordered set with a compatible topology, then between any two output values it takes, it also takes every value in between. The interval of all points between two outputs is contained within the set of values the function actually reaches. This generalizes the idea that a continuous function on an interval hits every intermediate value.

label: intervalIntegral.abs_integral_le_integral_abs
slogan: The absolute value of the integral of a real-valued function over an interval [a, b] is less than or equal to the integral of the absolute value of that function over the same interval. In simpler terms, taking absolute values before integrating gives a result that is at least as large as taking the absolute value after integrating. This holds for functions on real numbers with respect to a measure, assuming a ≤ b.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_add
slogan: The integral from a to b of the sum of two functions f and g is equal to the sum of their integrals from a to b, as long as both functions are integrable on that interval. This means that integrating a sum over an interval is the same as adding the separate integrals of the functions. The integral uses the standard real line measure restricted to the interval between a and b.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_add_adjacent_intervals
slogan: The integral of a function from a to b plus the integral from b to c equals the integral from a to c, as long as the function is integrable on both intervals. This means integrating over two connected intervals gives the same result as integrating over the entire interval from a to c. The function can take values in a normed vector space, and the integrals are with respect to a measure on the real line.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_comp_mul_deriv
slogan: If f is differentiable with a continuous derivative on the interval from a to b, and g is continuous, then the integral from a to b of g(f(x)) times f'(x) dx equals the integral from f(a) to f(b) of g(x) dx. This is the standard integration by substitution rule, derived from the chain rule. It allows changing the variable of integration from x to f(x) when computing definite integrals.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_comp_mul_deriv''
slogan: If f is continuous and differentiable with continuous derivative on an interval from a to b, and g is continuous on the range of f over that interval, then the integral from a to b of g(f(x)) times f'(x) dx equals the integral from f(a) to f(b) of g(u) du. This allows changing the variable of integration from x to u = f(x) when integrating a composed function. It is a form of the substitution rule for integrals.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_comp_neg
slogan: The integral of a function f(-x) from a to b is the same as the integral of f(x) from -b to -a. This means flipping the input of the function around zero is equivalent to flipping and negating the integration limits. The result holds for functions taking values in a normed vector space over the reals.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_const
slogan: The integral of a constant value c over the interval from a to b is just c multiplied by the length of the interval, which is b minus a. This holds for constant functions taking values in a complete normed real vector space, and uses the standard notion of length on the real line. The result matches the intuitive idea that integrating a constant accumulates it linearly over the interval.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_deriv_eq_sub'
slogan: If a function is differentiable at every point on a closed interval and its derivative is continuous there, then the integral of the derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a). This means the total change in the function over the interval can be found by integrating its instantaneous rate of change. The result applies to well-behaved real-valued functions under standard calculus conditions.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_deriv_of_contDiffOn_uIcc
slogan: If a function f from the real numbers to a complete normed vector space is continuously differentiable on the closed interval between a and b, then the integral of its derivative over that interval equals the difference between the values of f at b and a.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt
slogan: If a function has a derivative at every point between a and b, and its derivative is integrable, then the integral of the derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a). This means integrating the derivative of a function over an interval gives the total change in the function's values at the endpoints. The result applies to functions from the real numbers into a complete normed vector space.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt_of_le
slogan: If a function is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and has a derivative at every point inside the open interval (a, b), and if that derivative is integrable, then the integral of the derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a), as long as a is less than or equal to b.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDeriv_right
slogan: If a function is continuous on a closed interval from a to b and has a derivative at every point strictly greater than each point in the open interval between a and b, then the integral of its derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a), provided a <= b.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDeriv_right_of_le
slogan: If a function is continuous on a closed interval [a, b] and has a derivative at every point in the open interval (a, b) when approaching from the right, and if that derivative is integrable, then the integral of the derivative from a to b equals the difference f(b) - f(a).

label: intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right
slogan: If a function is integrable on intervals starting at a point and moving to the right, and it is continuous at that point, then the derivative from the right of the integral of the function at that point exists and equals the value of the function there. This means the rate at which the integral increases just to the right of the point is given by the function's value at the point. The result applies to functions from the real numbers into a complete normed vector space.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_hasStrictDerivAt_right
slogan: If a function is integrable on intervals ending at a point and is continuous at that point, then the derivative from the right of the integral function, as a function of its upper limit, equals the value of the function at that point. This means the instantaneous rate of change of the accumulated integral matches the function's value when approaching from the right. The result holds for functions into complete normed spaces with standard real measure and topology.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_mono
slogan: If two real-valued functions are integrable on a closed interval [a, b] and one function is less than or equal to the other at every point in that interval, then the integral of the smaller function over [a, b] is less than or equal to the integral of the larger function, using the standard Lebesgue measure.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_mul_deriv_eq_deriv_mul
slogan: If two functions are differentiable on a real interval and their derivatives are integrable, then the integral of one function times the derivative of the other equals the difference of their products at the endpoints minus the integral of the derivative of the first times the second function. This is integration by parts for real intervals, connecting the product rule for derivatives with integrals. It works for functions taking values in a complete normed algebra over the real numbers.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_same
slogan: The integral of any function over an interval from a real number a to itself is zero, because the interval has no length and thus no contribution to the integral. This holds for functions mapping real numbers to a normed vector space, using a standard measure. The result is always zero regardless of the function or measure used.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_symm
slogan: The integral of a function from a to b is the negative of the integral from b to a, meaning reversing the limits of integration changes the sign of the result. This holds for functions defined on the real numbers with values in a normed vector space, using a given measure. The interval integration is based on restricting the measure to the region between a and b.

label: intervalIntegral.integral_unitInterval_deriv_eq_sub
slogan: If a function is continuous on the closed interval from 0 to 1 and differentiable on the open interval from 0 to 1, then the integral of its derivative over [0, 1] equals the difference between the function's value at 1 and its value at 0.

label: intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_integral_norm
slogan: The absolute value of the integral of a function from a to b is at most the integral of the absolute value of the function from a to b, provided a is less than or equal to b. This applies to functions that take values in a normed space, like real or vector-valued functions, using standard integration with respect to a measure on the real line.

label: intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const
slogan: If a function's values never exceed a constant C in size over an interval from a to b, then the size of the integral of the function over that interval is at most C multiplied by the length of the interval, |b - a|.

label: inv_mul_cancel
slogan: Multiplying an element by its inverse, in either order, results in the identity element of the group.

label: inv_unique
slogan: In a commutative monoid, if two elements both act as inverses for a given element (when multiplied on either side), then those two inverses must be the same. This means each element can have only one inverse. The result follows from the commutativity and associativity of the operation.

label: irrational_pi
slogan: The number pi cannot be expressed as a fraction of two integers, meaning it is an irrational number.

label: irrational_sqrt_natCast_iff
slogan: The square root of a natural number, when treated as a real number, is irrational if and only if the natural number is not a perfect square. This means sqrt(n) cannot be expressed as a fraction of integers exactly when there is no natural number m such that m * m equals n.

label: irreducibleComponents
slogan: The irreducibleComponents function returns the set of all maximal irreducible subsets of a given topological space, where a subset is irreducible if it is nonempty and cannot be expressed as the union of two proper nonempty closed subsets, and maximal means no larger irreducible subset contains it.

label: isArtinianRing_iff_isNoetherianRing_krullDimLE_zero
slogan: A commutative ring has both ascending and descending chain conditions on ideals if and only if it is Noetherian and every prime ideal is maximal, which means the ring's Krull dimension is at most zero.

label: isClopen_empty
slogan: The empty set is both open and closed in any topological space because it is always open by definition and its complement, the whole space, is also open. This makes the empty set a clopen set.

label: isClosed_Icc
slogan: In a topological space with a preorder where sets of points greater than or equal to a given point and less than or equal to a given point are closed, the closed interval from a to b (all x such that a <= x <= b) is also closed. This is because the interval can be written as the intersection of the set of points >= a and the set of points <= b, both of which are closed. Since the intersection of closed sets is closed, the interval is closed.

label: isClosed_connectedComponent
slogan: The connected component of a point in a topological space is always a closed set, meaning it contains all its limit points. This set is the largest connected subset containing the point and remains unchanged when taking its closure. Being closed, it is equal to its own closure.

label: isClosed_eq
slogan: If two continuous functions map into a Hausdorff space, then the set of points where they are equal is closed. This means the subset of inputs that produce the same output under both functions forms a closed set. The result follows from the fact that the diagonal in the product space is closed when the space is Hausdorff.

label: isClosed_setOf_isCompactOperator
slogan: The set of compact operators between two normed spaces is closed under limits with respect to the operator norm, meaning that if a sequence of compact operators converges to some continuous linear operator, then the limit operator is also compact.

label: isCompactOperator_id_iff_finiteDimensional
slogan: The identity operator is compact if and only if the vector space is finite-dimensional, provided the base field is complete and has a nontrivial norm. In infinite-dimensional spaces over such fields, the identity operator is never compact. This result links compactness of the identity to the algebraic dimension of the space.

label: isCompactOperator_iff_isCompact_closure_image_closedBall
slogan: A linear operator is compact if and only if the closure of the image of any closed ball centered at zero with positive radius is a compact set. This means that when the operator is applied to all points in a closed ball of positive radius, the set of outputs, after including all its limit points, has the property that every sequence in it has a convergent subsequence. The result holds for operators between certain normed and topological vector spaces.

label: isCompactOperator_of_locallyCompactSpace_rng
slogan: If a continuous linear map goes from a locally compact topological vector space to another vector space, then it maps bounded sets to sets whose closures are compact. This means that in locally compact spaces, all continuous linear maps are automatically compact operators. The result relies on the fact that local compactness ensures bounded sets behave well under continuous linear transformations.

label: isCompact_iff_compactSpace
slogan: A topological space is compact if and only if its entire set of points is a compact set. This means the space is compact precisely when every open cover of the whole space has a finite subcover. The result equates the compactness of the space as a whole with the compactness of the universal set within it.

label: isCompact_iff_finite_subcover
slogan: A set is compact if and only if every collection of open sets that covers it has a finite subcollection that still covers it. This means that whenever open sets together contain the whole set, finitely many of them are already sufficient. The property connects compactness directly to the behavior of open covers.

label: isCompact_iff_isSeqCompact
slogan: In a topological space where the open sets can be described by a pseudo-metric, a subset is compact exactly when every sequence in it has a subsequence that converges to a point in the subset. This equivalence holds because the pseudo-metric ensures each point has a countable neighborhood basis, linking compactness defined by open covers to sequential compactness.

label: isCompact_iff_totallyBounded_isComplete
slogan: A set is compact exactly when it is both totally bounded and complete: it can be covered by finitely many small regions of any given size, and every Cauchy sequence or filter in the set converges to a point within the set.

label: isCompact_iff_ultrafilter_le_nhds
slogan: A set is compact if and only if every ultrafilter containing the set is contained in the neighborhood filter of some point in the set. This means compactness is equivalent to every ultrafilter on the set converging to a point within it. The condition links compactness to the convergence of ultrafilters via neighborhood systems.

label: isCompact_pi_infinite
slogan: A product of compact sets in topological spaces is compact in the product topology, even with infinitely many factors. This means that if every coordinate space has a compact subset, then the set of all functions choosing one element from each subset is also compact. The proof uses ultrafilters: if each coordinate filter converges, the whole filter converges in the product space.

label: isCompact_sphere
slogan: In a proper pseudometric space, any sphere (the set of points exactly a fixed distance from a center) is compact because it is a closed set contained within a compact closed ball.

label: isCompact_univ_pi
slogan: The product of any family of compact sets, one from each topological space indexed by some type, is itself compact in the product topology. This means that if every set in the family is compact, then the set of all functions choosing one element from each set is also compact. The result holds even for infinite products, using the standard topology where open sets depend on only finitely many coordinates.

label: isConj_iff
slogan: Two elements a and b in a group are conjugate if and only if there exists some element c such that multiplying c, then a, then the inverse of c gives b. This means a can be transformed into b by a change of perspective using c. The relation is symmetric and based on the group's multiplication and inversion rules.

label: isConnected_Icc
slogan: In a space with a dense and conditionally complete linear order under the order topology, any closed interval [a, b] where a ≤ b is connected, meaning it is not empty and cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets.

label: isCyclic_of_card_pow_eq_one_le
slogan: If in a finite group, the number of elements satisfying x^n = 1 is at most n for every positive n, then the group is cyclic. This means there exists a single element whose powers generate all elements of the group. The condition ensures the group structure is simple enough to be generated by one element.

label: isCyclic_of_prime_card
slogan: If a group has a prime number of elements, then it is cyclic, meaning there is one element whose repeated combinations give all the elements in the group.

label: isCyclic_tfae
slogan: For a finite field extension L/K where K contains all n-th roots of unity and n is the degree of the extension, the following are equivalent: the extension is cyclic and Galois, L is the splitting field of an irreducible polynomial of the form X^n - a over K, and L can be generated by adjoining a single element α to K such that α^n is in K.

label: isLUB_csSup
slogan: In a conditionally complete lattice, every nonempty set that has an upper bound also has a least upper bound, and this least upper bound is less than or equal to every other upper bound of the set.

label: isLittleO_log_rpow_atTop
slogan: The logarithm function grows slower than any positive power of x as x gets very large. Specifically, for any positive exponent r, the ratio log(x) / x^r approaches zero as x goes to infinity. This means log(x) is negligible compared to x^r in the limit.

label: isLittleO_rpow_exp_atTop
slogan: For any real number p, the function x^p grows much more slowly than exp(x) as x gets very large, so the ratio x^p / exp(x) approaches zero as x goes to infinity.

label: isLocalMax_of_deriv
slogan: If a function is continuous at a point and differentiable near that point (except possibly at the point itself), and if the derivative is non-negative to the left and non-positive to the right of the point, then the function has a local maximum at that point.

label: isLocalMin_of_deriv_Ioo
slogan: If a function f is continuous at a point b, differentiable on intervals just to the left and right of b, with nonpositive derivative on the left and nonnegative derivative on the right, then f has a local minimum at b.

label: isLocalMin_of_deriv_deriv_pos
slogan: If a function has a continuous value at a point, its first derivative is zero there, and its second derivative is positive, then the function has a local minimum at that point. This means the function curves upward like the bottom of a U-shape near that point.

label: isNoetherian_of_isNoetherianRing_of_finite
slogan: If a ring is Noetherian and a module over this ring is finitely generated, then the module is also Noetherian as an R-module. This means that all its submodules are finitely generated. The result follows from the preservation of finite generation under surjective maps from a Noetherian base ring.

label: isOpen_Ioo
slogan: In a topological space with a linear order where the order and topology are compatible, the open interval (a, b) — meaning all points strictly between a and b — is an open set. This is because the sets of points greater than a and less than b are open, and their intersection forms the open interval. The compatibility condition ensures that such intervals are open in the topology.

label: isOpen_connectedComponent
slogan: In a locally connected topological space, the connected component of any point is an open set. This means that the largest connected piece containing a point cannot be broken into smaller open parts and still remains open.

label: isOpen_empty
slogan: The empty set is always an open set in any topological space, as required by the definition of a topology. This means that no matter what space you're working with, the set containing no elements is included among the open sets.

label: isOpen_iff_mem_nhds
slogan: A set is open if and only if every point in the set has a neighborhood around it that is entirely contained within the set, meaning the set itself is a neighborhood of each of its points. This is equivalent to saying the set belongs to the neighborhood filter of each of its points. The theorem links the definition of open sets with the concept of neighborhood filters in topology.

label: isOpen_sUnion
slogan: The union of any collection of open sets is open, meaning that combining all elements from any number of open sets results in a set that is still considered open in the topology.

label: isPathConnected_compl_singleton_of_one_lt_rank
slogan: In a real vector space with dimension greater than one, removing a single point leaves the remaining space path-connected, meaning any two points not equal to the removed point can be connected by a continuous path that avoids it.

label: isPreconnected_Icc
slogan: In a linearly ordered space where every bounded set has a least upper bound, the order makes the space continuous and gaps impossible, and the topology is defined by the order, any closed interval [a, b] is preconnected, meaning it cannot be divided into two nonempty, disjoint, open subsets. This relies on the space being densely ordered, so there are always points between any two distinct elements. The result ensures that intervals behave like connected sets under these conditions.

label: isPreconnected_iff_ordConnected
slogan: A set in a linearly ordered space with a dense, conditionally complete order is preconnected (cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open parts) if and only if it contains every point between any two of its points. This means the set is topologically unbroken exactly when it is order-convex. The result holds when the topology matches the order structure.

label: isPreconnected_iff_subset_of_disjoint
slogan: A set is preconnected if whenever it is contained in the union of two disjoint open sets, it must lie entirely within one of them. This means the set cannot be split into two nonempty parts that are both open and separated from each other. In simple terms, if two open sets don't overlap and together cover the set, then the whole set has to be in just one of the two.

label: isPreconnected_sUnion
slogan: A union of sets is preconnected if all the sets are preconnected and share at least one common point. This means that if each set in a collection cannot be split by two disjoint open sets, and they all contain the same point, then their union also cannot be split in this way. The result holds in any topological space.

label: isProperMap_iff_isClosedMap_and_compact_fibers
slogan: A function between topological spaces is proper if and only if it is continuous, maps closed sets to closed sets, and the preimage of every point is a compact set. This means proper maps preserve closedness globally and have compact fibers locally. Properness combines continuity, closedness, and compactness of point preimages.

label: isQuotientCoveringMap_quotientMk_of_properlyDiscontinuousSMul
slogan: If a group acts properly discontinuously and continuously on a locally compact Hausdorff space, then the map sending each point to its orbit in the quotient space is a covering map, meaning the quotient space is locally homeomorphic to disjoint copies of neighborhoods in the original space, lifted by group actions.

label: isSemisimpleRing_iff_pi_matrix_divisionRing
slogan: A ring is semisimple if and only if it is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings, where each matrix ring consists of square matrices of a certain size over a division ring. The sizes of the matrices and the number of factors in the product are finite. This equivalence means the ring can be decomposed into simpler algebraic components that resemble linear algebra over division rings.

label: isSimpleGroup_of_prime_card
slogan: If a group has a prime number of elements, then it is simple: it is not the trivial group, and its only normal subgroups are the trivial subgroup and the whole group. This follows because the size of any subgroup must divide the group's size, and a prime number has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

label: isSimpleModule_iff_quot_maximal
slogan: A module is simple if it has no submodules other than zero and itself, and this happens exactly when the module is isomorphic to the quotient of the ring by a maximal ideal.

label: isSolvable_gal_of_irreducible
slogan: If a polynomial with coefficients in a field F is irreducible and has a root that can be expressed using radicals, then its Galois group is solvable. This means the symmetries among the roots of the polynomial form a group that can be built up from abelian groups through a series of extensions. The result connects solvability by radicals to the structure of the polynomial's Galois group.

label: isWellOrder_lt
slogan: In a type with a linear order, the less-than relation is well-founded and forms a strict well-order, meaning there are no infinite descending chains and every pair of elements is comparable with one less than, equal to, or greater than the other. This ensures that the ordering is transitive, trichotomous, and supports induction. The less-than relation on such a type satisfies all the conditions of a well-order.

label: is_const_of_deriv_eq_zero
slogan: If a function between certain kinds of vector spaces has a derivative of zero at every point, then the function's value doesn't change—it stays the same no matter the input. This holds when the function is defined on a space where derivatives make sense, like real or complex normed spaces. The result means zero rate of change leads to a constant function.

label: isometry_id
slogan: The identity function on any pseudometric space is an isometry, meaning it preserves all distances exactly. This holds even when distances can be infinite, as in spaces with an extended non-negative real-valued metric. Every point maps to itself, and so the distance between any two points remains unchanged.

label: iteratedDeriv
slogan: iteratedDeriv computes the n-th derivative of a function from the real numbers to a normed vector space, using recursion and the Fréchet derivative. It relies on iteratedFDeriv to define higher-order derivatives as continuous multilinear maps, and requires the target space to support a norm and scalar multiplication over a nontrivially normed field like the real numbers. The result at a point is an element of the target space representing the n-th order rate of change.

label: iteratedDerivWithin_cot_pi_mul_eq_mul_tsum_div_pow
slogan: The k-th derivative of the function pi * cot(pi * z) in the upper half of the complex plane equals (-1)^k times k factorial multiplied by the infinite sum over all integers n of 1 divided by (z + n) raised to the power k + 1. This holds for positive integers k and complex numbers z with positive imaginary part. The sum converges and is taken over all integers, positive and negative.

label: iteratedDeriv_comp_eq_sum_orderedFinpartition
slogan: The nth derivative of the composition of two functions g and f at a point x is equal to the sum over all ordered finite partitions of n, where each term in the sum is the product of the derivative of g of order equal to the number of parts, evaluated at f(x), and the product of the derivatives of f of orders given by the sizes of the parts.

label: iteratedDeriv_mul
slogan: The n-th derivative of the product of two functions at a point is the sum from k = 0 to n of (n choose k) times the k-th derivative of the first function times the (n-k)-th derivative of the second function, as long as both functions are sufficiently smooth at that point. This generalizes the product rule for derivatives to higher orders.

label: jacobiSym
slogan: The jacobiSym function takes an integer a and a natural number n and returns the Jacobi symbol (a|n), which is 1, -1, or 0 based on whether a is a quadratic residue modulo the prime factors of n, not a residue, or shares a common factor with n. It computes this by breaking n into its prime factors, applying the legendreSym function to each prime factor, and multiplying the results together using integer multiplication. The function relies on Nat.primeFactorsList to get the prime factors of n and uses List.pmap and List.prod to process and combine the individual Legendre symbols.

label: jacobiSym.mod_right
slogan: The Jacobi symbol (a | b) remains unchanged when a is replaced by its remainder modulo 4 times the absolute value of a, as long as b is an odd positive integer. This means the value of the symbol depends only on a modulo 4|a|, reflecting a modular reduction property in its definition. The result follows from how the Jacobi symbol is built from prime factorization and modular arithmetic.

label: jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity
slogan: For two odd positive integers a and b, the Jacobi symbol of a modulo b is equal to the Jacobi symbol of b modulo a multiplied by (-1) raised to the power of (a//2 * b//2), where // denotes integer division. This means the sign of the symbol flips only if both a and b leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 4, and stays the same otherwise. It extends the law of quadratic reciprocity from primes to all odd positive integers.

label: jacobiTheta
slogan: The function jacobiTheta takes a complex number tau and returns the sum over all integers n of exp(pi * i * n^2 * tau), where i is the imaginary unit and pi is the mathematical constant. This sum is defined as the limit of partial sums over finite sets of integers, using the exponential function on complex numbers. The result is a complex-valued function used in the study of modular forms.

label: jacobiTheta_S_smul
slogan: When you transform the input τ in the upper half of the complex plane using a specific modular operation S, the value of the Jacobi theta function at the transformed point equals the original theta value multiplied by a factor involving the imaginary unit i and the square root of -i times τ.

label: jacobiTheta_eq_tsum_nat
slogan: For any complex number tau with positive imaginary part, the Jacobi theta function equals 1 plus twice the infinite sum of exp(pi * i * (n + 1)^2 * tau) taken over all natural numbers n. This expresses the theta function as a series involving squares of integers shifted by 1. The sum converges due to the exponential decay caused by the imaginary part of tau.

label: jacobiTheta₂
slogan: The function jacobiTheta2 takes two complex numbers, z and tau, and returns the sum over all integers n of the exponential term exp(2 * pi * i * n * z + pi * i * n^2 * tau). This sum is taken in the sense of unconditional convergence over the integers. The result is a complex-valued function used in the theory of modular forms.

label: jacobiTheta₂_add_left
slogan: The two-variable Jacobi theta function has the property that shifting the first argument z by 1 does not change its value, meaning it is periodic in z with period 1. This means that for any complex numbers z and τ, the function evaluated at z + 1 and τ is the same as the function evaluated at z and τ.

label: jacobiTheta₂_add_left'
slogan: The function jacobiTheta2(z, τ) changes in a predictable way when you add τ to z: its value gets multiplied by a complex exponential factor involving pi, i, τ, and z. Specifically, shifting z by τ scales the function by exp(-pi * i * (τ + 2*z)). This describes a kind of periodic behavior up to a multiplicative factor.

label: jacobi_cross
slogan: For any three vectors u, v, and w in 3-dimensional space over a commutative ring, the sum of their cross products taken in a cyclic order—u cross (v cross w), plus v cross (w cross u), plus w cross (u cross v)—equals the zero vector. This identity reflects a fundamental symmetry property of the cross product operation.

label: killingForm
slogan: For a Lie algebra L that is finite and free over a commutative ring R, the killingForm defines a bilinear map from L × L to R by taking the trace of the composition of adjoint maps of elements in L. It is constructed using the trace of linear transformations associated with the Lie bracket. This bilinear form is symmetric and invariant under the Lie algebra action.

label: kuratowskiEmbedding
slogan: The Kuratowski embedding is a function that maps each point in a separable metric space into a bounded sequence of real numbers in such a way that the distance between any two points in the original space equals the supremum norm of the difference between their corresponding sequences. This embedding preserves the metric structure, meaning it is an isometry into the space l^∞(N, R).

label: le_gronwallBound_of_liminf_deriv_right_le
slogan: If a continuous function f on [a, b] starts at or below δ and its right-hand rate of change is bounded above by K times its value plus ε, then f(x) does not exceed the value gronwallBound δ K ε (x - a) at any point in [a, b]. This bound depends exponentially on K and linearly on ε and δ.

label: le_iff_lt_or_eq
slogan: In a partially ordered set, one element is less than or equal to another if and only if it is either strictly less than the other or exactly equal to it.

label: lebesgue_number_lemma
slogan: In a compact uniform space, there is always a positive distance (called a Lebesgue number) such that any subset smaller than this distance lies entirely within one of the sets from an open cover. This means every point in the compact set has a small neighborhood around it that fits completely into at least one set in the cover. The size of these neighborhoods is controlled uniformly across the space by the structure of the uniformity.

label: lebesgue_number_lemma_of_metric
slogan: In a compact pseudometric space, for any open cover of a set, there is a positive number r such that every ball of radius r centered at a point in the set is completely contained in at least one member of the cover. This means a single small radius can be chosen uniformly so that all such balls fit inside covering sets. The number r is called a Lebesgue number for the cover.

label: left_distrib
slogan: For any elements a, b, and c in a type with addition and multiplication, multiplying a by the sum of b and c is the same as first multiplying a with each of b and c, then adding the results: a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c.

label: left_inv_eq_right_inv
